Round this stage they fix a number of stakes, and when the cattle are brought up at night, each beast is tied to a separate stake with a strong rope made of the bark of trees. The cows are then milked, and four or five men stay upon the stage all night with their arms to guard them from the lions, tygers, and other wild beasts. Their huts are built in a very regular manner, they being round structures, placed in rows at a distance from each other to avoid fire, and each of them has a thatched roof somewhat resembling a high-crowned hat. They are also great huntsmen, and not only kill lions, tygers, and other wild beasts, but frequently go 20 or 30 in a company to hunt elephants; whose teeth they sell, and whose flesh they smoke-dry and eat, keeping it for several months together. As the elephants here generally go in droves of 100 or 200, they do great mischief by pulling up the trees by the roots, and trampling down the corn; to prevent which, when the natives have any suspicion of their coming, they make fires round their corn to keep them out. They are almost the only people who make butter, and sell cattle at some distance up the river. They are very particular in their dress, and never wear any other clothes but long robes of white cotton, which they make themselves. They are always very clean, especially the women, who keep their huts exceedingly neat. They are, however, in some particulars very superstitious: for if they chance to know that any person who buys milk of them boils it, they will from thenceforth on no consideration sell that person any more, from their imagining that boiling the milk makes the cows dry.

PHYSIOGNOMY

Pages 50-51

protuberance of the bone corresponds to an interior one; and this irregularity, which is found sometimes as a dif- ficult, and most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> at an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when the cerebral organs do not oppose the same resistance to the cranium, renders the practice of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">Gall</a>'s system, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, uncertain.] "Guided by these principles, Dr Gall examines the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the skull, compares the crania of animals and those of men analogous and different in faculties. His researches have proved to him, in a manner almost incontestable, not only the above truths, but that the faculties of animals are analogous to those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; that what we call <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> in animals is found also in the latter, such as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, cunning, circumcision, courage, &c.; that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the organs fixes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the genus of animals, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> proportion that of individuals; that the disposition originally given to each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> by nature may be called forth by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> and favourable circumstances, and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, but that it never can be created in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> where it has not been given by nature (c); that the accumulation of the organs takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a constant manner from the hind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> forwards, from the bottom to the top, in such a manner, that animals in proportion as they approach man in the quantity of their faculties have the superior and anterior part of the brain more expanded; and, in the last place, that in the most perfect animal, man, there are organs in the anterior and superior parts of the frontal bone, and of the parietals, destined for faculties which belong to them exclusively. It is under the latter point of view that the discoveries of Dr Gall agree perfectly with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the facial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, which seems still further to establish the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of them." Most of our readers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be satisfied with the short view which we have now given of this fanciful and visionary system; but such as wish for a fuller exposition of it, may consult the Philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, vol. xiv., p. 77, from which the above is extracted. We shall only add the names of a few of the organs, which the author of the system thinks he has discovered. Organ of the tenacity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Organ of music. Organ of fighting. Organ of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. Organ of cunning. Organ of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. Organ of thieving, &c.

a discourse concerning the growth, kind, and virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>.

PHYTON

a general of the people of Rhegium against Dionysius, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. He was taken by the enemy, and tortured, and his son was thrown into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>.

PI-HAHIROTH

Pages 163-163

(Moses); understood to be a mouth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, called Chiroth, or Eiroth, and lying not far from the bottom of the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Arabian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>; before which mouth the children of Israel encamped, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> before their entering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>).

a thin membrane which covers the brain and is in immediate contact with it. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PIABA

Pages 143-143

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, is a small fresh-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fish caught in all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and brooks in the Brazils, and in some other parts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is about the size of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINNOW">minnow</a>.

PIABUCU

Pages 143-143

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, is an American fish, eaten in many places by the natives. It is said to be so ravenous, and greedy of blood, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person go into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> with a wound in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his body, the piabucu <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make up to it to suck the blood. It seldom exceeds four inches in length. PIACENZA is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Parma, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 25'. N. Lat. 45°. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome city, whose name is derived from its pleasant situation, in a fruitful plain, on the Via Emilia, about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the Po. It is the see of a bishop suffragan of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, and has a university, but of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fame. It is defended by a wall and a strong citadel, and is reckoned about three miles in circumference, so that it is somewhat bigger than Parma. The houses are low, but well built; the great street called the Stradone is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line and of equal breadth, with a foot-way fenced with palisades on each side like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and is about 3000 feet long. The houses are generally built of brick, and some of them are prettily painted. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is an old structure, but well adorned within. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Parma, who is sovereign of Piacenza, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in the city built by Vignola. There are many excellent paintings in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. There are two chapels painted, one with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of St Catherine, and the other with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Christ, as also the altar of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Augustin, all by Perdonone. In the same church there is a fine picture of the blest virgin, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and St Paul, by Paolo Veronese. At the Capuchins there is a Francis by Guercino. There is a fountain said to have been erected here by Julius Caesar, and the equestrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the famous general Alexander I., duke of Parma and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, and of his son Ranuccio, both in the great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. In the palace of Scotti, there are a great many fine pictures by Lanfranco, who had been a page in their family, and among the rest the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of Helen, the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, the blest virgin, and St Francis. The trade of this city consists chiefly in their cheese, as at Parma, these cities being surrounded with the richest pasture grounds in Italy; though the greatest part of what is called Parmesan cheese is made in the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and particularly at Lodi. See Parmesan Cheese.—Without the walls, which are washed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Trebbia and Po, there is a large seminary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, magnificently erected by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Alberoni, a native of this city, but considerably hurt by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> in the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the city is the mouth of the river Trebbia, famous for the victory which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> obtained over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>.

PIANO FORTE

Pages 143-144
or Forte Piano, is a musical instrument, which is too well known to require any detailed description. We shall here, however, notice some of its peculiarities. The voice, it has been observed, is the original musical instrument; of this all other instruments are to be considered but as imitations; and it is remarkable with what promptitude, as well as accuracy, the voice of man obeys the impulse of the heart. Even a coarse ear is hurt by an error in its tone, amounting to what is called a comma; and a limited voice can execute melodies which include 12 notes, or an octave and a fifth. Between these extremes the motion of the glottis does not amount to one-twelfth of an inch, which must therefore be divided by the most ordinary finger into more than 1000 parts. All this too, without any seeming effort of thought, is done in an instant, and repeated with rapidity, without mistaking one of the divisions. The great object in the construction of musical instruments is, to bring them as near as possible to express the sounds produced by the human voice: the violin, however, and a few of the simple wind instruments, are the only ones found fully to express these momentary gradations of sentiment, and those tender and delicate emotions with which the heart is agitated. For the purpose of removing this defect of harmonic instruments, the swell was added to the organ. Similar improvements were also attempted on other instruments of the same kind, and in the same way. The harpsichord was flutted like the swell organ, and was opened by means of pedals, when the performer wished to enforce the sound. But as this was found not to succeed well, other methods were tried, and in particular unisons were added to each note, which were brought on, either by means of pedals, or by another set of keys; and in this way the power of the harpsichord was greatly improved. Among all the keyed instruments, the English piano forte seems to merit the preference, on account of the superior force of tone, adequate sweetness, and great variety of voice, of which, by the ingenuity of British artists, it has now become susceptible. It has been called a national instrument, because it is said to be an English contrivance, the invention of the celebrated poet, Mafon. Mr Mafon had seen some attempts that were made by the Germans to make keyed dulcimers, which were in some measure susceptible of the forte and piano; but as they were all constructed on one principle, and required a particular touch of the finger, which was of difficult acquisition, and which spoiled it for harpsichord practice; as they were also deficient in delicacy and justness; and as the performer was by no means certain of producing the very strength of sound intended, Mr Mafon removed all those imperfections, by detaching the mallet entirely from the key, and giving them only a momentary connection. It is by this improvement that the English piano forte is distinguished from all others. Mr Mafon's general principle may be fully understood by the following description. In the figure on Plate CCCXVIII. the parts are represented in their state of inaction. The key ABK turns, as usual, on the round edge of the bar E, and a pin P, driven into the bar, keeps it in its place. PIA The dot F represents a section of the string. ED is the mallet, having a hinge of vellum, by which it is attached to the upper surface of the bar E. At the other end is the head D, of wood, covered with some folds of prepared leather. The mallet lies in the position represented in the figure, its lower end resting on a cushion-bar K, which lies horizontally under the whole row of mallets. The key AR has a pin C, tipped with a bit of the softest cork or buckskin. This reaches to within \( \frac{1}{4} \)th of an inch of the shank of the mallet, but must not touch it. The distance Ee is about \( \frac{1}{4} \)d or \( \frac{1}{4} \)th of the length of the shank. When the end A of the key is pressed down on the stuffing (two or three thicknesses of the most elastic woollen felt) it raises the mallet, by means of the pin C, to the horizontal position Ed, within \( \frac{1}{4} \)th or \( \frac{1}{4} \)th of an inch of the wire F; but it cannot be so much pressed down as to make the mallet touch the wire. At the same time that the key raises the mallet by means of the pin C, it also lifts off the damper G (a bit of sponge) from the wire. This damper is fixed on the end of a little wooden pin Gg, connected with the lever gH; which has a vellum hinge at H. This motion of the damper is caused by the pin I, which is fixed into the key near to R. These pieces are so adjusted, that the first touch of the key lifts the damper, and, immediately after, the pin C acts on the shank of the mallet. As it acts so near to its centre of motion, it causes the head D to move briskly through a considerable arch Dd. Being made extremely moveable, and very light, it is thus lifted beyond the horizontal position Ed, and it strikes the wire F, which is now at liberty to vibrate up and down, by the previous removal of the damper G. Having made its stroke, the mallet falls down again, and rests on the soft substance on the pin C. It is of essential importance that this mallet be extremely light. Were it heavy, it would have too much force, after rebounding from the wire, that it would rebound from the pin C, and again strike the wire. For it will be recollected, that the key is, at this time, down, and the pin C raised as high as possible, so that there is very little room for this rebound. Lessening the momentum of the mallet by making it very light, making the cushion on the top of the pin C very soft, and great precision in the shape and figure of all the parts, are the only securities against the disagreeable rattling which these rebounds would occasion. In respect to the solidity and precision of workmanship, the British instruments are unrivalled, and vast numbers of them have been sent to all parts of the continent. As the blow of so light a mallet cannot bring much sound from a wire, it has always been found necessary to have two strings for each note. Another circumstance contributes to enfeeble the sound. The mechanism necessary for producing it makes it almost impossible to give any considerable extent to the belly or sound board of the instrument. There is seldom any more of it than what occupies the space between the tuning pins and the bridge. This is the more to be regretted, because the baffles are commonly covered strings, that they may be of a moderate length. The bass notes are also of brass, which has a considerably lower tone than a steel wire of the same diameter and tension. Yet even this substitution for steel in the bass strings is not enough. The highest of them are much too slack, and the lowest ones must be loaded, to compensate for want of length. This greatly diminishes the fullness, and still more the Piano Forte, mellowness and distinctness of the tone, and frequently makes the very lowest notes hardly appreciable. This inequality of tone about the middle of the instrument is somewhat diminished by constructing the instrument with two bridges; one for the steel, and the other for the brass wires. But still the bass notes are very much inferior to the treble.

PIASTUS

Pages 144-145

a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, was originally a wheelwright and the son of Cosifco, a citizen of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>. He flourished in the year 830, when on the extinction of the family of Popiel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disputes arose about his successor, and Cracow was afflicted with a severe famine. During this extremity, when the people were dropping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the streets, two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> forms, as the story is told, took up their residence with Piastus, who was celebrated for his piety and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. He had nothing left but a small cask of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> liquor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and this he presented to his new guests, who, charmed with his hospitality, promised him the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Poland. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of Piastus was equal to his other virtues: he implicitly believed the word of his guests; he piously followed their directions in every particular. He was ordered to distribute the liquor out of his little cask to the multitude: he did so, and found that it was inexhaustible. The people were astonished; all cried out, "A miracle!" and the electors determined to choose a person in whose favour Heaven had so visibly declared: Piastus was accordingly taken from his shop, and raised to the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Such is the relation of the canon of Cracow, which differs in many particulars from the account given by Guagnini, and several other historians. According to them, Piastus had prepared a small collation, to entertain some friends who were assembled at the birth of a child. Two pilgrims, Paul and John, afterwards murdered at Rome, came about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to Cracow. They begged charity at the door of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and were rudely repulsed; upon which they stumbled on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Piastus, and were kindly received. The miracle we have mentioned was wrought by them; and the two pilgrims, and not angels, were the instruments of the elevation of the hospitable wheelwright. Though we pay but little regard to the marvellous means by which Piastus ascended the ducal throne of Poland, it would be presumptuous entirely to omit a fact attested by all the writers upon this subject: it was proper, therefore, to take notice of it, and we leave the rest to the reader's judgement. Being now raised to the supreme dignity, he was not intoxicated with his prosperity. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> charity, benevolence, and sweetness of disposition, remained: nothing was altered but his power of doing good. He was truly called the father of his people: the injured never returned unredeemed, nor merit unrewarded. Piastus wiped the tear from the eyes of the widow; and was himself the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the orphan, and the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and distressed. His excellent inclinations served him in the room of great abilities; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> that his people enjoyed made them forget that their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was not born a statesman and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>. Several intestine commotions arose during his administration, all which he quelled by the mildness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> were ashamed Piafus ashamed of rebelling against a sovereign who devoted his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to render his people happy. He removed the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> from Cracow, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> which he detested, because it was the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of Piafus's crimes and tragic end, and fixed his residence at Gniezno, where he died beloved, esteemed, and even adored by his subjects. It is in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this excellent prince, that all the natives of Poland, who have been since promoted to the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> regal dignity, were called Piafus, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the foreigners. Piafus associated his son Ziemowit with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; a circumstance of much benefit to the people.

PIAZZA

Pages 145-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, popularly called piache, an Italian name for a portico, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covered walk, supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>.

PIBROCH

Pages 145-145

says Dr Beattie*, is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of tune peculiar I think, to the Highlands and Western Isles of Scotland. It is performed on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAGPIPE">bagpipe</a>, and differs totally from all other music. Its rhythm is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, and its notes, especially in the quick movement, so mixed and huddled together, that a stranger finds it almost impossible to reconcile his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to it, so as to perceive its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>. Some of these pibrochs, being intended to represent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, begin with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, then gradually quicken into the onset; run off with noisy confusion and turbulent rapidity, to imitate the conflict and pursuit; then dwindle into a few flourishes of triumphant joy; and perhaps <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with the wild and flow wailings of a funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">PICA</a>. See CORVUS, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. PICA Marina. See HÆMATOFUS, and ALCA, ORNITHOLOGY Index. Pica, in Medicine, a depravation of appetite, which makes the patient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> for what is unfit for food, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> incapable of nourishing; as chalk, ashes, coals, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>-lime, &c. See MEDICINE Index. Pica, or pyge, had formerly the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as ordinal, meaning a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or directory, pointing out the order in which the devotional services appointed for different occasions were to be performed. Accordingly we are told it is derived from πικ, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of πικαζ, a table; and by others from litera picta, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> at the beginning of some new order in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> was used in a similar sense by officers of civil courts, who called their calendars or alphabetical catalogues directing to the names and things contained in the rolls and records of their courts the pyges.

PICA

Pages 145-148
or Picus, John, prince of Mirandola and Concordia, was born in the year 1463, under the pontificate of Pius II. He was the youngest son of John Francis of Mirandola, and Julia, a lady of the noble family of Boiard. Some of the credulous historians of the time have related, that at his birth a globe of fire was seen to rest upon his mother's bed, portending, say they, by its shape the perfection of his genius, and by its element, the celestial turn of his mind. As soon as he was capable of receiving instruction, he was placed by his mother's care under the most able masters, and very early distinguished himself by the vigour of his application, and the strength of his memory; of which such prodigies are related as would be very difficult to credit, were we not assured by some modern instances, of the perfection to which that faculty may be carried. At the age of fourteen he was sent by his mother's direction, who was desirous that he should assume the clerical functions, to Bologna, at that time the principal resort of those who studied the pontifical law. After spending two years there, he became disgusted with this pursuit, although such was his industry, even at that early age, that he compiled an epitome of the pontifical epistles or decrets. His disposition, however, strongly led him to the pursuit of philosophy, with an eager curiosity to penetrate the secrets of nature and science; with this view he travelled over Italy and France, visited the most celebrated schools of each, and studied under the most famous teachers of both countries. After seven years spent in this course of instruction, and at the age of twenty-three, he went to Rome, and, after the fashion of the scholars of that time, brought himself into notice by publicly proposing literary questions for disputation. This sort of challenge was very common in that age, and, when printing was scarcely practised, and the name of a man of learning less rapidly extended than it is now, was almost the only method that a person of superior attainments had to make himself known. Mirandola proposed 999 questions, or as they were called conclusiones, in dialectics, mathematics, ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural philosophy, and divinity, drawn not only from the stores of the Latin and Greek, but from the mysteries of the Hebrews and the arcana of the Chaldæans and Arabians. In addition to the endless topics of metaphysics, theology, and the ordinary subjects of disputation, into which he entered very profoundly, the conclusiones involved the ancient and obscure philosophy of Pythagoras, Trismegistas, and Orpheus; the doctrines of the Cabala, or mystic interpretation of the sacred writings, according to the Hebrews, taught by Origen and Hilarius; the extent, uses, and learning of natural magic, which was vindicated from the vulgar reproach of impiety and necromancy. Seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmata of the author's invention were likewise proposed and defended. These propositions, according to the ostentatious practice on these occasions, were fixed in the most public places in Rome, and the proposer engaged to defray the expenses of any one who should come from a distance for the purpose of disputing with him. This challenge did not bring forward any disputants, but exposed Mirandola to much envy and jealousy, particularly from the professors of science at Rome, who felt the reflection that would be cast upon their credit by their declining a competition which they durst not encounter. Unable to injure his fame as a scholar, they made a much more dangerous attack upon the foundations of his faith; thirteen questions were selected, which were charged with the terrible suspicion of heresy and contempt of the ordinances of the church; a suspicion very readily listened to by the church when directed against great learning, which the increasing influence of philosophy and letters began to make her watch with extreme jealousy. Mirandola repelled this attack by publishing his Apologia, or Defence of the accused Propositions; which if he did not effectually clear away the suspicions he had incurred, tended to confirm his enemies in their dread of his learning and powers; and it must be owned that, overlook- ing the misapplication of talents to such subjects, the Apologia exhibits a command of profound and well digested learning and keen argument, truly astonishing at the age of twenty-three. This work, and the difficulties it contained of certain delicate points, added to some hints of the limits of pontifical control in matters of faith, were so disagreeable to Pope Innocent VIII. that he interdicted the reading both of the Apology and the disputed questions. The love of glory, however, was not Mirandola's only passion: his youth, splendid accomplishments, and the graces of his person, for which he is said to have been remarkable, attracted the admiration and carefess of many distinguished Roman ladies, who united the love of letters to that of pleasure, a taste very common amongst the Italian ladies of that age. The young philosopher yielded to the force of these allurements, or rather, according to the account of his nephew, and biographer, Francisco de Mirandola, eagerly followed the bent of his disposition, naturally inclined to obey the attractions of beauty. But this life of pleasure, however suitable to his condition and inclinations, was of a short continuance. Irritated by the relentless persecutions of his enemies, and obliged perpetually to defend himself against the imputation of heresy, the most formidable calamity which in that age any man could have to contend with, he detached himself from vicious pleasures, and regulated his manner of life by rigidly observing the laws of abstinence imposed by Christianity; for being a firm adherent to the Christian doctrines, the charge of infidelity and the vigilance of his enemies made him the more solicitous to guard against the appearance of disobeying them. Becoming from this time wholly devoted to learning, he soon acquired such celebrity that the most eminent scholars from all parts of Italy came to visit him for conversation or instruction. As a proof of the sincerity of his reformation, he committed to the flames five books of elegiac poetry which he had composed on the subject of his amours, together with numerous pieces in Tuscan verse, which had been addressed to his various mistresses. There is perhaps reason to lament that the zeal of a new convert would not be satisfied without this sacrifice. It must, however, be considered that the spirit of religion at that period exacted many sacrifices from the professors of Christianity, which the lenient temper of these times does not call for. An example of this severity is to be met with amongst the works that still remain of Mirandola; at the end of which, in the folio edition published by his nephew, we find a learned and entertaining comment, in the Italian language, upon a composition of his friend Girolamo Benivieni, entitled *Una Canzone de Amore secundo la mente et opusum de Platonici.* "A poetical treatise upon love, explaining the doctrines of the Platonists." The author, Girolamo, informs the reader, in a short preface, that he had determined to suppress this poem and comment out of regard to his friend's character and his own; deeming it unbecoming a professor of Christianity, in treating of celestial and divine love, "to treat of it as a Platonist and not as a Christian;" but that having lent it to some of his friends for their perusal, an imperfect and erroneous copy was printed, which obliged him, but not till after the death of Mirandola, to publish it correctly; and he takes care to allege, in excuse for himself, that he has apprized the reader of his plan by the title of the poem, and warned him in all places where Plato's opinions depart from those of Christ, that the doctrines of a gentile and a heathen are not entitled to the least weight compared with the reasonings of the Christian theologians, "and particularly the irrefragable arguments of the angelic doctor St Thomas of Aquino." The first fruit of Mirandola's devotion to sacred literature was the Heptaplus, or Comment upon the Six Days of the first Chapter of Genesis, which was written in 1491. Two years afterwards he published a treatise in ten chapters, *de Enne et Uno,* the object of which was to reconcile the doctrines of Plato and Aristotle, and to demonstrate that the disputes of their respective followers originated in a misconception of the opinions of these philosophers relative to the *Enn* and *Unum,* at that time a subject of mighty strife among the learned. This treatise was held in high esteem by both sides. It was the last work of consequence that the author lived to complete; but he had laid the plan of a vast and comprehensive work, which his early death prevented the execution of. This was no less than to confound the seven enemies of the Christian church, by examining and refuting all their errors. In the prosecution of this design, he had composed and perfected before his death twelve books against astrology, the most popular and the most pernicious superstition which then infected the world. Paulus Jovius, bishop of Nocera, has left a testimony to the merits of this work, which is above all other encomiums:—"In this excellent though unfinished work, Mirandola attacked the astrologers with such erudition and keenness, and so ably exposed the absurdity and vanity of the whole art of divination, that he seems to have deterred the professors of the occult sciences from writing." This great design, as well as many others which Mirandola had formed, particularly that of a more complete effay towards reconciling the opinions of Plato and Aristotle, was frustrated by his death. From the time that he left Rome, which was soon after the publication of the Apologia, Mirandola generally resided either at Ferrara or at Florence. The friendship of the prince of Ferrara and its vicinity to his paternal seat attracted him to the former place; but Florence was the most agreeable to him, on account of the society of literary men which it afforded, and particularly of Politian and Lorenzo de Medici, with whom he entertained a close friendship. Besides these two illustrious men, his society was cultivated by other eminent scholars, among whom was the learned and unfortunate Hieronymus Savonarola, and Hermolans Barbarus: Petrus Crinitus, the pupil of Politian, mentions him as excelling all his companions in the erudition and eloquence of his conversation. The same author has left us an account of his diligent, laborious studies; for when Politian had expressed in his presence high admiration of his great genius and learning, Mirandola with singular modesty answered, c. 2., that he deserved no praise but for his affluence of application.—"Gratulandum potius, intelligite, affiduis vigilis atque lucubrationibus, quam nostro ingenio plaudendum." His library likewise is celebrated by the same writer, c. 2., and is said by Francisco de Mirandola to have cost 7000 pieces of gold. His accomplishments were not confined to subjects of abstruse literature; in his youth he was much attached to music, in which he acquired such skill, that... that some of his melodies were publicly received, and held in great esteem. It might also be concluded, from an anecdote related by Petrus Crinitus, that he was not unacquainted with physic; for according to that author, when Hermolaus Barbarus was seized at Rome with a dangerous fever, Mirandola sent him from Florence a medicine prepared by himself. No man ever testified a more sincere devotion for learning and philosophy, to the contempt of all other qualifications, than the Prince of Mirandola. He possessed a very large estate, which he bestowed almost entirely upon works of charity, except what was spent in collecting books, and entertaining and providing for literary men. At length, however, about three years before his death, he made over to his nephew Franciscus his principalities and possessions in Mirandola, and obtained a confirmation of the grant from Maximilian, the Roman emperor, to whom that principality was subject. He referred to himself only enough to purchase a small estate near Ferrara, where he spent the remainder of his life, except when he resided at Florence, in elegant and learned retirement. His mother, under whose care he received his education, had destined him for the church; and he was often urged by his friends to embrace the sacred profession, with the certainty of the highest honours and emoluments: but nothing could induce him to quit the life that he had chosen. He died of a fever at Florence, in the year 1494, in the thirty-first year of his age, on the same day that Charles IX. of France entered that city on his famous expedition into Italy. That monarch, hearing of Mirandola's illness, as he approached the city, sent two of his own physicians to his assistance; but in spite of their aid, the violence of his disorder put an end to his existence in thirteen days. With respect to the works of this author, something has already been said, and little more remains to be observed. The Conclusions afford a very complete specimen of the learning of the age, and of what were deemed the most valuable purposes to which learning could be applied. However useless and unprofitable these purposes may appear to us, it will not be denied by anyone, who has the curiosity to look through the Conclusions, that the mass of learning, which must have been possessed by the proposer of them, is prodigious; when it is recollected that, at the time he propounded them, he was no more than twenty-three years of age. For there is not the least reason to suppose, that a person whose works prove him to have been a man of profound learning, and who, in an age and nation distinguished by some of the brightest scholars that ever appeared, was ranked by their own judgment among the first, should have challenged the discussion of any of the proposed subjects, without being well provided with the knowledge necessary for such a debate. The manner in which the questions were propounded leave little room to doubt that the author was deeply versed in the respective subjects of them; and the Apology for the accused propositions, particularly those de Salute Origenis and de Magia atque Cabalae, discover familiarity with the writings of the Fathers, as well as with the Greek and Hebrew classics, and a facility of language and argument that could not be acquired at that age without extraordinary powers of mind. It would be worth while to transcribe the whole of this curious piece for the amusement of such of our readers as may not have access to the original, but our limits do not admit of it. It is curious to observe how greatly the sudden growth of learning outstripped that of solid science. No age, perhaps, was ever so remarkable for the learning which it produced as the period from the middle of the fifteenth century to the beginning of the sixteenth; yet, except the ineffable obligations we owe to the learned men of that time for their editions of the classics, later ages have been little benefited by their works, which are either lost or neglected, and even the sciences they treated of exploded and ridiculed. School-divinity and metaphysics, though the most attended to, were not the only studies in which the vast erudition of that age was wasted. The mysterious doctrines of the Cabala formed a favourite study of some of the most learned scholars. The proposition which laid Pica open to the indignation of the church, was that in which he asserted the orthodoxy of Origen; for Origen, notwithstanding his meritorious labours in the cause of Christianity, his daring zeal and self-martyrdom, and notwithstanding the defence of Eusebius, was configned by the sentence of the church to inevitable damnation, on account of his errors in the mysteries of the faith. To question his perdition, therefore, was to deny that the church was the interpreter of the divine intentions. The defence of this part of the Conclusions is written with a boldness that could hardly be expected from an Italian of the fifteenth century. But the hardest of these propositions was that in which it is asserted, that faith is not in a man's own power. In defending this and the other propositions, which were taxed with heresy, Pica probably relied less on the spirit and ability of his justification, than on his own high rank and station, together with the countenance and protection of his powerful friends, particularly the Medici, whose liberality of sentiment in regard to religious points was so notorious, that even Leo X. has been directly charged, not only with heresy, but infidelity.* * Milner's Hist. of the Church, vol. iv. By the Cabala, a term at this time generally misapprehended, was understood sometimes a species of divine magic operating by the agency of good spirits, as magic commonly so called was supposed to do by that of evil beings; but the true definition of it, as received by the best of its professors, is given by Reuchlinus (a), in his treatise addressed to Lorenzo de Medici, Divinae Revelationis ad salutarem Dei et formarum separatarum contemplationem traditae symbolica receptio,—a symbolic acceptance of the Mosaic history (for that is meant by divina revelation) which produced a pure and perfect acquaintance with the nature of the divinity and of spirits; and according to the opinions of some, which seem to be revived by the modern Swedenborgians, this knowledge, when sublimed to the highest perfection it was capable of, and accompanied with perfect purity, was believed to (a) This treatise, which contains the whole learning upon a subject once held in the highest veneration by men of learning, is very curious, and is to be found in the folio edition of Mirandola's works, published at Basil, in 1557. to raise the mind to an absolute familiarity with good angels, by whose affluence the professors of the cabalistic secrets were enabled to do miraculous things. This art was derived from the rabbinical doctors, who were at first called Thalmudists; and, about the middle of the 15th century, according to Pica de Mirandola, its professors were denominated Cabalists, Cabalists, or Cabalists, according to their different degrees of perfection: they afterwards, however, departed from their masters the Thalmudists; the latter, according to Reuchlinus, being chiefly intent upon the law and the explanation of it, while the former, paying less regard to what concerned human affairs, aimed chiefly at elevation of mind and thought. The ideas and doctrines of the Cabalists seem to have been well known to Milton, and perhaps fuggetted some pallages in Paradise Lost. In Reuchlinus's Exposition of their mysteries there is a curious passage describing the speech of the Deity to the heavenly spirits after the fall of Adam, with the future prospect of redemption by the incarnation of the Messiah, whom the Cabalists recognised in the character of a celestial Adam (b); and, among the books relating to these doctrines, which are said to be lost, mention is made of Liber Bellorum Domini. The mysteries of the Pythagorean philosophy, which, according to Philolaus apud Reuchlinum, sprung from the same source, were also studied and taught with great fervency during this period. Mirandola and Paulus Riccius were the first who explained the Cabalistic mysteries in Latin, and the former, in his Apology, has employed much labour and learning in defending them, as well as the science of natural magic, from the vulgar idea that necromancy was at the bottom of them. His writings, however, upon that subject were few, and we do not know whether they still exist; but it may be collected from the following proposition in his Conclusions, and some others of a similar nature, that he, like all the scholars of his time, had bestowed much attention upon this useless learning: "Qui scierit quid sit denarius in Arithmetica formalis, et cognoverit natura primi numeri sphærici, sciet secretum quinquaginta portarum intelligentiae et magni jubelaei, et millesimae generationis, et regnum omnium seculorum." Those who are well acquainted with the tenets of the modern millenniums will be able to tell whether there be any connection between them and the allusions in the concluding part of this proposition. Magic also entered deeply into the learning of this era. This comprises two distinct sciences, that of natural magic, and that of demonology: the first was concerned only in the properties of numbers and figures, and some of the more hidden properties of nature. This knowledge enabled its professors to produce many effects from natural causes, which, when science was less diffused than at present, appeared to be the effect of something superior to the common limits of human power. Albertus, commonly called Magnus, the friend and tutor of Roger Bacon, was the most celebrated of those who excelled in this sort of knowledge. This science has been productive of many admirable discoveries in mathematics and chemistry. Magic, in its common signification, or necromancy, was also eagerly studied at this time, as appears from Cornelius Agrippa's strange work upon that subject; and we may judge of the estimation in which it was held, by the confession that writer makes in his book De vanitate omnium Scientiarum, that while he professed that science, he derived more credit and profit from it, than from any other use he ever could make of his learning. The first matter in this way was said to be Solomon, whose magic ring and glaifs are still famous in eastern demonology. But the most dangerous, the most popular, and the most pernicious delusion which the darkness of the preceding ages had entailed upon mankind, was astrology, which will perhaps never be utterly exterminated from the minds of the vulgar, but which then possessed all ranks. When these considerations are taken into the account, it must be looked upon as no despicable application of learning and talents, to have exposed the fallacy and absurdity of this delusion; and when we recollect the great learning and credit of some of its upholders, among whom our countryman Roger Bacon was the most esteemed; the almost universal belief entertained of it, and the few lights which mankind then possessed, as to the real and constant laws obeyed by the celestial bodies; it cannot be denied that the twelve books written by Mirandola against astrology, the effect of which, in opening men's eyes upon that subject is testified by a respectable contemporary author, were the work of a very superior and enlightened mind. When we congratulate ourselves upon our freedom from these superstitions, we ought not to forget, that we owe something to those who gave the first blow to them. Proud of the lights of the age we live in, when astrology and such like cheats are no longer in vogue, we are too apt to overlook the merit of those exertions which first exposed and refuted them; and to persuade ourselves, that in these days of genius and philosophy, such exertions would have been unnecessary; not recollecting that if we enjoy many superiorities of this kind, we are less indebted for them to our own genius than to the labours of those who first paved the way for the detection of superstitious errors; our merit is, that we do not shut our eyes to the light of science; but while we enjoy its blaze, we ought to be grateful to those who struck the first sparks. John Pica of Mirandola has been represented by writers; whose ideas are taken from the encomiums of his contemporaries, as a mighty prodigy of learning and genius. The dilliance which the present times entertain towards those subjects upon which he wrote, renders it very difficult, upon a review of his works, to think those encomiums justified. But making allowance for this change of opinion, and weighing the impartial testimony of his equals, and the early age at which he obtained their admiration, it may be fairly concluded, he was in reality, a man of very extraordinary powers. These memoirs are principally collected from his letters, and the account given of him by his nephew Francisco, himself (b) Conjicimus fane, alterum esse Adam caelestem angelis in coelo demonstratum, unum ex Deo, quem verbo fecerat, et alterum esse Adam terrenum, repulsum a Deo, quem ex luto manibus suis finxerat. Reuchlinus, p. 750.

PICARD

Pages 148-150

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which arose in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in the 15th century. Picard, the author of this sect, from whom it derived its name, drew after him, as has been generally said, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men and women, pretending he would restore them to the primitive state of innocence wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was created; and accordingly he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>. With this pretence he taught his followers to give themselves up to all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>; saying that therein consisted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the sons of God; and that all those not of their sect were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. He first published his notions in Germany and the Low Countries, and persuaded many people to go naked, and gave them the name of Adamites. After this he seized on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the river Laufnecz, some leagues from Thabor, the head <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of Zizka, where he fixed himself and his followers. His women were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, but none were allowed to enjoy them without his permission: so that when any man desired a particular woman, he carried her to Picard, who gave him leave in these words, Go, increase, multiply, and fill the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. At length, however, Zizka, general of the Hussites, (famous for his victories over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Sigismund), hurt at their abominations, marched against them, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of their island, and put them all to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> except two; whom he spared, that he might learn their doctrine. Such is the account which various writers, relying on the authorities of Æneas Sylvius and Varillas, have given of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICARDS">Picards</a>, who appear to have been a party of the Vaudois, that fled from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> in their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and sought refuge in Bohemia. It is indeed doubtful whether a sect of this denomination, chargeable with such wild principles and such licentious conduct, ever existed: and it is certainly astonishing that Mr Bayle, in his art, Picards, should adopt the reproachful representations of the writers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned: for it appears probable at least that the whole is a calumny invented and propagated in order to disgrace the Picards, merely because they deserted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> and protested against the errors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. Lafitius informs us, that Picard, together with 40 other persons, besides women and children, settled in Bohemia in the year 1418. Balbinus the Jesuit, in his Epitome Rerum Bohemicarum, lib. ii. gives a similar account, and charges on the Picards none of the extravagancies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> crimes ascribed to them by Sylvius. Schlecta, secretary of Ladislaus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Bohemia, in his letters to Erasmus in which he gives a particular account of the Picards, says that they considered the pope, cardinals, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Rome, as the true Antichrists, and the adorers of the consecrated elements in the eucharist as downright idolaters; that they denied the corporal presence of Christ in this ordinance; that they condemned the worship of saints, prayers for the dead, auricular confession, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> imposed by priests, the feasts and vigils observed in the Romish church; and that they confined themselves to the observance of the Sabbath, and of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> feasts of Christmas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>. From this account, it would appear that they were no other than the Vaudois; and M. de Beaufobre has shown that they were both of the same sect, though under different denominations. Besides, it is certain that the Vaudois were settled in Bohemia in the year 1178, where some of them adopted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the Greek, and others those of the Latin church. The former were pretty generally adhered to till the middle of the 14th century, when the establishment of the Latin rites caused great disturbance. On the commencement of the national troubles in Bohemia, on account of the opposition to the papal power (see Moravians), the Picards more publicly avowed and defended their religious opinions; and they formed a considerable body in an island by the river Launitz or Laufneez, in the district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BECHIN">Bechin</a>, and recurring to arms, were defeated by Zifca. Encyclop. art. Picards.

PICARDY

Pages 150-150

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in France, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Hainault, Artois, and the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>; on the east by Champagne; on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France; and on the west by Normandy and the English channel (a). This province is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and narrow, being usually compared to a bent arm; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is nearly 150 miles in length, but not above 40 in breadth, and in many places not above 20. It is generally a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and produces wine, fruit of all kinds, plenty of corn, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of hay: but wood being scarce, most of the inhabitants burn turf. They have, however, some pit-coal, but it is not so good as that of England. It was united to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France in the year 1643; and is supposed to contain 533,000 inhabitants. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>, the Oise, the Canche, the Lanthie, the Lys, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a>, the Scarpe, and the Deule. The situation of this province on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, its many navigable rivers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, with the industry of the inhabitants, render it the seat of a flourishing trade. In it are made beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs, woollen stuffs, coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; it also carries on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trade in corn and pit-coal. In the districts of Calais and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a> are annually bred 5000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 6000 colts, which being afterwards turned loose in the pastures of Normandy, are sold for Norman horses. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> on this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> are also very advantageous. This province was formerly divided into Upper, Middle, and Lower Picardy; and again subdivided into four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>-governments. The principal town is Amiens.

PICCOLOMINI

Pages 150-154

Alexander, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRAS">Patras</a>, and a native of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, where he was born about the year 1508, was of an illustrious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, which came originally from Rome, but afterwards settled at Sienna. He composed with success for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>; but he was not more distinguished by his genius, than by the purity of his manners, and his regard to virtue. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>; and was chiefly exerted in relieving the necessities of men of letters. He has left behind him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of works in Italian. The most remarkable of which are, 1. Various Dramatic Pieces, which laid the first foundation of his character as a writer. 2. A Treatise on the Sphere. 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">Theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">Planets</a>. 4. A Translation of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s Art of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, in 4to. 5. A System of Piccolomini Morality, published at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1575, in 4to; translated into French by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de Larivey, in 4to; and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1581. These, with a variety of other works, prove his extensive knowledge in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. He was the first who made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> upon philosophical subjects. He died at Sienna the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1578, aged 70. A particular catalogue of his works may be seen in the Typographical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. There is one performance ascribed to this author, entitled Dialogo della bella Creanza delle Donne, (printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, 1558, and at Venice, 1574, in 8vo.) which but ill suits the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a prelate. It is filled with maxims which have an evident tendency to hurt the morals of young women. Piccolomini's name, indeed, is not in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> page; and it has all the appearance of being a juvenile production. It is very scarce; and the public would sustain no loss by its being entirely out of print. It was translated into French by F. d'<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBOISE">Amboise</a>, and published at Lyons, in 16mo, under the title of Instruction des jeunes dames. It was afterwards reprinted in 1583, under that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> & Devis des Demoiselles. Piccolomini, Francis, of the same family with the foregoing, was born in 1520, and taught philosophy with success, for the space of 22 years, in the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and afterwards retired to Sienna, where he died, in 1624, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 84. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> went into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His works are, 1. Some Commentaries upon Aristotle, printed at Mayence, 1608, in 4to. 2. Universa Philosophia de Moribus, printed at Venice, 1583, in folio. He laboured to revive the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, and endeavoured also to imitate the manners of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. He had for his rival the famous James Zabarella, whom he excelled in facility of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> and neatness of discourse; but to whom he was much inferior in point of argument, because he did not examine matters to the bottom as the other did, but prefaced too rapidly from one proposition to another. Piccolomini of Arragon, Octavius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the Empire, a general of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the order of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">Fleece</a>, was born in 1599. He first bore arms among the Spanish troops in Italy. He afterwards served in the army of Ferdinand II, who sent him to the relief of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and entrusted him with the command of the imperial troops in 1634. After having signalized himself at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Norlingue, he made Marshal de Châtillon raise the siege of St Omer. He had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a victory over Marquis de Feuquieres in 1639; nor did the loss of the battle of Wolfenbuttel, in 1651, impair his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. He died on the 10th of August 1656, being five years after, aged 57, without issue; and with the character of an able negotiator and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> general. The celebrated Caprara was his nephew. Piccolomini, (a) The origin of the name of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> does not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> earlier than A.D. 1200. It was an academical joke; an epithet first applied to the quarrelsome humour of those students in the university of Paris who came from the frontier of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and hence to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> Valerii Notitia Galliarum, p. 447. Lorgues, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> de la France, p. 52. Piccolomini, James, whose proper name was Ambrosianus, took that of Piccolomini in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Pius II. He was born in a village near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> in 1422. He became bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSA">Massa</a>, afterwards of Frejcati; a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> in 1461, under the name of Cardinal de Pavie; and died in 1479, at the age of 57, of an indigestion of figs. He left 8,000 pittoles in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, which Pope Sixtus IV claimed; and of which he gave a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> of the Holy Ghost. His works, which consist of some Letters, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, were printed at Milan, in 1521, in folio. His history, entitled Commentaries, commences the 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1464, and ends the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1469. They may very properly be considered as a sequel of Pope Pius II's Commentaries, which end with the year 1463. Piccolomini, Aeneas Sylvius. See Pius II. Picentia, (Strabo, Pliny), the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Picentini, whose territory, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">Ager</a> Picentinus, a small district, lay on the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from the Promontorium Minervae, the south boundary of Campania on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, to the river Silarus, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> boundary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, extending within <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> as far as the Samnites and Hirpini, though the exact termination cannot be assigned. The Greeks <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> confound the Picentini with Picentes, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> carefully distinguish them. The former, with no more than two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> that can be named, Silernum and Picentia; the situation of both doubtful: only Pliny says the latter food within land, at some distance from the sea. Now thought to be Bicenza, (Holtenius), in the Principato Citra of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. Picenum, (Cæsar, Pliny, Florus); Picenum Ager, (Cicero, Sallust, Livy, Tacitus); Ager Picentium, (Varro): a territory of Italy, lying to the east of Umbria, from the Apennine to the Adriatic; on the coast extending from the river Aesis on the north, as far as the Picentium to the south. In the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> northern part of their territory the Umbri excluded them from the Apennine, as far as Camerium, (Strabo); but in the lower or southern part they extended from the Adriatic to the Apennine. A very fruitful territory, and very populous. Picentes, the people, (Cicero); from the singular Picen, (Livy): different from the Picentini on the Tuscan sea, though called so by the Greeks; but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> calls them Piceni, as does also Pliny. Their territory at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> is supposed to form the greatest part of the March of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>, (Cluverius). Pickford, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Salop in England; on the south-east side of Shrewsbury, near Condover. It is noted for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of pitchy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> (from whence some derive its name), on the top of which there always flows a sort of liquid bitumen. Over most of the coal pits in this neighbourhood there lies a stratum of blackish rock; of which, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>, they make pitch and tar, and also distil an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from it. Pichincha, or Pinchinca, a mountain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. See Peru, No. 56. Pickering, in the north riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in England, 13 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a>, and 125 from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, on a hill among the wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Blakeworth; having the forest of Pickering on the north, and Pickering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on the south. It is said to have been built 270 years before Christ by Peridurus, Pickering, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Britons, who was buried here. It had once a castle, the ruins of which are still to be seen; to whose jurisdiction many of the neighbouring villages were subject; and the adjacent territory, commonly called Pickering-Lath, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> or forest of Pickering, was given by Henry III. to his son Edmund <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Lancaster. A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> is kept here for all actions under 40s. arising within the honour of Pickering. Pickery, in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, petty theft, or stealing things of small value. Pickets, in fortification, flakes sharp at one end, and sometimes shod with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, used in laying out the ground, of about three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; but, when used for pinning the falcons of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, they are from three to five feet long. Pickets, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, are about five or six feet long, shod with iron, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, in laying out the boundaries of the park. Pickets, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, are also flakes of about six or eight inches long, to fallen the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> cords, in pitching the tents; also, of about four or five feet long, driven into the ground near the tents of the horsemen, to tie their horses to. Picket, an out-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> posted before an army, to give notice of an enemy approaching. Picket, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> so called, where a soldier stands with one foot upon a sharp pointed flake; the time of his standing is limited according to the offence. Pickle, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> or liquor, commonly composed of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c., sometimes with the addition of spices, wherein meat, fruit, and other things, are preserved and seasoned. Pico, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, is so called from some lofty mountains on it; or rather from one very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, terminating like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a> in a peak, and reputed by some writers equal to it in height. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lies about four leagues south-west from St George, twelve from Terceira, and about three leagues south-east of Fayal; in W. Long. 28° 21' and N. Lat. 39° 29'. The mountain Pico, which gives name to the island, is filled with dismal dark caverns or volcanoes, which frequently vomit out flames, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and ashes, to a great distance. At the foot of this mountain towards the east is a spring of fresh water, generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but sometimes heated with the subterraneous fire, as to rush forth in torrents with a kind of ebullition like boiling water; equalling that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and feeding forth a stream of fulminous feld vapours, liquefied <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, minerals, and flakes of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> all on fire, in such quantities, and with such violence, as to have formed a kind of promontory vulgarly called Mysterios, on the declivity of the coast, and at the distance of 1200 paces from the fountain. Such at least is the account of Ortelius; though we do not find this last circumstance of the promontory confirmed by later observations. The circumference of Pico is computed at about 15 leagues: and its most remarkable places are Pico, Lagosas, Santa Cruz or Cruz, San Sebastian, Pequin, San Rocko, Playa, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDALENA">Magdalena</a>; the inhabitants of which live wholly on the produce of the island, in great plenty and felicity. The cattle are various, numerous, and excellent in their several kinds: it is the same with the vine; and its juice, prepared into different wines, the best in the Azores. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, they have a kind of wood which they call teixo, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and hard as iron; and veined, when finely polished, like a rich scarlet tabby; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> it has in great perfection. The longer it is kept, the more beautiful it grows: hence it is, that the teixo tree is felled only for the king's use or by his order; and is prohibited from being exported as a common article of trade. Pico Marina, a sea fish common at Kongo in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, derives its name from the resemblance of its mouth to the beak of a woodpecker.
