It is of a large size, and prodigious strength, has four fins on its back, three under its belly, and one on each side of its head; its tail is large and forked, by which it cuts the waves with surprising force and velocity. It is at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with every fish that swims, and with everything it meets in its way, without being intimidated by the largest vessels; a surprising instance of which intrepidity, we are told by some mariners, whose ship was attacked by one of them, near these coasts, in the dead of night. The violence of the shock which it gave to the vessel quickly awakened the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and the rest of the people; who immediately ran to the ship's side, where they perceived, by moonlight, this huge monster fastened by its forehead to the vessel, and making the strongest efforts to disengage itself; upon which some of them tried to pierce him with their pikes, but he got off before they could accomplish their aim. On the next morning, upon visiting that side of the vessel, they found a piece of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> snout stuck fast into the wood, and two or three inches of it projecting outwards. In the inside of the ship, there was discovered about five or six inches more of the point of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, which had penetrated through the plank. But we must observe, that the credulity of the times probably rendered this animal thus formidable. Picquering, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> war, or skirmish, made by foldiers detached from two armies for pillage, or before a main battle begins. Picquet, or Picquet. See Picquet. Picramnia, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class; and in the natural method ranking with those that are doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Picrania amara, or Bitter Wood, is a tall and beautiful timber tree, common in the woods of Jamaica, belonging to the pentandra class of plants. The name is expressive of its sensible qualities. Every part of this tree is intensely bitter; and even after the tree has been laid for floors many years, whoever rubs or scrapes the wood, feels a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bitterness in their mouth or throat. Cabinet-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> made of this wood is very useful, as no insect <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> live near it. This tree has a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> to the Quassia Amara of Linnaeus; in lieu of which it is used as an antiseptic in putrid fevers. When used, less of it will do than of the Quassia Amara of Surinam. See Quassia, Botany and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> Index. Picris, Ox-tongue; a genus of plants, belonging to the syngenesia class. See Botany Index. Picrium, a genus of plants, belonging to the tetrandria class; and in the natural method ranking with those that are doubtful. See Botany Index. Picet, Benedict, a celebrated divine, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, in 1655, of a distinguished family, and prosecuted his studies with great success. After having traveled into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and England, he taught theology in his own country with an extraordinary reputation. The university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, after the death of Spanreina, solicited him to come and fill his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but he thought that his own country had the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to his services; and for that generosity he received its thanks by the mouth of the members of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. A languishing disorder, occasioned by too much fatigue, hastened his death: which happened on the 9th of June 1724, at the age of 69 years. This minister had much sweetness and affability in his manner. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> found in him a comforter and a father. He published a great number of works in Latin and French, which are much esteemed in Protestant countries. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these are, 1. A System of Christian Theology in Latin, 3 vols. in 4to; the best edition of which is that of 1712. 2. Christian Morality, printed at Geneva, 1710, 8 vols. in 12mo. 3. The History of the 11th and 12th centuries; intended as a sequel to that of Sueur, printed in 1713, 2 vols. in 4to. The Continuator is held in higher estimation than the first author. 4. Several Controversial Treatises. 5. A great number of tracts on morality and piety; among which we must distinguish "the Art of Living and Dying well;" published at Geneva, 1725, in 12mo. 6. Some Letters. 7. Some Sermons, from 1697 to 1721; 4 vols. in 8vo. With a vast number of other books, the names of which it would be tedious to mention; but which, as Mr Sennebier says, "all show evident marks of piety and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>." Picet, John-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, a counsellor of Geneva, born in 1739, was of the same family. He was member of the Council of Two Hundred; Counsellor of State and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNDIC">Syndic</a>; and died in 1781. He applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and made several voyages into France and England for his improvement. Few men were ever blest with a clearer or more enlightened understanding. He has left in manuscript the "Journal of a Voyage which he made to Russia and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> in 1768 and 1769, in order to observe the transit of Venus over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s disk." A work very interesting, from the lively descriptions which it gives both of men and of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Pictland. See Pentland. Picts, the name of one of those nations who anciently possessed the north of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is generally believed that they were so called from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> their bodies; an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which Camden supports with great erudition. (See Gough's edition, Vol. I. p. xci. of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>). It is certainly liable, however, to considerable objections; for as this custom prevailed among the other ancient inhabitants of Britain, who used the glaifum of Pliny and the virum of Mela for the like purpose, it may be asked, Why the name of Picti was confined by the Romans to only one tribe, when it was equally applicable to many others? Why should they dignify them only by an epithet, without ever annexing their proper name? Or why should they impose a new name on this people only, when they give their proper name to every other tribe which they have occasion to speak of? As these questions cannot be answered in any satisfactory manner, it is plain we must look for some other derivation of the name. The Highlanders of Scotland, who speak the ancient language of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALEDONIA">Caledonia</a>, express the name of this once fa- Picts mous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Pictish; a name familiar to the ears of the most illiterate, who could never have derived it from the Roman authors. The word Pictish means pilferers or plunderers. The appellation was probably imposed upon this people by their neighbours, or assumed by themselves, some time after the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>, when the ungarded state of the Roman province, on which this people bordered, gave them frequent opportunities of making incursions thither, and committing depredations. Accordingly this name seems to have been unknown till the end of the 3rd century. Eumenius the panegyrist is the first Roman author who mentions this people under their new name of Pictish, or, with a Latin termination, Pisci. When we say that this name may have been probably assumed for the reason <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now mentioned, we must observe, that, in those days of violence, the character of a robber was attended with no disgrace. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to form his schemes well, and to execute them successfully, he was rather praised than blamed for his conduct; providing he made no encroachments on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of his own tribe or any of its allies. We <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> this as no peculiar stigma upon the Picts; for other nations of antiquity, in the like rude state, thought and acted as they did. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, lib. iii. p. 3. and Virg. Aen. vii. 745 et 749. Concerning the origin of the Picts, authors are much divided. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> derives them from the Agathyrsi, Pomponius Laetus from the Germans, Bede from the Scythians, Camden (A) and Father Innes from the ancient Britons, Stillingfleet from a people inhabiting the Cimbrica Cheronesus, and Keating and O'Flaherty, on the authority of the Cathol Pfister, derive them from the Thracians. But the most probable opinion is, that they were the descendants of the old Caledonians. Several reasons are urged in support of this opinion by Dr Macpherson; and the words of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUMENES">Eumenes</a>, "Caledonum, aliorumque Pictorum, filvas," &c. plainly imply that the Picts and Caledonians were one and the same people. As there has been much dispute about the origin of the Picts, so there has been likewise about their language. There are many reasons which make it plain that their tongue was the Gaelic or Celtic; and these reasons are a further <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of their having been of Caledonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. Through the east and north-east coasts of Scotland (which were possessed by the Picts) we meet with an innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of names of places, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, mountains, &c., which are manifestly Gaelic. From a very old <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the priory of St Andrew's (Dalrymple's Collections, p. 122.) it appears, that in the days of Hungus, the last Pictish king of that name, St Andrew's was called Mubrofs; and that the town now called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEENSFERRY">Queensferry</a> had the name of Ardochinnachan. Both these words are plain Gaelic. The first signifies "the heath or promontory of boars;" and the latter, "the height or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Kenneth." In the list of Pictish kings published by Father Innes, most of the names are obviously Gaelic, and in many instances the same with the names in the list of Scottish or Caledonian kings published by the same author. Had Innes understood anything of this language, he would not have supposed with Camden that the Picts spoke the British tongue. It was unlucky that the two words on which they built their conjecture (Strath and Aber) are as common in the Gaelic as they could have been in the British, and at this day make a part of the names of places in countries to which the Pictish empire never extended. The names of Strathfillan and Lochaber may serve as instances. The venerable Bede, as much a stranger to the Celtic as either of the antiquaries just now mentioned, is equally unhappy in the specimen which he gives of the Pictish language in the word penauhel, "the head of the wall." Allowing the commutation of the initial p into c, as in some other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, this word has still the same meaning in Gaelic which Bede gives it in the Pictish. It is true, there might have been then, as well as now, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between various dialects of the Celtic; and thus, perhaps, that pious author was led to discover five languages in Britain agreeably to the five books of Moses: a contest from which the good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> derived a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of harmless satisfaction. The Picts of the earliest ages, as appears from the Territory, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> testimony of all writers who have examined the subject, possessed only the east and north-east coast of Scotland. On one side, the ancient Drumalbin, or that ridge of mountains reaching from Lochlomond near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUMBARTON">Dumbarton</a> to the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">Tain</a>, which separates the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a> from a part of Ross, was the boundary of the Pictish dominions. Accordingly we find in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Columba, that, in travelling to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Bruidis, king of the Picts, he travelled over Drumalbin, the Dorfium Britanniae of Adamnan. On the other side, the territory of the Picts was bounded by the Roman province. After Britain was relinquished by the emperor Honorius, they and the Saxons by turns were masters of those countries which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between the frith of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and the river Tweed. We learn from Bede, that the Saxons were masters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> when he finished his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> History. The Picts, however, made a conquest of that country soon after; so that, before the extinction of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, all the territories bounded on the one side by the Forth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, and on the other by the Tweed and Solway, fell into their hands. The history of the Picts, as well as of all the other ancient inhabitants of Britain, is involved in obscurity. The Irish historians give us a long list of Pictish kings, who reigned over Pictavia for the space of 11 or 13 centuries before the Christian era. After them Innes, in his Critical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a>, gives us a list of above fifty, of whom no less than five held the sceptre, each for a whole century. It is probable that these writers had confounded the history of the Picts with that of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> the old Caledonians. In any other view, their accounts of them are highly fabulous; and have been long ago confuted by Dr Macpherson of Slate, an antiquary of much learning and research. The Picts, as has been already. (a) See Gough's edition of Camden, Vol. I. Preface, p. xc. and the Ancient Universal History, Vol. XVII. p. 39, &c. Picts already oblerved, were probably not known by that name before the 2d or 3d century. Adamnan, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONA">Iona</a>, is the first author that expressly mentions any Pictish king; and the oldest after him is Bede. We are informed by these two writers, that St Columba converted Brudius king of the Picts to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Columba came into Britain in the year of the vulgar era 565. Before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> we have no general record to ascertain so much as the name of any Pictish king. The history of Druft or Dreft, who is said to have reigned over the Picts in the beginning of the fifth century, when St Ninian first preached the gospel to that nation, has all the appearance of fiction (b). His having reigned a hundred years, and his putting an end to a hundred wars, are stories which exceed all the bounds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>. Brudius, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> of Columba, is the first Pictish king mentioned by any writer of authority. What <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> his ancestors made, or who were his successors on the throne of Pictavia, cannot be ascertained. Bede informs us, that, during the reign of one of them, the Picts killed Egfred king of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in battle, and destroyed the greatest part of his army. The same author mentions another of their kings called Naitan, for whom he had a particular regard. It was to this Naitan that Ceolfrid, abbot of Wiremouth, wrote his famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> concerning Easter and the Tonfure (c); a letter in which Bede himself is supposed to have had a principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Roger Hoveden and Simon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> mention two other Pictish kings Onnus and Kinoth, the first of whom died in 761, and the latter flourished about the 774, and gave an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to Alfred of Northumberland, who was much about that time expelled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The accounts given by the Scots historians of several other Pictish kings cannot be depended on; nor are the stories told by the British historians, Geoffrey of Monmouth and the author of the Eulogium Britanniae, worthy of much greater <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. In the ninth century the Pictish nation was totally subdued by the Scots in the reign of Kenneth Macalpin. Since that time their name has been lost in that of the conquerors, with whom they were incorporated after this conquest; however, they seem to have been treated by the Scottish kings with great lenity, so that for some ages after they commanded a great deal of respect. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> of Hogulthead, an old English historian, relates, that they made a considerable figure in the army of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> the Saint, in his disputes with Stephen king of England. In a battle fought in the year 1136, by the English on one side, and the Scots and Picts on the other, the latter insisted on their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> right of leading the van of the Scots army, and were indulged in that request by the king, The principal seat of the Pictish kings was at Abernethy. Brudius, however, as appears from the accounts given by Adamnan, in his life of Columba, had a palace at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, which was probably near the extremity of his territory in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; for there is no good reason for believing, with Camden, that this king had any property in the Western Isles, or that he had made a gift of Iona to St Columba when he visited him in that place. With respect to the manners and customs of the Picts, there is no reason to suppose they were any other than those of the old Caledonians and Scots, of which many particulars are related in the Greek and Roman writers who have occasion to speak of those nations. Upon the decline of the Roman empire, cohorts of barbarians were raised, and Picts were invited into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, by Honorius, when peace was everywhere restored, and were named Honoriaei. Those under Constantine opened the passes of the Pyrenean mountains, and let the barbarous nations into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. From this period we date the civilization of their manners, which happened after they had by themselves, and then with the Scots, ravaged this Roman province. Picts Wall, in antiquity, a wall begun by the emperor Adrian, on the northern bounds of England; to prevent the incursions of the Picts and Scots. It was first made only of turf strengthened with palisades, till the emperor Severus, coming into Britain in person, built it with solid <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This wall, part of which still remains, began at the entrance of the Solway frith in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and running north-east extended to the German ocean. See Adrian and Severus.

PICTURE

Pages 154-154

a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a subject represented in colours, on wood, canvas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or the like. See PAINTING.

PICTURESQUE BEAUTY

Pages 154-156

says a late writer on that subject, refers to "such beautiful objects as are suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>." This epithet is chiefly applied to the works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, though it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> often apply to works of art also. Those objects are most properly denominated picturesque, which are disposed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of nature with a mixture of varied rudeness, simplicity, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. A plain neat garden, with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and no striking grandeur in its position, displays too much of art, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and uniformity, to be called picturesque. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of neat and smooth (says Mr Gilpin), instead of being picturesque, in fact disqualify the object in which they reside from any pretensions to picturesque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Nay, farther, we do not scruple to assert, that roughness forms the most essential point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the beautiful and the picturesque; as it seems to be that particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> which makes (b) According to Camden, this conversion happened about the year 630, in the southern Pictish provinces; while the northern, which were separated by fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, were converted by Columba. (c) We are told by some authors that Columba taught the Picts to celebrate Easter always on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> between the 14th and 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and to observe a different method of tonsure from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, leaving an imperfect appearance of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. This occasioned much dispute till Naitan brought his subjects at length to the Roman rule. In that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> many of the Picts went on a pilgrimage to Rome, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the times; and amongst the rest we find two persons mentioned in the antiquities of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Aelverius <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of the Picts, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYRA">Syra</a> with his countrymen, performed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a>. P H I Pictorial makes objects chiefly pleasing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> roughness; but properly speaking roughness relates only to the surfaces of bodies: when we speak of their delineation, we use the word ruggedness. Both ideas, however, equally enter into the picturesque, and both are observable in the smaller as well as in the larger parts of nature; in the outline and bark of a tree, as in the rude summit and craggy sides of a mountain. Let us then examine our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, and try how far these qualities enter into the idea of picturesque beauty, and how far they mark that difference among objects which is the ground of our inquiry. "A piece of Palladian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> may be elegant in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; the proportion of its parts, the propriety of its ornaments, and the symmetry of the whole, may be highly pleasing; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we introduce it in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, it immediately becomes a formal object, and ceases to please. Should we wish to give it picturesque beauty, we must use the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a> instead of the chisel; we must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> one half of it, deface the other, and throw the mutilated members around in heaps; in short, from a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> we must turn it into a rough ruin. No painter who had the choice of the two objects would hesitate a moment. "Again, why does an elegant piece of garden-ground make no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> on canvas? The shape is pleasing, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the objects harmonious, and the winding of the walk in the very line of beauty. All this is true; but the smoothness of the whole, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and as it should be in nature, offends in picture. Turn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> into a piece of broken ground, plant rugged oaks instead of flowering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the edges of the walk, give it the rudeness of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, mark it with wheel tracks, and scatter around a few <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and brushwood; in a word, instead of making the whole smooth, make it rough, and you make it also picturesque. All the other ingredients of beauty it already possesses." On the whole, picturesque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> consists in uniting in one whole, a variety of parts, and these parts can only be obtained from rough objects. It is possible, therefore, to find picturesque objects among works of art, and it is possible to make objects so; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of picturesque beauty is nature in all its original variety, and in all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> grandeur. "We seek it (says our author) among all the ingredients of landscape, trees, rocks, broken grounds, woods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, plains, valleys, mountains, and distances. These objects in themselves produce infinite variety; no two rocks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trees are exactly the same; they are varied a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by combination; and almost as much a third time by different lights and shades and other aerial effects. Sometimes we find among them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of a whole, but oftener we find only beautiful parts." Sublimity or grandeur alone cannot make an object picturesque: for, as our author remarks, "however grand the mountain or the rocks may be, it has no claim to this epithet, unless its form, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, or its accompaniments, have some degree of beauty. Nothing can be more sublime than the ocean; but wholly unaccompanied, it has little of the picturesque. When we talk therefore of a sublime object, we always understand that it is also beautiful; and we call it sublime or beautiful only as the ideas of sublimity or simple beauty prevail. But it is not only the form and the composition of the objects of landscape which the picturesque eye examines; it connects them with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, and feels for all those various effects which are produced from that vast and wonderful storehouse of nature. Nor is there in travelling a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> than when a scene of grandeur bursts unexpectedly upon the eye, accompanied with some accidental circumstance of the atmosphere which harmonizes with it, and gives it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> value." There are few places so barren as to afford no picturesque scene. Believe the muse, She does not know that insipidious spot Where beauty is thus niggard of her store. Believe the muse, through this terrestrial waste The seeds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> are sown, profusely sown, Even where we least may hope. Mr Gilpin mentions the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> road between <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> and Carlisle as the most barren tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in England; and yet there, he says, there is "always something to amuse the eye. The interchangeable patches of heath and green-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> make an agreeable variety. Often too on these vast tracts of intersecting grounds we see beautiful lights, softening off along the sides of hills; and often we see them adorned with cattle, flocks of sheep, heath-cocks, grouse, plover, and flights of other wild fowl. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of cattle standing in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> on the edge of a dark hill, and relieved by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> distance beyond them, will often make a complete picture without any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPANIMENT">accompaniment</a>. In many other situations also we find them wonderfully pleasing, and capable of making pictures amidst all the deficiencies of landscape. Even a winding road itself is an object of beauty; while the richness of the heath on each side, with the little hillocks and crumbling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, give many an excellent lesson for a foreground. When we have no opportunity of examining the grand scenery of nature, we have everywhere at least the means of observing with what a multiplicity of parts, and yet with what general simplicity, she covers every surface. "But if we let the imagination loose, even scenes like these administer great amusement. The imagination can plant hills; can form rivers and lakes in valleys; can build castles and abbeys; and, if it find no other amusement, can dilate itself in vast ideas of space." Mr Gilpin, after describing such objects as may be called picturesque, proceeds to consider their sources of amusement. We cannot follow our ingenious author through the whole of this consideration, and shall therefore finish our article with a short quotation from the beginning of it. "We might begin (says he) in moral style, and consider the objects of nature in a higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than merely as amusement. We might observe, that a search after beauty should naturally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the mind to the great origin of all beauty; to the first good, first perfect, and first fair. But though in theory this seems a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> climax, we infall the less upon it, as in fact we have scarce ground to hope that every admirer of picturesque beauty is an admirer. PIE Picturcous admirer also of the beauty of virtue; and that every lover of nature reflects, that Beauty is but a name for an effect, Whole cayce is God. If, however, the admirer of nature can turn his amusements to a higher purpose; if its great scenes can inspire him with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> awe, or its tranquil scenes with that complacency of mind which is so nearly allied that benevolence, it is certainly the better. Apponat lucro. It is so much into the bargain; for we dare not <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> him more from picturesque travel than a rational and agreeable amusement. Yet even this may be of some use in an age teeming with licentious pleasure; and may in this light at least be considered as having a moral tendency."

PICUPINIMA

Pages 156-156

is the Brazilian name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pigeon, which is so very small as scarcely to exceed the lark in size. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PICUMNUS">PICUMNUS</a> and PILUMNUS, were two Roman deities, who presided over the auspices required before the celebration of nuptials. Pilumnus was supposed to patronize children, as his name seems in some manner to indicate quod pellat nulla infantiae. The maturing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> was first invented by Picumnus, from which reason he is called Sterquilinus. Pilumnus is also invoked as the god of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> and millers, as he is said to have first invented the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> corn.

PICUS

Pages 156-156

the WOODPECKER, a genus of birds belonging to the order of picce. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Picus (fab. hist.), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Latium, son of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>. He married Venilia, also called Canens, by whom he had Faunus. He was tenderly loved by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Pomona, and he returned her affection. As he was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> hunting in the woods, he was met by Circe, who became deeply enamoured of him, and who changed him into a woodpecker, called by the name of picus among the Latins. His wife Venilia was so disconsolate when she was informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, that she pined away. Some suppose that Picus was the son of Pilumnus, and that he gave out prophecies to his subjects by means of a favourite woodpecker; from which circumstance originated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of his being metamorphosed into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. Picus, John Francis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRANDOLA">Mirandola</a>, nephew of John <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICA">Pica</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Picus, mentioned above, was born about the year 1469. He cultivated learning and the sciences after the example of his uncle; but he had a principality and dominions to superintend, which involved him in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> troubles, and at last cost him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was twice driven from his principality, and twice restored; and at last, in 1533, was, together with his eldest son Albert, affianced in his own castle by his nephew Galeotti. He was a great lover of letters; and such of his works as were then composed were inserted in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> edition of his uncle's in 1554, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in future impressions, besides some others which were never collected.

PIECE

Pages 156-156

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> pieces of the shield are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, fess, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, crois, faltier, chevron, and in general all those which may take up one-third of the field, when alone, and in what manner forever it be. See HERALDRY.

PIECES

Pages 156-156

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, include all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns and mortars. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERING">Battering</a> pieces are the larger sort of guns used at sieges for making the breaches; such are the 24-pounder and culverine, the one carrying a 24 and the other an 18 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. Field-pieces are 12-pounds, demi-culverines, 6-pounders, fackers, minions, and 3-pounders, which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and encamp always behind the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line, but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. A soldier's firelock is likewise called his piece.

PIEDMONT

Pages 156-157

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, having formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Savoy and Italy; on the west by France; on the south by the Mediterranean and the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; and on the east by the duchies of Montferrat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; extending about 150 miles from north to south, but much less from east to west. It is called Piedmont, and in Latin Piedmontium, from its situation at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which separate France from Italy. This country is in some parts mountainous, but is everywhere very fruitful. The plains produce fine corn, and Montferrat and the Milanese yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> wheat, which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> serves for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and with which the people of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> mix rye; the pods are used for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and the stalks being thick serve to mend the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>. The hills produce plenty of wine, which, like the Italian wines, is very delicious when new, especially the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. There is also a tartish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine called vino brufco, said to be very wholesome for fat people, and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the sweet wine is recommended as a stomachic. The neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> is famous for its fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> walks of chestnut and mulberry trees, which produce both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and profit. Marons, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> chestnuts, are a favourite dainty among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people. They are put into an oven, and, when thoroughly hot, and cooled in red wine, are dried a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the oven, and afterwards eaten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. Truffles grow here in such abundance, that Piedmont has obtained the name of the truffle country. Some are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, others white marbled with red. Their price is rated according to their size. Sometimes they are found of 12 or 14 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and many country people earn from 60 to 70 dollars a-year merely by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> for them. The trade in cattle is said to bring into Piedmont no less than three millions of livres per annum. The cultivation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> is also a profitable article, the Piedmontese silk being, on account of its fineness and strength, esteemed the best in Italy. The Piedmontese gentry breed vast numbers of silk-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> under the care of their tenants, who have the eggs and mulberry leaves delivered to them, and in return they give half the silk to their masters. This principality comprehends eleven small provinces: Piedmont proper, the valleys between France and Italy, the valley of Saluzza, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, the marquisate of Sula, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Aoët, the Canavese, the lordship of Vettai, Piedmont, fail, the county of Aft, and the Langes. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, but now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, and lies at the foot of the Alps, which separate France from Italy. It contains many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains, among which there are rich and fruitful valleys, as pleasant and populous as any part of Italy. In the mountains are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of several kinds, and the forests afford a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, among which the tumor is an useful animal. "The mules (says Mr Watkins) are very fine in this country; but the inhabitants have other beasts, or rather monsters which they find very serviceable, though vicious and obstinate. These are produced by a cow and an ass, or mare and bull, and called jumarres or gimerri (A). I cannot say that I have ever seen any of them, but I am told they are very common." The Piedmontese are said to be more intelligent than the Savoyards, but less sincere. Some authors represent them as lively, artful, and witty, the inhabitants of the mountain of Aoita excepted, who are farther distinguished by large wens, as even their horses, dogs, and other animals. Mr Baretti, however, in his Account of Italy, vol. ii. p. 116, gives the following account of them. "One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> qualities (says he), which distinguish the Piedmontese from all other Italians, is their want of cheerfulness. Piedmont never produced a single good poet, as far as the records of the country can go, whereas there is no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Italy but what can boast of some poet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>; and yet the Piedmontese are not deficient in several branches of learning, and some of them have succeeded tolerably well in civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, physic, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. It is likewise observed of this people, that none of them ever attained to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence in the polite arts, and it is but lately that they can boast of a painter, Cavaliere Bontempe; a flautist, Signor Lodetto; and some architects, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTE">Conte</a> Alferi, Signor Borra, and others, who yet, to say the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, are far inferior to numberless artists produced by the other provinces of Italy. They have, on the other hand, greatly advanced when considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>; though their troops have never been very numerous, every body conversant in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> knows the brave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> they made for some centuries past against the French, Spaniards, and Germans, whenever they have been invaded by these nations. The skill of the Piedmontese in fortification is likewise very great, and their Bertolas and Pintos have shown as much genius as the Vaubans and Cohorns, in rendering impregnable several places which inferior engineers would only have made secure." The chief trade of this principality consists in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and silk. Indeed, so great is their trade in raw silk, that the English alone have purchased to the value of 200,000 lib. in a year. The silk worm thrives so well, that many peasants make above (B) 100 lib. of silk annually; and it is not only abundant, but universally known to be stronger and finer than any in Italy. The land owners divide the profit with their tenants. The Piedmontese workmen, however, are said to want <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, though they finish their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> equally well with those of other nations. The high duty and land carriage on mules likewise tend to lessen the value of this trade. They have besides corn, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, wine, fruits, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and cattle. In the valleys of Lucerne, Peyrouse, and St Martin, which have always belonged to Piedmont, live the celebrated Waldenses or Vaudois, a name which signifies people of the valleys. These have rendered themselves famous in history for their dissent from the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> long before the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and Calvin, and for the persecutions they have suffered on that account; but since the year 1730 they have not been openly molested for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, but, in order to suppress them by degrees, a papal church has been built in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. They are heavily taxed, and labour under great oppressions. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people in these valleys scarce at present exceeds 15,000, of which 1000 are Catholics. The chief river of Piedmont is the Po, which flows out of Mount Vilo. The river Sesia, the Doria, Baltea, the ancient Drunta, the Tenaro, and several others, run into it. The Var, anciently called the Varus, rises in the county of Nice, and after watering it empties itself into the Mediterranean. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Piedmontese is a mixture of French and Italian. In this country are about 50 earldoms, 15 marquises, a multitude of lordships, and 20 abbeys. Though the country be entirely popish, except some valleys inhabited by the Waldenses, the king reserves to himself the greatest part of the power in church affairs, which in many other places is given up to the pope, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> unigenitus is here universally opposed. Towards the end of the 17th century, the French king persuaded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy to drive them out of the country; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which 200,000 of them retired to Germany, England, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and yet they are not all extirpated, though, as we have observed, they are obliged to have a Roman Catholic church in every parish. Turin, formerly the residence of the king of Sardinia, to whom this principality belonged, is the chief <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. See Turin. The number of inhabitants, Mr Watkins says, in Piedmont and Savoy, amount to 2,695,727 souls, of which Turin contains about 77,000. Piedmont, as well as the rest of Italy, few of our readers need be informed, is now subject to the overgrown power of France.

PIENES

Pages 157-157

a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, opposite to the harbour of Saccat, is famed not only for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its walks, to which crowds of people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but for a deity worshipped there, to which vast numbers of persons devote themselves. They go from his temple to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> side, where they enter into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> provided (A) These equivocal animals, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> them, are so generally mentioned by travellers in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, that we have no doubt of their existence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of their being found hardy and serviceable as labourers. (B) Each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> is valued in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> at 18s. The little village of La Tour, in the valley of Lucerne, makes above 50,000 lb. annually, and the exports every year to the single city of Lyons amount to more than 160,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">Sterling</a>.

PIEPOUDRE

Pages 157-158
COURT OF, the lowest, and at the same time the most expeditious, court of justice known to the law of England. It is called PIEPOUDRE, (curia pedis pulverizata), from the dusty feet of the jurors; or, according to Sir Edward Coke, because justice is there done as speedily as dust can fall from the foot: Upon the same principle that justice among the Jews was administered in the gate of the city, that the proceedings might be the more speedy, as well as public. But the etymology given us by a learned modern writer is much more ingenious and satisfactory; it being derived, according to him, from pied pulvérieux, "a pedlar," in old French, and therefore signifying the court of such petty chapmen as refer to fairs or markets. It is a court of record incident to every fair and market; of which the steward of him who owns or has the toll of the market is the judge. It was instituted to administer justice for all commercial injuries done in that very fair or market, and not in any preceding one. So that the injury must be done, complained of, heard, and determined, within the compass of one and the same day, unless the fair continues longer. The court hath cognizance of all matters of contract that can possibly arise within the precinct of that fair or market; and the plaintiff must make oath that the cause of an action arose there. From this court a writ of error lies, in the nature of an appeal, to the courts at Westminster. The reason of its institution seems to have been, to do justice expeditiously among the variety of persons that resort from distant places to a fair or market; since it is probable, that no other inferior court might be able to serve its process, or execute its judgements, on both or perhaps either of the parties; and therefore, unless this court had been erected, the complaint must necessarily have referred even in the first instance to some superior judicature.

PIERIA

Pages 158-158

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, contained between the mouths of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Ludias and Peneus; extended by Strabo beyond the Ludias, to the river Axios on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and on the south farther than the Aiacmon, along the west side of the Sinus Thermaicus.—Another Pieria of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Antiochana, situated on the Sinus Ilicus, and lying next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> to the north-west.

PIERIDES

Pages 158-158

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the daughters of Pierus a Macedonian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, presuming to dispute with the mules for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, were turned into magpies. The name of Pierides was also given to the mules, from Mount Pieris in Thessaly, which was consecrated to them; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, from Pieris, a Thessalian poet, who was the first who sacrificed to them.

PIERINO DEL VAGA

Pages 158-158

an eminent Italian painter, born of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> parents in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, about the year 1500. He was placed apprentice with a grocer in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and got some instructions from the painters to whom he was sent with colours and pencils; but a painter named Vaga taking him to Rome, he was called Del Vaga, from living with him, his real name being Buonaccorsi. He studied anatomy with the sciences necessary for his profession; and had somewhat of everything that was good in his compositions. After Raphael's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he joined with Julio Romano and Francisco Penni to finish the works in the Vatican, which were left imperfect by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; and to confirm their friendship married Penni's sister. He gained the highest reputation by his performances in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Doria at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; but the multiplicity of his business, and the vivacity of his imagination, drained his spirits in the flower of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; for he died in the year 1547. Of all Raphael's disciples, Pierino kept the character of his master longest, i.e., his exterior character and manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>; for he fell very short of the fineness of Raphael's thinking. He had a particular genius for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> of places according to their customs. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> in that kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> was full of ingenuity; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and order are everywhere to be met with, and his dispositions, which are ordinary in his pictures, are wonderful in his ornaments: some of these he has made little, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and placed them both with so much art, that they set off one another by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. His figures are disposed and designed according to Raphael's gusto; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Raphael gave him at first some slight sketches of ornaments, as he did to Giovanni d'Udine, he executed them to admiration. The tapestries of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, in seven pieces, which Pierino designed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POITIERS">Poitiers</a>, and which were, when De Piles wrote, with Monsieur the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, flows sufficiently what he was, and that the above character does not exceed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.

PIERIS

Pages 158-159

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain which is thought to have given name to Picaria of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; taking its name from Pierus a poet, who was the first that sacrificed to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, thence called Pierides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> may be given to an ancient scholiast on Juvenal. PIERRE D'AUTOMNE is a French name, translated from the Chinese, of a medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, celebrated in the east for curing all disorders of the lungs. Many imagine it had its name of the autumn-stone from its being only to be made at that season of the year; but it may certainly be made equally at all times. The Chinese chemists refer the various parts of the body to the several seasons of the year, and thus they refer the lungs to autumn. This is evident in their writings, and thus the stone for dilutes of the lungs came to be called autumn-stone. It is prepared as follows: They put 30 pints of the urine of a strong and healthy young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pot, and let it over a gentle fire. When it begins to boil, they add to it, drop by drop, about a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-cup-full of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. They then leave it on the fire till the whole is evaporated to a thick substance like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mud. It is then taken out of the pot, and laid on a flat iron to dry, so that it may be powdered very fine. This powder is moistened with fresh oil, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> is put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> crucible, surrounded with coals, where it stands till it be thoroughly dried again. This is again powdered, and put into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a> veffel, which being covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> cloth and a double <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, they pour on it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which makes its way, drop by drop, through these coverings, till so much is got in as is sufficient to reduce it to a paste. This paste is well mixed together in the veffel it is kept in, and this is put into a veffel of water, and the whole set over the fire. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> thus becomes again dried in balne mariae, and is then finished. Obferv. fur les Cout. de l'Afie, p. 218.

PIERRE

Pages 159-159

St. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a>, was built in 1665, in order to overawe the mutineers of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> who rebelled against its proprietors, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, who were at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the proprietors of all the French Antilles. It is situated on the western side of the island. The town extends along the shore, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> that commands the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is erected on the west side, which is washed by the river Royolan, or St Peter. The town is divided into three wards; the middle, which is properly St Peter's, begins at the fort, and runs westward to the battery of St Nicholas. Under the walls of the second <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> ships at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> ride more securely than under the fort, on which account this ward is called the Anchorage. The third ward, called the Gallery, extends along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> side from Fort St Peter to the Jesuits River, and is the most populous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The houses of St Peter's ward are neat, commodious, and elegant, particularly those of the governor of the island, the intendant, and the other officers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Peter is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> which belonged to the Jesuits, with a noble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the Doric order. The church of the Anchorage, which belongs to the Jacobite friars, is likewise of stone. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable trade, and is built with tolerable regularity. The houses are mostly constructed of a gray pumice-stone or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, which is found on the strand; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-street is, according to Dr Hert, above an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length. It is supposed to contain about 2000 houses, and 30,000 inhabitants, including <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>. St Pierre, with the whole of the flourishing island of Martinico, was taken from the French in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1794, by the British troops: 125 vessels loaded with the produce of the island, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value, were captured, 71 of which were in the harbour of St Pierre.

PIETISTS

Pages 159-159

otherwise called the Brethren and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">Sisters</a> of the Pious and Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">Schools</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> formed in the year 1678 by Nicholas Barre, and obliged by their engagements to devote themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> children of both sexes.

PIETOLA

Pages 159-159

anciently called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> within two Italian miles of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, famous for being the birthplace of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>.

PIETY

Pages 159-160

is a virtue which denotes veneration for the Deity, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and tenderness to our friends. This distinguished virtue, like many others, received among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> divine honours, and was made one of their gods. Acilius Glabrio first erected a temple to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, which he did upon the spot on which a woman had fed with her own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> her aged father, who had been imprisoned by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and deprived of all aliments. The story is well known, and is given at length in authors which are in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of every schoolboy. See Cicero de div. i. and Valerius Maximus, v. c. 4. and our article FILLAL Piety. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> piety was thus practised and thus honoured in Heathen antiquity, it surely ought not to be less so, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, to whom its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is better defined, and to the practice of which they have motives of greater cogency. A learned and elegant writer has said that the want of piety arises from the want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>; and his observations and arguments are so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> and so well expressed, that we cannot do better than transcribe them. "It appears to me (says Dr Knox), that the mind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, when it is free from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> defects and acquired corruption, feels no less a tendency to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> than to virtuous love, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to any other of the more refined and elevated affections. But debauchery and excess contribute greatly to destroy all the susceptible delicacy with which nature usually furnishes the heart; and, in the general extinction of our better qualities, it is no wonder that so pure a sentiment as that of piety should be one of the first to expire. "It is certain that the understanding may be improved in a knowledge of the world, and in the arts of succeeding in it, while the heart, or whatever constitutes the seat of the moral and sentimental feelings, is gradually receding from its proper and original perfection. Indeed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> seems to evince, that it is hardly possible to arrive at the character of a complete man of the world, without losing many of the most valuable sentiments of uncorrupted nature. A complete man of the world is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> being; he has discarded many of the native and laudable tendencies of his mind, and adopted a new system of objects and propensities of his own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. These are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>, coarse, lordly, selfish, and sensual. All, or either of these attributes, tend directly to blunt the senses of every thing liberal, enlarged, disinterested; of every thing which participates more of an intellectual than of a sensual nature. When the heart is tied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> by lust and avarice, it is not extraordinary that the eye should be Pietv. seldom lifted up to heaven. To the man who spends his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> (because he thinks the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> fit for little else) in the counting-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in travelling, in the tavern, or in the brothel, those who go to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> appear as fools, and the busines they go upon as nonsense. He is callous to the feelings of devotion; but he is tremblingly alive to all that gratifies his senses or promotes his interests. "It has been remarked of those writers who have attacked Christianity, and represented all religions merely as diversified modes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, that they were indeed, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, men of a metaphysical and a disputatious turn of mind, but usually little distinguished for benignity and generosity. There was, amidst all their pretensions to logical sagacity, a cloudiness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, and a coldness of heart, which rendered them very unfit judges on a question in which the heart is chiefly interested; in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of nature is more expressive and convincing, than all the dreary subtleties of the dismal metaphysicians. Even the reasoning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, on which we so greatly value ourselves, may be perverted by excessive refinement; and there is an abstruse, but vain and foolish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which philosophizes us out of the noblest parts of our noble nature. One of those parts of us is our instinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, of which not one of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> which the philosophers most admire, and to whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> they wish to reduce us, is found in the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to participate. "Such philosophers may be called, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> sense, the enemies of mankind. They not only endeavour to entice man from his duty, but to rob him of a most excellent and natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Such, surely, is the pleasure of devotion. For when the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> rises above this little orb, and pours its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> at the throne of celestial majesty, the holy fervour which it feels is itself a rapturous delight. Neither is this a declamatory representation, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> felt and acknowledged by all the sons of men; except those who have been defective in sensibility, or who hoped to gratify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> or the malignity of their hearts by singular and pernicious speculation. "Indeed all disputatious, controversial, and metaphysical writings on the subject of religion, are unfavourable to genuine piety. We do not find that the most renowned polemics in the church militant were at all more attentive than others to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> offices of religion, or that they were actuated by any peculiar degree of devotion. The truth is, their religion centered in their heads, whereas its natural region is the heart. The heart! confined, alas! in colleges or <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, unacquainted with all the tender charities of husband, father, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, friend; some of them have almost forgotten that they possess a heart. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ceased to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> with the pulsations of love and sympathy, and has been engrossed by pride on conquering an adversary in the syllogistic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, or by impotent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> on a defeat. With such habits, and so defective a system of feelings, can we expect that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the Sorbonne, or the disputing professor of divinity, should ever feel the pure <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of piety that glowed in the bosoms of Mrs Rowe, Mrs Talbot, or Mr Nellon? "It is however certain, that a devotional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> are very desirable in themselves, exclusive of their effects in meliorating the morals and disposition, and promoting present and future felicity. They add <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, pleasure, and security to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>: but to old age they are the most becoming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, the most substantial support, and the sweetest comfort. In order to preserve them, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary to preserve our sensibility; and nothing will contribute so much to this purpose as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, innocence, and simplicity." Of piety, as it denotes love and tenderness to our friends, there have been many distinguished instances both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">FILIAL</a> Piety, FRATERNAL and PARENTAL Affection, &c. The following example of filial piety in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, taken from P. Du Halde's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, will not we trust be disagreeable to our readers. "In the commencement of the dynasty of the Tang, Lou-tao-tsong, who was disaffected to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, being accused of a fault, which touched his life, obtained leave from those who had him in custody, to perform the duties of the Tao to one of his deceased friends. He managed matters so well, that giving his keepers the slip, he fled to the house of Lou Nan-kin, with whom he had a friendship, and there hid himself. Lou Nan-kin, notwithstanding the strict search that was made, and the severity of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> against those who conceal prisoners that have escaped, would not betray his friend. However, the thing coming to be discovered, Lou Nan-kin was imprisoned; and they were just on the point of proceeding against him, when his younger brother presenting himself before the judge, It is I, Sir, said he, who have hidden the prisoner; it is I who ought to die, and not my elder brother. The eldest maintained, on the contrary, that his younger brother accused himself wrongfully, and was not at all culpable. The judge, who was a person of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sagacity, fitted both parties to effectually, that he not only discovered that the younger brother was innocent, but even made him confess it himself: It is true, Sir, said the younger all in tears, I have accused myself falsely; but I have very strong reasons for so doing. My mother has been dead for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and her corpse is not yet buried; I have a sister also who is marriageable, but is not yet disposed of: these things which my brother is capable of managing, I am not, and therefore desire to die in his stead. Vouchsafe to admit my testimony.
