The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> gave an account of the whole affair to the court, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> at his solicitation pardoned the criminal."

PIG

Pages 160-160

see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUS">Sus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>-Pig, see Mus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. PIG of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a fother, amounting to 250 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. PIGANIOL de la Force, John Aymar de, a native of Auvergne, of a noble family, applied himself with ardour to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a> and of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of France. With the view of improving himself in this study, he travelled into different provinces; and, in the course of his travels, made some important observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. These observations were of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to him in compiling the works he has left behind him, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> are, 1. An Historical and Geographical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of France; the largest edition of which is that of 1753, in 15 vols. 12mo. It is the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which has hitherto appeared upon that subject, though it contains a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inaccuracies and even errors. 2. A Description of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 10 vols. 12mo; a work equally entertaining and instructive, and much more complete than the description given by German Brice: besides, it is written with an elegant simplicity. He published an abridgement of it in 2 vols. 12mo.

PIGEON

Pages 160-162

see Columba, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Pigeon-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> is a house erected full of holes within, for the keeping, breeding, &c. of pigeons, otherwise called a dove-cot. Any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> may build a pigeon-house on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but a tenant cannot do it without the lord's licence. When persons shoot at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kill pigeons within a certain distance of the pigeon-house, they are liable to pay a forfeiture. In order to erect a pigeon-house to advantage, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to pitch upon a convenient situation; of which none is more proper than the middle of a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-yard, because pigeons are naturally of a timorous disposition, and the least noise they hear frightens them. With regard to the size of the pigeon-house, it must depend entirely upon the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of birds intended to be kept; but it is better to have it too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> than too little; and as to its form, the round should be preferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> ones; because rats cannot so easily come at them in the former as in the latter. It is also much more commodious; because you may, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LADDER">ladder</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> upon an axis, easily visit all the nests in the house, without the least difficulty; which cannot so easily be done in a square house. In order to hinder rats from climbing up the outside of the pigeon-house, the wall should be covered with tin plates to a certain height, about a foot and a half will be sufficient; but they should project out three or four inches at the top, to prevent their clambering any higher. The pigeon-house should be placed at no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that the pigeons may carry it to their young ones; and their carrying it in their bills will warm it, and render it more wholesome in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. The boards that cover the pigeon-house should be well joined together, so that no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> may penetrate through it; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> should be covered with hard <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-washed within and without, white being the most pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to pigeons. There must be no window, or other opening in the pigeon-house to the eastward; these should always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> the south, for pigeons are very fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, especially in winter. The nests or covers in a pigeon-house should consist of square holes made in the walls, of a size sufficient to admit the cock and hen to stand in them. The first range of these nests should not be less than four feet from the ground, that the wall underneath being smooth, the rats may not be able to reach them. These nests should be placed in quincunx order, and not directly over one another. Nor must they be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> any higher than within three feet of the top of the wall; and the upper row should be covered with a board, projecting a considerable distance from the wall, for fear the rats should find means to climb the outside of the house. M. Duhamel thinks that pigeons neither feed upon the green corn, nor have bills strong enough to search for its seeds in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but only pick up the grains that are not covered, which would infallibly become the prey of other animals, or be dried up by the sun. "From the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the sprouting of the corn," says he, "pigeons live chiefly upon the seeds of wild uncultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and therefore lessen considerably the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of weeds that would otherwise <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up; as will appear from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> estimate of the quantity of grain necessary to feed all the pigeons of a well-stocked dove-house." But Mr Worlidge and Mr Litle allege facts in support of the contrary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. The latter relates, that a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> in his neighbourhood assured him he had known an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> sown with peas, and rain coming on so that they could not be harrowed in, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a> was fetched away in half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s time by pigeons; and the former says, "It is to be observed, that where the flight of pigeons falls, there they fill themselves and away, and return again where they first rose, and so proceed over a whole piece of ground, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they like it. Although you cannot perceive any grain above the ground, they know how to find it. I have seen them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> so much upon a piece of about two or three acres sown with peas, that they devoured at least three parts in four of the seed, which, I am sure, could not be all above the surface of the ground. That their smelling is their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, I have observed; having sown a small plot of peas in my garden, near a pigeon-house, and covered them so well that not a pea appeared above ground. In a few days, a parcel of pigeons were hard at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in discovering this hidden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; and in a few days more I had not above two or three peas left out of about two quarts that were planted; for what they could not find before, they found when the buds appeared, notwithstanding they were hoed in, and well covered. Their smelling alone directed them, as I supposed, because they followed the ranges exactly. The injury they do at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> on the peas, vetches, &c. is such that we may <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> them among the greatest enemies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> husbandman meets withal; and the greater, because he may not erect a pigeon-house, whereby to have a share of his own spoils; none but the rich being allowed this privilege, and so severe a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> being also made to protect these winged thieves, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> cannot encounter them, even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. You have therefore no remedy against them, but to affright them away by noises or such like. You may, indeed, shoot at them; but you must not kill them; or you may, if you can, take them in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, cut off their tails, and let them go; by which means you will impound them; for when they are in their houses, they cannot bolt or fly out of the tops of them, but by the strength of their tails; after thus weakening of which, they remain prisoners at home." Mr Worlidge's impounding the pigeons reminds us of a humorous story of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, who, upon a neighbouring farmer's complaining to him, that his pigeons were a great nuisance to his land, and did sad mischief to his corn, replied jokingly, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">Pound</a> them, if you catch them trespassing." The farmer, improving the hint, steeped a parcel of peas in an infusion of coccinellus indicus, or some other intoxicating drug, and strewed them upon his grounds. The pigeons swallowed them, and soon remained motionless on the field: upon which the farmer threw a net over them, inclosed them in it, and carried ried them to an empty barn, from whence he sent the gentleman word that he had followed his directions with regard to the pounding of his pigeons, and desired him to come and release them. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">Carrier</a>-Pigeon. See Carrier-Pigeon and Columba, Ornithology Index. Pigeon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Francis, curate of St Peter du Regard, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Bayeux, was one of the priests lately belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s house at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>. He was born in Lower Normandy, of honest and virtuous parents, and of a decent fortune. His inclinations early led him to embrace the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state, from which neither the solicitations of his friends, nor the prospect of a more ample fortune on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, could withdraw him. Several of his schoolfellows and masters, who are now resident in the king's house at Winchester, bear the most ample testimony to his affability, regularity, piety, and the sweetness of his disposition, during the whole course of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. The sweetness of temper, in particular, was so remarkable, and so clearly depicted on his countenance, as to have gained him the esteem and affection of such of the inhabitants of Winchester as by any means had become acquainted with him. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, or, as we should call it, curate, of a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in the diocese of Seze, where his virtues and talents had ample scope for exertion. His practice was to rise at five o'clock every morning, and to spend the whole time till noon (the usual time of dinner for persons in his station) in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The rest of the day, till evening, he devoted to visiting the sick, and other exterior duties of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. In 1789, the year of the French revolution, M. Pigeon was promoted to a curacy, or rather a rectory, in the diocese of Bayeux, called the parish of St Peter du Regard, near the town of Condé sur Noëre. It was easy for him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the good-will and the protection of his parishioners; but a Jacobin club in the above-mentioned town seemed to have no other subject to deliberate upon than the various ways of harassing and persecuting M. Pigeon and certain other priests in the neighbourhood, who had from motives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> refused the famous civic oath. It would be tedious to relate the many cruelties which were at different times exercised upon him, and the imminent danger of losing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to which he was exposed, by the blows that were inflicted on him, by his being thrown into water, and being obliged to wander in woods and other solitary places, without any food or place to lay his head, in order to avoid his persecutors. We may form some judgement of the spirit of his persecutors from the following circumstance. Being disappointed on a particular occasion in the search they were making after M. Pigeon, with the view of amusing themselves with his sufferings, they made themselves amends by seizing his mother, a respectable lady of 74 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and his two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, whom they placed upon asses with their faces turned backwards, obliging them in derision to hold the tails of these animals. Thus they were conducted in pain and ignominy throughout the whole town of Condé, for no other alleged crime except being the nearest relations of M. Pigeon. At length the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> for transporting all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> arrived; and this gentleman, with several others, after having been stripped of all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, was shipped from Port Belfin, and landed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, where he was shortly after received into the establishment at Foxton, and, upon that being dissolved in order to make room for prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, into the king's house at Winchester. Being of a studious turn, he was accustomed, as many of his brethren also were, to betake himself to the neighbouring lanes and thickets for the sake of greater solitude. With this view having, about ten o'clock in the morning, Aug. 28, 1793, retired to a certain little valley, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east side of a place called Oram's Arbour, the same place where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> elections for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a> are held, he was there found, between three and four o'clock in the afternoon, murdered, with the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his skull absolutely broken from the lower part, and a large hedge-stake, covered with blood, lying by him, as were the papers on which he had been transcribing a manuscript sermon, with the hearing of which he had been much edified, and the sermon itself which he was copying, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, imbrued in blood. His watch was carried away, though part of the chain, which had by some means been broken, was left behind. He was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the word paradise, the last letters of which remained unwritten when the fatal blow was given him, which appears evidently to have been discharged upon him from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> in a hedge which was immediately behind him. At first the suspicion of this cruel <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> fell upon the French democrats, who, to the number of 200, are prisoners of war, at the neighbouring town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALRESFORD">Alresford</a>, as one of that number, who had broken his parole, had, about three weeks before, been taken up in Winchester, and both there and at Alresford had repeatedly threatened to murder his uncle, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, whom he understood to be then at Winchester, not without fervent wishes of having it in his power to murder the whole establishment, consisting of more than 600 persons. However, as no French prisoner was seen that day in the neighbourhood of Winchester, as none of them were known to have left Alresford, it is evidently reasonable to acquiesce in the verdict of the coroner; namely, that the murder was committed by a person or persons unknown. The most noble marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, whose munificence and kindness to those conscientious exiles, the emigrant French clergy, can only be conceived by those who have been witnesses of the same, with the truly respectable corps of the Buckinghamshire <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, then quartered at Winchester, joined in paying the last mark of respect to the unfortunate deceased, by attending his funeral, which was performed at the Roman Catholic burying-ground, called St James's, near the said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, on Saturday, Aug. 29. He was just 38 years of age when he was murdered.

PIGMENTS

Pages 162-162

preparations used by painters, dyers, &c., to impart colours to bodies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to imitate particular colours. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>-Making, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a>. PIGNEROL is a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 15' N. Lat. 44° 45', situated on the river Chizou, 10 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, at the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and the confines of Dauphiny. The town is small, but populous, and extremely well fortified by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>. It is defended by a citadel, on the top of the mountain near which is the castle of Peroufe, which was built at the entrance of the valley of that name.

PIGUS

Pages 162-163

PIGUS, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, is the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-mouthed fish, very much resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> carp; being of the same shape and size, and its eyes, fins, and fleshy palate, exactly the same; from the gills to the tail there is a crooked dotted line; the back and sides are bluish, and the belly reddish. It is covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> scales; from the middle of each of which there rises a fine pellucid prickle, which is very sharp. It is an excellent fish for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, being perhaps preferable to the carp; and it is in season in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and April. It is caught in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and is mentioned by Pliny, though without a name. Artedi says it is a species of cyprinus, and he calls it the cyprinus, called ploco and pigus.

PIISSKER

Pages 163-164

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, is a fish of the mustela kind, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the fossile mustela, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fossile fish. This fish is generally found as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as an ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and as thick as the finger; but it sometimes grows much longer: the back is of gray with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of spots and transverse streaks, partly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and partly blue; the belly is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and spotted with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and black; the white are the larger, the others look as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were made with the point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>; and there is on each of the sides a longitudinal black and white line. There are some fleshy excrescences at the mouth, which are expanded in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>; and when out of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, they are contracted. These fishes run into caverns of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in the sides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, in marshy places, and penetrate a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way, and are often dug up at a distance from waters. Often, when the waters of brooks and rivers swell beyond their banks, and again cover them, they make their way out of the earth into the water; and when it deserts them, they are often left in vast numbers upon the ground, and become a prey to swine. It is thought to be much of the same kind with the figum fish; and it is indeed possible that the pecilia of Schonefeldt is the same. PIKE. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESOX">Esox</a>, Ichthyology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The pike never swims in shoals as most other fish do, but always lies alone; and is so bold and ravenous, that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon almost any thing less than himself. Of the ravenous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this fish we shall give the following instances. At Rycoot in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, in the year 1749, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOAT">moat</a> surrounding the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABINGDON">Abingdon</a>'s seat, there was a jack or pike of such a monstrous size, that it had destroyed young swans feathers and all. An old cobb swan having hatched five young, one after another was lost till four were gone. At length an under gardener <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the fish seize the fifth. The old one fought him with their beaks, and with the assistance of the gardener, released it although he had got it under water. In the year 1765 a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pike was caught in the river Ouse, which weighed upwards of 28 pounds, and was sold for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a>. On gutting the fish, a watch with a black ribbon and two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> seals were found in its stomach, which, by the maker's name, &c. was found to belong to a person who had been drowned about six weeks before. This fish breeds but once in a year, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. It is found in almost all fresh waters; but is very different in goodness, according to the nature of the places where it lives. The finest pike are those which feed in clear rivers; those in ponds and meres are inferior, and the worst of all are those of the fen ditches. They are very plentiful in these last places, where the water is foul and coloured, and their food, such as frogs and the like, very plentiful, but very coarse; so that they grow large, but are yellowish and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> bellied, and differ greatly from those which live in the clearer waters. The fishermen have two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ways of catching the pike; by the ledger, and by the walking-bait. The ledger-bait is fixed in one certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and may continue while the angler is absent. This must be a live bait, a fish or frog; and among fish, the dace, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, and gudgeon, are the best; of frogs, the only caution is to choose the largest and yellowest that can be met with. If the bait be a fish, the hook is to be stuck through the upper lip, and the line must be 14 yards at least in length; the other end of this is to be tied to a bough of a tree, or to a stick driven into the ground near the pike's haunt, and all the line wound round a forked stick, except about half a yard. The bait will by this means keep playing so much under water, and the pike will soon lay hold of it. If the bait be a frog, then the arming wire of the hook should be put in at the mouth, and out at the side; and with a needle and some strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, the hinder leg of one side is to be fastened by one flitch to the wire-arming of the hook. The pike will soon seize this, and must have line enough to give him leave to get to his haunt, and poach the bait. The trolling for pike is a pleasant method also of taking them: in this a dead bait serves, and none is so proper as a gudgeon. This is to be pulled about in the water till the pike seizes it; and then it is to have line enough, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to swallow it: the hook is small for this sport, and has a smooth piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> fixed at its end to sink the bait; and the line is very long, and runs through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> at the end of the rod, which must not be too slender at top. The art of feeding pike, so as to make them very fat, is the giving them eels; and without this it is not to be done under a very long time; otherwise perch, while small, and their prickly fins tender, are the best food for them. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">Bream</a> put into a pike-pond are a very proper food: they will breed freely, and their young ones make excellent food for the pike, who will take care that they shall not increase over much. The numerous shoals of roaches and rudds, which are continually changing place, and often in floods get into the pike's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, are food for them for a long time. Pike, when used to be fed by hand, will come up to the very shore, and take the food that is given them out of the fingers of the feeder. It is wonderful to see with what courage they will do this, after a while practising; and it is a very diverting fight when there are several of them nearly of the same size, to see what striving and fighting there will be for the best bits when they are thrown in. The most convenient place is near the mouth of the pond, and where there is about half a yard depth of water; for, by that means, the offal of the feedings will all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in one place, and the deep water. will serve for a place to retire into and rest in, and will be always clean and in order. Carp may be fed in the same manner as pike; and though by nature a fish as remarkably shy and timorous as the pike is bold and fearless, yet by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> they will come to take their food out of the person's hand; and will, like the pike, quarrel among one another for the nicest bits. **Pike**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>*, an offensive weapon, consisting of a wooden shaft, 12 or 14 feet long, with a flat steel head, pointed, called the *spear*. This weapon was long in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the infantry; but now the bayonet, which is fixed on the muzzle of the firelock, is substituted in its stead. It is still used by some of the officers of infantry, under the name of *spontoon*. The Macedonian phalanx was a battalion of pikemen. See PHALANX. **Pila marina**, or the *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>*, in *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>*, is the name of a substance very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on the shores of the Mediterranean, and elsewhere. It is generally found in the form of a ball about the size of the balls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> dung, and composed of a variety of fibrils irregularly complicated. Various conjectures have been given of its origin by different authors. John Bauhine tells us, that it consists of small hairy fibres and straws, such as are found about the sea plant called *algae vivariarum*; but he does not ascertain what plant it owes its origin to. Imperatus imagined it consisted of the exuviae both of vegetable and animal bodies. Mercatus is doubtful whether it be a congeries of the fibrils of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, wound up into a ball by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the sea water, or whether it be not the workmanship of some sort of beetle living about the sea shore, and analogous to our common dung beetle's ball, which it elaborates from dung for the reception of its progeny. Schreckius says it is composed of the filaments of some plant of the reed kind; and Welchius supposes it is composed of the papous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the reed. Maurice Hoffman thinks it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a> of the hippopotamus; and others think it that of the phoca or sea calf. Klein, who had thoroughly and minutely examined the bodies themselves, and all what authors had conjectured concerning them, thinks that they are wholly owing to, and entirely composed of, the calliaments which the leaves, growing to the woody stalk of the *algae vivariarum*, have when they wither and decay. These leaves, in their natural state, are as thick as a wheat straw, and they are placed so thick about the tops and extremities of the stalks, that they enfold, embrace, and lie over one another; and from the middle of these clusters of leaves, and indeed from the woody substance of the plant itself, there arise several other very long, flat, smooth, and brittle leaves. These are usually four from each tuft of the other leaves; and they have ever a common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a>, which is membranaceous and very thin. This is the style of the plant, and the *pila marina* appears to be a cluster of the fibres of the leaves of this plant, which cover the whole stalk, divided into their constituent fibres; and by the motion of the waves first broken and worn into short threads, and afterwards wound up together into a roundish or lengthened ball. **Pila**, was a ball made in a different manner according to the different games in which it was to be used. Playing at ball was very common amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a>, and was looked upon as a manly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, which contributed both to amusement and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The pila was of four sorts: 1st, *Follis* or balloon; 2d, *Pila Trigonalis*; 3d, *Pila Paganica*; 4th, *Harpagium*. All these come under the general name of pila. For the manner of playing with each of them, see the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> FOLLIS, TRIGONALIS.

PILASTER

Pages 164-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. See there, No 50, &c. **Pilate**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pontius Pilate, was governor of Judea when our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> was crucified. Of his family or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> we know but little, though it is believed that he was of Rome, or at least of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. He was sent to govern Judea in the room of Gratius, in the year 26 or 27 of the vulgar era, and governed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> for ten years, from the 12th or 13th year of Tiberius to the 22d or 23d. He is represented both by Philo and Josephus as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an impetuous and obstinate temper, and as a judge who used to sell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and to pronounce any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> that was desired, provided he was paid for it. The same authors make mention of his rapines, his injuries, his murders, the torments that he inflicted upon the innocent, and the persons he put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> without any form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. Philo, in particular, describes him as a man that exercised an excessive cruelty during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, who disturbed the repose of Judea, and gave occasion to the troubles and revolt that followed after. St Luke (xiii. 1, 2, &c.) acquaints us, that Pilate had mingled the blood of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALILEANS">Galileans</a> with their sacrifices; and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> having been related to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, he said, "Think you that these Galileans were greater sinners than other Galileans, because they suffered this calamity. I tell you nay; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you do not repent, you shall all perish in like manner." It is unknown upon what occasion Pilate caused these Galileans to be slain in the temple while they were sacrificing; for this is the meaning of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of mingling their blood with their sacrifices. Some think they were disciples of Judas the Gaulonite, who taught that the Jews ought not to pay tribute to foreign princes; and that Pilate had put some of them to death even in the temple; but there is no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this fact. Others think that these Galileans were <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">Samaritans</a>, whom Pilate cut to pieces in the village of Tirataba, as they were preparing to go up to Mount Gerizim, where a certain Antig. lib. impolior had promised to discover treasures to them; but this event did not happen before the year 35 of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> era, and consequently two years after the death of Jesus Christ. At the time of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, Pilate made some endeavours to deliver him out of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Jews. He knew they had delivered him up, and purified his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> with so much violence, only out of malice and envy (Matt. xxvii. 18.). His wife also, who had been disturbed the night before with frightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, sent to tell him she desired him not to meddle in the affair of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> person (ib. 19.). He attempted to appease the wrath of the Jews, and to give them some satisfaction, by whipping Jesus Christ (John xix. 1. Matt. xxvii. 26.). He tried to take him out of their hands, by proposing to deliver him or Barabbas, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the festival of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>. Lastly, he had a mind to discharge himself from pronouncing judgement against him, by sending him to Herod <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Galilee (Luke xxiii. 7, 8.). When he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> all this would not satisfy the Jews, and that they even threatened him in some manner, saying he could be no friend to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> if he let him go (John xix. 12, 15.), he caused <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to be brought, washed his hands before all the people, and publicly declared himself innocent of the blood of that just person (Matt. xxvii. 23, 24.); yet at the same time he delivered him up to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, that they might crucify him. This was enough to justify Jesus Christ, as Calmet observes, and to show that he held him as innocent; but it was not enough to vindicate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> and integrity of a judge, whose duty it was as well to assert the cause of oppressed innocence as to punish the guilty and criminal. He ordered to be put over our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, as it were, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of his sentence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> (John xix. 9.), Jesus of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAZARETH">Nazareth</a>, king of the Jews, which was written in Latin, Greek, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>. Some of the Jews found fault with it, and remonstrated to Pilate that he ought to have written Jesus of Nazareth, who pretended to be king of the Jews. But Pilate could not be prevailed with to alter it, and gave them this peremptory answer, That what he had written he had written. Towards evening, he was applied to for leave to take <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the bodies from the cross, that they might not continue there the following day, which was the passover and the Sabbath-day (John xix. 31.). This he allowed, and granted the body of Jesus to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> of Arimathea, that he might pay his last duties to it, (ib. 33.). Lastly, when the priests, who had solicited the death of our Saviour, came to desire him to set a watch about the sepulchre, for fear his disciples should steal him away by night, he answered them, that they had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and might <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them there themselves (Matt. xxvii. 65.). This is the substance of what the gospel tells us concerning Pilate. <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-JUSTIN_MARTYR">Justin <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>, Tertullian, Eusebius, and after them several others both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, assure us, that it was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for Roman magistrates to prepare copies of all verbal proceedings and judicial acts which they passed in their several provinces, and to send them to the emperor. And Pilate, in compliance to this custom, having sent word to Tiberius of what had passed relating to Jesus Christ, the emperor wrote an account of it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, in a manner that gave reason to judge that he thought favourably of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Jesus Christ, and showed that he should be willing they would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> divine honours to him. But the senate was not of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and so the matter was dropped. It appears by what Justin says of these acts, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of Jesus Christ were mentioned there, and even that the soldiers had divided his garments among them. Eusebius intimates that they spoke of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> and ascension. Tertullian and Justin refer to these acts with so much confidence as would make one believe they had them in their hands. However, neither Eusebius nor St Jerome, who were both inquisitive, understanding persons, nor any other author that wrote afterwards, seem to have seen them, at least not the true and original acts; for as to what we have now in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, they are not authentic, being neither ancient nor uniform. There are also some pretended letters of Pilate to Tiberius, giving a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of our Saviour, but they are universally allowed to be spurious. Pilate being a man that, by his excessive cruelties and rapine, had disturbed the peace of Judea during the whole time of his government, was at length deposed by Vitellius the proconsul of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in the 36th year of Jesus Christ, and sent to Rome to give an account of his conduct to the emperor. But though Tiberius died before Pilate arrived at Rome, yet his successor Caligula banished him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, where he was reduced to such extremity that he killed himself with his own hands. The evangelists call him governor, though in reality he was no more than procurator of Judea, not only because governor was a name of general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, but because Pilate in effect acted as one, by taking upon him to judge in criminal matters; as his predecessors had done, and other procurators in the small provinces of the empire where there was no proconsul, constantly did. See Calmet's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, Eckhard's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Dictionary, and Beaupré's Annotations. With regard to Pilate's wife, the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> is, that she was named Claudia Procula or Procula; and in relation to her dream, some are of opinion that she had intelligence of our Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, and knew by his character that he was a righteous person; her imagination, being struck with these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, did naturally produce the dream we read of; but others think that this dream was sent providentially upon her, for the clearer manifestation of our Lord's innocence.

PILATRE DU ROZIER

Pages 165-165

French, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1756. He was first apprentice to an apothecary there, and afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in quest of farther improvement. He applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and had already acquired some reputation, when the discovery of M. de Montgolfier had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> astonished the learned world. On the 25th of October 1783, he attempted an aerial voyage with the Marquis d'Arlande. He performed several other excursions in this way with brilliant success, in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family of France, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. He then resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into England by means of his aerial vehicle, and for that purpose he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>, whence he rose about 7 o'clock in the morning of the 1st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1785; but in half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after he set out, the balloon took fire, and the aeronaut, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> M. Romaine, were crushed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of that machine, which was more ingenious, perhaps, than useless*. Pilatre's social virtues *See Aerostation, the regret of his friends for his loss. His merit as a chemist, and his experiments as an aeronaut, procured him some pecuniary reward, and some public appointments. He had a pension from the king, was intendant of Monseigneur's cabinets of natural philosophy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, and natural history, professor of natural philosophy, a member of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of Monseigneur's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>.

PILCHARD

Pages 165-166

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a fish which has a general resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, but differs in some essential particulars. The body of the pilchard is less compressed than that of the herring, being thicker and rounder: the nose is shorter in proportion, and turns up; the under jaw is shorter. The back is more elevated; the belly less sharp. The dorsal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a> of the pilchard is placed exactly in the centre of gravity, so that when taken up by it, the body preserves an equilibrium, whereas that of the herring dips at the head. The scales of the pilchard adhere very closely, whereas those of the herring very easily drop off. The pilchard is in general less than the herring; but it is fatter, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more full of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The pilchard appears in vast shoals off the Cornish coasts about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, disappearing the beginning of winter, yet sometimes a few return again after Christmas. Their winter retreat is the same with that of the herring, and their motives for migrating the same. They affect, during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, a warmer latitude; for they are not found in any quantities on any of our coasts except those of Cornwall, that is to say, from Fowey harbour to the Scilly isles, between which places the shoals keep shifting for some weeks. The approach of the pilchard is known by much the same signs as those that indicate the arrival of the herring. Persons, called in Cornwall hurrs, are placed on the cliffs, to point to the boats stationed off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> the course of the fish. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a> of James I. c. 23, fishermen are empowered to go on the grounds of others to hue, without being liable to actions of trespass, which before occasioned frequent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits. The emoluments that accrue to the inhabitants of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and are best expressed in the words of Dr W. Borlase, in his Account of the Pilchard Fishery. "It employs a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, training them thereby to naval affairs; employs men, women, and children, at land, in salting, pressing, washing, and cleaning, in making boats, nets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, casks, and all the trades depending on their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> is fed with the offal of the captures; the land with the refuse of the fish and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; the merchant finds the gains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; the fisherman, the gains of the fish. Ships are often freighted hither with salt, and into foreign countries with the fish, carrying off at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our tin. The usual number of hogheads of fish exported each year, for ten years, from 1747 to 1756 inclusive, from the four ports of Fowey, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, and St Ives, in all amounts to 29,794; since it appears that Fowey has exported yearly 1732 hogheads; Falmouth, 14,631 hogheads and two-thirds; Penzance and Mounts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, 12,140 hogheads and one-third; St Ives, 1282 hogheads. Every hoghead for ten years last past, together with the bounty allowed for each when exported, and the oil made out of each, has amounted, one year with another at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, to the price of £1. 13s. 3d.; so that the cash paid for pilchards exported has, at a medium, annually amounted to the sum of £49,552.10s." The numbers that are taken at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out of the nets is amazingly great. Mr Pennant says, that Dr Borlase assured him, that on the 5th of October 1767, there were at one time inclosed in St Ives's bay 7000 hogheads, each hoghead containing 35,000 fish, in all 245,000,000.

PILE

Pages 166-166

among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> built of wood, whereon were laid the bodies of the deceased to be burnt. It was partly in the form of an altar, and differed in height according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the person to be consumed. Probably it might originally be considered as an altar, on which the dead were consumed as a burnt offering to the internal deities. The trees made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in the erection of a funeral pile were such as abounded in pitch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rosin, as being most combustible; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they used any other wood, it was split that it might the more easily catch fire. Round the pile were placed cypress boughs to hinder the noisome smell.

PILES

Pages 169-169

in Medicine, the same with haemorrhoids. See MEDICINE, No. 249, &c.

PILEUS

Pages 169-169

in Roman antiquity, was the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hat worn at public shows and sacrifices, and by the freedmen. It was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rewards assigned to such gladiators as were slaves, in token of their obtaining freedom.

PILEWORT

Pages 169-169

the root. This is a very small plant, found in moist meadows and by hedge sides. The roots consist of slender fibres with some little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> among them, which are supposed to resemble the haemorrhoids. From thence it has been concluded, that this root must needs be of wonderful efficacy for the cure of that distemper: to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, it is little other than mucilaginous; and although still retained in several of the foreign pharmacopoeias, it is hardly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

PILGRIM

Pages 169-169

one who travels through foreign countries to visit holy places, and to pay his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the relics of dead saints. See PILGRIMAGE. The word is formed from the Flemish pelgrim, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Italian pellegrino, which signifies the same; and those originally from the Latin peregrinus, a "stranger or traveller."

PILGRIMAGE

Pages 169-170

a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, which consists in taking a journey to some holy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in order to adore the relics of some deceased saint. Pilgrimages began to be made about the middle ages of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but they were most in vogue after the end of the 11th century, when every one was for visiting places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, not excepting kings and princes themselves; and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> made no difficulty of being absent from their churches on the same account. The places most visited were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a> (A), and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>; but the greatest numbers now --- (A) It deserves to be remarked here, that in the year 1428, under the reign of Henry VI., abundance of licences were granted from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England to captains of English ships, for carrying numbers of devout persons to the shrine of St James of Compostella in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; provided, however, that those pilgrims should first take an oath not PIL Pilgrimage refers to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORETTO">Loretto</a>, in order to visit the chamber of the blest virgin, in which she was born, and brought up her son <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> till he was 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. For the pilgrimage of the followers of Mahomet, see Mahometanism. In every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPERY">popery</a> was established, pilgrimages were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; and in those countries which are still papish, they continue. In England, the shrine of St Thomas à Becket was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the pious; and in Scotland, St Andrews; where, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> informs us, was deposited a leg of the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> they still continue; for, from the beginning of May till the middle of August every year, crowds of papish penitents from all parts of that country resort to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near the centre of Lough-foo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Lake, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DONEGAL">Donegal</a>, to the amount of 3000 or 4000. These are mostly of the poorer sort, and many of them are proxies for those who are richer; some of which, however, together with some of the priests and bishops on occasion, make their appearance there. When the pilgrim comes within sight of the holy lake, he must uncover his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, and thus walk to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-side, and is taken to the island for inspection. Here there are two chapels and 15 other houses; to which are added <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFESSIONAL">confessional</a>, so contrived, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> cannot see the person confessing. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a> varies according to the circumstances of the penitent; during the continuance of which (which is sometimes three, six, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days) he subsists on oatmeal, sometimes made into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. He traverses sharp <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> on his bare <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> or feet, and goes through a variety of other forms, paying inspection at every different confession. When all is over, the priest bores a gimblet-hole through the pilgrim's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> near the top, in which he fastens a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> peg; gives him as many holy pebbles out of the lake as he cares to carry away, for amulets to be presented to his friends, and so disposes him, an object of veneration to all other papists not thus initiated, who no sooner see the pilgrim's cross in his hands, than they kneel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to get his blessing. There are, however, other parts of Ireland sacred to extraordinary worship and pilgrimage; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and miraculous cures, &c., produced by them, is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. That such things should exist in this enlightened age, and in a Protestant country, is indeed strange; but our wonder ceases, when we reflect that it is among the lowest; and perhaps the worst of the people. They who carry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, and place that confidence in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> which belongs only to the spirit of it, are seldom distinguished either for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> or their virtue. We do not deny, however, that they who carry matters to the other extreme, may be equally destitute of real knowledge and genuine morality. Dr Johnson, in his Rasselas, gives us some observations on pilgrimage, which are so much to the purpose, that we think we cannot do better than lay them before our readers. "Pilgrimage (said Imalac, into whose mouth the observations are put), like many other acts of piety, may be reasonable or superstitious according to the principles upon which it is performed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> journeys in search of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> are not commanded. Truth, such as is necessary to the regulation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, is always found where it is honestly sought: change of place is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> cause of the increase of piety, for it inevitably produces dissipation of mind. Yet since men go every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to view the fields where great actions have been performed, and return with stronger impressions of the event, curiosity of the same kind may naturally dispose us to view that country whence our religion had its beginning: and I believe no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> surveys those awful scenes without some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of holy resolutions. That the Supreme Being may be more easily propitiated in one place than in another, is the dream of idle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; but that some places may operate upon our own minds in an uncommon manner, is an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which hourly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> justify. He who supposes that his vices may be more successfully combated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, will, perhaps, find himself mistaken; yet he may go thither without folly: he who thinks they will be more freely pardoned, dishonours at once his reason and religion."

PILKINGTON

Pages 170-170

Letitia, a famous poetical genius, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Dr Van Lewin, a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, where she was born in 1712. She was married very young to the Rev. Matthew Pilkington, a poet also of no inconsiderable merit; and the two wits, as is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, lived very unhappily together. They were at length totally separated, on the husband accidentally discovering a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in her bedchamber at two o'clock in the morning; a circumstance which she accounted for in a very unsatisfactory manner. The story is told at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>; where she says, "Lovers of learning, I am sure, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> me, as I solemnly declare it was the attractive charms of a new book, which the gentleman would not lend me, but consented to stay till I read it through, that was the sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of my detaining him." As there are not wanting some who form objections to marrying learned wives, the chance of such literary affinities may perhaps be added to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of them. After this unlucky adventure, Mrs Pilkington came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and having recourse to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> for subsistence, through the means of Colley Cibber, she lived for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on the contributions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. She was however thrown into the Marshalsea for debt; and being set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, opened a pamphlet shop. She raised at length a handsome subscription for her Memoirs; which are written with great sprightliness and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, containing several entertaining anecdotes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift, with whom she was intimate, as well as many pretty little pieces of her own <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. This ingenious woman is said at last to have killed herself with drinking. She died at Dublin, in 1750.

PILLAR

Pages 171-171

in the manège, is the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> manege-ground, round which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> turns, whether there be a pillar in it or not. Besides this, there are pillars on the circumference or sides of the manege-ground, placed at certain distances, by two and two, from whence they are called the two pillars, to distinguish them from that of the centre. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the pillar in the centre is for regulating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, that the manege upon the volts may be performed with method and justness, and that they may <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, by rule and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, upon the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of the volts; and also to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> unruly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-metelled horses, without endangering the rider. The two pillars are placed at the distance of two or three paces one from the other; and the horse is put between those, to teach him to ride before and yerk out behind, and put himself upon raised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, &c., either by the aids or chastisements. Pompey's PILLAR. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>.

PILLARS

Pages 171-171

in antiquarian topography, are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> single <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> set up perpendicularly. Those of them which are found in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> have been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>; but as they are the most simple of all monuments, they are unquestionably more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> than druidism itself. They were placed as memorials recording different events; such as remarkable instances of God's mercies, contracts, singular victories, boundaries, and sometimes sepulchres. Various instances of these monuments erected by the patriarchs occur in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>: such was that raised by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> at Luz, afterwards by him named <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a>; such also was the pillar placed by him over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> of Rachel. They were likewise marks of exorcitations and magical talismans. These stones, from having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been considered as objects of veneration, at length were by the ignorant and superstitious idolatrously worshipped; therefore, after the introduction of Christianity, some had crosses cut on them, which was considered as sanctifying them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. Vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of a later <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> has led the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people to consider them as persons transformed into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of some crime, generally that of Sabbath-breaking; but this tale is not confined to single stones, but is told also of whole circles: witness the monuments called the hurlers in Cornwall, and Rollorick Stones in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>. The first are by the vulgar supposed to have been men once, and thus transformed as a punishment for playing on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> called hurling; the latter, a pagan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILTON">Wilton</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> has a very magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, there is a pillar of one piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, which was brought from the temple of Venus Genetrix at Rome, near 14 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and 22 inches diameter, with an inscription to Ashtarte <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Venus.

PILLORE

Pages 171-171

is an engine made of wood to punish offenders, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> them to public view, and rendering them infamous. There is a statute of the pillory, 51 Hen. III. And by statute it is appointed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>, foretellers, and those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> false weights, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, forgery, &c. 3 Inst. 219. Lords of leets are to have a pillory and tumbrel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the cause of forfeiture of the leet; and a village may be bound by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> to provide a pillory, &c. 2 Hawk. P. C. 73.

PILOT

Pages 171-172

the officer who superintends the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, either upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> on the main ocean. It is, however, more particularly applied by our mariners to the person <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a ship's course on or near the sea-coast, and into the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, bays, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, havens, &c., within his respective district. Pilots of ships, taking upon them to conduct any ship from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, &c., to any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> up the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, are to be first examined and approved by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and wardens of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, &c., or shall forfeit 10l. for the first offence, 20l. for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and 40l. for every other offence; one moiety to the informer, the other to the master and wardens; but any master or mate of a ship may pilot his own vessel up the river: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any ship be lost through the negligence of any pilot, he shall be for ever after disallowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a pilot. 3 Geo. I. c. 13. Also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-warden of the cinque ports may make rules for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of pilots, and order a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to ply at sea to conduct ships up to the Thames: 7 Geo. I. c. 21. No person shall act as a pilot on the Thames, &c. (except in collier ships) without a licence from the master and wardens of Trinity House at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, on pain of forfeiting 20l. And pilots are to be subject to the government of that corporation; and pay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dues, not exceeding 1s. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> thereof. Stat. 5 Geo. II. c. 20. By the former laws of France, no person could be received as pilot till he had made several voyages and passed a strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>; and after that, on his return in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages, he was obliged to lodge a copy of his journal in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>; and if a pilot occasioned the loss of a ship, he had to pay 100 livres fine, and to be for ever deprived of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of pilotage; and if he did so designedly, be punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Lex Mercat. 79, 71. The laws of Oleron ordain, That if any pilot designedly misguide a ship, that it may be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> away, he shall be put to a rigorous death, and hung in chains: and if the lord of a place, where a ship be thus lost, abet such villains in order to have a share of the wreck, he shall be apprehended, and all his goods forfeited for the satisfaction of the persons suffering; and his person shall be fastened to a stake in the midst of his own mansion, which, being fired on the four corners, shall be burned to the ground, and he with it. Leg. Ol. c. 25. And if the fault of a pilot be so notorious, that the ship's crew see an apparent wreck, they may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>, and strike off his head; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> denies this hasty execution: an ignorant pilot is sentenced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> thrice under the ship's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> by the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. Lex Mercat. 70.
