The regulations with regard to pilots in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> are as follow: "The commanders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s ships, in order to give all reasonable encouragement to so useful a body of men as pilots, and to remove all their ob- jections to his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, are strictly charged to treat them with good usage, and an equal respect with warrant-officers. "The purser of the ship is always to have a set of bedding provided on board for the pilots; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> is to order the boatswain to supply them with hammocks, and a convenient place to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in, near their duty, and apart from the common men; which bedding and hammocks are to be returned when the pilots leave the ship. "A pilot, when conducting one of his majesty's ships in pilot-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, shall have the sole <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> and command of the ship, and may give orders for steering, setting, trimming, or furling the sails; tacking the ship; or whatever concerns the navigation: and the captain is to take care that all the officers and crew obey his orders. But the captain is diligently to observe the conduct of the pilot; and if he judges him to behave so ill as to bring the ship into danger, he may remove him from the command and charge of the ship, and take such methods for her preservation as shall be judged necessary; remarking upon the log book, the exact <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the pilot was removed from his office, and the reasons assigned for it. "Captains of the king's ships, employing pilots in foreign parts of his majesty's dominions, shall, after performance of the service, give a certificate thereof to the pilot, which being produced to the proper naval officer, he shall cause the same to be immediately paid; but if there be no naval-officer there, the captain of his majesty's ship shall pay him, and send the proper vouchers, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, to the navy-board, in order to be paid as bills of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. "Captains of his majesty's ships, employing foreign pilots to carry the ships they command into or out of foreign ports, shall pay them the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> due by the establishment or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, before they discharge them: whose receipts being duly vouched, and sent, with a certificate of the service performed, to the navy-board, they shall cause them to be paid with the same exactness as they do bills of exchange." Regulations and Instructions of the Sea Service, &c. PILOT-FISH. See Gasterosteus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Ofsec tells us, that they are shaped like those mackerels which have a transverse line upon the body. "Sailors (continues he) give them the name of pilots, because they closely follow the dog-fish, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> shoals round it on all sides. It is thought that they point out some prey to the dog-fish. They are not only not touched, but also preferred by it against all their enemies. It likewise follows the shark, apparently for the purpose of devouring the remains of its prey. It is pretended that it acts as its pilot. The manner in which it attends the shark, according to M. Daubenton, may have given rise to this name. It is said to swim at the height of a foot and a half from the snout of this voracious animal, to follow and imitate all its movements, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its prey which the shark allows to escape, and which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUOY">buoy</a> up towards the surface of the water. When the shark, which has its mouth below, turns to seize any fish, the pilot-fish starts away; but as soon as the shark resumes his ordinary position, it returns to its former place. It is said, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> those fishes follow ships for the sake of the offal and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> excrements; and hence the Dutch give them the name of dungen-fish. It is remarkable, that though so small they can keep pace with ships in their swiftest course.

PILTON

Pages 172-172

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, which lies in Courland properly so called, derives its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Pilton, built by Valdemar II., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> about the year 1220, when he founded a bishop's see in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for the more effectual conversion of its Pagan inhabitants. This district afterwards successively belonged to the Germans, then again to the king of Denmark, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Courland, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; and by virtue of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of regency drawn up for this district in the year 1717, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is lodged in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Polish senators or councillors, from whom an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> lies to the king. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMOGITIA">Samogitia</a> also styles himself bishop of Pilton. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this district is the promontory of Domeinfs, which projects northward into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. From this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a>, a sand-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> runs four German miles farther into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, half of which lies under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and cannot be discerned. To the east of this promontory is an unfathomable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>, which is never observed to be agitated. For the safety of vessels bound to Livonia, two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> beacons have been erected on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, near Domeinfs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, opposite to the sand bank, and facing each other. One of these is twelve fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the other eight; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fire is kept <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> on them from the first of August to the first of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>. When the mariners see these fires appear as one in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line, they may conclude that they are clear of the extremity of the sand bank, and consequently out of danger; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they see both beacons, they are in danger of running upon it. The district of Pilton contains seven parishes, but no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> worthy of notice. The inhabitants are chiefly of the Lutheran persuasion.

PILUM

Pages 172-172

a missile weapon used by the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> darted upon the enemy. Its point, we are told by Polybius, was so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and small, that after the first discharge it was generally so bent as to be rendered useless. The legionary soldiers made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the pilum, and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> carried two. The pilum underwent many alterations and improvements, inasmuch that it is impossible with any precision to describe it. Julius Scaliger laboured much to give an accurate account of it, and would have effected success on this head amongst the greatest blessings of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. This weapon appears, however, to have been sometimes round, but most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, to have been two cubits long in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, and to have had an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> point of the same length hooked and jagged at the end. Marius made a material improvement in it; for during the Cimbrian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, he so contrived it, that when it stuck in the enemy's shield it should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> where the wood was connected with the iron, and thus become useless to the person who received it.

PIMENTO

Pages 172-173

PIEMENTO, Jamaica <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Allspice, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRTUS">myrtus</a>. See Myrtus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. "The pimento trees grow spontaneously, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance, in many parts of Jamaica, but more particularly on hilly situations near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the northern side of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; where they form the..." PIM most delicious groves that can possibly be imagined; filling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with fragrance, and giving reality, though in a very distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the globe, to our great poet's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of those balmy gales which convey to the delighted voyager 'Sabean odours from the spicy shore Of Araby the blest. Chear'd with the grateful smell, old ocean smiles.' This tree is purely a child of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and seems to mock all the labours of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in his endeavours to extend or improve its growth: not one attempt in fifty to propagate the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, or to raise them from the seeds, in parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where it is not found growing spontaneously, having succeeded. The usual method of forming a new pimento plantation (in Jamaica it is called a walk) is nothing more than to appropriate a piece of woodland, in the neighbourhood of a plantation already existing, or in a country where the scattered trees are found in a native state, the woods of which being fallen, the trees are suffered to remain on the ground till they become rotten and perish. In the course of twelve months after the first season, abundance of young pimento plants <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found growing vigorously in all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, being without doubt produced from ripe berries scattered there by the birds, while the fallen trees, &c., afford them both shelter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. At the end of two years it will be proper to give the land a thorough cleaning, leaving such only of the pimento trees as have a good appearance, which will then soon form such groves as those I have described, and, except perhaps for the first four or five years, require very little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> afterwards. Soon after the trees are in blossom, the berries become fit for gathering; the fruit not being suffered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> on the tree, as the pulp in that state, being moist and glutinous, is difficult to cure, and when dry becomes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and tasteless. It is impossible, however, to prevent some of the ripe berries from mixing with the refuse; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the proportion of them be great, the price of the commodity is considerably injured. It is gathered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; one labourer on the tree, employed in gathering the small branches, will give employment to three below (who are generally women and children) in picking the berries; and an industrious picker will fill a bag of 70 lbs. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The returns from a pimento walk in a favourable season are prodigious. A single tree has been known to yield 150 lbs. of the raw fruit, or one cwt. of the dried spice; there being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of one third in curing; but this, like many other of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> productions, is exceedingly uncertain, and perhaps a very plentiful crop occurs but once in five years."

PIMPINELLA

Pages 173-173

Burnet Saxifrage; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Pimple, in Medicine, a small pustule arising on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>. By mixing equal quantities of the juice of horseradish (Cedum minus), passed through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and of spirit of wine rectified by itself, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> coagulum of a very volatile <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is formed, which Dr Bughart commends for curing pimples of the face; and says, that the thin liquor separated from it with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDY">candy</a> is an excellent remedy for thick viscid phlegm in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>.

PIN

Pages 173-173

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a little necessary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>-wire, chiefly used by women in fastening and adjusting their dress. In the year 1543, by statute 34 and 35 of Henry VIII, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6, it was enacted, "That no person shall put to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> any pinnes but only such as shall be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>-headed, and have the heads foldered fast to the flank of the pins, well smoothened, the flank well-flapen, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> well and round filed, cauted, and sharpened." From the above extract it should appear that the art of pin-making was but of late <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, probably introduced from France; and that our manufactories since that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> have wonderfully improved. Though pins are apparently simple, their manufacture is, however, not a little curious and complex. We shall therefore give our readers an account of it from Ellis's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. When the brass-wire, of which the pins are formed, is first received at the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>, it is generally too thick for the purpose of being cut into pins. The first operation therefore is that of winding it off from one wheel to another with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> velocity, and causing it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between the two, through a circle in a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> of smaller diameter: the wire, being thus reduced to its proper dimensions, is strained by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it between iron pins fixed in a board in a zig-zag manner, but so as to leave a straight line between them: afterwards it is cut into lengths of three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four yards, and then into smaller ones, every length being sufficient to make six pins; each end of these is ground to a point, which was performed when I viewed the factory by boys who sat each with two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> before him, turned by a wheel. Taking up a handful, he applies the ends to the coarsest of the two stones, being careful at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to keep each piece moving round between his fingers, so that the points may not become flat: he then gives them a smoother and sharper point, by applying them to the other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and by that means a lad of 12 or 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> is enabled to point about 16,000 pins in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. When the wire is thus pointed, a pin is taken off from each end, and this is repeated till it is cut into six pieces. The next operation is that of forming the heads, or, as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, head-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>; which is done by means of a spinning-wheel, one piece of wire being thus with astonishing rapidity wound round another, and the interior one being drawn out, leaves a hollow tube between the circumvolutions: it is then cut with shears; every two circumvolutions or turns of the wire forming one head; these are softened by throwing them into iron pans, and placing them in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> till they are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot. As soon as they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, they are distributed to children, who fit with anvils and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a> before them, which they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with their feet, by means of a lathe, and taking up one of the lengths, they thrust the blunt end into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the heads which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> before them, and catching one at the extremity, they apply them immediately to the anvil and hammer, and by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or two of the foot, the point and the head are fixed together in much less time than it can be described, and with a dexterity only to be acquired by practice; the spectator being in continual <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>.

PINACIA

Pages 173-174

among the Athenians, were tablets of brafs <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with the names of all those citizens in each tribe who were duly qualified and willing to be judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">Areopagus</a>. These tablets were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into a vessel provided for the purpose, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of beans, a hundred being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and all the rest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, were thrown into another. Then the names of the candidates and the beans were drawn out one by one, and they whose names were drawn out together with the white beans were elected judges <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> senators. In Solon's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> there were only four tribes, each of which chose 100 senators; but the number of tribes afterwards increasing, the number of senators and judges increased to so many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> more.

PINANG

Pages 174-174

the Chinese name of the Areca catechu Lin. See Areca, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PINCHEBECK

Pages 174-174

a factitious metallic substance, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an alloy of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> three parts, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, four. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PINDAR

Pages 174-175

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of lyric poets, was born at Thebes, about 520 years B.C. He received his first musical instructions from his father, who was a flutist-player by profession; after which, according to Suidas, he was placed under Myrtilis, a lady of distinguished abilities in lyric <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. It was during this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> that he became acquainted with the poetess Corinna, who was likewise a student under Myrtilis. Plutarch tells us, that Pindar profited from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> which Corinna, more advanced in her studies, gave him at this school. It is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to suppose, that the first poetical effusions of a genius so full of fire and imagination as that of Pindar would be wild and luxuriant; and Lucian has preserved five verses, said to have been the exordium of his first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>; in which he crowded almost all the subjects for song which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> then furnished. Upon communicating this attempt to Corinna, she told him smiling, that he should fow with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and not empty his whole flask at once. Pindar, however, soon quitted Pindar, the leading strings of these ladies, his poetical nurture, and became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a>, now arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>: after which he soon surpassed all his masters, and acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation over all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; but, like a true prophet, he was less honoured in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than elsewhere; for at Thebes he was frequently pronounced to be vanquished, in the musical and poetical contests, by candidates of inferior merit. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of having these public trials of skill in all the great cities of Greece was now so prevalent, that but little fame was to be acquired by a musician <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poet any other way than by entering the lists; and we find, that both Myrtilis and Corinna publicly disputed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> with him at Thebes. He obtained a victory over Myrtilis, but was vanquished five different times by Corinna. The judges, upon occasions like these, have been frequently accused of partiality or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, not only by the vanquished, but by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the merit of Pindar was pronounced inferior to that of Corinna five several times, it was, says Pausanias, because the judges were more sensible to the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> than to those of music and poetry (a). Was it not strange, said the Scythian Anacharsis, that the Grecian artists were never judged by artists, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>? Pindar, before he quitted Thebes, had the vexation to see his Dithyrambics traduced, abused, and turned into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>, by the comic poets of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and Athenaeus tells us, that he was feverishly censured by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> lyrics, for being a lipogrammatist, and composing an ode from which he had excommunicated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> S. Whether these censures proceeded from envy or contempt cannot now be determined; but they were certainly useful to Pindar, and it was necessary that he should be lauded for such puerilities. Thebes seems to have been the purgatory of our young bard: when he quitted that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, as his judgement was matured, he avoided most of the errors for which he had been chastised, and suddenly became the wonder and delight of all Greece. Every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, prince, and potentate, deafuous of lasting fame, courted the muse of Pindar. He seems frequently to have been present at the four great festivals, of the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games, as may be inferred from several circumstances and expressions in the odes which he composed for the victors in them all. Those at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, who were ambitious of having their achievements celebrated by Pindar, applied to him for an ode, which was first sung in the Prytaneum or town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of Olympia, where there was a banqueting-room, set apart for the entertainment of the conquerors. Here the ode was rehearsed by a chorus, accompanied by instruments. It was afterwards performed in the same manner at the triumphal entry of the victor into his own country, in processions, or at the sacrifices that were made with great pomp and solemnity on the occasion. (a) Pausanias says, that Corinna was one of the most beautiful women of her time, as he judged by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of her which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> at Tanagris at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the public exercises were performed. She was represented with her head ornamented by a ribbon, as a memorial of the victories she had obtained over Pindar at Thebes. Pindar, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Isthmian ode, has apologized for the mercenary custom among poets, of receiving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for their compositions. "The world (says he) is grown interested, and thinks in general with the Spartan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> Aristostratus, that money only makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>: a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which this sage himself experienced, having with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> lost all his friends." It is supposed that Pindar here alludes to the avarice of Simonides, who first allowed his muse to sell her favours to the highest bidder. There is no great poet in antiquity whose moral character has been less censured than that of Pindar. Plutarch has preferred a single <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of his Epicedium or Dirge that was sung at his funeral; which, short and simple as it is, implies great praise: This man was pleasing to strangers, and dear to his fellow-citizens. His works abound with precepts of the purest morality: and it does not appear that he ever traduced even his enemies; comforting himself, for their malignity, by a maxim which he inserted in his first Pythic, and which afterwards became proverbial, That it is better to be envied than pitied. Paulanias says, that the character of poet was truly consecrated, in the person of Pindar, by the god of verse himself; who was pleased, by an express oracle, to order the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> to set apart for Pindar one half of the first-fruit offerings brought by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> to his shrine, and to allow him a conspicuous place in his temple, where, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, he used to sit and sing his hymns in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of that god. This chair was remaining in the time of Paulanias, several centuries after, and shown to him as a relic not unworthy of the sanctity and magnificence of that place. But though Pindar's muse was patronized at Delphi, and well paid by princes and potentates elsewhere, she seems, however, sometimes to have sung the spontaneous strains of pure friendship. Of this kind were, probably, the verses bestowed upon the musician <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, who had twice obtained the palm of victory by his performance on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> at the Pythic games (b). It is in his 12th Pythic ode that Pindar celebrates the victory of Midas over all Greece, upon that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> herself had invented (c). Fabricius tells us, that Pindar lived to the age of 90; and, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Dr Blair, he died 435 years B.C. aged 86. His fellow citizens erected a monument to him in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPODROME">Hippodrome</a> at Thebes, which was still subsisting in the time of Paulanias; and his renown was so great after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, that his posterity derived very considerable honours and privileges from it. When Alexander the Great attacked the city of Thebes, he gave express orders to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to spare the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and family of Pindar. The Lacedemonians had done the same before this period; for when they ravaged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a> and burned the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, the following words were written upon the door of the poet: Forbear to burn this house, it was the dwelling of Pindar. Respect for the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this great poet <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, that, even in Plutarch's time, the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sacred victim at the Theoxenian festival was appropriated to his descendants.

PINDARIC ODE

Pages 175-175

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, an ode formed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the manner of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. See POETRY, no 136, &c.

PINDUS

Pages 175-175

a Doric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Aetolia, situated on the cognominal river, which falls into the Cephissus (Strabo).

PINEA

Pages 175-176
or **FIGNE**, in commerce, is a term used in Peru and Chili, for a kind of light, porous masses, or lumps, formed of a mixture of mercury and silver-dust from the mines. The ore, or mineral, of silver, when dug out of the veins of the mine, is first broken and then ground in mills for the purpose, driven by water with iron pestles, each of 200 pounds weight. The mineral, when thus pulverized, is next fitted, and then worked up with water into a paste; which, when half dry, is cut into pieces, called cuerpos, a foot long, weighing each about two thousand five hundred pounds. Each piece or cuerpo is again kneaded up with sea-salt, which, dissolving, incorporates with it. They then add mercury, from 10 to 20 pounds for each cuerpo, kneading the paste afresh until the mercury be incorporated therewith. This office, which is exceedingly dangerous on account of the noxious qualities of the mercury, is always made the lot of the poor Indians. This amalgamation is continued for eight or nine days; and some add lime, lead, or tin ore, &c. to forward it; and, in some mines, they are obliged to use fire. To try whether or no the mixture and amalgamation be sufficient, they wash a piece in water; and if the mercury be white, it is a proof that it has had its effect; if black, it must be still farther worked. --- (b) This Midas is a very different personage from his long-eared majesty of Phrygia, whose decision in favour of Pan had given such offence to Apollo; as is manifest, indeed, from his having been contemporary with Pindar. (c) The most extraordinary part of this musician's performance that can be gathered from the scholiast upon Pindar, was his finishing the solo, without a reed or mouth-piece, which broke accidentally while he was playing. The legendary account given by the poet in this ode, of the occasion upon which the flute was invented by Minerva, is diverting: "It was (says he) to imitate the howling of the Gorgons, and the hissing of their snakes, which the goddess had heard when the head of Medusa (one of these three anti-graces) was cut off by Perseus." When finished, it is sent to the lavatories, which are large basins that empty successively into one another. The palls, &c., being laid in the uppermost of these, the earth is then washed from it into the rest by a rivulet turned upon it; an Indian, all the while, stirring it with his feet, and two other Indians doing the like in the other basins. When the water runs quite clear out of the basins, the mercury and silver are found at bottom incorporated. This matter they call *pella*, and of this they form the pineas, by expressing as much of the mercury as they can; first, by putting it in woollen bags, and pressing and beating it strongly; then, by stamping it in a kind of wooden mould, of an octagonal form, at bottom whereof is a brass plate pierced full of little holes. The matter, when taken out of the mould, is laid on a trivet, under which is a large vessel full of water; and the whole being covered with an earthen head, a fire is made round it. The mercury still remains in the mass, and is thus reduced into fumes, and, at length condensing, it is precipitated into the water, leaving behind it a mass of silver grains of different figures, which, only joining or touching at the extremes, render the matter very porous and light. This, therefore, is the pinea, or pigne, which the workmen endeavour to sell secretly to vessels trading to the South Sea; and from which those, who have ventured to engage in so dangerous a commerce, have made such vast gains. Indeed the traders herein must be very careful; for the Spanish miners are arrant knaves, and to make the pignes weigh the more, they often fill the middle with sand or iron. **PINEAL GLAND.** See Brain, Anatomy Index.

PINEAU

Pages 176-176

GABRIEL DU,** a distinguished lawyer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGERS">Angers</a> in 1573. He went afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and pled with eclat before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. Upon his return to Angers, he became a counsellor in the prefidial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. He was consulted by all the neighbouring provinces, and had an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in all the great affairs of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> de Medicis conferred upon him the office of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of requests, and in her disgrace wished to support herself by his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> and counsels; but Du Pineau, always attentive to what he owed on the one hand to the mother of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and on the other to the king himself, never ceased to inspire that princess with sentiments of peace. In 1632 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. by way of reward, appointed him mayor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Angers; a situation in which he merited the flattering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Father of the People. He had no respect of persons; for he was equally accessible to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and the great. This worthy citizen died the 15th of October 1644, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 71. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was a kind of academy, where regular conferences were held, and attended by young officers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>, and other literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In these conferences every one freely stated the difficulties which occurred to him upon subjects either of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and when Pineau spoke, all was made clear; but he was always the last in delivering his sentiments, because he perceived that too much deference was paid to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. His writings are, 1. Latin notes, in addition to those of Du Moulin, upon the canon law, and printed along with the works of that eminent lawyer by the care of Francis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">Pinion</a>. 2. Commentaries, observations, and consultations, upon several important questions respecting the laws both of Anjou and of France, with some dissertations upon different subjects, &c., reprinted in 1725, in 2 vol. folio, by the care of Livoniere, who has enriched them with very useful remarks. The editor says, that "Du Pineau is a little inferior to the celebrated Du Moulin on the civil law, but that he is more accurate than the other upon the canon law."—Menage made these two verses upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>: *Pinellus peritit, Themidis pius ille sacerdos, In proprio judex limine perpetuus.*

PINEDA

Pages 176-176

JOHN,** a writer of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> of a noble family, and entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Jesuits in 1572. He taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> in several colleges; and devoted his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Holy Scriptures. That he might render that study the easier, he made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the oriental languages. We have of his writings, 1. Two volumes of Commentaries upon the book of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, in folio. 2. Two upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTES">Ecclesiastes</a>. 3. A General History of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, in Spanish, 4 vol. in folio. 4. A History of Ferdinand III. in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, in folio. He died in 1637, much regretted by the members of his society, and by the public in general.

PINELLI

Pages 176-178

JOHN VINCENT,** a distinguished literary character, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and was son of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Pinelli, a noble Genoese, who had settled in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and had acquired a handsome fortune in the way of trade. After receiving a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>, and repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where he took up his residence at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 24. Being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lover of science, he gave a preference to that city on account of its famous university, which brought to it a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of learned men. He had an excellent library, which consisted of a choice collection of books and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to enrich till the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. His literary correspondence, not only in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but through the most of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, procured him all the new works which were worthy of a place in his collection. The authors themselves were often forward to pay their respects to him. In many cities of Italy he had persons employed to search, at least once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, the stalls of those artificers who make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of old parchments, such as lute-makers, sievers, and others; and by this means he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> often to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> from destruction some valuable fragments. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for knowledge embraced all the sciences; but <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, medals, antiquities, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history, and particularly <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, were his favourite studies. He was consulted from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his acquaintance with the learned world was very great. He corresponded with Justus Lipsius, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger, Sigonius, Poffevin, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Pithou, and a great many others, who have all paid the highest compliments to his erudition. Indifferent to all the pleasures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and acquainted only with those of the mind, he had a great dislike to plays, entertainments, shows, and everything which most excites the curiosity of other men. During the space of 43 years that he lived at Padua, he was never known to be out of the city but twice; once on occasion of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> which infested it; and afterwards on a voyage to Naples, which he made at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitation of his friends. In short, Pinelli was generous, Pinguicula, Butterwort; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diandra class. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Pinguin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Penguin, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a genus of birds of the order anseres. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APTENODYTES">Aptenodytes</a>, Ornithology Index, or page 507. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">Pinion</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, an arbor, or spindle, in the body whereof are several notches, which catch the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a wheel that serves to turn it round; or it is a lesser wheel that plays in the teeth of a larger. Pink, a name given to a ship with a very narrow stern; whence all vessels, however small, whose stems are fashioned in this manner, are called pink-floored. Pink. See Dianthus, Botany Index. Pinna, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a genus of shell-fish belonging to the order of vermes testacea. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> Index.—Pliny, who gives some account, perhaps not very correct, of the history of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus, (lib. ix. 51.) says, the smallest of all the kinds is called the pinnoterex, and therefore liable to injury; this has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> to hide itself in the shells of oysters. Again, lib. ix. 66. he says, the pinna is of the genus of shell-fish; it is produced in muddy waters, always erect, nor ever without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, which some call the pinnoterex, others the pinophylax. This sometimes is a small squill, sometimes a crab, that follows the pinna for the sake of food. The pinna, upon opening its shell, exposes itself as a prey to the smallest kind of fishes; for they immediately assault her, and, growing bolder upon finding no resistance, venture in. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, watching its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, gives notice by a bite; upon which the pinna, closing its shell, shuts in, kills, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of whatever happens to be there to its companion. The pinna and the crab together dwell, For mutual succour, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> shell. They both to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a livelihood combine; That takes the prey, when this has given the sign. From hence this crab, above his fellows fam'd, By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks was pinnoterex nam'd.—Oppian. Pinnace, a small vessel navigated with oars and sails, and having generally two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, which are rigged like those of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOONER">schooner</a>. Pinnace is also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> usually rowed with eight oars. See the article Boat. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINNACLE">Pinnacle</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the top or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, terminating in a point. This kind of roof among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> was appropriated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; their ordinary roofs were all flat, or made in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> way. Pinnated leaves. See Botany Index. Pinnatifid leaves. See Botany Index. Pinnoterus, or Pinnothylax, is a kind of crab-fish, furnished with very good eyes. It is said to be the companion of the pinna marina. They live and and lodge together in the same shell, which belongs to the latter. When it has occasion to eat, it opens its valves, and feeds out its faithful purveyor to procure food. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> during their labour the pinnoterus perceives the polypus, it immediately returns to warn its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> friend of the danger, when, by shutting its valves, it escapes the rage of its enemy; but when the pinnoterus loads itself with booty without molestation, it makes a gentle noise at the opening of the shell, and when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a>- --- Pinelli, sympathizing, and compassionate, particularly to men of letters, whose wants he often anticipated. His zeal for the progress and advancement of science rendered him very communicative of his knowledge and of his books; but this was always done with judgement and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. He died in 1621, aged 68, without having published any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Paul Gualdo, who has written Pinelli's life, does not specify the number of volumes of which his rich library consisted: he only informs us, that when it was transported by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to Naples, it was packed up in 130 chests, of which 14 contained manuscripts; but it did not go wholly to his heirs. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> caused their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> to be set upon the manuscripts, and took away whatever concerned the affairs of the republic, to the number of 200 pieces. "I compare (says <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> de Thon) Pinelli to Titus Pomponius; for, as that illustrious Roman was called Atticus, Pinelli also bore the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Venetian, on account of the great affection which the republic of Venice had for him. Pinet, Antony du, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of Noroy, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writer, lived in the 16th century, and was a native of Besançon. He was strongly attached to the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and a bitter enemy to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome. His book, entitled La Conformité des Églises Réformées de France, et de l'Église primitive, printed at Lyons, 1564, in 8vo; and the notes which he added to the French translation of the Fees of the Pope's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>, which was printed at Lyons, in 8vo, 1564, and reprinted at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1700, in 12mo, plainly discover his sentiments. He published the last-mentioned performance under this title: Taxe des parties castrales de la Législature du Pape, in Latin and French, with some notes taken from decrees, councils, and canons, in order to ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> anciently observed in the church. In the epistle dedicatory, he affirms the tone of a declared enemy to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome. He apologizes for having presented this book "to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> so holy as yours (the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>), in which are heard only hymns, psalms, and praises, to the Lord our God: but it is proper to throw to the villain his villany, and the fool his folly, lest one should be thought to resemble them." We see by this specimen, that Pinet had no more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> in his style than in his manners. His translation of Pliny's Natural History, printed at Lyons in 2 vol. folio, 1566, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1608, was formerly much read. Though there are a good many errors in it, it is yet very useful at present, especially for those who understand Pliny's Latin, on account of the translator's researches, and a great number of marginal notes. Pinet also published Plans of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fortresses in the world at Lyons, 1564, in folio. Ping-leang fou, a city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Chen-fu. It is one of the most considerable cities of the western part of the province, and is situated on the river Kin-ho. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> here is mild; and the agreeable views which the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> present, added to the streams which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, render it a very delightful residence. It has under its jurisdiction three cities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> class and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of the third. In this district is a valley so deep and narrow, that it is almost impervious to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>: a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> highway, paved with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, runs through it. Vol. XVI. Part II. mitted the two friends feast on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of its industry. See Pinna, &c.

PINT

Pages 178-178

a vessel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, used in estimating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of liquids, and even sometimes of dry things.—Budeus derives the word from the Greek πίναξ; others from the German pint, a little measure of wine; Nicod from the Greek πίνω, "to drink." The English pint is twofold; the one for wine measure, the other for beer and ale measure. See Measure.

PINTLES

Pages 178-178

certain pivots <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hooks fastened upon the back <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>, with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> downwards, in order to enter into, and rest upon, the goosings, fixed in the stern-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, to hang the rudder. See Helm.

PINTOR

Pages 178-178
PETER, physician, was born at Valencia in Spain, in the year 1420, and was physician to Alexander VI., whom he followed to Rome, where he practised with great success. He has left behind him two performances of considerable merit, 1. Aggregator Sententiarum Doctorum de Curatione in Pestilentia, printed at Rome 1499, in folio. 2. De Morbo Fado et Occulto his Temporibus Affigentis, &c. printed at Rome, 1503, in 4to, black letter: a book extremely scarce, unknown to Luini and Afruc, and which traces the venerable disease to the year 1496. Pintor died at Rome in 1503, aged 83 years.

PINTURICCO

Pages 178-178

BERNARDINO, a celebrated Italian painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERUGIA">Perugia</a> in 1454. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Perugino, under whom he became so good an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, that he employed him on many occasions as his assistant. He principally painted <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a>; but he also excelled in portraits, among which those of Pope Pius II. and Innocent VIII., of Giulia Farnese, Caesar Borgia, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Isabella of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, are particularly distinguished. The most memorable performance of Pinturicchio is the history of Pius II., painted in ten compartments in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Siena; in which undertaking, Raphael, then a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and bred under the same <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, assisted him so far as to sketch out cartoons of many parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The story of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is worth relating, especially as it illustrates his character. The last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he was engaged in was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a> for the monastery of St Francis at Siena: the monks accommodated him with a chamber to work in, which they cleared of all the furniture, except one old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> that appeared too rotten to move; but Pinturicchio, naturally polite and peevish, insisted on its being taken away, and the monks, willing to gratify him, complied. It was no sooner stirred than one of the planks bursting, out tumbled 500 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which had been secreted there for many years. The monks were overjoyed at finding this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, and the painter proportionably mortified at losing his chance of the discovery by his indiscreet obstinacy: it affected his spirits so much that he survived but a few months, and it was generally considered as the cause of his death.

PINUS

Pages 178-183

the Pine-tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the coniferae class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The pine-tree was well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and has been described and celebrated both by their philosophers and poets. Pliny enumerates no less than six <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of trees of this genus; and it is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> both in his Eclogues, his Georgics, and his Aeneid; by Horace in his Odes; by Ovid in his Metamorphoses; by Statius; and by Catullus, &c. Macrobius relates an anecdote concerning the cones of pine-trees, which in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> were called poma pinæa, "pine-apples." There lived in the Augustan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> one Vatinius, who by some means had irritated the Roman people so much that they pelted him with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. When he entertained them with gladiators, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself from such treatment for the future, he procured an edict from the ediles, that no person should throw any thing but apples in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. It accidentally happened that at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Cæcilius, eminent for his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> as well as knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, was consulted on the question, whether a pine-apple (the cone of the pine) was legally included in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> pomum, "an apple"? It is an apple (said he) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you intend to fling it at Vatinius*. A decision by which the edict in his favour did not much mend his situation: for Martial represents it dangerous rap. 6. to come under this tree, because the cones in his time were of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a size and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, probably enlarged by cultivation for ages. Nuces Pinææ. Poma furnus Cybeles: procul hinc discedite, visior, Ne cadat in infernum nostra ruina caput†. Lib. xiii. There are generally reckoned 14 species of this genus; of which the most remarkable are these following: 1. The pinea, pineager, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wild pine, grows naturally on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and the south of France. It grows to the size of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tree; the branches extend to a considerable distance; and while the trees are young, they are fully furnished with leaves, especially where they are not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as to exclude the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> from those within; but as they advance in age, the branches appear naked, and all those which are situated below become unfruitful in a few years; for which reason they are now much less in esteem than formerly. 2. The pinus pinæa, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> pine, is a tall evergreen tree, native of Italy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It delights in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> loam, though like most others it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow well in almost any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Respecting the uses of this species, Hanbury tells us that "the kernels are eatable, and by many preferred to almonds. In Italy they are served up at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in their shells."—They are exceeding wholesome, being good for coughs, colds, consumptions, &c. on which account only this tree deserves to be propagated." Hanbury continues: "It may be very proper here to take notice of a very great and dangerous mistake Mr Miller has committed, by saying, under this article of stone-pine, that seeds kept in the cones will be good, and grow if they are sown ten or twelve years after the cones have been gathered from the trees; whereas the seeds of this sort, whether kept in the cones or taken out, are never good after the first year; and though sometimes a few plants will come up from the seeds that are kept in the cones for two years before, yet this is but seldom; neither must a tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a crop be expected. This caution is the more necessary, as several gentlemen who had cones, upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> Mr Miller's book, and finding the seeds would take no damage when kept there, deferred the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> for a season or two, when they thought they should have more conveniency either of men or ground for their purpose; and were afterwards wholly disappointed, no plants appearing," pearing, the seeds being by that time spoiled and worth nothing." 3. The rubra, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Scots fir or pine. It is common throughout Scotland, whence its name; though it is also found in most of the other countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. M. du Hamel, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences, mentions his having received some seeds of it from St Domingo in the West Indies; and thence concludes, that it grows indifferently in the temperate, frigid, and torrid zones. The wood of this tree is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, which is the most durable of any of the kinds yet known. The leaves of this tree are much shorter and broader than those of the former sort, of a grayish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, growing two out of one fleath; the cones are small, pyramidal, and end in narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> colour, and the seeds are small. 4. The pinus picea, or yew-leaved fir, is a tall evergreen, and a native of Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and Germany. This species includes the silver fir and the balm of Gilead fir. The first of these is a noble upright tree. Mr. Marshall says, "The tallest trees I have seen were spruce and silver firs in the valleys in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> several firs in the dockyards in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and one of 39 yards was 18 inches diameter at the small end. I was told they came from Switzerland." The branches are not very numerous, and the bark is smooth and delicate. The leaves grow singly on the branches, and their ends are slightly indented. Their upper surface is of a fine strong green colour, and their under has an ornament of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> running lengthwise on each side the midrib; on account of which silvery look this sort is called the silver fir. The cones are large, and grow erect; and when the warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> comes on, they soon shed their seeds; which should be a caution to all who wish to raise this plant, to gather the cones before that happens. The balm of Gilead fir has of all the sorts been most coveted, on account of the great fragrance of its leaves; though this is not its only good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>: for it is a very beautiful tree, naturally of an upright growth, and the branches are so ornamented with their balmy leaves, as to exceed any of the other sorts in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. The leaves, which are very closely set on the branches, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and their ends are indented. Their upper surface, when healthy, is of a fine dark-green colour, and their under has white lines on each side the midrib lengthwise, nearly like those of the silver fir. These leaves when bruised are very finely scented; and the buds, which swell in the autumn for the next year's shoot, are very ornamental all winter, being turgid, and of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> colour: and from these also exudes a kind of fine turpentine, of the same kind of (though heightened) fragrancy. The tree being wounded in any part, emits plenty of this turpentine; and Hanbury says, "it is supposed by many to be the sort from whence the balm of Gilead is taken, which occasions this tree being so called. But this is a mistake; for the true balm of Gilead is taken from a kind of terebinth: though I am informed, that what has been collected from this tree has been sent over to England from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> (where it grows naturally), and often sold in the shops for the true sort." The silver fir is very hardy, and will grow in any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> or situation, but always makes the greatest progress in rich loamy <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The balm of Gilead fir must be planted in deep, rich, good earth; nor will it live long in any other. The soil may be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mould, or of a sandy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, if it be deep enough, and if the roots have room enough to strike freely. 5. The pinus abies, or European spruce fir, a native of the northern parts of Europe and of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, includes the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> spruce and long-coned Cornish fir. The former of these is a tree of as much beauty while growing as its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> is valuable when propagated on that account. Its growth is naturally like the silver, upright; and the height it will attain to may be easily conceived, when we say that the white deal, so much coveted by the joiners, &c., is the wood of this tree; and it may perhaps satisfy the curious reader to know, that from this fir pitch is drawn. The leaves are of a dark-green colour; they stand singly on the branches, but the younger shoots are very closely garnished with them. They are very narrow; their ends are pointed; and they are peopled of such beauties as to excite admiration. The cones are eight or ten inches long, and hang downwards. The better the soil is, the faster will the spruce fir grow, though it will thrive very well in most of our English lands. In strong loamy earth it makes a surprising progress; and it delights in fresh land of all sorts, which never has been worn out by ploughing, &c., though it be ever so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The long-coned Cornish fir differs scarcely in any respect from the Norway spruce, except that the leaves and the cones are larger. 6. The pinus Canadensis, American or Newfoundland spruce fir, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America, includes three varieties. The white Newfoundland spruce, the red Newfoundland spruce, and the black Newfoundland spruce. These, however, differ so little, that one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is common to them all. They are of a gentle upright growth, though they do not float so freely or grow so fast with us as the Norway spruce. The leaves are of the same green, and garnish the branches in the same beautiful manner as those of that species; only they are narrower, shorter, and stand closer. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is observable in the cones; for these are no more than about an inch in length, and the scales are closely placed. In the cones, indeed, consists the difference of these three sorts: those of the white species are of a very light brown colour; those of the red species more of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>-brown or reddish colour; and those of the black species of a dark or blackish colour. Besides this, there is scarcely any material difference; though it is observable, that this trifling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> seems to be pretty constant in the plants raised from the like seeds. These sorts will often flower, and produce cones when only about five or six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and indeed look then very beautiful: but this is a sign of weaknesses in the plant, which it does not often fairly get over. 7. The pinus balsamea, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a> fir, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> and Canada, possesses as little beauty as any of the fir tribe; though, being rather scarce in proportion, it is deemed valuable. It is called by some the yew-leaved fir, from the resemblance of the leaves to those of the yew-tree. It is a tree of low growth, with but few branches; and these are long and slender, and spread abroad without order. The leaves do not garnish the branches... Pinus branches so plentifully as those of any other sort of fir. The cones are very small and rounded; they are about half an inch long; and the scales are loosely arranged. We receive these cones from America, by which we raise the plants; though this caution should be given to the planter, that this tree is fond of moist rich ground, and in such a kind of soil will make the greatest progress. 8. The *pinus orientalis*, or oriental fir, a native of the East, is a low but elegant tree. The leaves are very short, and nearly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The fruit is exceeding small, and hangs downward; and the whole tree makes an agreeable variety with the other kinds. 9. The *abies* <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Weymouth's pine, or North American white pine. This grows sometimes to the height of 100 feet and upwards, and is highly valued on account of its beauty. The bark of the tree is very smooth and delicate, especially when young; the leaves are long and slender, five growing out of one sheath; the branches are pretty closely garnished with them, and thus make a fine appearance. The cones are long, slender, and very loose, opening with the first warmth of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; so that if they are not gathered in winter, the scales open and let out the seeds. The wood of this sort is esteemed for making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> for ships. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s time there was a law made for the preservation of these trees, and for the encouragement of their growth in America. Within these last 50 years they have been propagated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in considerable plenty. With respect to the culture of this species, Mr Hanbury, after some more general directions, continues thus, "I have known gentlemen, who, in attempting to raise these trees, have seen the young plants go off without perceiving the cause; and the more watering and pains they have taken, have found the plants perish in this way more and more, to their great mortification and afflamentment. In the spring following these plants should be pricked out in beds half a foot under each way; and here they may stand two years, when they may be either finally planted out, or removed into the nursery, at the distance of one foot under, and two feet in the rows. If care has been taken of them in the nursery, they may be removed at a considerable height with great assurance of success: for it is much easier to make this pine grow than any of the other sorts: so that where they are wanted for ornament in parks, open places, &c., a show of them may be made in a little time. "The soil the Weymouth pine delights in most is a sandy loam; but it likes other soils of an inferior nature: and although it is not generally to be planted on all lands like the Scotch fir, yet I have seen it luxuriant and healthy, making strong shoots, on blue and red clays, and other sorts of strong ground. On stony and flat ground, likewise, I have seen some very fine trees; so that I believe whoever is desirous of having plantations of this pine, need not be curious in the choice of his ground." 10. The *pinus taeda*, or swamp-pine, is a tall evergreen tree, a native of the swamps of Virginia and Canada. There are several varieties of this genus which Hanbury enumerates and describes: such as, 1st, The three-leaved American swamp-pine. 2d, The two-leaved American pine. 3d, The yellow American pine, the yellow tough pine, and the tough pine of the plains; among which there is but little variety. 4th, The battard pine. 5th, The frankincense pine. And 6th, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> pine.
