"There are (continues our author) many other sorts of American pines, which we receive from thence with the like cant names of those of the above, which I have chosen to retain, as they will probably be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be sent over; and that the gardener receiving them as such may best know what to do with them. In many of those sorts I see at present no material difference; so I am induced to think they are the same, sent over with different names. Some of the sorts above-mentioned differ in very few respects; but I have chosen to mention them, as a pedon may be supplied with the seeds from Pennsylvania, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, Virginia, Carolina, &c., where they all grow naturally; and having once obtained the seeds, and from them plants, they will become pleasing objects of his nicest observations." 11. The *pinus cedrus*, ranked by Tournefort and others under larix, famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, is that popularly called by us the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> of Lebanon, by the ancients *cedrus magna* or the great cedar; also *cedrela*, *cedrata*; and sometimes the Phoenician or Syrian cedar, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where it grows in its greatest perfection. It is a coniferous evergreen, of the biggest sort, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> large roundish cones of smooth scales, standing erect, the leaves being small, narrow, and thick set.—They sometimes counterfeit cedar, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> wood of a reddish hue: but the smell discovers the cheat, that of true cedar being very aromatic. In some places, the wood of the cajou-tree passes under the name of cedar, on account of its reddish colour and its aromatic smell, which somewhat resemble that of fantal. Cedar-wood is reputed almost immortal and incorruptible; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> which it owes chiefly to its bitter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> cannot endure. For this reason it was that the ancients used cedar tablets to write upon, especially for things of importance, as appears from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of Periurus, *Et cedra ligna locuitur*. A juice was also drawn from cedar, with which they smeared their books and writings, or other matters, to preserve them from rotting; which is alluded to by Horace: by means of which it was, that Numa's books, written on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPYRUS">papyrus</a>, were preserved entire to the year 535, as we are informed by Pliny. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple, as well as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, were both of this wood. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Hiram several cities for the cedars he had furnished him on these occasions. Cortes is said to have erected a palace at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, in which were 7000 beams of cedar, most of them 120 feet long, and 12 in circumference, as we are informed by Herrera. Some tell us of a cedar felled in Cyprus 130 feet long, and 18 in diameter. It was used for the main-mast in the galley of King Demetrius. Le Bruyn affirms us, that the two biggest he saw on Mount Lebanon, measured, one of them 57 palms, and the other 47, in circumference. In the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> at Utiaca, there were cedar trees near 2000 years old; which yet were nothing to that beam in an oratory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> at Seguntum in Spain, said to have been brought thither 2000 years before the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. Cedar is of so dry a nature, that it will not endure to be fastened with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> nails, from which it usually shrinks; so that they commonly fasten it with pins of the same wood." The statue (says Hanbury) of the great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> at Ephesus was made of this material; and, if this tree abounded with us in great plenty, it might have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> share in our most superb edifices. The ethereal constantly emitted from its wood are said to purify the air, and make rooms wholesome. Chapels and places set apart for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties, being wainscoted with this wood, inspire the worshippers with a more solemn awe. It is not obnoxious to worms; and emits an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> which will preserve cloth or books from worms or corruption. The sawdust will preserve <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>; and is therefore said to be plentifully used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a>, where practised. It is remarkable that this tree is not to be found as a native in any other part of the world than Mount Libanus, as far as hath yet been discovered. What we find mentioned in Scripture of the lofty cedars can nowise applicable to the common growth of this tree; since, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> we have of those now growing in England, as also from the testimony of several travellers who have visited those few remaining trees on Mount Libanus, they are not inclined to grow very lofty, but on the contrary extend their branches very far; to which the allusion made by the Psalmist agrees very well, when he is describing the flourishing state of a people, and says, "They shall spread their branches like the cedar-tree." Rauwolf, in his Travels, says, there were not at that time (i.e. anno 1574) upon Mount Libanus more than 26 trees remaining, 24 of which stood in a circle; and the other two, which stood at a small distance, had their branches almost confused with age; nor could he find any younger tree coming up to succeed them, though he looked about diligently for some. These trees (he says) were growing at the foot of a small hill, on the top of the mountains, and amongst the snow. Those having very large branches, commonly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the tree to one side, but are extended to a great length, and in so delicate and pleasant order, as if they were trimmed and made even with great diligence, by which they are easily distinguished, at a great distance, from fir-trees. The leaves (continues he) are very like to those of the larch-tree, growing close together in little branches upon small brown thorns. Maundrel, in his Travels, says, there were but 16 large trees remaining when he visited the mountain, some of which were of a prodigious bulk, but that there were many more young ones of a smaller size: he measured one of the largest, and found it to be 12 yards six inches in girth, and yet found, and 37 yards in the spread of its boughs. At about five or six yards from the ground it was divided into five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, each of which was equal to a great tree. What Maundrel hath related was confirmed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who was there in the year 1722, with this difference only, viz. in the directions of the branches of the largest tree, which he measured, and found to be 22 yards diameter. Now, whether Mr Maundrel meant 37 yards in circumference of the spreading branches, or the diameter of them, cannot be determined by his words; yet either of them well agrees with this last account. There is another species, viz. the larch tree, which the old botanists ranked under larix, with deciduous leaves, and oval obtuse cones. It grows naturally upon the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> and Apennines, and of late has been very much propagated in Britain. It is of quick growth, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> rises to 50 feet or more; the branches are slender, their ends generally hanging downward, and are garnished with long narrow leaves which arise in clusters from one point, spreading open above like the hairs of a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>; they are of a light green, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> away in autumn. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> appear, which are disposed in form of small cones; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers are collected into oval obtuse cones, which in some species have bright purple tops, and in others they are white; these differences are accidental; the cones are about an inch long, obtuse at their points; the scales are smooth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> over each other; under each <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> there are generally lodged two seeds, which have wings. There are other two varieties of this tree, one of which is a native of America, and the other of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The cones of the American kind which have been brought to Britain seem in general to be larger than those of the common sort. Many encomiums (says Hanbury when speaking of this species) have been bestowed on the timber of the larch; and we find such a favourable account of it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors, as should induce us to think it would be proper for almost any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Evelyn recites a story of Witten, a Dutch writer, that a ship built of this timber and cypress had been found in the Numidian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, twelve fathoms under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and entire, and reduced to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> as to resist the sharpest tool, after it had lain submerged above 1490 years. Certain it is this is an excellent wood for ship and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. At Venice this wood is frequently used in building their houses, as well as in Switzerland, where these trees abound; so that, without all doubt, the larch excels for masts for ships, or beams for houses, doors, windows, &c., particularly as it is said to resist the worm. In Switzerland (A) their houses are covered with boards of this wood cut out a foot square; and, as it emits a resinous substance, it so diffuses itself into every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> and crevice, and becomes so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and close, as well as so hardened by the air, as to render the covering <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> against all weather. But, as such covering for houses would cause great devastation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fire, the buildings (A) "Between Bex and Bevieux (says Coxe in his Travels in Switzerland), I observed the larch in great plenty. Painters, from the time of Pliny to that of Raphael, trusted their works to this wood, which the Roman naturalist titles immortale lignum. The wood is reckoned excellent for all works which are to lie under water; and the borderers on the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a> prefer it for building their vessels. In these parts I saw most beautiful woods of chestnut. Haller says that they extend some leagues; he also informs us, that they are found in other parts of Switzerland, and even in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> places in some of the transalpine parts. Accident must have brought them thither, as it appears from Pliny that these trees were first introduced into Europe from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>." buildings are confined to a limited distance by an order of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> from the magistrates. The wood when first laid on the houses, is said to be very white; but this colour, in two or three years is changed, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, to a black, which appears like a smooth shining <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>." Of the common larch there are several varieties. The flowers which the commonest sort exhibits early in the spring are of a delicate red colour; another sort produces white flowers at the same season, and these have a delightful effect among those of the red sort; whilst another, called the Black Newfoundland larix, increases the variety, though by an aspect little differing from the others. There are also larches with greenish flowers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> red, &c., all of which are accidental varieties from seeds. These varieties are easily distinguished, even when out of blow: the young shoots of the white-flowering larch are of the lightest green, and the cones when ripe are nearly white. The red flowering larch has its shoots of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, and the cones are of a brown colour; whilst the cones and shoots of the black Newfoundland larch are in the same manner proportionally tinged. The cones, which are a very great ornament to several sorts of the pines, are very little to these. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> beauty consists in the manner of their growth, the nature and beauty of their pencilled leaves and fair flowers; for the cones that succeed them are small, of a whitish, a reddish, or a blackish-brown colour, and make no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The pinus cedrus and pinus larix are propagated by sowing in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of light earth exposed to the morning sun. The seed must be covered half an inch thick with fine light earth, and the beds watered at times when the weather is dry. In about six weeks the plants will appear; they must at this time be carefully guarded from the birds, shaded from the sun and winds, and kept very clear of weeds. In the latter end of April the following year, they may be removed into beds of fresh earth, placing them at ten inches distance every way. They are to be kept here two years, and such of them as seem to bend must be tied up to a stake to keep them upright. They may afterwards be planted in the places where they are to remain. They thrive well on the sides of barren hills, and make a very pretty figure there. Respecting the uses of this tree, Dr Pallas, in his Flora Rossica, informs us, that if it is burnt, and the wood consumed, the internal part of the wood distils copiously a drying reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, a little less glutinous than gum arabic, somewhat of a resinous taste, but wholly soluble in water. At the instigation of M. Kinder, this gum has lately been sold in the Russian shops under the name of gummi Orenburgensis, but which our author thinks should be called gummi Uraliensis or laricii. It is eaten by the Wogulis as a dainty, and is said to be nutritious and antiseptic. Some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a> was gathered from the green leaves, but it could never be condensed. The Russians use the boletus laricius as an emetic in intermittents, and to check the leucorrhea. At Bafchir and Siberia the inhabitants sprinkle the dry powder on the wounds of oxen and horses, as a detergent and anthelmintic. The nuts of the pinus cembra, the same author affirms, are eaten as luxuries in Russia, and are even exported with the same view. The unripe cones give a very fragrant oil, termed balsamic. The inhabitants of Siberia use the tender tops, and even the bark rubbed off in the spring, as an antiseptic. The kernels of the nuts of the amygdalus nana give a very pleasing flavour to brandy; and, when pressed, afford a bitter oil in large quantities. The way of destroying the bitter is by digesting it in the sun with spirit of wine, and it then becomes sweet and extremely agreeable. From the larch-tree is extracted what is erroneously called Venice turpentine. This substance, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> balsam, flows at first without incision; when it has done dropping, the poor people who wait in the fir woods make incisions at about two or three feet from the ground into the trunks of the trees, into which they fix narrow troughs about 20 inches long. The end of these troughs is hollowed like a ladle; and in the middle is a small hole bored for the turpentine to run into the receiver which is placed below it. As the gummy substance runs from the trees, it passes along the sloping gutter or trough to the ladle, and from thence runs through the holes into the receiver. The people who gather it visit the trees morning and evening from the end of May to September, to collect the turpentine out of the receivers. When it flows out of the tree, Venice turpentine is clear like water, and of a yellowish white; but, as it grows older, it thickens and becomes of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> colour. It is procured in the greatest abundance in the neighbourhood of Lyons, and in the valley of St Martin near St Lucern in Switzerland. Though we have already noticed the manner of cultivating some of the particular species of this genus, and have also remarked the uses of some of them, we shall finish the article with a few general observations on the culture and uses of the whole. Culture. All the sorts of pines are propagated by seeds produced in hard woody cones. The way to get the seeds out of these cones is to lay them before a gentle fire, which will cause the cells to open, and then the seeds may be easily taken out. If the cones are kept entire, the seeds will remain good for some years; so that the surest way of preserving them is to let them remain in the cones till the time for sowing the seeds. If the cones are kept in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, they will open and emit the seeds; but if they are not exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, they will remain close for a long time. The best season for sowing the pines is about the end of March. When the seeds are sown, the place should be covered with nets to keep off the birds; otherwise, when the plants begin to appear with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a> of the seed on the top of them, the birds will peck off the tops, and thus destroy them. Uses. From the first species is extracted the common turpentine, much used by farriers, and from which is drawn the oil of that name. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of making pitch, tar, resin, and turpentine, from these trees, is very familiar. In the spring time, when the sap is most free in running, they pare off the bark of the pine tree, to make the sap run <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into a hole which they cut at the bottom to receive it. In the way, as it runs down, it leaves a white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> like cream, but a little thicker. This is very different from all the kinds of resin and turpentine in use, and it is generally sold to be used in the making of flambéaux instead of white bees wax. The matter that is received in the hole at the bottom is taken up with ladles, and put in a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>. A great part of this immediately runs through, and this is the com- mon turpentine. This is received into stone or earthen pots, and is ready for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. The thicker matter, which remains in the basket, they put into a common alembic, adding a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water. They distil this as long as any oil is seen floating upon the water. This oil they separate from the surface in large quantities, and this is the common oil or spirit of turpentine. The remaining matter at the bottom of the still is common yellow resin. When they have thus obtained all that they can from the sap of the tree, they cut it down, and hewing the wood into billets, they fill a pit dug in the earth with these billets, and, setting them on fire, there runs from them, while they are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, a black thick matter. This naturally falls to the bottom of the pit, and this is the tar. The top of the pit is covered with tiles, to keep in the heat; and there is at the bottom a little hole, out of which the tar runs like oil. If this hole be made too large, it sets the whole quantity of the tar on fire; but, if small enough, it runs quietly out. The tar, being thus made, is put up in barrels; and if it be to be made into pitch, they put it into large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> vessels, without adding anything to it. It is then suffered to boil a while, and being then let out, is found when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> to be what we call pitch. A decoction of the nuts or seeds of the first species in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, or of the extremities of the branches pulled in spring, is said, with a proper regimen, to cure the most inveterate scurvy. The wood of this species is not valued; but that of the Scots pine is superior to any of the rest. It is observable of the Scots pine, that when planted in bogs, or in a moist soil, though the plants make great progress, yet the wood is white, soft, and little esteemed; but when planted in a dry soil, though the growth of the trees is there very slow, yet the wood is proportionably better. Few trees have been applied to more uses than this. The tallest and straightest are formed by nature for masts to our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. The timber is resinous, durable, and applicable to numberless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> purposes, such as flooring and wainscoting of rooms, making of beds, chests, tables, boxes, &c. From the trunk and branches of this, as well as most others of the pine tribe, tar and pitch is obtained. By incision, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>-ras, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> pitch, and turpentine, are acquired and prepared. The resinous roots are dug out of the ground in many parts of the Highlands, and, being divided into small splinters, are used by the inhabitants to burn, instead of candles.—At Loch-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROSS_SHIRE">Ross-shire</a> the fishermen make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> of the inner bark; but hard <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> has taught the inhabitants of Sweden, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, and Kamtchatka, to convert the same into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. To effect this, they, in the spring season, make choice of the tallest and fairest trees; then stripping off carefully the outer bark, they collect the soft, white, succulent interior bark, and dry it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. When they have occasion to use it, they first toast it at the fire, then grind, and after steeping the flour in warm water to take off the resinous taste, they make it into thin cakes, which are baked for use. On this strange food the poor inhabitants are sometimes constrained to live for a whole year; and, we are told, through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, become at last even fond of it. Linnaeus remarks, that this same bark-bread will fatten swine; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> obliges us to wish, that men might never be reduced to the necessity of robbing them of such a food. The interior bark, of which the above-mentioned bread is made, the Swedish boys frequently peel off the trees in the spring, and eat raw with greedy appetite. From the cones of this tree is prepared a diuretic oil, like the oil of turpentine, and a resinous extract, which has similar virtues with the balsam of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. An infusion or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> of the buds is highly commended as an antiscorbutic. The farina, or yellow powder, of the male flowers, is sometimes in the spring carried away by the winds, in such quantities, where the trees abound, as to alarm the ignorant with the notion of its raining bitumen. The tree lives to a great age; Linnaeus affirms to 400 years.

PIONEERS

Pages 183-183

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, are such as are commanded in from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> for mending the ways, for working on intrenchments and fortifications, and for making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and approaches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are likewise employed for all these purposes. Most of the foreign regiments of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> have half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of pioneers, well instructed in that important branch of duty. Our regiments of infantry and cavalry have three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four pioneers each, provided with aprons, hatchets, saws, spades, and pick-axes. Each pioneer must have an axe, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, and an apron; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bearskin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, on which is to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s crest in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> ground; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the regiment is to be on the back <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it.

PIPE

Pages 183-184

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c., a canal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conduit, for the conveyance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and other liquids. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">Pipes</a> for water, water-engines, &c., are usually of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or wood: the latter are usually made of oak or elder. Those of iron are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in forges; their usual length is about two feet and a half; several of these are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> fastened together by means of four screws at each end, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> or old hat between them, to stop the water. Those of earth are made by the potters; these are fitted into one another, one end being always made wider than the other. To join them closer, and prevent their breaking, they are covered with tow and pitch: their length is usually about that of the iron pipes. The wooden pipes are trees bored with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> iron augers, of different sizes, beginning with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and then proceeding with a larger successively; the first being pointed, the rest being formed like spoons, increasing in diameter, from one to six inches or more: they are fitted into the extremities of each other (as represented fig. 2), and are sold by the foot. Wooden pipes are bored as follows. The machine represented fig. 1, is put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> by the wheel A, which is moved by a current of water; upon the axle of this wheel is a cog-wheel B, which causes the lanterns C, D, to turn horizontally, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> axis is consequently in a perpendicular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> D turns at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> two cog-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>, E and F: the first, E, which is vertical, turns the auger which bores the wood; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, F, which is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, causes the carriage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the piece to advance by means of the arms H, I, which take hold of the notches. Pipes in the wheel K. The first, H, by means of the notches, draws the wheel towards F; and the other, I, pushes the under-polt of the wheel in an opposite direction; both which motions tend to draw the carriage towards F, and consequently cause the augre to pierce the wood. The augre being from 9 to 12 feet in length, and of a proportionable bigness, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary to have two pieces, as L, L, to support its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, and cause it to enter the piece to be bored with the same uniformity. For the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of leaden pipes, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLUMBERY">PLUMBERY</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a>-Pipes. See Air-Pipe. Pipes of an Organ. See Organ. Bag Pipe. See Bag-Pipe. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>-Pipe. See Hornpipe. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>-Pipe, a machine used in the smoking of tobacco, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> tube, made of earth or clay, having at one end a little cafe, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, called the bowl, for the reception of the tobacco, the fumes whereof are drawn by the mouth through the other end. Tobacco pipes are made of various fashions; long, short, plain, worked, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, varnished, unvarnished, and of various colours, &c. The Turks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> pipes three or four feet long, made of rushes, or of wood bored, at the end whereof they fix a kind of a pot of baked earth, which serves as a bowl, and which they take off after smoking. Pipe, also denotes a vessel or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for wine, and things measured by wine-measure. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">Barrel</a> and Measure. Pipe, in Mining, is where the ore runs forwards endwise in a hole, and doth not sink downwards or in a vein. Pipe, Pipa, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a roll in the exchequer, called also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> roll. See the next article. Pipe-Office, is an office wherein a person called the clerk of the pipe, makes out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-lands, by warrant from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, or commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer. The clerk of the pipe makes out also all accounts of sheriffs, &c., and gives the accountants their quietus of. To this office are brought all accounts which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the remembrancer's office, and remain there, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any stated debt be due from any person, the same may be drawn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into the great roll of the pipe: upon which the comptroller issues out a writ, called the summons of the pipe, for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> thereof; and if there be no goods or chattels, the clerk then draws down the debts to the lord treasurer's remembrancer, to write ejectments against their lands. All tallies which vouch the payment of any sum contained in such accounts are examined and allowed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> secondary of the pipe. Besides the chief clerk in this office, there are eight attorneys or sworn clerks, and a comptroller. Pipe-Fish. See Syngnathus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> Pipes, the trivial name of univalve shells belonging to the genus Dentalis. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> Index.

PIPER

Pages 184-185

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIGLA">Trigla</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Piper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">Pepper</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the Piper dandria clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. There are 25 species, of which the most remarkable is the firiboa, with oval, heart-shaped, nervèd leaves, and reflexed spikes. This is the plant which produces the pepper so much used in food. It is a shrub whose root is small, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>; it rises into a stem, which requires a tree <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prop to support it. Its wood has the same sort of knots as the vine; and when it is dry, it exactly resembles the vine-branch. The leaves, which have a strong smell and a pungent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, are of an oval shape; but they diminish towards the extremity, and terminate in a point. From the flower-buds, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and are sometimes placed in the middle and sometimes at the extremity of the branches, are produced small berries resembling those of the currant tree. Each of these contains between 20 and 30 corns of pepper; they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> gathered in October, and exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight days. The fruit which was green at first, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, when stripped of its covering affirms the appearance it has when we see it. The largest, heaviest, and least shrivelled, is the best. The pepper plants flourishes in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a> (a), and Ceylon, and more particularly on the Malabar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. It is not sown, but planted; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> nicety is required in the choice of the shoots. It produces no fruit till the end of three years; but bears plentifully the three succeeding years, that some plants yield between five and seven pounds of pepper. The bark then begins to shrink; and the shrub declines so fast, that in 12 years <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it ceases <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>. The culture of pepper is not difficult: it is sufficient to plant it in a rich <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and carefully to pull up the weeds that grow in great abundance round its roots, especially the three first years. As the sun is highly necessary to the growth of the pepper plant, when it is ready to bear, the trees that support it must be lopped to prevent their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> from injuring the fruit. When the season is over, it is proper to crop the head of the plant. Without this precaution, there would be too much wood, and little fruit. The pepper exported from Malabar, which was formerly entirely in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Portuguese, and was afterwards divided between the Dutch, British, and French, amounted to about 10,000,000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETEL">Betel</a>, or betle, is a species of this genus. See Betel. It is a creeping and climbing plant like the ivy; and its leaves a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> resemble those of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, though they are longer and narrower at the extremity. It grows in all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, but thrives best in moist places. The natives cultivate it as we do the vine, placing props for it to run and climb upon; and it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice to plant it against the tree which bears the areca-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>. At all times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and even in the night, the Indians chew the leaves of the betel, the bittermels of which is corrected by the areca that is wrapped up in them. There is constantly mixed with it the chimam, (a) See a copious account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of cultivating pepper in Sumatra, in Mr Marsten's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Sumatra, or in the New Annual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a> for 1783, p. 147. a kind of burnt lime made of shells. The rich frequently add perfumes, either to gratify their vanity or their sensuality. It would be thought a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> among the Indians to take leave for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time, without presenting each other with a purée of betel. It is a pledge of friendship that relieves the pain of absence. No one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to speak to a superior unless his mouth is perfumed with betel; it would even be rude to neglect this precaution with an equal. The women of gallantry are the most lavish in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of betel, as being a powerful incentive to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Betel is taken after meals; it is chewed during a visit; it is offered when you meet, and when you separate; in short, nothing is to be done without betel. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it is prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, it afflicts and strengthens the stomach. At least, it is a general fashion that prevails throughout India. The piper amalago, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> pepper, and the piper ingeale, or long pepper of Jamaica, with some other species, are indigenous, and known by the names of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> wood, or peppery elder. The first bears a small spike, on which are attached a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small seeds of the size of mustard. The whole of the plant has the exact taste of the East India black pepper. The long pepper bush grows taller than the amalago. The leaves are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, smooth, and shining. The fruit is similar to the long pepper of the shops, but smaller. The common people in Jamaica season their messes with the black pepper. To preserve both, the fruit may be slightly scalded when green, then dried, and wrapped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Perhaps hereafter they may be deemed worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>.

PIQUET

Pages 185-186
or Picket, a celebrated game at cards, much in use throughout the polite world. It is played between two persons, with only 32 cards; all the duces, threes, fours, fives, and fixes, being set aside. In reckoning at this game, every card goes for the number it bears, as a ten for ten; only all count cards go for ten, and the ace for eleven; and the usual game is one hundred up. In playing, the ace wins the king, the king the queen, and so down. Twelve cards are dealt round, usually by two and two; which done, the remainder are laid in the middle: if one of the gamesters finds he has not a court card in his hand, he is to declare he has carte-blanche, and tell how many cards he will lay out, and define the other to discard, that he may show his game, and satisfy his antagonist that the carte-blanche is real; for which he reckons ten. Each person discards, i.e., lays aside a certain number of his cards, and takes in a like number from the stock. The first of the eight cards may take three, four, or five; the dealer all the remainder, if he pleases. After discarding, the eldest hand examines what suit he has most cards of; and reckoning how many points he has in that suit, if the other have not so many in that or any other suit, he tells one for every ten of that suit. He who thus reckons most is said to win the point. The point being over, each examines what sequences he has of the same suit, viz., how many tierces, or fe- quences of threes, quartes or fours, quintes or fives, six- emes, or fixes, &c. For a tierce they reckon three points, for a quarte four, for a quinte fifteen, for a fixieme sixteen, &c. And the several sequences are distinguished in dignity by the cards they begin from: thus ace king, and queen, are called tierce major; king, queen, and knave, tierce to a king; knave, ten, and nine, tierce to a knave, &c. and the best tierce, quarte, or quinte, i.e., that which takes its descent from the best card, prevails, so as to make all the others in that hand good, and destroy all those in the other hand. In like manner, a quarte in one hand sets aside a tierce in the other. The sequences over, they proceed to examine how many aces, kings, queens, knaves, and tens, each holds; reckoning for every three of any sort, three: but here too, as in sequences, he that with the same number of threes has one that is higher than any the other has, e.g., three aces, has all his others made good hereby, and his adversary's all set aside. But four of any sort, which is called a quatorze, always sets aside three. All the game in hand being thus reckoned, the eldest proceeds to play, reckoning one for every card he plays above a nine, and the other follows him in the suit; and the highest card of the suit wins the trick. Note, un- less a trick be won with a card above a nine (except the last trick), nothing is reckoned for it, though the trick serves afterwards towards winning the cards; and that he who plays last does not reckon for his cards unless he wins the trick. The cards being played out, he that has most tricks reckons ten for winning the cards. If they have tricks alike, neither reckons anything. The deal being fin- ished, and each having marked up his game, they pro- ceed to deal again as before, cutting afresh each time for the deal. If both parties be within a few points of being up, the carte-blanche is the first thing that reckons, then the point, then the sequences, then the quatorzes or threes, then the tenth cards. He that can reckon 30 in hand by carte-blanche, points, quintes, &c., without playing, before the other has reckoned anything, reckons 90 for them; and this is called a repique. If he reckons above 30, he reckons to many above 90. If he can make up 30, part in hand and part play, ere the other has told any- thing, he reckons for them 60. And this is called a pique. Where the name of the game. He that wins all the tricks, instead of ten, which is his right for winning the cards, reckons 40. And this is called a capot. Mr de Moivre, who has made this game the object of mathematical investigation, has proposed and solved the following problems: 1. To find at piquet the prob- ability which the dealer has for taking one ace or more in three cards, he having none in his hand. He con- cludes from his computation, that it is 29 to 28 that the dealer takes one ace or more. 2. To find at piquet the probability which the eldest has of taking an ace or more in five cards, he having no ace in his hand. Answer: 232 to 91, or 5 to 2, nearly. 3. To find at piquet the probability which the eldest hand has of taking an ace and a king in five cards, he having none in his hand. Answer: the odds against the eldest hand taking an ace and a king are $331$ to $315$, or $21$ to $20$ nearly. 4. To find at piquet the probability of having 12 cards dealt to, without king, queen, or knaves, which case is commonly called cartes-blanches. Answer; the odds against cartes-blanches are $1791$ to $1$ nearly. 5. To find how many different sets, essentially different from one another, one may have at piquet before taking in. Answer; $28,967,278$. This number falls short of the sum of all the distinct combinations, whereby 12 cards may be taken out of 32, this number being $225,792,840$; but it must be considered that in that number several sets of the same import, but differing in suit, might be taken, which would not introduce an essential difference among the sets. The same author gives also some observations on this game, which he had from an experienced player. See Doctrine of Chances, p. 179, &c. M. de Monmort has treated of piquet in his Analyse des Jeux de Hazard, p. 162.

PIRA

Pages 186-186

is a name by which a variety of foreign fishes are distinguished. The pira-aca is a little horned fish of the West Indies, called by Clusius and others the monoceros <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> unicorn-fish. The pira acanaga is the name of a Brazilian fish, which resembles the perch both in size and shape. It seldom exceeds four or five inches in length; its mouth is small; its tail forked. On the back it has only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>, which is supported by rigid and prickly spines. This fin can depress at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and sink within a cavity made for it in the back. Its scales are of a silvery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; it is wholesome and well tasted. Pira bebe is the name of the milvus, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KITE">kite</a>-fish. Pira coaba is an American fish of the trutaceous kind, of a very delicate flavour. It grows to the length of 12 inches; its nose is pointed, and its mouth <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; the upper jaw is longer than the under one, and hangs over like a cartilaginous prominence; its eyes are very large, and its tail is forked; under each of the gill fins there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> made of six white filaments, and covered with silvery scales. Pira jurumenbeca is a Brazilian fish, otherwise called bocca molle. It lives in the muddy bottom of the American seas, and is a long-bodied not flat-tailed fish. It grows to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> size, being found <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, and sometimes even ten or eleven, feet long, and two feet and a half thick. It has one long fin on the back, the anterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is thin and pellucid. There is also a cavity on the back, as in the pira acanaga, into which the fin can be depressed at pleasure; the tail is not forked, and the scales are all of a silvery colour and brightish. The fish is very well tasted; the pira pixanga is another Brazilian fish of the turdus or waffle kind, and called by some the gutujoche. It is generally about four or five inches long; its mouth is pretty large, and furnished with very small and very sharp teeth; its head is small, but its eyes are large and prominent, the pupil being of a fine turmoule colour, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> in a variety of shades. The coverings of the gills end in a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and are terminated by a short spine or prickle; its scales are very small, and so evenly arranged, and closely laid on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, that it is very smooth to the touch; its tail is rounded at the end; its whole body, head, tail, and fins, are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow colour, variegated all over with very beautiful blood-coloured spots; these are round, and of the bignets of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>-feed on the back and sides, and something larger on the belly; the fins are all spotted in the same manner, and are all marked with an edge of red. It is caught among the rocks, and about the shores, and is a very well tasted fish. Piranha is an American fish, more generally known by the name piraya. Piraquiba, or ipiraquiba, is the name of a fish originally Brazilian, which some writers apply to the remora or sucking fish.

PIRACY

Pages 187-187

the crime of robbery and depredation upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> seas. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, piracy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> committed by a subject, was held to be a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, being contrary to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; and by an alien, to be felony only: but now, since the statute of treasons, 25 Edw. III. c. 2, it is held to be only felony in a subject. Formerly it was only cognizable by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> courts, which proceed by the rules of the civil law. But, it being inconsistent with the liberties of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> should be taken away, unless by the judgement of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the common law of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, the statute 28 Hen. VIII. c. 15, established a new jurisdiction for this purpose; which proceeds according to the course of the common law. The offence of piracy, by common law, consists in committing those acts of robbery and depredation upon the high seas, which, if committed upon land, would have amounted to felony there. But, by statute, some other offences are made piracy also; as, by statute 11 and 12 W. III. c. 7, if any natural-born subject commits any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of hostility upon the high seas, against others of his majesty's subjects, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> from any foreign power; this, though it would only be an act of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in an alien, shall be construed piracy in a subject. And farther, any commander, or other seafaring person, betraying his trust, and running away with any ship, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, ordnance, ammunition, or goods; or yielding them up voluntarily to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>; or confining to do these acts; or any person assaulting the commander of a vessel, to hinder him from fighting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his ship; or confining him, or causing or endeavouring to cause a revolt on board; shall, for each of these offenses, be adjudged a pirate, felon, and robber, and shall suffer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, whether he be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, or merely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> by setting forth such pirates, or abetting them before the fact, or receiving or concealing them or their goods after it. And the statute 4 Geo. I. c. 11, expressly excludes the principals from the benefit of clergy. By the statute 8 Geo. I. c. 24, the trading with known pirates, or furnishing them with ammunition, or fitting out any vessel for that purpose, or in anywise consulting, combining, confederating, or corresponding with them; or the forcibly boarding any merchant vessel, though without seizing or carrying her off, and destroying or throwing any of the goods overboard; shall be deemed piracy: and such accessories to piracy as are described by the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> William are declared to be principal pirates; and all pirates convicted by virtue of this act are made felons without benefit of clergy. By the same statutes also, (to encourage the defence of merchant-vessels against pirates), the commanders or seamen wounded, and the widows of such seamen as are slain, in any piratical engagement, shall be entitled to a bounty to be divided among them, not exceeding one-fiftieth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the value of the cargo on board: and such wounded seamen shall be entitled to the pension of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; which no other seamen are, except only such as have served in a ship of war. And if the commander shall behave cowardly, by not defending the ship, if she carry guns or arms; or shall discharge the mariners from fighting, so that the ship falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of pirates; such commander shall forfeit all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, and suffer six months imprisonment. Lastly, by statute 18 Geo. II. c. 30, any natural-born subject or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a>, who in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of war shall commit hostilities at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> against any of his fellow-subjects, or shall assist an enemy on that element, is liable to be tried and convicted as a pirate.

PIRAEUS PORTUS

Pages 186-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a celebrated port to the west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, consisting naturally of three harbours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> basins, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>); which lay neglected, till Themistocles put the Athenians on making it a commodious port, (Nepos); the Phalerus, a small port, and not far from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, being what they used before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, (Paufanias, Nepos). Piraeus was originally a village of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, (Paufanias), an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, (Strabo); and though distant 40 stadia from Athens, was joined to it by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> walls, (Thucydides), and itself locked or walled round, (Nepos): A very commodious and safe harbour. The whole of its compass was 60 stadia, including the Munichia. Not far from the Piraeus stood the sepulchre of Themistocles; whither his friends conveyed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNESIA">Magnesia</a>, into the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, (Cicero, Plutarch, Paufanias). The entrance of the Piraeus is narrow, and formed by two rocky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, one belonging to the promontory of Eetion, the other to that of Alcimus. Within were three stations for shipping; Kantharos, so named from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>; Aphrodium, from a temple of Venus; and Zea, the refort of vessels laden with grain. By it was a demos or borough town of the same name before the time of Themistocles, who recommended the exchanging its triple harbour for the single one of Phalerum, both as more capacious and as better situated for navigators. The wall was begun by him when archon, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of the 75th Olympiad, 477 years before Christ; and afterwards he urged the Athenians to complete it as the importance of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> deserved. This whole fortification was of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, without cement or other material, except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which were used to hold together the exterior ranges or facings. It was so wide that loaded carts could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> on it in different directions, and it was 40 cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which was about half what he had designed. The Piraeus, as Athens flourished, became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> emporium of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Hippodamus an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, celebrated, besides other monuments of his genius, as the inventor of many improvements in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, was employed to lay out the ground. Five porticoes, which uniting formed the Long Portico, were erected by the ports. Here was an agora or market-place, and, farther from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, another called Hippodamia. By the vessels were dwellings for the mariners. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was opened, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were raised, and the Piraeus, which surpassed the city in utility, began to equal it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The cavities and windings of Munichia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, were filled with houses; and the whole settlement, comprehending Phalerum and the ports of the Piraeus, with the aréna, the storehouses, the famous armory of which Philo was the architect, and the fleets for 300, and afterwards 400, triremes, resembled the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, which had been planned by the same Hippodamus. The ports, on the commencement of the Peloponnesian... Piraeus, Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were secured with chains. Centinels were stationed, and the Piraeus was carefully guarded. The Piraeus was reduced with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty by Sulla, who demolished the walls, and set fire to the armory and arsenals. In the civil war it was in a defenseless condition. Calenus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> to Caesar, seized it, invested Athens, and ravaged the territory. Strabo, who lived under the emperors Augustus and Tiberius, observes, that the many wars had destroyed the long walls, with the fortresses of Munychia, and had contracted the Piraeus into a small settlement by the ports and the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Saviour. This fabric was then adorned with wonderful pictures, the works of illustrious artists, and on the outside with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. In the second century, besides houses for triremes, the temple of Jupiter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> remained, with their images in bronzes, and a temple of Venus, a portico, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Themistocles. The port of the Piraeus has been named Porto Liona, from the marble lion seen in the chart, and also Porto Dracco. The lion has been described as a piece of admirable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, 10 feet high, and as resting on its hinder parts. It was pierced, and, as some have conjectured, had belonged to a fountain. Near Athens, in the way to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, was another, the posture couchant; probably its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. Both these were removed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> by the famous general Morosini, and are to be seen there before the arsenal. At the mouth of the port are two ruined piers. A few vessels, mostly small craft, frequent it. Some low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> at the head seems an incroachment on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The buildings are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> customhouse, with a few sheds; and by the shore on the east side, a warehouse belonging to the French; and a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> dedicated to St Spiridon. On the opposite side is a rocky ridge, on which are remnants of the ancient wall, and of a gateway towards Athens. By the water-edge are vestiges of building; and going from the customhouse to the city on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, traces of a small theatre in the side of the hill of Munychia.

PIRATE

Pages 187-188

(πειρατής, Gr.) a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-robbler, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an armed ship that roams the seas without any legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and seizes or plunders every vessel she meets indiscriminately, whether friends or enemies. The colours usually displayed by pirates are said to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> field, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>'s head, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-axe, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>-glass. The last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> is generally supposed to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> allowed to the prisoners, whom they take, to consider whether they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> join the pirates in their felonious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, or be put to death, which is often perpetrated in the most cruel manner. Amongst the most celebrated pirates of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> is recorded Alvida, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> named Sigaraius. She embraced this occupation to deliver herself from the violence imposed on her inclination, by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with Alf, son of Sigaraius king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. She dressed herself as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and composed her band of rowers, and the rest of her crew, of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young women attired in the same manner. Amongst the first of her cruises, she touched at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of pirates bewailed the death of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. The strangers were captivated with the agreeable manners of Alvilda, and chose her for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. By this reinforcement she became formidable upon the sea, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Alf came to engage her. She sustained his attacks for a considerable time; but, in a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, Alf boarded her vessel, and having killed the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of her crew, seized the captain, namely herself; whom nevertheless he knew not, because the princess had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASQUE">casque</a> which covered her visage. Being <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of her person, he removed the casque; and in spite of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, instantly recognized her, and offered her his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in wedlock.

PIRENE

Pages 188-188

(Pliny); a fountain sacred to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, springing below the top of the Acrocorinthus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and steep mountain which hangs over Corinth. Its waters were agreeable to drink, (Pausanias); extremely clear, (Strabo); very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, (Atheneus); and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, (Periplus): having relation either to the grief of Pirene, mother of Cenchrea, from whose tears this fountain arose, (Pausanias); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the paleness brought on by the too eager pursuits of the muses.

PIROMALLI

Pages 188-188

PAUL, a Dominican of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, was sent a missionary into the east. He remained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, where he had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to bring back to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> many schismatics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUTYCHIANS">Eutychians</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> himself, who had before thrown every obstacle in his way. He afterwards passed into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, then into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of Pope Urban VIII's nuncio, in order to appease the disturbances which had been occasioned there by the disputes of the Armenians, who were very numerous in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Piromalli reunited them in the profession of the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and observance of the same ceremonies. In his return to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he was taken by some corsairs who carried him prisoner to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. As soon as he was ransomed, he went to Rome, and gave an account of his mission to the pope, who conferred upon him some signal marks of his esteem. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> entrusted him with the revival of an Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, and sent him again into the east, where he was promoted, in 1655, to the bishopric of Nasirvan. After having governed that church for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years, he returned to Italy, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the church of Bafgiano, where he died three years after in 1667. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, his zeal, and other virtues, did <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the Episcopal office. There are extant of his writings, 1. Some works of Controversy and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>. 2. Two Dictionaries; the one a Latin-Perfian, and the other an Armenian-Latin. 3. An Armenian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>. 4. A Directory, which is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in correcting Armenian books. All these works equally distinguish him for virtue and for learning.

PIRON

Pages 188-189
ALEXIS, a French poet, was born at Dijon in July 1689, where his father was an apothecary, and where he passed more than 30 years in idle and destructive dissipation. He was at length obliged to quit the place of his nativity, in order to avoid the reproaches of his fellow citizens, on account of an ode which he had written, and which gave great offence. His relations not being able to give him much assistance, he supported himself at Paris by means of his pen, the strokes of which were as beautiful and fair as those of an engraver. He lived in the house of M. de Bellisle as his secretary, and afterwards with a financier, who did not know that he had a man of genius under his roof. His reputation as a writer commenced with some pieces which he published for the entertainment of the populace, and which showed strong marks of original invention; but what fully established his character in this way was his comedy intitled Metromancy, which was the best that had appeared in France since Regnard's Gamellet. This performance, in five acts, well conducted, replete with genius, wit, and humour, was acted with the greatest success upon the French stage in 1738. The author met with every attention in the capital which was due to a man of real genius, and whose flashes of wit were inexhaustible. We shall insert a few anecdotes of him, which will serve to show his character and turn of mind. In Burgundy the inhabitants of Beaune are called the Affet de Beaune. Piron often indulged his satirical disposition at their expense. One day as he was taking a walk in the neighbourhood of that city, he diverted himself with cutting down all the thistles which he met with. When a friend asked him his reason for doing so, he replied, "J'ai à me plaindre des Beaunois; je leur coupe les vivres," i.e., "I am sorry indeed for the Beaunois; for I am cutting down their food." Being told again that these people would certainly be revenged of him, Allez, (says he) Allez : je ne crains point leur impuissant courroux; Et quand je serais seul, je les battrais tous. "Get you gone, get you gone: I fear not their feeble revenge; for though alone, I should beat them all." Going into a theatre one time where a play was acting, he asked what it was? The Cheats of Scapin, gravely replied a young Beaunian. "Ah! Sir, (says Piron, after thanking him), I took it to be the Cheats of Orefles." In the time of the play, some body addressed the company with "Silence there, gentlemen, we don't hear." "It is not at least (cried Piron) for want of ears." A bishop one day asked Piron, during the disputes about Jansenism, "Did you read my mandate, Mr Piron?" No, my lord; and you—The conversation turning very warm, the bishop reminded him of the difference which birth and rank had put between them. "Sir (says Piron), I have plainly the superiority over you at this moment; for I am in the right, and you are in the wrong."—Voltaire's Semiramis did not meet with a very favourable reception the first time it was acted. The author finding Piron behind the scenes, asked him what he thought of his performance? "I think (replied he) you would have been pleased that I had been the author of it." The performer of the character Ferdinand Cortez (the title of one of Piron's tragedies) having requested some corrections to be made on the play the first time it was acted, Piron fired at the word corrections. The player, who was deputed to wait upon the author with this request, cited the example of Voltaire, who corrected some of his pieces in order to gratify the taste of the public. "The cases are widely different (replied Piron); Voltaire works in chequer-work, and I cast in brafs." If this answer be not very modest, we must allow that it does not want wit. He thought himself, if not superior, at least equal to Voltaire. Some person congratulating him on having composed the best comedy of this age, he answered, with more frankness than modesty, "Add too, and the best tragedy." The following verses are well known, in which he says: *En deux mots voulez-vous distinguer et connoitre* *Le rimeur Dijonnois et le Parisien?* *Le premier ne fut rien, et ne voulut rien être;* *L'autre voulut tout être, et ne fut presque rien.* We see by these different traits that Piron had a sufficient stock of self-conceit. What helped to increase it, and make him fancy himself superior to the most celebrated of his contemporaries, was, that his company, on account of his original humour, of which he had an uncommon share, was more courted than that of Voltaire, who was otherwise too lively, too captious, and crabbed. But those who have favoured us with an account of his many witticisms in conversation, would have done more honour to his memory if they had passed over such as were either indecent or infipid. A thing often pleases over a glass of wine, which will not give the same satisfaction when it is repeated, especially if, in repeating it, you want to make it appear of some importance. Be that as it may, Piron's mischievous ingenuity was partly the cause which excluded him from the French Academy.—"I could not (said he) make thirty-nine people think as I do, and I could less think as thirty-nine do." He called that celebrated society very unjustly *les invalides du bel esprit*, "the invalids of wit;" and yet he often endeavoured to be one of those invalids. His death was hastened by a fall which he got a little before. He died the 21st of January 1773, at the age of 83. He had prepared for himself the following epitaph, in the way of an epigram: *Ci git Piron, qui ne fut rien,* *Pas même académicien.* "Here lies Piron, who was nothing, not even an academician." His wife Maria Theresa Quenandon, who died in 1751, he describes as a sweet and most agreeable companion. They lived together for several years; and no husband ever discharged his duty with more fidelity and attention. A collection of his works appeared in 1776, in 7 vols 8vo, and 9 vols 12mo. The principal pieces are, The School of Fathers; a comedy acted in 1728 under the title of Ungrateful Sons. Callithene; a tragedy, the subject of which is taken from Juvin. The Mysterious Lover, a comedy. Gustavus and Ferdinand Cortez, two tragedies; some scenes of which discover an original genius, but the versification neither pleases the ear nor affects the heart. Metromany, a comedy. The Courtes of Tempe, an ingenious pastoral, in which the manners both of the town and country are pleasantly drawn. Some odes, poems, fables, and epigrams. In this last kind of poetry he was very successful, and he may be placed after Marot and Rousseau. There was no occasion for loading the public with 7 vols of his works; the half of that number might have sufficed. For, excepting Metromany, Gustavus, the Courtes of Tempe, some odes, about 20 epigrams, three or four fables, and some epistles, the rest are but indifferent, and have no claim to any extraordinary merit.

PISA

Pages 189-190

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the river Arno, 12 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>.
