It was a famous republic, till subdued, first by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and then by the Florentines in the year 1406. Before it lost its freedom, it is said to have contained near 150,000 inhabitants, but now it has not above 16,000 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 17,000. It was founded, we are told, by the Pisans of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, and afterwards became one of the 12 municipia of Tuscany. Its neighbourhood to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, which is now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> port in the Mediterranean, though formerly of little or no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> for trade, has contributed greatly to the decay of Pisa, which, however, begins to lift up its head again, under the auspices of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> duke, who has made it his winter residence. Between Pisa and Leghorn is a canal 16 Italian miles in length.—Its territory is very fruitful; abounding in corn, wine, and fruit, and fine cattle. The houses are well built, and the streets even, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and well paved; but in many places overrun with grass. The university is well endowed, and has able professors, but is not in a very flourishing condition. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> is a stately structure, but little frequented. The grand duke's galleys are built, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> stationed here. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> residence of the order of St Stephen, and the see of an archbishop. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, a large Gothic pile, contains a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent paintings and other curiosities. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is dedicated to St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; is very advantageously situated in the middle of a large <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIAZZA">piazza</a>, and built out of a great heap of wrought marble, such as pillars, pedestals, capitals, cornices, and architraves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the spoils which the Pisans took in their eastern expeditions, when the republic was in a flourishing condition. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is supported by 76 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> marble pillars of different colours, and finely gilt. Both the church and the cupola are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. The choir is painted by good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The brazen doors are curiously wrought with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, by Bonanno, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statuary. The chapel of St Rainerius is richly adorned with gilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, columns of porphyry, and fine paintings. In the middle of the nave of the church you see two brazen tombs, raised upon pillars. The marble pulpit was carved by John Pifano, and the choir by Julian da Majana. Joining thereto is the altar, over which is preferred a hollow globe or vessel of marble, wherein they kept the sacrament for the new baptized, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Father Mabillon. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> before the church, you see a pillar upon which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the ancient Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>. In the same square with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a>, stands the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISTERY">baptistery</a>, a round fabric supported by fluted pillars, and remarkable for a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">echo</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the cathedral is the burying-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, called Campo Santo, being covered with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> brought from the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. This burying-place is inclosed with a broad portico, well painted, and paved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Here are a great many ancient tombs, among the rest that of Beatrice, mother of the countess Mathilda, with marble basso-relievos, which the Pisans brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, where you see the hunt of Meleager, which assisted Nicholas of Pisa in the reformation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>. The walls of the Campo Santo are painted by the best masters of their times. Giotto has drawn six historical pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>; and Andrea Orgagna has given a fine piece of the last judgement. Under the portico there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the city, ordering the inhabitants to wear <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> a year for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cesar. Near the church you see a steeple in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, to which you ascend by 153 steps; it inclines 15 feet on one side, which some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to art, but others to the sinking of the foundation. Its inclination is so great that a plumb-line let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the top touches the ground at the distance of almost 15 feet from the bottom. It was built by John of Infruck and Bonanno of Pisa, in 1174. Near this steeple is a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, dependent on that of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Nuova in Florence. The steeple of the church of the Augustinians is also very fine, being an octagon, adorned with pillars, and built by Nicholas of Pisa. In the great market-place there is a statue of Plenty, by Pierino da Vinci. In the church of St Matthew, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> of the ceiling by the brothers Mclani, natives of this city, is an admired performance. The church of the knights of St Stephen, decorated with the trophies taken from the Saracens, is all of marble, with marble steps, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> adorned with marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>. In the square there is a statue of Cosimo I. upon a very fine pedestal. Contiguous to the church is the convent or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the knights, which is worth seeing, as also the churches Della Madonna and Della Spina; the last of which was built by a beggar, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> you may see on the outside of the wall. It is pretended that one of the thorns of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> which was placed on our Saviour's head is preserved here. Belonging to the university there is a great number of colleges, the chief of which is the Sapienza, where the professors read their public lectures; next to which are the colleges Puteano, Ferdinando, Ricci, and others. Besides the public palace, and that of the grand duke, there are several others with marble fronts, the finest of which is that of Lanfranchi, which, with the rest along the banks of the Arno, makes a very fine appearance. There is here a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>, where they build the galleys, which are conveyed by the Arno to Leghorn. They have a famous aqueduct in this town, consisting of 9000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, which conveys the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the hills at five miles distance. This water is esteemed the best in Italy, and is carried in flasks to Florence and Leghorn. The neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> produces great store of corn and wine, but the latter is not much esteemed. They have very good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> in this neighbourhood, which is a scarce commodity in Italy. The city for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>, walls, a castle, fort, and citadel; the last of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> work. The Arno is of a considerable breadth here, and has three bridges over it, one of them of marble: two leagues below the town it falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The physic garden is very spacious, contains a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and is decorated with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER_WORKS">water-works</a>: over the door leading into it are these words, Hic Argus sed non Briareus est: i.e. "Employ the eyes of Argus, but not the hands of Briareus." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is said to be unwholesome here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, on account of the neighbouring marshes. Many buffaloes are bred in the neighbouring country, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is commonly eaten. Between Pisa and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> are hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 17'. N. Lat. 43° 43'.

Pages 190-190

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> statutes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s waters.

PISCES

Pages 190-190

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, the 12th sign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> constellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>.

PISCINA

Pages 190-190

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin in a public <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, where the Roman youth learned to swim: and which was surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall, to prevent filth from being thrown into it.—This word is also used for a lavatory among the Turks, placed in the middle <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of a mosque or temple, where the Mussulmans wash themselves before they offer their prayers.

PISIDIA

Pages 190-190

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. PISIDIA Erythrina, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Dogwood-tree, is employed to intoxicate fish. For this purpose, the bark is pounded Pisidina, small, put into bags, and soaked in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The juice, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>, which is of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, makes the fish stupid, so that they are easily taken.

PISISTRATUS

Pages 190-193

an Athenian who early distinguished himself by his valour in the field, and by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and eloquence at home. After he had rendered himself the favourite of the populace by his liberality and by the intrepidity with which he had fought their battles, particularly near <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, he resolved to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Everything seemed favourable to his ambitious views; but Solon alone, who was then at the head of affairs, and who had lately enforced his celebrated laws, opposed him, and discovered his duplicity and artful behaviour before the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. Pisistratus was not disheartened by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of his relation Solon, but he had recourse to artifice. In returning from his country-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he cut himself in various places; and after he had exposed his mangled body to the eyes of the populace, deplored his misfortunes, and accused his enemies of attempts upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, because he was the friend of the people, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the reliever of the oppressed, he claimed a chosen body of 50 men from the populace to defend his person in future from the malevolence and the cruelty of his enemies. The unsuspicious people unanimously granted his request, though Solon opposed it with all his influence; and Pisistratus had no sooner received an armed band on whose fidelity and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> he could rely, than he seized the citadel of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>. The people too late perceived their credulity; yet, though the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> was popular, two of the citizens, Megacles and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, conspired together against him, and by their means he was forcibly ejected from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. His house and all his effects were exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; but there was found in Athens only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who would buy them. The private dissensions of the friends of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> proved favourable to the expelled tyrant; and Megacles, who was jealous of Lycurgus, secretly promised to restore Pisistratus to all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges in Athens, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would marry his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. Pisistratus consented; and by the affiance of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he was soon enabled to expel Lycurgus, and to re-establish himself. By means of a woman called Phya, whose shape was tall, whose features were noble and commanding, he imposed upon the people, and created himself adherents even among his enemies. Phya was conducted through the streets of the city, and showing herself subservient to the artifice of Pisistratus, she was announced as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and the patroness of Athens, who came <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from Heaven to re-establish her favourite Pisistratus in a power which was sanctioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of Heaven, and favoured by the affection of the people. In the midst of his triumph, however, Pisistratus found himself unsupported; and some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, when Pisistratus, when he repudiated the daughter of Megacles, he found that not only the citizens, but even his very troops, were alienated from him by the influence, the intrigues, and the bribery of his father-in-law. He fled from Athens where he no longer could maintain his power, and retired to Euboea. Eleven years after he was drawn from his obscure retreat, by means of his son Hippias, and he was a third time received by the people of Athens as their master and sovereign. Upon this he sacrificed to his resentment the friends of Megacles, but he did not lose sight of the public good, and while he fought the aggrandizement of his family, he did not neglect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Athenian name. He died about 528 years before the Christian era, after he had enjoyed the sovereign power at Athens for 33 years, and he was succeeded by his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIPPARCHUS">Hipparchus</a>. Pisistratus claims our admiration for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, his liberality, and his moderation. If he was dreaded and detested as a tyrant, the Athenians loved and respected his private virtues and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a> as a fellow-citizen; and the opprobrium which generally falls on his head may be attributed not to the severity of his administration, but to the republican principles of the Athenians, who hated and exclaimed against the moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> of the mildest sovereign, while they flattered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and gratified the guilty desires of the most tyrannical of their fellow subjects. Pisistratus often refused to punish the insolence of his enemies; and when he had one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> been virulently accused of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, rather than inflict immediate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> upon the man who had criminated him, he went to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">areopagus</a>, and there convinced the Athenians that the accusations of his enemies were groundless, and that his life was irreproachable. It is to his labours that we are indebted for the preservation of the poems of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; and he was the first, according to Cicero, who introduced them at Athens in the order in which they now stand. He also established a public library at Athens; and the valuable books which he had diligently collected were carried into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> made himself master of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. Hipparchus and Hippias the sons of Pisistratus, who had received the name of Pisistratides, rendered themselves as illustrious as their father; but the flames of liberty were too powerful to be extinguished. The Pisistratide governed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> moderation, but the name of tyrant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sovereign was unsupportable to the Athenians. Two of the most respectable of the citizens, called Harmodius and Aristogeiton, conspired against them, and Hipparchus was dispatched in a public assembly. This murder was not, however, attended with any advantages; and though the two leaders of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>, who have been celebrated through every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> for their patriotism, were supported by the people, yet Hippias quelled the tumult by his uncommon firmness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and for a while preserved that peace in Athens which his father had often been unable to command. This was not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> to continue. Hippias was at last expelled by the united efforts of the Athenians and of their allies, and he left Attica, when he found himself unable to maintain his power and independence. The rest of the family of Pisistratus followed him in his banishment; and after they had refused to accept the liberal offers of the princes of Thessaly, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, who wished them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in their respective territories, the Pisistratide retired to Sigeum, which their father had in the summit of his power conquered and bequeathed to his posterity. After the banishment of the Pisistratide, the Athenians became more than <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> jealous of their liberty, and often sacrificed the most powerful of their citizens, apprehensive of the influence which popularity and a well-directed liberality might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> among a fickle and unsettled populace. The Pisistratide were banished from Athens about 18 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Pisistratus. Pismires, or Ants, are a kind of insects very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; of which there is so great a variety, and such innumerable swarms, that they destroy not only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the ground but sometimes even men and beasts in little time as one single night; and would, without all doubt, prove more fatally destructive to the inhabitants, were they not so happily destroyed by a proportionable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of monkeys and other animals, who greedily devour them. The far greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the vast continent of Africa is afflicted with these and some other grievous plagues, and particularly with the horrid visitation of locusts, which seldom fail a year of laying waste some of the provinces. Piso, Lucius Calpurnius, surnamed Frugi on account of his frugality, was descended of the illustrious family of the Pisos, which gave so many great men to the Roman republic. He was tribune of the people in the year 149 before Christ, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. During his tribuneship, he published a law against the crime of concupiscence or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTORTION">extortion</a>, intitled Lex Calpurnia de pecuniae repetundis. He happily ended the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. To reward the services of one of his sons, who had distinguished himself in that expedition, he left him by his will a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, weighing 20 pounds. Piso joined to the qualities of a good citizen the talents of a lawyer, an orator, and historian. Piso, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Calpurnius, a Roman consul in the year 67 before Christ, was author of the law which forbade canvassing for public offices, intitled Lex Calpurnia de ambitu. He displayed all the firmness worthy of a consul in one of the most stormy periods of the republic. The Roman people, deceived by the flattery of Marcus Palicanus, a turbulent and factious fellow, were on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of loading themselves with the greatest disgrace, by putting the supreme authority into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of this man, who deserved punishment rather than honours. The tribunes of the people, by their harangues, inflamed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> fury of the multitude, already sufficiently mutinous of themselves. In this situation, Piso mounted the rostrum, and being asked if he would declare Palicanus consul, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the suffrages of the people should concur in the nomination, he instantly replied, that "he did not think the republic was yet involved in such darkness and despair as to be capable of committing so infamous an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>." Being afterwards strongly and repeatedly called upon to say, "what he would do, if the thing should happen?" his answer was, "No, I would not name him." By this firm and laconic answer he deprived Palicanus of the dignity to which he aspired. Piso, according to Cicero, was not possessed of a quick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, but he thought maturely, and with judgment, and, by a proper firmness, he appeared to be an abler man than he really was. Piso, Cnecius Calpurnius, was consul in the reign of Augustus, and governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> under Tiberius, whose confidant he was. It is said, that by the order of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> he caused Germanicus to be poisoned. Being accused of that crime, and seeing himself abandoned by every body, he laid violent hands on himself in the 26th year of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. He was a man of infupportable pride and excessive violence. Some instances of his wicked cruelty have been handed down to us. Having given orders in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to conduct to punishment a folder, as guilty of the death of one of his companions, because he had gone out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> with him and returned without him, no prayers or intreaty could prevail with Piso to suspend the execution of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> until the affair should be properly investigated. The folder was led without the entrenchments, and had already presented his head to receive the fatal stroke, when his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> whom he was accused of having killed made his appearance again. Whereupon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CENTURION">centurion</a>, whose office it was to see the sentence executed, ordered the executioner to put up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> into the scabbard. Those two companions, after embracing each other, are conducted to Piso, amidst the acclamations of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and a prodigious crowd of people. Piso, foaming with rage, ascends his tribune, and pronounces the same sentence of death against the whole three, without excepting the centurion who had brought back the condemned folder, in these terms: "You I order to be put to death because you have been already condemned; you, because you have been the cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of your comrade; and you, because having got orders to put that folder to death, you have not obeyed your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>." Pissasphaltum, or Asphaltum, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>-pitch; a fluid, opaque, mineral body, of a thick consistence, strong smell, readily inflammable, but leaving a residuum of greyish ashes after <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. It arises out of the cracks of the rocks, in several places in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and some other places in the East Indies, where it is much esteemed in paralytic disorders. There is a remarkable mine of it in the island of Bua, (see BUA), of which the following curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given us by the Abbé Fortis. "The island is divided into two promontories between the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west. Cropping over the top of the latter, which is not half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and descending in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, one is conducted to a hole well known to the inhabitants. This hole extends not much above 12 feet, and from its bottom above 25 feet perpendicular, arise the marble <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> which sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> masses that sur-round the top of the mountain. This piffalphaltum is of the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and shining, very pure, odoriferous, and cohesive; and it comes out almost liquid, but hardens in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> drops when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> sets. On breaking many of these drops on the spot, I found that almost every one of them had an inner cavity full of very clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. "The greatest breadth of the tears that I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> was two inches, and the common breadth is half an inch. The chinks and fissures of the marble, from whence this bituminous pitch tranfudes, are not more than the thickness of a thread; and for the most part are so imperceptible, that were it not for the pitch itself, whereby they are blackened, they could not by any means be distinguished by the naked eye. To the narrowness of these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> is, no doubt, in part owing the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of piffalphaltum that tranfpires." After some conjectures about the origin of this mine, our author proceeds to inform us that the piffalphaltum of Bua is correspondent to that fossil production which by Haefelquilt, in his Travels, is called mumia minerales, and mumia nativa Persiana by Kempfer, which the Egyptians made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to embalm their kings (A). It is found in a cave of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, which is kept shut, and carefully guarded by order of the king of Persia. One of the qualities assigned by M. Linnæus to the finest bitumen is to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> when laid on the fire, as ours does, emitting a smell of pitch not disagreeable. He believes it would be very good for wounds, as the oriental mummia is, and like the pitch of Caltro, which is frequently used by the Roman surgeons for fractures, contusions, and in many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> applications. See ASPHALTUM, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Pissellæum Indicum, Barbados Tar; a mineral fluid of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the thicker bitumens, and of all others the most approaching, in appearance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and consistence, to the true piffalphaltum, but differing from it in other respects. It is very frequent in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where it is found trickling down the sides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in large quantities, and sometimes floating on the surface of the waters. It has been greatly recommended internally in coughs and other disorders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and lungs. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PISTACIA">Pistacia</a>, Turpentine-tree, Pistachia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> and Macfick-tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The terebinthus, or pistachia-tree, which grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, Persia, and Syria, whence the nuts are annually brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In those countries it grows to the height (A) "Mumiahi, or native Persian mummy. It proceeds from a hard rock in very small quantity. It is a bituminous juice, that tranfudes from the stony superficies of the hill, resembling in appearance coarse thomakers wax, as well in its colour as in its density and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCTILITY">ductility</a>. While adherent to the rock it is left <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, but is formed by the warmth of the hands. It is easily united with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, but repels water; it is quite void of smell, and very like in substance to the Egyptian mummy. When laid on burning coals, it has the smell of sulphur tempered a little with that of naphtha, not disagreeable. There are two kinds of this mummy; the one is valuable for its scarcity and great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. The native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the best mummy is far from the access of men, from habitations, and from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of water, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Daraab. It is found in a narrow cave, not above two fathoms deep, cut like a well out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, at the foot of the rugged mountain Caucasus."—Kempfer. Amoen. Pers. This description agrees perfectly with the piffalphaltum or fossil mummy of Bua, differing only in the privation of smell, which it is difficult to imagine is totally wanting in the Persian mummy. height of 25 or 30 feet; the bark of the stem and old branches is of a dark rufous colour, but that of the young branches is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. These are garnished with winged leaves, composed sometimes of two, at other times of three, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of lobes, terminated by an odd one: these lobes approach towards an oval shape, and their edges are turned backward; and these, when bruised, emit a smell similar to that of the shell of the nut. Some of these trees produce <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and some have both male and female on the same tree. The male flowers come out from the sides of the branches in loose bunches or catkins. They have no petals, but five small stamens crowned by large four-cornered summits filled with farina; and when this is discharged, the flowers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off. The female flowers come out in clusters from the sides of the branches: they have no petals, but a large oval germen supporting three reflexed styles, and are succeeded by oval nuts. 2. The lentifcus, or common mastic tree, grows naturally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Being an evergreen, it has been preferred in this country in order to adorn the green-houses. In the countries where it is a native, it rises to the height of 18 or 20 feet, covered with a grey bark on the stem; but the branches, which are very numerous, are covered with a reddish brown bark, and are garnished with winged leaves, composed of three or four pair of small spear-shaped lobes, without an odd one at the end. 3. The orientalis, or true mastic tree of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, from which the malachite is gathered, has been confounded by most botanical writers with the lentifcus, or common mastic tree, above described, though there are considerable differences between them. The bark of the tree is brown; the leaves are composed of two or three pair of spear-shaped lobes, terminated by an odd one: the outer lobes are the largest; the others gradually diminish, the innermost being the least. These turn of a brownish colour towards the autumn, when the plants are exposed to the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; but if they are under glasses, they keep green. The leaves continue all the year, but are not so thick as those of the common sort, nor are the plants so hardy. Culture. The first species is propagated by its nuts, which should be planted in pots filled with light <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden earth, and plunged into a moderate hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> to bring up the plants; when these appear, they should have a large share of air admitted to them, and by degrees they should be exposed to the open air, which at last they will bear in all seasons, though not without great danger of being destroyed in severe winters. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort is commonly propagated by laying down the branches, though it may also be raised from the seed in the manner already directed for the pistacia-nut tree; and in this manner also may the true mastic-tree be raised. But this being more tender than any of the other sorts, requires to be constantly sheltered in winter, and to have a warm situation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Pistacia nuts are moderately large, containing a kernel of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> greenish colour, covered with a reddish skin. They have a pleasant, sweet, unctuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, resembling that of almonds; and they abound with a sweet and well-tasted oil, which they yield in great abundance on being pressed after bruising them: they are reckoned amongst the analeptics, and are wholesome and nutritious, and are by some esteemed very proper to be prescribed by way of restoratives, eaten in small quantity, to people emaciated by long illness.

PISTIL

Pages 193-193

among botanists, the little upright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> which is generally found in the centre of every flower. According to the Linnaean system, it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, whose office is to receive and secrete the pollen, and produce the fruit. It consists of three parts, viz. germen, style, and stigma. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. PISTOIA is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, situated on the river Stella, in a beautiful plain near the foot of the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. By Pliny it is called Pyllorium, and is said to have been once a Roman colony. At present it is a bishop's see, suffragan of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. The streets are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and regular, the houses tolerably well built, but poorly inhabited for want of trade. Formerly it was an independent republic, but since it was subdued by the Florentines in 1200, it has been in a declining condition. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> has a very handsome cupola, and a magnificent staircase to ascend to it. In the chapel dedicated to St James, where his relics are preserved, the walls are almost covered with plates of silver. Here are four marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of very good workmanship. The marble pulpit, the belfry, relieves, the vessel that holds the holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> steeple, are the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of John Pifano. The Jesuits have a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and the Franciscans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>, and Augustinians, good churches. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Madonna dell' Umiltà there are two statues, one of Leo X. and the other of Clement VII. The public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, situated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> square, is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; several of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> have also very good houses. In the neighbouring mountains, called by the name of Pistoia, there are many large villages, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is that of S. Marcello, belonging to the family of Cartoli. These mountains are a part of the Apennines, and border on the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Vernio; higher up is the source of the river Reno. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Pistoia, especially towards Florence, is exceeding fertile and delightful, covered with all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, corn, wine, &c. &c. containing a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, wealthy villages, and country seats, so as to be reckoned the richest and most beautiful in all Tuscany. It is about 20 miles N.W. of Florence, and 30 N.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 29'. N. Lat. 43° 55'.

PISTOL

Pages 193-193

the smallest piece of fire-arms, borne at the fadde-bow, on the girdle, and in the pocket.

PISTOLE

Pages 193-193

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, struck in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and in several parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, &c.—The pittole has its augmentations and diminutions, which are quadruple pittoles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> pittoles, and half pittoles. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">Money</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>.

PISTON

Pages 193-193

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, is a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> of metal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substance, fitted exactly to the cavity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> or body of the pump. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a>.

PISUM

Pages 193-195

Pease; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diadelphia clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are, 1. The sativum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> greater garden-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, whose lower stipules are roundish, indented, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> foot-stalks, and many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on a foot-stalk. 2. The humile, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> pea, with an erect branching stalk, and leaves having two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of round lobes. 3. The umbellatum, rose or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-pea, with four pointed acute stipules, and foot- stalks. stalks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> many flowers, which terminate the stalks. 4. The maritimum, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-pea, with foot-stalks which are plain on their upper side, an angular stalk, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>-pointed stipulae, and foot-stalks bearing many flowers. 5. The Americanaum, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a> pea, with an angular trailing stalk, whose lower leaves are spear-shaped, sharply indented, and those at the top arrow-pointed. 6. The ochrus, with membranaceous running foot-stalks, having two leaves and one flower upon a foot-stalk. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of garden-peas now cultivated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which are distinguished by gardeners and seedmen, and have their different titles; but as great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of these have been seminal variations, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not very carefully managed, by taking away all those plants which have a tendency to alter before the seeds are formed, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> degenerate into their original state: therefore all those persons who are curious in the choice of their seeds, look carefully over those which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> for seeds at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they begin to flower, and draw out all the plants which they dislike from the other. This is what they call roguing their peas; meaning hereby the taking out all the bad plants from the good, that the farina of the former may not impregnate the latter; to prevent which, they always do it before the flowers open. By thus diligently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> out the bad, referring those which come earliest to flower, they have greatly improved their peas of late years, and are constantly endeavouring to get forwarder varieties; so that it would be to little purpose in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to attempt giving a particular account of all the varieties now cultivated: we shall therefore only mention the names by which they are commonly known, placing them according to their time of coming to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or gathering for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> hotspur. Nonpareil. The Chartop. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> dwarf. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a> hotspur. Sickle pea. Mutter's hotspur. Marrowfat. Effex hotspur. Rose or crown pea. The dwarf pea. Runcival pea. The sugar pea. Gray pea. Spanish Morotto. Pig pea; with some others. The English sea-pea is found wild upon the shore in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> and several other counties in England, and is undoubtedly a different species from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pea. The fifth species hath a biennial root, which continues two years. This was brought from Cape Horn by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Anson's cook, when he passed that cape, where these peas were a great relief to the sailors. It is kept here as a curiosity, but the peas are not so good for eating as the worst sort now cultivated in Britain. It is a low trailing plant; the leaves have two lobes on each foot-stalk: those below are spear-shaped, and sharply indented on their edges; but the upper leaves are small, and arrow-pointed. The flowers are blue, each foot-stalk sustaining four or five flowers; the pods are taper, near three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and the seeds are round, about the size of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARES">tares</a>. The sixth sort is annual. This grows naturally among the corn in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, but is here preserved in botanic gardens for the sake of variety. It hath an angular stalk, rising near three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the leaves stand upon winged foot-stalks, each sustaining two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> lobes. The flowers are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, shaped like those of the other sort of pea, but are small, each foot-stalk sustaining one flower; these are succeeded by pods about two inches long, containing five or six roundish seeds, which are a little compressed on their sides. These are by some persons eaten green; but unless they are gathered very young, they are coarse, and at best not so good as the common pea. It may be sown and managed in the same way as the garden pea. For an account of the method of cultivating the several sorts of garden peas, so as to continue them throughout the season, see <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>. The gray and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> winter peas are seldom cultivated in gardens, because they require a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of room; they are therefore usually sown in fields. For the proper method of managing them, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> Rusticum, vol. i. p. 109, we find the following method of preparing peas for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, which we shall give in the words of the ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> who communicated it. "A few years ago (says he), I had a plentiful crop of peas on a ten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> piece, which lies near my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>: when they were full podded and nearly ripe, I had them hooked in the usual manner; but before I could get them in, there came a heavy shower of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> which wetted them through and through; and the dull heavy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, with frequent showers which followed, prevented their drying for a considerable time. "I caused the wads to be from time to time turned, to prevent the haulm from rotting; and at length a few days sunshine dried them enough to be mowed; for as they lay hollow, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> was greatly assistant to the operation. "Before I got them in, on examining some of the pods, I found that the peas were all sprouted to a considerable length; this was what I had expected, as I gave my crop over for loft, till after a little recollection, as the weather still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> fine, I determined to thresh them in the field. "This was accordingly done; and the corn, after it was <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and riddled to separate it from the rubbish, was dried on my malt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>. "When this operation was over, I began to reflect in what manner I should dispose of my peas, being sensible that they could not be proper for feed, and standing no chance of disposing of them to any advantage in the market. "At length, as it was then a time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and of course there was a great demand for pork for the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, I determined to buy a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lean hogs, that I might by their means consume this crop on my own premises, and in that manner make the most of it. "My expectations were more than answered; for I found, by repeated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that three bushels of the peas I have mentioned went nearly as far in fattening the hogs I bought as four bushels got in dry and hard in the manner usually practised. "This discovery I made several years ago, and it has turned out to my advantage; for since that time I have been quite indifferent as to the weather in which my peas are hooked, being rather better pleased, as far as relates to them, with wet than dry weather;" PIT ther; but if the weather happens to be dry at the time they are ripe, I always cause as many as I want for feeding my hogs, which are not a few in a year, to be regularly malted in the same manner nearly as my barley: this management has of late succeeded very well with me, and I therefore intend to continue it. "Besides feeding my hogs with these malted pease, I have often given them to my horses, with which they agree very well, and are heartening food. "Turkeys will fatten apace on them also, and be fine meat. "I have applied my malted pease to many other uses, which I have not at present time to enumerate: but were they only used for feeding hogs and horses, it is still worth while to prepare some in this manner every year."

PITCAIRNE

Pages 195-198

Dr Archibald, an eminent physician and ingenious poet, was descended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family of the Pitcairnes of Pitcairne in Fifehire, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1652. He commenced his studies at the school of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALKEITH">Dalkeith</a>; and from thence he was removed to the university of Edinburgh, where he improved himself in classical learning, and completed a regular course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. His friends, according to the authors of the Biographia Britannica, were delirious that he should follow the profession of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. The unpleasant gloom, however, which at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> hung over <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and its professors Pitcairne in Scotland, could not but very ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with that native cheerfulness of temper and liberality of mind which made him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, a mark for the arrows of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> and grimace. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> seems to have been his own choice, and to this science he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. With an ardour peculiar to himself, and an ambition to excel in whatever he undertook, he pursued it with so much intensity, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> began to be impaired. On this account, his physicians advised him to let out for the south of France. By the time he reached <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was happily so far recovered, that he determined to renew his studies; but being informed that there was no able professor of law in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and finding several gentlemen of his acquaintance engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic, he went with them to the lectures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and employed himself in this manner for several months till his affairs called him home. On his return, he applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. It is not usual to see the briars of this science and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> growing in the same foil. Here, however, they were happily united; and to this union perhaps was owing that singular command of judgement, over one of the liveliest of fancies, which appears in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his works. His intimacy with Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Gregory, the celebrated mathematical professor, began about the same time; and probably conduced to cherish his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> aptitude for this study. It was then in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, new to him; it soon became his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> delight; his progress in it was rapid, and correspondent to his progress in other pursuits. His improvements on the method of infinite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> then adopted, which Dr Wallis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> afterwards published, were a conspicuous and early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his abilities in this science. Had Dr Pitcairne <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to prosecute the study of the law, and could he have moulded his principles to the times, the first offices and honours of the state might have been looked for without presumption as the probable reward of such talents as he possessed. Struck, however with the charms of mathematical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> which had been lately introduced into the philosophy of medicine, and hoping to reduce the healing art to geometrical method, he unalterably determined on this less aspiring profession. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when he formed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the medical world, already sufficiently confused, were still farther jumbled by the discovery of the circulation of the blood, which had as yet produced nothing but doubt, uncertainty, and astonishment. In Edinburgh at that time there was no school, no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, no opportunity of improvement but the chamber and the shop. He therefore soon after returned to Paris. Genius and industry are unhappily not often united in the same character: of such an union, however, Dr Pitcairne is a celebrated instance. During his residence in France, he cultivated the object of his pursuit with his natural enthusiasm, and with a steadfastness from which he could not be diverted by the allurements of that joy which, in his hours of social and festive intercourse, he always felt and always gave. Among his various occupations, the study of the ancient physicians seems to have had a principal share. This appears from a treatise which he published some time after his return; and it shows, that he wisely determined to know the progress of medicine from its earliest periods, before he attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> and improve that science. On the 13th of August 1689, he received, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>; which, on the 7th of August 1699, was likewise conferred on him by the university of Aberdeen; both being attended with marks of peculiar distinction. Other medical honours are said to have been conferred on him in France and elsewhere; but nothing affords a more unequivocal testimony to his abilities than that which the surgeons of Edinburgh gave, in admitting him, freely and unostentatiously, a member of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. None had such opportunities of judging of his merit as a practitioner, and on no physician did they ever bestow the same public mark of respect. Soon after his graduation at Rheims, he returned to Edinburgh; where, on the 29th of November 1681, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> College of Physicians was instituted; and his name, among others, graced the original patent from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. In his Soluto Problematis de Inventoribus, the treatise above alluded to, he discovers a wonderful degree of medical literature, and makes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in a manner that does great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> both to his head and his heart. His object is to vindicate Dr Harvey's claim to the discovery of the circulation of the blood. The discovery was, at first, controverted by envy, and reproached by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. When at length its truth was fully established, many invidiously attempted to tear the laurels from the illustrious Englishman, and to plant them on the brows of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> and others. Had the attempt been directed against himself, the generous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of Pitcairne could not have exerted more zeal in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; and his arguments remain unanswered. During his residence in Scotland, his reputation became so considerable, that, in the year 1691, the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> solicited him to fill the medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, at that time vacant. Such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimony of respect, from a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and from such an university, cannot perhaps be produced in the medical biography of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The lustre of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> reflects honour on their profession, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which has the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> of giving them birth; and serves to give the individuals of that country not only a useful estimation in their own eyes, but in those also of the rest of the world. Dr Pitcairne's well-known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles excluded him from public honours and promotion at home; he therefore accepted the invitation from abroad; and, on the 26th of April 1692, delivered, at Leyden, his elegant and masterly inaugural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>: Oratio qua ostenditur medicinam <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> omni philo- (A) Dr Boerhaave gives the following character of these and some other of Dr Pitcairne's dissertations, which were collected and published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, anno 1701: "Hec scripta optima sunt et perfecta, five legas Dissertacionem de Motu Sanguinis per Pulmones, five alia opuscula, five ultimum tractatum de Opio." Methodus studii, ab Hallero edita, p. 509. (B) He had been married before to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> James Hay of Pitfour, by whom he had a son and daughter, who both died young. (C) Vide Pitcairnii Poemata.—Several of his poems, however, are obscure, and some of them totally unintelligible without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>. In those of them which are of a political kind, he wished not to express himself too clearly; and in others, he alludes to private occurrences which were not known beyond the circle of his companions. His poem (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">Ad</a> Lindeium), addressed to his friend Lindley, is commented on by the authors of the Biographia Britannica; and it is to be regretted that it is the only one on which they have been solicitous to throw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. exerted in the cure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, still operate to the good of posterity. The discovery of the circulation, while in some measure it exploded the chemical and Galenical doctrines, tended to introduce mathematical and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> reasoning in their stead. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> (n) Dr Pitcairne was the principal support, and the first who introduced it into Britain. A mathematical turn of mind, and a wish for mathematical certainty in medicine, biased him in its favour, and he pushed it to its utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. One is at a loss whether most to admire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> regret such a waste of talents in propounding a theory which, though subversive of former ones, was to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> before others but a little more satisfactory than itself. Mechanical physicians expected more from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> than that science could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>. They made it the foundation instead of an auxiliary to their inquiries, and applied it to parts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> not admitting mathematical calculations. By paying more attention afterwards to the supreme influence of the living principle, the source of all the motions and functions of the body, it was found that these could not be explained by any laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> or mechanism. They are still, however, involved in obscurity; and notwithstanding the numberless improvements which have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the sciences connected with medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps remain incurable while <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> continues in his present stage of existence. In a science so slowly progressive as that of medical practice, Dr Pitcairne did a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>. By labouring in vain for truth in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, he saved many the same drudgery, and thereby showed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of another. He not only exploded many false notions of the chemists and Galenists which prevailed in his time, but many of those too of his own feet. In particular, he showed the absurdity of referring all diseases and their cures to an alkali or an acid (r). He refuted the idea of secretion being performed by pores differently shaped (v), Bellini's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of effervescences in the animal spirits with the blood, and Bonelli's of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> entering the blood by respiration (g). He proved the continuity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> and veins (h); and seems to have been the first who showed that the blood flows from a smaller capacity into a larger; that the aorta, with respect to the arterial system, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> of a cone (i). In this therefore he may be considered as the latent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the discoveries respecting the powers moving the blood. He introduced a simplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> unknown in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> before his time (k); and such was the state of medicine in this country, that scarcely have the works of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> or preceding author been thought worthy even of preservation (l). As to the errors of his philosophy, let it be remembered, that no theory has as yet stood the test of many years in an enlightened period. His own hung very loosely. light. "Some parts (fay they) of this poem, are hardly intelligible, without knowing a circumstance in the doctor's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which he often told, and never without some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>. It is a well known story of the two <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophers, who promised one another, that whichever died first should make a visit to his surviving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. This story being read by Mr Lindley and our author together, they being both then very young, entered into the same engagement. Soon after, Pitcairne, at his father's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Fife, dreamed one morning that Lindley, who was then at Paris, came to him, and told him he was not dead, as was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reported, but still alive, and lived in a very agreeable place, to which he could not yet carry him. By the course of the poet news came of Lindley's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened very suddenly the morning of the dream. When this is known, the poem is easily understood, and shines with no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. "Lyndell! Stygiæ jamdudum vesta per undas, "Stagnaque Cocytii non adeunda mihi; "Exeunte paulisper Lethæi vincula somni, "Ut feriant animum carmina nostra tuum. "Te nobis, te redde tuis, promissa datus "Gaudia; sed proavo sis comitante redux: "Namque novos viros mutataque regna videbis, "Pallaque Teutonicæ sceptræ Britannæ manus *." * Written in 1689. "He then proceeds to explain against the principles and practices which produced this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> violence upon the British sceptre; and concludes with a wish, that Lindley might bring Rhadamantus with him to punish them. "Unus abest fcelerum vindex Rhadamantus; amice, "Dil faciant redditus fit comes ille tui. "Every one sees how much keener an edge is given to the satire upon the Revolution, by making it an additional reason for his friend's keeping his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to return him a visit after his death." (n) See the article Physiology. (e) Pitcarnii Diffutationes, Edin. edit. 1713. De <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> quam praestant corpora acida vel alkalica in curatione morborum. (f) De circulatione sanguinis per vaia minima. (g) De diversa <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> qua sanguis fluit per pulmones. (h) De circulatione sanguinis per vaia minima. (i) De circulatione sanguinis in animalibus genitis et non genitis. (k) Elementa Medicinae, lib. i. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 21. et passim. (l) The first medical publication which distinguished this country, after Dr Pitcairne's, was that of the Edinburgh Medical Essays, in the year 1732. Vid. the article Monro. PITCAIRNE loosely about him (m); and the present generally received practice differs from his very little in reality. He treated inflammatory and hemorrhagic diseases by bleeding, purging, and blistering, as has been done uniformly and solely on the different theories since. His method of administering <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> and the bark is observed at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and with respect to febrile, nervous, glandular, and tropical affections, they seem to be as often the opprobrium of the art now as they were then. Dr Pitcairne was universally considered as the first physician of his time. No one appeared ever to have had so much practice in this country, or so many consultations from abroad; and no one, from all accounts, ever practised with greater sagacity and success. The highest thought themselves honoured by his acquaintance, and the lowest were never denied his assistance and advice. The emoluments of his profession must have been great; but his charities are known to have been correspondent. The possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he postponed to more liberal objects; he collected one of the finest private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in the world; which was purchased, after his death, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> of Muscovy. Notwithstanding the fatigues he underwent in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his profession, his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was naturally delicate. About the beginning of October 1713, he became affected with his last illness; and on the 23rd he died, regretted by science as its ornament, by his country as its boast, and by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> as its friend. He left a son and four daughters: of whom only one of the latter now survives. The present noble family of Kelly are his grandchildren. Some anonymous publications are attributed to Dr Pitcairne, particularly a treatise De Legibus Historiae Naturalis, &c.; but the only ones he thought proper to legitimate are his Dissertationes Medicae, and a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> De Salute. PITCAITHLY. See PITCAITHLY.

Pages 198-198

a tenacious oily substance, drawn chiefly from pines and firs, and used in shipping, medicine, and various arts: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is more properly tar infusitated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> it over a slow fire. See TAR. Fossil PITCH. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETROLEUM">PETROLEUM</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PITCHING

Pages 198-198

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-affairs, may be defined the vertical vibration which the length of a ship makes about her centre of gravity; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the movement by which she plunges her head and after-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> alternately into the hollow of the sea. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> may proceed from two causes: the waves which agitate the vessel; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> upon the sails, which makes her stoop to every blast thereof. The first absolutely depends upon the agitation of the sea, and is not susceptible of inquiry; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is occasioned by the inclination of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, and may be submitted to certain established maxims. When the wind acts upon the sails, the mast yields to its effort, with an inclination which increases in proportion to the length of the mast, to the augmentation of the wind, and to the comparative <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and distribution of the ship's lading. The repulsion of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to the effort of gravity, opposes itself to this inclination, or at least sustains it, by as much as the repulsion exceeds the momentum, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> effort of the mast, upon which the wind operates.
