At the end of each blast, when the wind fulfils its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, this repulsion lifts the vessel; and these succussive inclinations and repulsions produce the movement of pitching, which is very inconvenient; and, when it is considerable, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> greatly retard the course, as well as endanger the mast, and strain the vessel.

PITCOAL

Pages 195-195
or STONE-COAL. See COAL, MINERALOGY Index, and COALERY. The coal-trade is of infinite importance to Great Britain, which never could have arrived at its present commercial eminence without it; and this eminence it will be impossible to retain if coal should ever become scarce. This we trust is not likely to be the case, though Mr Williams expresses great fears for it, and informs us that at Newcastle and in many parts of Scotland, the mines near the sea are already wasted, the first consequence of which must be an enormous rise in the price. See his observations on this subject in his href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History of the Mineral Kingdom. This author says, that coal was not discovered till between the middle of the 12th and beginning of the 13th centuries: it is therefore, according to him, 400 years since it was first discovered in Britain, but they have not been in common use for more than 200 years. The same author makes many excellent observations on the appearances and indications of coal, instructions about searching for it, remarks on false and doubtful symptoms of coal; for all which, together with his observations on the different kinds of Scots coal, we shall refer our readers to the work itself; the first part of which, occupying a large proportion of it, is upon the strata of coal, and on the concomitant strata. See GEOLOGY and STRATA of the earth. PITAHAYA (Cactus Pitahaya). Lin. Syb. Vegetabilium. Jacquin Amer. 151. ed. 2d. p. 75. M. E. Carthagena), a shrub peculiar to California, the fruit of which forms the greatest part of the harvest of the natives. Its branches are finely fluted, and rise vertically from the stem, so as to form a very beautiful top. The fruit is like a horse-chestnut; in some white, in others yellow, and in others red, but always exquisitely delicious, being a rich sweet, tempered with a grateful acid. See CACTUS, BOTANY Index.

PITHO

Pages 198-198

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of perfusion among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. She was supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> and Venus, and was represented with a diadem on her head, to intimate her influence over the hearts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. One of her arms appeared raised in the attitude of an orator haranguing in a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>; and with the other she holds a thunderbolt and fetters, made with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, to signify the powers of reasoning and the attractions of eloquence. A caduceus, as a symbol of persuasion, appears at her feet, with the writings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a> and Cicero, the two most celebrated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, who understood how to command the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of their audience, and to rouse and animate their various passions.—A Roman courtezan. She received this name on account of the allurements which her charms possessed, and of her winning expressions.

PITHOM

Pages 198-198

one of the cities that the children of Israel built for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> (Exod. i. ii.) during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their servitude. This is probably the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with Pathumos mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, which he places upon the canal made by the kings <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECHO">Necho</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> to join the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, and by that means with the Mediterranean. We find also in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> geographers, that there was an arm of the Nile called Pathmeticus, Phatnicus, Phainicus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Phainiticus. Bochart says, that Pithom and Raamles are about five leagues above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Nile, and beyond this river; but this assertion has no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> from antiquity. This author contents himself with relating what was said of Egypt in his own time. Marsha <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have Pithom to be the same as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELUSIUM">Pelusium</a> or Damietta. PITHOU or PITHOEUS, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, a Frenchman of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> literary eminence, was descended from an ancient and noble family in Normandy, and born at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TROYES">Troyes</a> in 1539. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature appeared very early, and his father cultivated it to the utmost. He first studied at Troyes, and was afterwards sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he became first the scholar, and then the friend, of Turenne. Having finished his pursuits in languages and the belles lettres, he was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, and placed under Cujacius in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His father was well skilled in this profession, and has left no inconsiderable --- (m) Patet (says he) medicinam esse memoriam eorum quae cuilibet morbo usus ostendit usu utilia. Nam notas non esse corporum intra venas fluentium aut consistentium naturas, adeoque sola observatione innotescere quid cuique morbo conveniat postquam siuepius eadem eadem morbo profuisset comperimus. De Div. Morb.

PITKEATHLY

Pages 198-199
or Pitcaithly, is the name of Pitkeathly, an estate in Strathern in Scotland, famous for its mineral waters. An intelligent traveller* gives the following account of it. "The situation of the mineral spring at Pitcaithly, the efficacy with which its waters through the Western Counties of Scotland are said to operate in the cure of the diseases for which they are used, and the accommodations which the neighbourhood affords, are all of a nature to invite equally the sick and the healthy. Two or three houses are kept in the style of hotels for the reception of strangers. There is no long-room at the well; but there are pleasing walks through the adjoining fields. Good roads afford easy access to all the circumjacent country. This delightful tract of Lower Strathern is filled with houses and gardens, and situations from which wide and delightful prospects may be enjoyed; all of which offer agreeable points to which the company at the well may direct their forenoon excursions; conversation, music, dances, whist, and that best friend to elegant, lively, and social converse, the tea-table, are sufficient to prevent the afternoons from becoming languid; and in the evenings nothing can be so delightful as a walk when the setting sun sheds a soft glancing light, and the dew has just not begun to moisten the grasses.—Thus is Pitcaithly truly a rural watering-place. The company cannot be at any one time more in number than two or three families. The amusements of the place are simply such as a single family might enjoy in an agreeable situation in the country; only the society is more diversified by the continual change and fluctuation of the company." The waters of this place are of a sulphureous nature.

PITOT

Pages 199-200

John, the biographer, was born in 1560, at Aulton in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, and educated at Wykeham's school, near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, till he was about 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; when he was sent to New-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and admitted probationer fellow. Having <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in that university not quite two years, he left the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> as a voluntary Roman exile, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>; thence he went to the English college at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, where he remained about a year; and then proceeded to Rome, where he continued a member of the English college near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, and was made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. In 1589 he returned to Rheims; and there, during two years, taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> and the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He now quitted Rheims on account of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> in France; and retired to Pont à Mousson in Lorraine, where he took the degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts and bachelor in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. Hence he travelled into Germany, and resided a year and a half at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIER">Trier</a>, where he commenced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICENTIATE">licentiate</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>. From Trier he visited several of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities in Germany; and continuing three years at Ingolstadt in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in divinity. Thence having made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he returned once more to Lorraine; where he was patronized by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, who preferred him to a canonry of Verdun; and about two years after he became confessor to the duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Lorraine. During the leisure he enjoyed in this employment, he wrote in Latin the lives of the kings, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, apostolic men, and writers of England. The last of these, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known and quoted by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, De illybris Angliae scriptoribus, was published after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The three first remain still in manuscript among the archives of the collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Liverdun. The duke of Cleves dying after Pitts had been about twelve years confessor to the duchess, he returned to Lorraine, attended by our author, who was promoted to the deanery of Liverdun, which, with a canonry and officialship, he enjoyed to the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He died in 1616, and was buried in the collegiate church. Pitts was undoubtedly a scholar, and not an inelegant writer; but he is justly accused of ingratitude to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>, from whom he borrowed his materials, without acknowledgment. He quotes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> familiarity, without ever having seen his book: his errors are innumerable, and his partiality to the Roman writers most obvious; nevertheless we are obliged to him for his account of several popish authors, who lived abroad at the beginning of the Reformation.

PITSCUS

Pages 199-199

Samuel, a learned antiquary, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, and was rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and afterwards of St Jerome at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, where he died on the 1st of February 1717, aged 90. He wrote: 1. Lexicon Antiquitatum Romanarum, in two volumes folio; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which is esteemed. 2. Editions of many Latin authors, with notes; and other works.

PITT

Pages 202-205

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> William, was the fourth child of that illustrious orator and consummate statesman, William Pitt, the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, and was born on the 28th of May 1759. Nicholas Pitt, who lived in the reign of Henry VI., was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ancestor of the noble families of Chatham, Camelford, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">Rivers</a>. Thomas Pitt, the first of the name who attained any considerable eminence, was governor of Fort St George in the East Indies, where he purchased, as noticed in the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, for 20,400l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, the extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> called the regent, weighing 127 carats, and which was sold to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France for the enormous sum of 135,000l. sterling. This diamond it is said, now occupies a conspicuous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the imperial diadem of Bonaparte. Bonaparte. By means of this vast sum he was enabled to purchase a considerable estate in Cornwall; yet his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-children were poorly provided for, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> earl of Chatham, but what he wanted in opulence was abundantly supplied by the uncommon talents and abilities, which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> conferred upon him in the profusest manner. Although he betook himself for support to the profession of arms, he never rose higher than to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a cornet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, of which Sir Robert Walpole, with unexampled meanness, deprived him, because he had the boldness and integrity to oppose his administration. This, however, proved no real obstacle to his preferment in the state, for in the year 1756 he became prime minister. As the present earl of Chatham was destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and another son James <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Chatham resolved to train up William to the profession of a statesman. Having therefore confided the care of his other two sons to others, he took William under his own immediate inspection, whose rapid progress cheered the solitude, and illumined the declining days of this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who already began to prefigure his future greatness. His school exercises were performed under the care of a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, a Mr. afterwards Dr Wilson, while his noble father embraced every opportunity of conversing with him on every interesting topic with the utmost freedom, in order to expand his mind, and mature his judgement. He also made him declaim from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, well knowing that the gift of eloquence is a valuable acquisition for a young man who wishes to arrive at eminence, and that it had supplied the deficiencies of fortune in his own person. It was resolved on, at a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, to send William to one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and on this occasion <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> was preferred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, from a decided <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> entertained by many, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> doctrines inculcated at the former were more liberal than those usually propagated at the latter. He was accordingly placed under the tuition of Dr Turner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>. Dr Prettyman, afterwards bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, also participated in the care of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and was his private instructor. During his residence at Cambridge, it appears certain that the morals and conduct of Mr Pitt were unimpeachable, not in the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> contaminated by the powerful example of the young <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. Here he took his bachelor's degree, and also that of A.M. and acquired such reputation in the university for talents, industry, and propriety of deportment, as proved of great advantage to him in his subsequent pursuits through life. When Mr Pitt left the university, he was entered at Lincoln's Inn, much about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with Mr Addington, whose father had been both the physician and friend of his family, and was enabled to be called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> in the space of three years, having received some marks of favour on account of his degree. He made choice of the western circuit as the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his first efforts; but having little practice as an lawyer, he had of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> but little celebrity; and it is probable that he was ill qualified, on the score of patient and laborious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, for a pursuit in which nothing great can be accomplished, without the persevering industry of a whole life. Fortune at this time seemed eager to heap favours upon him of another kind. Being bred a statesman, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons was of course the place where he was to begin his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. He was advised by numerous friends to propose himself a candidate for the university of Cambridge, but he failed of success from the want of sufficient influence. Accident, however, brought about what the designs of his friends could not accomplish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Rutland asked Sir James Lowther (afterwards earl of Lonsdale), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could possibly make room in any of his boroughs, to bring in his young friend Mr Pitt, who had thus lost his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> for Cambridge. He was chosen member for the borough of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPLEBY">Appleby</a>. About this time the American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was raging with unabated violence, which Mr Pitt, following the example and advice of his father, reproached as one of the most shameful and ruinous conflicts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. Having espoused the constitutional and popular side of this important question, his opening talents were displayed to no common advantage, and he was not only regarded as a promising speaker, but as destined at some future period to rank <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the councils of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This was truly honourable to so young a man, when it is remembered that one horse could then boast of a Rockingham, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, and a Shelburne, and the other of a Savile, a Dunning, a Burke, a Barré, and a Fox. Yet there was still room for our juvenile orator, and the recollection of the eloquence, the talents, and the meritorious services of his father, contributed greatly to fix the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of mankind on the deportment of a favourite son. About this time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> engaged the attention both of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> and the public, and a vote of the commons, "that the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> had increased, was increasing, and ought to be diminished," plainly pointed to an object, whether real or imaginary, which occasioned a considerable degree of discontent. Mr Burke, then in the zenith of his popularity, encouraged by numerous symptoms of jealousy, once more brought forward his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of economy, which being founded on a progressive retrenchment, appeared admirably calculated to diminish the influence of the crown. It is needless to add that it was opposed by the minister (Lord <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>), but it was ably supported by Mr Pitt, who forcibly ridiculed every objection that could be brought against it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> was rejected after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> debate, but afterwards introduced at a more auspicious period, and to a certain extent carried into effect. Mr Fox having moved that ministers should immediately take every possible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for concluding a peace with our American colonies, he was powerfully supported by Mr Pitt, whose commanding eloquence engaged the whole attention of the house, while he reproved the cruelty and impolicy of the contest with our colonies. He declared that it was conceived in injustice, nurtured and brought forth in folly, and its footsteps were marked with blood, slaughter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, and devastation. Many handsome compliments were paid him by two eminent judges of real merit, we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the lord advocate of Scotland (now Viscount Melville), and Mr Wilkes. The former, in particular, declared that his powerful abilities and brilliant eloquence were universally acknowledged proofs, that the astonishing extent and force of an exalted understanding had descended, in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> line, from the late illustrious possessor of them, to a son equally endowed with all the fire, and strength, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> of oratory. A more equal representation of the people in parliament was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects to which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> directed its attention, next to the American war. It was admitted to be the undoubted prerogative of the crown to declare war; but as the supplies were entrusted to the management of the representatives of the people, it was affirmed by some that ministers could not have carried on a contest accompanied with the waste of so much blood and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, had it not been owing to the corruption and venality of parliament. To derive advantage from past <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; to confer on the people their due importance in such a mixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> as that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and restore the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to its original purity, became by this time the grand object of Mr Pitt's exertions. He was, as yet untainted by the fascinating charms of power and authority, and considered a well-earned fame as the best, the only reward of his laudable endeavours. He accordingly brought the principles and conduct of his opponents to such a test as they successfully employed against himself, in order to wound his feelings, and convict him of inconsistency, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> his back on his once favourite sentiments. When many cities and counties endeavoured to obtain a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> in parliament, Mr Pitt actually sat in a convention of delegates, met together in the neighbourhood of the place where the legislature held its sittings. The American war in the mean time was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> to a termination, and the spoils of the office of the former minister became the reward of those who opposed him. During the short existence of the Rockingham administration, contractors were excluded from the house of commons; officers belonging to the customs and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> were declared unqualified to vote at elections; the proceedings respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a> election were rescinded; and while a more liberal policy was adopted with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, many superstitious offices were abolished in England by means of a reform bill, which tended powerfully to destroy corruption. Many more important reforms would have been accomplished, had not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the distinguished Rockingham brought about great and sudden changes. Mr Fox retired in consequence of new arrangements, and Lord Shelburne, as first lord of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, made choice of Mr Pitt as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer, who, declared, although only 23 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, that he would accept of no inferior office. Peace now seemed to be an object generally desirable at any rate, and without much regarding what sacrifices might be made in order to procure it; but the terms met with powerful opposition from two men formerly considered as mortal enemies, viz. Lord North and Mr Fox, the latter of whom retired from office. Soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of Mr Fox, Mr Pitt again brought forward the question respecting a reform in parliament, which he fondly hoped would be the means of restoring him to his wonted popularity, and pave the way to the increase of his power. He therefore submitted three different motions to the consideration of the house; but although in these motions he was ably supported, he was left in a minority. The coalition ministry, as it was called, had still a considerable majority in parliament, notwithstanding the popularity belonging to the name and talents of Mr Pitt, but the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> bill was productive of a change. This bill owed its origin to Mr Burke, but it received a regular and systematical opposition from the ex-chancellor of the exchequer. It was carried, however, in the house of commons by a great majority, but in the house of lords it was opposed by the duke of Richmond, Lord Thurlow, and Earl Temple (afterwards marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>); and on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1783, it was finally rejected by a majority of 19. The king in the meantime determined on an entire change of administration, and the two secretaries were informed on the 18th of December 1783, about 12 o'clock at night, that his majesty had no further occasion for their services. In consequence of this change, the important offices of first lord of the treasury and chancellor of the exchequer were bestowed on Mr Pitt, who thus became prime minister before he was full 24 years of age. Thurlow was created lord chancellor, the duke of Richmond keeper of the privy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; the marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERNARVON">Caernarvon</a> then and Lord Sidney were chosen secretaries of state, and Mr Dundas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the navy. Much about this time Mr Pitt brought forward a new bill for the better government of India. He proposed that a board of control should be instituted, the nomination of whose members was to be vested in the crown, and to them the dispatches of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> were to be submitted. He also proposed that the appointment of the commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> should belong to his majesty, and having thus secured the political interests of the company, he left those of a commercial nature entirely to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of directors. This bill, after a short debate, was rejected by a majority of eight. Such was the present temper of the house of commons, that a coalition or immediate dissolution became absolutely necessary; and the former having been unsuccessfully attempted, the latter was suddenly adopted, on the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1784. Mr Pitt having been returned for the university of Cambridge, again brought forward his bill in an amended state for the regulation of India, and carried it in triumph through both houses of parliament. The remaining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the session gave birth to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> for the better prevention of smuggling, and the commutation act, by virtue of which certain duties were transferred from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> to windows. When Mr <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">Alderman</a> Sawbridge (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 16th 1784) made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> for inquiring into the present state of the commons of Great Britain in parliament, Mr Pitt, whose political sentiments had undergone a revolution, felt himself considerably embarrassed, as he was reminded that he had brought forward questions on the same subject upon a former occasion. Mr Pitt, however, declined it, on account of the pressure of public business, and observed that, in his opinion, the present was not the proper time for bringing forward the question, and that it might be urged with greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of success on some future occasion. He did not wish it to be discussed in a precipitate manner, yet the business itself should have every support he was able to afford it. Having now attained the summit of power and influence as prime minister, Mr Pitt exercised every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of his important office, without any check or control. Possessed of a great majority in both houses of parliament, as well as in the cabinet, his whole deportment, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of his opponents, seems to have become lofty in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>; and he paid little or no regard to that popularity which he had formerly courted. A commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> about this time was entered into with France, the terms of which have been generally acknowledged. acknowledged to be advantageous to Britain. Mr Pitt, who deserves great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> for giving the plan his countenance, adopted, much about the same time, another respecting the finances, from which he derived a high degree of reputation; and, as he pointed at a period when the national debt might, in all probability, be extinguished, the country, if it was not altogether satisfied, appeared to be at least contented under his administration; and it is not a little to the credit of his financial system, that his opponents, when in power, not only approved, but adopted and extended it. In this manner a commercial country began again to flourish, by turning its attention to the arts of peace; but, during his administration, its prosperity was threatened to be interrupted by the preparations for an attack upon Russia at one time, and by an open rupture with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> at another, relative to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOOTKA">Nootka</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. In both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the blow was warded off by negotiation, and a good understanding restored. The restoration of the tradeholder, by the intervention of a Prussian army, and his strenuous opposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>'s appointment to the regency during the king's indisposition, were also two important <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> pursued and discussed in the course of his ministry. Soon after the commencement of the French revolution, Mr Pitt deemed a war with that country inevitable. But for a full detail of the events of this war, see BATTAIN. Having held the reins of government during 18 years, Mr Pitt, and all the members of the cabinet, suddenly retired from office in 1801. On this occasion all parties appeared to rejoice at the appointment of Mr Addington; and France, from that moment, as some affect, seemed to have neither friends nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the treaty of Amiens were debated in the house of commons, Mr Pitt defended the new minister with the whole force of his abilities and influence. On the 15th of March 1804, Mr Pitt made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> attack on the administration; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> board was accused by him of imbecility. He zealously supported Mr Fox's proposition relative to the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> bill for the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, which was lost on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. The minister's majority having dwindled to 37, on the army of reserve suspension bill, Mr Addington and some of his friends retired, and the ex-minister resumed his former seat. When parliament met on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1805, Mr Pitt warmly defended the war with Spain; and, on the motion for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, he had a majority of 207. But, in the meantime, a gouty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, the predisposing causes of which appear to have been hereditary, and which, perhaps, was increased by his own manner of living, seized on a constitution never very strong. It is alleged, by his opponents, that this, combined with the miscarriage of his schemes, and the aspect of affairs on the continent, preyed so much upon his mind, that he is said to have died of a broken heart, at his house near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUTNEY">Putney</a>, between four and five on Wednesday morning, January 23, 1806, in the 47th year of his age. As a financier, no man has obtained more praise, who ever presided at the board of exchequer. During his ministry some of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> languished, but many flourished, and our exports were greatly increased. As a speaker he was unrivalled, and his generous scorn of wealth must be admired. In 20 years his debts amounted only to 40,000l. They were paid out of the public purse. The house of commons also passed a vote, that the expenses of his funeral, and a monument to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, should be defrayed by the nation.

PITTAUS

Pages 205-205

a native of Mitylene in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>, was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wise men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>: his father's name was Hyrradus. With the assistance of the sons of Alcaeus, he delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from the oppression of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> Melanchrus; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> which the Athenians waged against Lesbos, he appeared at the head of his countrymen, and challenged to single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> Phrynon, the enemy's general. As the event of the war seemed to depend upon this combat, Pittacus had recourse to artifice; and when he engaged, he entangled his adversary in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> which he had concealed under his shield, and easily dispatched him. He was amply rewarded for this victory; and his countrymen, sensible of his merit, unanimously appointed him governor of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with unlimited authority. In this capacity Pittacus behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>; and after he had governed his fellow-citizens with the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and after he had established and enforced the most salutary laws, he voluntarily resigned the sovereign power after having enjoyed it for 10 years, observing, that the virtues and innocence of private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were incompatible with the power and influence of a sovereign. His disinterestedness gained him many admirers; and, when the Mitylenians wished to reward his public services by presenting him with an immense tract of territory, he refused to accept more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> than what should be contained in the distance to which he could throw a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>. He died in the 70th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, about 579 years before Christ, after he had spent the last 10 years of his life in literary ease and peaceful retirement. The following maxims and precepts are ascribed to Pittacus: The first office of prudence is to foresee threatening misfortunes, and prevent them. Power discovers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Never talk of your schemes before they are executed; lest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you fail to accomplish them, you be exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> mortification of disappointment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>. Whatever you do, do it well. Do not that to your neighbour which you would take ill from him. Be watchful for opportunities. Many of his maxims were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>'s temple at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a>, to show to the world how great an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> the Mitylenians entertained of his abilities as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a moralist, and a man. By one of his laws, every fault committed by a man when intoxicated deserved double <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>.

PITTENWEEM

Pages 205-206

a small town situated on the frith of Forth, towards the eastern extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Fife in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It takes its name from a small cave in the middle of it, anciently called a queens; and is remarkable for nothing but the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which is sometimes called an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> and sometimes a priory. Which of these is the proper denomination it is hardly worth while to inquire; but it appears from the arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, still preserved over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> gate, that the superior, by whatever <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> he was called, had the privilege of wearing a mitre. This edifice, which seems never to have been <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, was, with other monuments of mistaken piety, alienated from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at the Reformation; and what parts of it now remain are are put to very different uses. Some of the cells of the monks furnish habitations tolerably convenient for the servants of him who, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of change of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, has got possession of the lands which formerly belonged to them. That which seems to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> is a decent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church. The porch of the chapel, the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> which exists, has been alternately employed as a stable and a slaughterhouse; and the meat killed there has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> in the lower part of the steeple of that edifice which is now dedicated to the offices of parochial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Had the moralizing traveller*, who composed the beautiful and pathetic meditation on the ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONA">Iona</a>, considered to visit Pittenweem, he would not have viewed the abbey without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>. Insignificant as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at present is, it seems to have been of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the last century; and we are led to infer, from the following extract from the records, that the inhabitants were opulent, and that the town was fortified. "Pittenweem, decimo quarto Feb. 1651. The bailies and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> being convened, and having received information that his majesty is to be in progress with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> tomorrow, and to stay at Anstruther house that night, have thought it expedient, according to their bounden duty, with all reverence and due respect, and with all the same solemnity they can, to wait upon his majesty, as he comes through this his majesty's burgh, and invite his majesty to eat and drink as he passes; and for that effect hath ordained, that the morn afternoon the town's colours be put upon the belfry of the steeple, and that at three o'clock the bells begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>, and ring on still till his majesty comes hither, and passes to Anstruther: And sickly, that the minister be spoken to, to be with the bailies and council, who are to be in their best apparel, and with them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of 24 of the ablest men, with partizans, and other 24 with muskets, all in their best apparel, William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a> commanding as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the guard; and to wait upon his majesty, and to receive his highnesses at the West Port, bringing his majesty and court through the town, until they come to Robert Smith's* best carpet: and that George Hetherwick have in readiness, of fine flour, some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burns, and other wheat-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> of the best order, taken with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, and other spices fitting; and that James Richardson and Walter Airth have care to have ready eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ten gallons of good strong ale, with Canary, sack, Rhenish wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and claret wines, that his majesty and his court may eat and drink; and that in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, when his majesty is present, the guard do diligently attend about the court; and so soon as his majesty is to go away, that a sign be made to Andrew Tod, who is appointed to attend the colours on the steeple head, to the effect he may give sign to those who attend the cannon of his majesty's departure, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> thirty six cannons to be all foot at once. It is also thought fitting, that the minister, and James Richardson the oldest bailie, when his majesty comes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, show the great joy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> this burgh has of his majesty's condescension to visit the same, with some other expressions of loyalty. All which was acted." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of this town, in 1790, was computed at 1157. N. Lat. 56. 11. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 49.

PITTOSPORUM

Pages 206-206

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. PITUITARY GLAND. See Anatomy Index.

PITYOCAMPASIS

Pages 206-206

in Entomology, the caterpillar of the pine-tree, received its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> name from that substance. It was considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, and as a remedy, according to its different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of application. Our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> information concerning this caterpillar, is derived from M. Reaumur, who has attentively observed its manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The animal cannot bear much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and is therefore never found in the higher latitudes. It is styled procectionary, because it never leaves its hold, where many families reside, till the evening, when it feeds in trains, led on by two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three, and this train leaves a ribbon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> in its way; for those behind follow exactly the steps of those which preceded, and each leaves its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> of silk. Their nests are found in autumn; they are produced in the middle of September, become torpid in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, and recover their strength again in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. They then descend from the trees, plunge into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and undergo their last change. It is the bombix pityocampa of Fabricius, (Manissa Insector, tom. ii. p. 114, No. 66.), and greatly resembled the procectionary caterpillar of the oak. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used it as a vesicatory, and the acrimony seems to reside chiefly in a dust which is concealed in receptacles on its back. This is its offensive weapon, for it is thrown out at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and produces very troublesome effects, though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of the animal and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its body seem to have a similar, but weaker power. The effect is also weaker in winter; but this may depend on the diminished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRRITABILITY">irritability</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, as well as on the torpid state of the insect. Their silk is not sufficiently strong for the loom, and in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> melts almost to a paste. In the earth it forms nests of stronger silk, but it is then found with difficulty: in boxes its silk is extremely tender. Adding to all these inconveniences, handling the cones produces all the bad effects of the dust. Matthiolus recommends them as a styptic, and perhaps they may serve for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> on the skin instead of moxa, the downy silk of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTEMISIA">artemisia</a>. The ancients, afraid of its hurtful qualities, used them with caution, and enacted laws against their being sold profanously: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> planter is chiefly afraid of them, because they destroy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of his trees, and he endeavours to collect the eggs by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off the branches, which are burnt immediately.

PIVAT'

Pages 206-209
or PIVOT, a foot or shoe of iron or other metal, usually conical or terminating in a point, whereby a body, intended to turn round, bears on another fixed at rest, and performs its revolutions. The pivot usually bears or turns round in a sole, or piece of iron or brass hollowed to receive it. PIUS II. (Aeneas-Sylvius Piccolomini), was born on the 18th of October 1405, at Corfigni in the Sienese, the name of which he afterwards changed into that of Pienza. His mother Victoria Forteguerra, when she was with child of him, dreamed that she should be delivered of a mitred infant; and as the way of degrading clergymen at that time was by crowning them with a paper mitre, she believed that Aeneas would be a disgrace to his family. But what to her had the appearance of being a disgrace, was a prelude of the greatest honors. Aeneas was carefully educated, and made considerable proficiency in the belles lettres. After ha- Pius ving finished his studies at Sienna, he went in 1431 to the council of Bale with Cardinal Capranica, named De Fermo, because he was entrusted with the government of that church. Aeneas was his secretary, and was then only 26 years of age. He afterwards acted in the same capacity to some other prelates, and to Cardinal Albergati. The council of Bale honoured him with different commissions, in order to recompense him for the zeal with which he defended that assembly against Pope Eugene IV. He was afterwards secretary to Frederic III, who decreed to him the poetical crown, and sent him ambassador to Rome, Milan, Naples, Bohemia, and other places. Nicholas V advanced him to the bishopric of Trieite, which he quitted some time after for that of Sienna. At last, after having distinguished himself in various negotiations, he was invested with the Roman purple by Calixtus III, whom he succeeded two years after, on the 27th of August 1458. Pius II now advanced to the holy see, made good the proverb, Honores mutant mores. From the commencement of his pontificate, he appeared jealous of the papal prerogatives. In 1460 he issued a bull, "declaring appeals from the pope to a council to be null, erroneous, detestable, and contrary to the sacred canons." That bull, however, did not prevent the procurator-general of the parliament of Paris from appealing to a council in defence of the Pragmatic Sanction, which the pope had strenuously opposed. Pius was then at Mantua, whither he had gone in order to engage the Catholic princes to unite in a war against the Turks. The greater part of them had agreed to furnish troops or money; others refused both, particularly France, who from that moment incurred his holiness's aversion. That aversion abated under Louis XI, whom he persuaded in 1461 to abolish the Pragmatic Sanction, which the parliament of Paris had supported with so much vigour. The following year 1462, was rendered famous by a controversy which took place between the Cordeliers and Dominicans, whether or not the blood of Jesus Christ was separated from his body while he lay in the grave. It was also made a question whether it was separated from his divinity. The Cordeliers affirmed that it was, but the Dominicans were of an opposite opinion. They called each other heretics; which obliged the pope to issue a bull, forbidding them under pain of censure to brand one another with such odious epithets. The bull which his holiness published on the 26th of April, retracting what he had written to the council of Bale when he was its secretary, did not redound much to his honour. "I am a man (says he), and as a man I have erred. I am far from denying that a great many things which I have said and written may deserve condemnation. Like Paul, I have preached through deception, and I have persecuted the church of God through ignorance. I imitate the blessed Augustin, who having suffered some erroneous sentiments to creep into his works, retracted them. I do the same thing; I frankly acknowledge my ignorance, from a fear lest what I have written in my younger years should be the occasion of any error that might afterwards be prejudicial to the interests of the holy see. For if it be proper for any one to defend and support the eminence and glory of the first throne of the church, it is in a peculiar manner my duty, whom God, out of his mercy and goodness alone, without any merit on my part, has raised to the dignity of vicar of Jesus Christ. For all these reasons, we exhort and admonish you in the Lord, not to give credit to those writings of ours which tend in any degree to hurt the authority of the apostolic see, and which establish opinions that are not received by the Roman church. If you find, then, anything contrary to her doctrine, either in our dialogues, in our letters, or in other of our works, despite these opinions, reject them, and adopt our present sentiments. Believe me rather now that I am an old man, than when I addressed you in my earlier days. Esteem a sovereign pontiff more than a private person; except against Aeneas Sylvius, but receive Pius II." It might be objected to his holiness, that it was his dignity alone which had made him alter his opinion. He anticipates that objection, by giving a short account of his life and actions, with the whole history of the council of Bale, to which he went with Cardinal Capranica in 1431; "but (says he) I was then a young man, and without any experience, like a bird just come from its nest." In the mean time, the Turks were threatening Christendom. Pius, ever zealous in the defence of religion against the infidels, forms the resolution of fitting out a fleet at the expense of the church, and of passing over into Asia himself, in order to animate the Christian princes by his example. He repaired to Ancona with a design to embark; but he there fell sick with the fatigue of the journey, and died on the 16th of August 1464, aged 59 years. Pius was one of the most learned men of his time, and one of the most zealous pontiffs; but being of an ambitious and pliant disposition, he sometimes sacrificed to that ambition. His principal works are, 1. Memoirs of the council of Bale, from the suspension of Eugenius to the election of Felix. 2. The history of the Bohemians, from their origin to the year 1458. 3. Two books on cosmography. 4. The history of Frederic III, whose vice-chancellor he had been. This performance was published in 1785 in folio, and is believed to be pretty accurate and very particular. 5. A treatise on the education of children. 6. A poem upon the passion of Jesus Christ. 7. A collection of 432 letters, printed at Milan, 1473, folio, in which are found some curious anecdotes. 8. The memoirs of his own life, published by John Gobelin Peronne his secretary, and printed at Rome in 4to in 1584. There is no doubt of this being the genuine production of that pontiff. 9. Historia rerum ubicumque gestarum, of which only the first part was published at Venice in 1477 in folio. His works were printed at Helmstadt in 1700, in folio, at the beginning of which we find his life. That verse of Virgil's Aeneid (lib. i. 382.) which begins thus, Sum pious Aeneas, and the end of the following verse, fama super aethera notus, have been applied to him. Pius IV. (John Angel, Cardinal de Medicis), of a different family from that of Florence, was born at Milan in 1499. He was son to Bernardin de Medechini, and brother of the famous Marquis de Marignan, Charles V.'s general. He raised himself by his own merit, and filled several important offices under Popes Clement VII. and Paul III. Julius III. who had entrusted him with several legations, honoured him with a cardinal's hat. hat in 1549. After the death of Paul IV. he was advanced to St Peter's chair on the 23rd of December 1559. His predecessor had rendered himself detestable to the Romans, who treated his memory with every mark of indignity, and Pius IV. commenced his pontificate by pardoning them. He did not, however, extend the same clemency to the nephews of Pope Paul IV.; for he caused Cardinal Caraffe to be strangled in the cattle of St Angelo, and his brother, the prince de Palliano, to be beheaded. His zeal was afterwards directed against the Turks and heretics. In order to stop, if possible, the progress of these last, he renewed the Council of Trent, which had been suspended. He knew well (says Abbe de Choisy), that that council might make some regulations which would have the effect to lessen his authority; but, on the other hand, he perceived that great inconveniences might result from its not being assembled; and "in the man (said he to his confidants) it is better to feel evil for once than to be always in dread of it." In 1561 he dispatched nuncios to all the Catholic and Protestant princes, to present them with the bull for calling that important assembly. An end was, however, put to it by the industry of his nephew, S. Charles Borromeus, in 1563; and, on the 26th of January the year following, he issued a bull for confirming its decrees. In 1565 a conspiracy was formed against his life by Benedict Acolti, and some other visionaries. Those madmen had taken it into their head that Pius IV. was not a lawful pope, and that after his death they would place another in St Peter's chair, with the title of Pope Angelicus, under whom errors might be reformed, and peace restored to the church. The conspiracy was discovered, and the fanatic Benedict put to death. This pontiff died a little time after, on the 9th of December 1565, aged 66 years, carrying to the grave with him the hatred of the Romans, whom his severity had exasperated. He was a man of great address, and very fruitful in his resources. He adorned Rome with several public edifices; but these ornaments tended greatly to impoverish it. If he was the instrument of raising his relations in the world, it must be allowed, at least, that the greater part of them did him honour. Pius V. (S. Michael Ghilieri), born at Bofchi or Bofco, in the diocese of Fortona, on the 17th of January 1504, was, according to Abbé de Choisy, son to a senator of Milan. He turned a Dominican friar. Paul IV. informed of his merit and virtue, gave him the bishopric of Sutri, created him cardinal in 1557, and made him inquisitor-general of the faith among the Milanese and in Lombardy; but the severity with which he exercised his office obliged him to quit that country. He was sent to Venice, where the ardour of his zeal met with still greater obstacles. Pius IV. added to the cardinal's hat the bishopric of Mondovi. After the death of that pontiff, he was advanced to St Peter's chair in 1566. The Romans expressed but little joy at his coronation: he was very sensible of it, and said, "I hope they will be as sorry at my death as they are at my election;" but he was mistaken. Raised by his merit to the first ecclesiastical preferment in Christendom, he could not divest himself of the severity of his character; and the situation in which he found himself rendered, perhaps, that severity necessary. One of his first objects was to repel the luxury of the clergy, the pride of the cardinals, and the licentious manners of the Romans. He caused the decrees of reformation enacted by the Council of Trent to be put in execution; he prohibited bull-baiting in the Circus; he expelled from Rome the women of the town; and allowed the cardinals to be prosecuted for their debts. The errors which overflowed the Christian world gave him great uneasiness. After having employed gentle and lenient measures in the reclaiming of heretics, he had recourse to severity, and some of them ended their days in the flames of the inquisition. He particularly displayed his zeal for the grandeur of the holy see in 1568, by ordaining that the bull In coena domini, which was published at Rome every year on Maunday Thursday, and which Clement XIV. suppressed, should be published likewise throughout the whole church. That bull, the work of several sovereign pontiffs, principally regards the jurisdiction of the ecclesiastical and civil power. It anathematizes those who appeal from the decrees of popes to a general council; those who favour the appellants; the universities which teach that the pope is subject to a general council; the princes who would restrain the ecclesiastical jurisdiction, or who exact contributions from the clergy. It was rejected by all the sovereign states, excepting a very few. In 1580, some bishops having endeavoured to introduce it into their dioceses, the parliament caused their temporalities to be seized upon, and declared those guilty of high treason who should imitate the fanaticism of those prelates. Pius V. for some time meditated an expedition against the Turks. He had the courage to make war on the Ottoman empire, by forming a league with the Venetians and Philip II., king of Spain. This was the first time that the standard of the two keys was seen displayed against the crescent. The naval armies came to an engagement, on the 7th of October 1571, in Lepanto bay, in which the confederate Christian princes obtained a signal victory over the Turks, who lost above 30,000 men, and near 200 galleys. This success was principally owing to the pope, who exhausted both his purse and person in fitting out that armament. He died of the gravel six months after, on the 30th of April 1572, aged 68. He repeated often, in the midst of his sufferings, "O Lord! increase my pains and my patience." His name will forever adorn the list of Roman pontiffs. It is true, that his bull against Queen Elizabeth, and his other bull in favour of the inquisition, with his rigorous prosecution of heretics both in France and Ireland, prove that he had more zeal than sweetness in his temper; but in other respects he possessed the virtues of a saint and the qualities of a king. He was the model of the famous Sixtus Quintus, to whom he gave an example of amassing in a few years such savings as were sufficient to make the holy see be regarded as a formidable power. Sultan Selim, who had no greater enemy than this pope, caused public rejoicings to be made at Constantinople for his death during the space of three days. The pontificate of Pius is also celebrated for the condemnation of Baius, the extinction of the order of Humilites, and the reformation of that of the Cistercians. He was canonized by Clement XI. in 1712. There are extant several of his letters, printed at Antwerp in 1649, in 4to. Felibian, in 1672, published his Life, translated from the Italian of Agatio di Somma; but we cannot vouch for the fidelity of the translation. PIX. See MINT-MARKS.

PIZARRO

Pages 209-209

Francis, a celebrated Spanish general, the discoverer and conqueror of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, in conjunction with Diego <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMAGRO">Almagro</a>, a Spanish navigator. They are both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with horrid cruelties to the inhabitants; and they fell victims to their own ambition, jealousy, and avarice. Almagro revolting, was defeated and beheaded by Pizarro, who was afterwards joined by Almagro's friends in 1541. See PERU.

PLACE

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, a general name for all kinds of fortresses where a party may defend themselves. Thus, 1. A strong <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fortified place is one flanked, and covered with battions. 2. A regular place, one whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, sides, battions, and other parts, are equal; and this is usually denominated from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its angles, as a pentagon, hexagon, &c. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">Irregular</a> place is one whose sides and angles are unequal.—4. Place of arms is a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town pitched upon for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; or, in a city or garrison, it is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> open spot of ground, usually near the centre of the place where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> kept, and the garrison holds its rendezvous at reviews, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of alarm to receive orders from the governor. 5. Places of arms of an attack, in a siege, is a spacious place covered from the enemy by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> or epaulette, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are posted ready to sustain those at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in the trenches against the soldiers of the garrison. 6. Place of arms particular, in a garrison, a place near every battalion, where the soldiers sent from the grand place to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> assigned them relieve those that are either upon the guard or in fight. 7. Place of arms without, is a place allowed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> way for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> of cannon, to oblige those who advance in their approaches to retire. 8. Place of arms in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, a large place at the head of the camp for the army to be ranged in and drawn up in battalia. There is also a place for each particular body, troop, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, to assemble in. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> PLACE. See COMMON-PLACE.

PLACENTA

Pages 209-209

in Anatomy and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>, a soft roundish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, found in the womb of pregnant women; which, from its resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, was called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> hepatis uterini, uterine liver.

PLACENTIA

Pages 209-209

called by the natives Placentia, is Placentia, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, with a bishop's see. It is seated about 100 paces from the river Po, in a very fertile pleasant plain, watered by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rivulets, and surrounded with hills, abounding in all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. In its territory there are <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, from which they make a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> salt; and there are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, woods, and warrens. It contains a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and is reckoned three miles in circumference. Its fortifications are inconsiderable, but the citadel is pretty strong. The streets are straight, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street called Stradone, is 25 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> paces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and 3000 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line, with 600 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> posts, for separating the foot from the carriage-way, and on both sides are 11 spacious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>. The other buildings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> are not very remarkable, though it contains 45 churches, 28 convents, and two almshouses. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is pretty much in the Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Augustines is reckoned the most beautiful, and esteemed worthy of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, the celebrated Vignoli. The ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, though <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, makes no great appearance externally; but within there are some good apartments. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> before the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> stand two admirable bronz <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of Alexander and Renatus IV. both of the house of Farnese, and dukes of Parma and Placentia. The bishop is suffragan to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. At this city begins the Via Emilia, which extends as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a> on the Adriatic. The number of the inhabitants is about 30,000, among whom there are 2000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>. This city has been taken several times in the wars of Italy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> took possession of it in 1744, it being ceded to him by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; but it was taken from him in 1746, after a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The French got possession of it in 1796. It has a famous university, and the inhabitants are much esteemed for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>. There is a great fair here every year on the 15th of April, which is much frequented. Placentia is about 32 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Parma and 83 east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. E. Long. 10° 24'. N. Lat. 45° 5'.

PLAGIARY

Pages 209-209

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILOLOGY">Philology</a>, the purloining another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s works, and putting them off as our own. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, plagiarus was properly a person who bought, sold, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> retained a freeman for a slave; and was so called, because, by the Flavian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, such persons were condemned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> plagas, "to be whipped." Thomasius has an express treatise De plagis literario; wherein he lays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the laws and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> which authors have to one another's writings.—"<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> writers, at least such as meddle with arts and sciences (as is pertinently observed by Mr Chambers), seem exempted from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> laws of neum et tuum: they do not pretend to set up on their own bottom, nor to treat you at their own cost. Their works are supposed, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, compositions of other peoples; and what they take from others, they do it avowedly, and in the open fun.—In effect, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> gives them a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to every thing that may be for their purpose, wherever they find it; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they rob, they do not do it any otherwise than as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a> does, for the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Their occupation is not pillaging, but collecting contributions; and, if you ask them their authority, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce you the practice of their predecessors of all ages and nations."

PLAGUE

Pages 210-213

Pestilence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pestilential Fever, is a very acute, malignant, and contagious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; being a putrid fever of the worst kind, and seldom failing to prove mortal. Though it is generally defined a malignant fever, Diemerbrock thinks they ought to be distinguished, since the fever is not the essence of the disease, but merely a symptom or effect of it. See Medicine, No. 221. The plague, as is generally agreed, is never bred or propagated in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, but always imported from abroad, especially from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, &c., where it is very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Sydenham has remarked that it rarely infects this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> oftener than once in 40 years, and happily we have been free of it for a much longer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. Authors are not as yet agreed concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this dreadful distemper.
