Some think that insects are the cause of it, in the same way that they are the cause of blights, being brought in swarms from other climates by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, when they are taken into the lungs in respiration; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which is, that they mix with the blood and juices, and attack and corrode the viscera. Mr. Boyle, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, thinks it originates from the effluvia or exhalations breathed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> from noxious minerals, to which may be added stagnant waters and putrid bodies of every kind. Mr. Gibbon thinks that the plague is derived from damp, hot, and stagnating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> of animal substances, especially locusts. See Gibbon's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, 4to edit. vol. iv. p. 327—332, where there is also a very particular account of the plague which depopulated the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian. The Mahometans believe that the plague proceeds from certain spirits, or goblins, armed with bows and arrows, sent by God to punish men for their sins; and that when the wounds are given by spectres of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, they certainly prove fatal, but not so when the arrows are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> by those that appear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. They therefore take no precaution to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> themselves against it. The wisest professors of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, however, at present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> otherwise; for we find a receipt recommended by Sidi Mohammed Zerroke, one of the most celebrated Marabouts, prefaced with these remarkable words: "The lives of us all are in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of God, when it is we must die. However, it hath pleased him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> many persons from the plague, by taking every morning while the infection rages, one pill or two of the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; viz. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a> two parts, saffron one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, of aloes two parts, of syrup of myrtle berries, &c." But this remedy is confined to the more enlightened; for the bigotry of the lower sort is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> as to make them despise all precautions which people of other nations <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Of this extreme and foolish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> Dr. Chandler gives an interesting account when speaking of the plague at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>. This learned author is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the disease arises from animals, which he supposes to be invisible. See Chandler's Travels in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, p. 279, &c. It is a remarkable fact, that plagues are sometimes partial, and that they only attack particular animals, or a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of persons, avoiding others altogether, or attacking them but lightly. Thus Ferneius informs us of a plague, or murrain, in 1514, which invaded only cats. Dionysius Halicarnaeus mentions a plague which attacked none but maids; and that which raged in the time of Gentius, killed scarcely any women, and very few but lusty men. Boterus mentions another plague, which assaulted none but the younger sort; and we have instances of the same kind of a later standing (a). Cardan speaks of a plague at Baille, with which the Switzers were infected, and the Italians, Germans, or French, exempted: and John Utenhovius takes notice of a dreadful one at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, which, though it raged among the Danes, spared the Germans, Dutch, and English, who went with all freedom, and without the least danger, to the houses of the infected. During the plague which ravaged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> in 1760, it was observed that people of the fowdest constitutions were the most liable to it, and that the weak and delicate were either spared or easily cured. It was most fatal to the Moors; and, when it attacked them, it was generally incurable. When the plague raged in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1636, a young girl was seized with it, had three carbuncles, and was removed to a garden, where her lover, who was betrothed to her, attended her as a nurse, and slept with her as his wife. He remained uninfected, and the recovered, and was married to him. The story is related by Vine. Fabricius in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>. Cur. Ann. II. Olst. 188. Many methods have been adopted in different countries to prevent the importation of this dreadful scourge of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, and to stop the progress of infection after it has been imported. In England, mayors, bailiffs, head officers of corporations, and justices of peace, have power to tax inhabitants, houses, and lands, &c. within their precincts, for the relief of persons infected with the plague; and justices of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> may tax persons within five miles round, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>'s inability; the tax to be levied by distress and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of goods, or in default thereof by imprisonment. Infected persons going abroad, after being commanded to keep <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for avoiding farther infections, may be visited by watchmen, &c., and punished as vagrants, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have no fires upon them; and if they have infectious sores on them it is felony. Justices of the peace, &c., are to appoint searchers, examiners, and buriers of the dead, in places infected, and administer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to them for the performance of their duties, &c.; flat. 1 Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 31. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUARANTINE">QUARANTINE</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a> having, in the year 1770, invented a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a>-powder, which, from several other experiments, had proved efficacious in preventing the infection of the plague; in order more fully to ascertain its virtue in that respect, it was determined, (a) See the account of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> fever under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">PHILADELPHIA</a>, where it appears that the disease was less fatal to some sorts of persons than to others. Plague. determined, towards the end of the year, that ten malefactors under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> should, without undergoing any other precautions than the fumigations, be confined three weeks in a lazaretto, be laid upon the beds, and drestled in the clothes, which had been used by persons sick, dying, and even dead, of the plague in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. The experiment was accordingly tried, and none of the ten malefactors were then infected, or have been since ill. The fumigation powder is prepared as follows. Powder of the first strength.] Take leaves of juniper, juniper-berries pounded, ears of wheat, guaiacum wood pounded, of each five pounds; common <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a> pounded, eight pounds; sulphur pounded, five pounds; Smyrna tar, or myrrh, two pounds: mix all the above ingredients together, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of the powder of fumigation of the first strength. [N.B. A pound is 40 pounds Russian, which are equal to 35 pounds and a half or 36 pounds English avoirdupoise.] Powder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> strength.] Take southernwood cut into small pieces, four pounds; juniper berries pounded, three pounds; common saltpetre pounded, four pounds; sulphur pounded, two pounds and a half; Smyrna tar, or myrrh, one pound and a half: mix the above together, which will produce half a pound of the powder of fumigation of the second strength. Odoriferous powder.] Take the root called kalmus cut into small pieces, three pounds; leaves of juniper cut into small pieces four pounds; frankincense pounded grossly, one pound; storax pounded, and rose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, half a pound; yellow <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> pounded, one pound; common saltpetre pounded, one pound and a half; sulphur, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pound: mix all the above together, which will produce <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pounds and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the odoriferous powder. Remark on the powder of fumigation.] If guaiacum cannot be had, the cones of pines or firs may be used in its stead; likewise common tar of pines and firs may be used instead of the Smyrna tar, or myrrh, and mugwort may supply the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of southernwood. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a>, who was himself infected, lib. ii. gives us an account of a dreadful plague which happened at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> about the year before Christ 430, while the Peloponnesians under the command of Archidamus waited all her territory abroad; but of these two enemies the plague was by far the most dreadful and severe. The most dreadful plague that ever raged at Rome was in the reign of Titus, A.D. 80. The emperor left no remedy unattempted to abate the malignity of the distemper, acting during its continuance like a father to his people. The same fatal disease raged in all the provinces of the Roman empire in the reign of M. Aurelius, A.D. 167, and was followed by a dreadful famine, by earthquakes, inundations, and other calamities. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> believed that Ascalaphus sometimes entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, and cured the plague. About the year 430 the plague visited Britain, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> after the Picts and Scots had made a formidable invasion of the southern part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The plague raged with uncommon fury, and swept away most of those whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and famine had spared, so that the living were scarcely sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the dead. About the year 1348 the plague became almost general over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many authors give an account of this plague, which is said to have appeared first in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Cathay in the year 1346, and to have proceeded gradually westward to Constantinople and Egypt. From Constantinople it passed into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and by degrees along the coasts of the ocean into Britain and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and afterwards into Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> and the other northern kingdoms. According to Antoninus archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> the distemper carried off 60,000 people in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, among whom was the historian John Villani. In the year 1656 the plague was brought from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, being introduced into the city by a transport with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> on board. It raged with excessive violence, carrying off in less than six months 400,000 of the inhabitants. The distemper was at first called by the physicians a malignant fever; but one of them affirming it to be pestilential, the viceroy, who was apprehensive lest such a report would occasion all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Naples to be broke off, was offended with this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, and ordered him to be imprisoned. As a favour, however, he allowed him to return and die in his own house. By this proceeding of the viceroy, the distemper being neglected, made a most rapid and furious progress, and filled the whole city with consternation. The streets were crowded with confused processions, which served to spread the infection through all the quarters. The terror of the people increased their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and it being reported that a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> had prophesied that the pestilence would cease upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a hermitage for her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> nuns upon the hill of St Martin's, the edifice was immediately begun with the most ardent zeal. Persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> strove who should perform the meanest offices; some loading themselves with beams, and others carrying baskets full of lime and nails, while persons of all ranks stripped themselves of their most valuable effects, which they threw into empty hogheads placed in the streets to receive the charitable contributions. Their violent agitation, however, and the increasing heats, diffused the malady through the whole city, and the streets and the stairs of the churches were filled with the dead; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of whom, for some time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, amounted daily to 15,000. The viceroy now used all possible precautions to abate the fury of the distemper, and to prevent its spreading to the provinces. The infection, however, defoliated the whole kingdom, excepting the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a> and the Farther <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, and the cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORRENTO">Sorrento</a>, Paolo, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELVEDERE">Belvedere</a>. The general calamity was increased in Naples by malecontents, who infamated that the distemper had been designingly introduced by the Spaniards, and that there were people in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> who went through the city fowling poisoned dust. This idle rumour enraged the populace, who began to insult the Spanish soldiers, and threaten a sedition; so that the viceroy, to pacify the mob, caused a criminal to be broke upon the wheel, under pretence that he was a disperser of the dust. A violent and plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> falling about the middle of August, the distemper began to abate; and on the eighth of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> the physicians made a solemn declaration that the city was entirely free from infection. Of the dreadful plague which raged at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1665, the reader will find an account in the article LONDON, No. 21. In 1720 the city of Marseille was visited with this destructive disease, brought in a ship from the Levant; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months, during which time it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, it carried off not less than 60,000 people. This defoliation is not yet obliterated from the minds of the inhabitants; some survivors remained alive but a few years ago to transmit a traditional account of it to after ages. There are two fine pictures, painted by Puget, representing some of the horrid scenes of that time. "They are (says Lady Craven) only too well executed. I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> several dying figures taking leave of their friends, and looking their last, anxious, kind, and watchful prayers on their sick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>, that made the tears flow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. I was told the physicians and noblemen who were afflicting the sick and dying, were all portraits: I can easily conceive it; for in some faces there is a look of reflection and concern which could only be drawn from the life." Letters, p. 34, 35. This fatal event has caused the laws of quarantine to be very strictly enforced in the lazaretto here, which is an extensive insulated building. The ravages of this disease have been dreadful wherever it has made its appearance. On the first arrival of the Europeans at the island of Gran Canaria, it contained 14,000 fighting men, soon after which, two thirds of the whole inhabitants fell a sacrifice to the plague, which had doubtless been introduced by their new visitors. The destruction it has made in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Europe, and particularly in Constantinople, must be known to every reader; and its fatal effects have been particularly heightened there by that firm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> which prevails among the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a>, &c., as has been already mentioned. It is generally brought into European Turkey from Egypt; where it is very frequent, especially at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. To give even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of all the plagues which have defoliated many flourishing countries, would extend this article beyond all bounds; and minutely to describe them all, would be impossible. For the plague at Smyrna, we refer to Chandler's Travels as above. Relating that which raged in Syria in 1762, we refer to the Abbé Mariti's Travels through Cyprus, Syria, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, vol. i. p. 278—296. This plague was one of the most malignant and fatal that Syria ever experienced; for it scarcely made its appearance in any part of the body when it carried off the patient. In addition to what the reader will find upon this subject in the article MEDICINE, and the observations which have now been offered, we beg leave to state the sentiments of Berthier on this subject, in his account of Bonaparte's expedition into Syria. "At the time of our entry into Syria, (says he) all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> were infected by the plague; a malady which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarity render so fatal in the east. Those who are affected by it give themselves up for dead; they are immediately abandoned by every body, and are left to die, when they might have been saved by medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. "Citizen Degenettes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, displayed a courage and character which entitle him to the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>. When our soldiers were attacked by the least fever, it was supposed that they had caught the plague, and these maladies were founded. The fever <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> were abandoned by the officers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and their attendants. Citizen Degenettes repaired in person to the hospitals, visited all the patients, felt the glandular swellings, drested them, declared and maintained that the distemper was not the plague, but a malignant fever with glandular swellings, which might easily be cured by attention, and keeping the patient's mind easy." The views of Degenettes in making this distinction were worthy of the highest commendation; but Dr Mofley maintains that this fever was actually the plague. The physician, however, carried his courage so far, as to make two incisions, and to inoculate the suppuration <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from one of these buboes above his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and under his armpits, but was not affected with the malady. He thus eased the minds of the soldiers, the first step to a cure; and, by his fidelity and constant attendance in the hospitals, a number of men attacked with the plague were cured. His example was followed by other officers of health. "There are, says Dr Mofley, annual or seasonal disorders, more or less severe, in all countries; but the plague, and other great depopulating epidemics, do not always obey the seasons of the year. Like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>, their course is eccentric. They have their revolutions; but from whence they come, or whether they go after they have made their revolution, no mortal can tell. "Diseases originating in the atmosphere <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> some, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by others; and act exclusively on bodies graduated to receive their impressions; otherwise whole nations would be destroyed. In some constitutions of the body the access is easy, in some difficult, and in others impossible. "The air of confined places may be so vitiated as to be unfit for the purposes of the healthy existence of any person. Hence gaol, hospital, and ship fevers. But, as these distempers are the offspring of a local cause, that local cause, and not the distempered people, communicate the disease. "The infection, were it not in the atmosphere, would be confined within very narrow limits; have a determinate sphere of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; and none but physicians and attendants on the sick would suffer; and these must suffer; and the cause and the effects would be palpable to our senses. Upon this ground, the precaution of quarantine would be rational. But who then would visit and attend the sick, or could live in hospitals, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, and lazarettos?" The author is convinced from these reasonings, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUBO">bubo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a>, of which we hear so much in Turkey, and read so much in our own history of plagues, arise from heating food and improper treatment; that they contain no infection; and consequently that they are not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> deposit of the morbid virus separated from the contagion. Speaking of the plague, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a> says, "the first symptoms are said to be thirst; 2. Cephalalgia; 3. A stiff and uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, with redness and tumour about the eyes; 4. Watering of the eyes; 5. White pustules on the tongue. Not uncommonly, all these have successively shown themselves, yet the patient has recovered; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, where suppuration has had place, the skin always remains discoloured, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> of a purple hue. Many who have been bled in an early stage of the disorder, have recovered without any fatal symptoms;" symptoms; but whether from that or any other cause, does not appear certain." <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">Oil</a> rubbed into the skin acts as a preventive, as well as a cure of the plague. When the operation is performed to prevent infection, it is successfully performed with that view at Smyrna, as often as the plague makes its appearance in the city. As it is not done for the purpose of promoting perspiration, it is not requisite that it should be performed with the same speed as when for curing the disorder; nor is it necessary to abstain from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and to use soups; but it will be proper to use only fowls or veal for some days, without any seasoning. It will in fine be necessary to guard against indigestible food, and such liquors as might put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or inflame the maws of the blood. This interesting discovery merits the attention of all medical men; for if olive oil has been found efficacious in curing or preserving against one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of infection, it is not absurd to suppose, that the same or other kinds of oil might be productive of much benefit in other malignant infectious diseases. We hope soon to hear of some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> being made with it in this country. Would it be of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the yellow fever, so prevalent in the western world?

PLAIN

Pages 213-213
or Plane, in general, an appellation given to whatever is smooth and even, or simple, obvious, and easy to be understood; and, consequently, stands opposed to rough, enriched, or laboured. A plain figure, in geometry, is an uniform surface; from every point of whose perimeter right lines may be drawn to every other point in the same. A plain angle is one contained under two lines, or surfaces, in contradiction to a solid angle. See Angle under Geometry. The doctrine of plain triangles, as those included under three right lines, is termed plain trigonometry. See the article Trigonometry. PLAIN Chart. See the article Chart. PLAIN-Sailing. See Navigation.

PLAISE

Pages 213-213

the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pleuronectes. See Pleuronectes, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLAN

Pages 213-213

in general, denotes the representation of something drawn on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; such as maps, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTS">charts</a>, ichnographies, &c. See Map, Chart, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> plan, however, is particularly used for a draught of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, such as it appears, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is intended to appear, on the ground, showing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, and distribution of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> or ground-plot into apartments, rooms, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, &c. A geometrical plan is that wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and vacant parts are represented in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> proportions. The raised plan of a building is the same with what is otherwise called an elevation or orthography. See Orthography. A <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> plan is that exhibited by degradations or diminutions, according to the rules of perspective. See Perspective. To render plans intelligible, it is usual to distinguish the materials with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> wash; the projections on the ground are drawn in full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and those supposed over them in dotted lines. The augmentations or alterations to be made are distinguished by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> different from what is already built; and the tints of each plan made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> as the stories are raised. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> buildings it is usual to have three several plans for the three first stories.

PLANCUS

Pages 213-213

Francis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, was born at Amiens in 1696, and died on the 19th of September 1765, aged 69 years. He is the author of some works which have had considerable reputation. 1. A complete System of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, in 2 vols in 12mo; a treatise much recommended by surgeons to their pupils. 2. A choice Library of Medicine, taken from periodical publications, both French and others: this curious collection, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> and completed by M. Coulin, makes 9 vols in 4to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 18 vols in 12mo. 3. A Translation of Vander Wiel's Observations on Medicine and Surgery, 1758, 2 vols in 12mo. Plancus was also the editor of various editions of works on medicine and surgery, which he enriched with notes.

PLANE

Pages 213-213

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, denotes a plain surface, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one that lies evenly between its bounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>: and as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line is the shortest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> from one point to another, so a plane surface is the shortest extension from one line to another. In <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, conics, &c., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> plane is frequently used for an imaginary surface, supposed to cut and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies; and on this foundation is the whole doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">conic sections</a> built. See Astronomy, Conic Sections, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, planes are either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, or inclined thereto. See Mechanics. The determining how far any given plane deviates from an horizontal line, makes the whole business of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a>. See the article Levelling. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, the planes of reflection and refraction are those drawn through the incident and reflected or refracted rays. See Optics. In <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> we meet with the perspective plane, which is supposed to be pellucid, and perpendicular to the horizon; the horizontal plane, supposed to pass through the spectator's eye, parallel to the horizon; the geometrical plane, likewise parallel to the horizon, wherein the object to be represented is supposed to be placed, &c. See Perspective. The plane of projection in the stereographic projection of the sphere, is that on which the projection is made, corresponding to the perspective plane. See Projection. Plane, in joinery, an edged tool or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for paring and shaving of wood smooth. It consists of a piece of wood very smooth at bottom, as a stock or shaft; in the midst of which is an aperture, through which a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> edge, or chisel, placed obliquely, passes; which, being very sharp, takes off the inequalities of the wood along which it slides. PLANE-Tree, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Platanus.

PLANET

Pages 213-214

a celestial body, revolving round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> as a centre, and continually changing its position with respect to the fixed stars; whence the name planet, which is a Greek word, signifying "wanderer." The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are usually distinguished into primary and secondary. The primary ones, called by way of eminence planets, are those which revolve round the sun as a centre; and the secondary planets, more usually called satellites <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moons, are those which revolve round a primary planet as a centre, and constantly attend it in its revolution round the sun. The primary planets are again distinguished into superior and inferior. The superior planets are those farther from the sun than our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, and the Georgium Sidus; and the inferior planets are those nearer the sun than our earth, as Venus and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>. For an account of the planets lately discovered, see Vesta. That the planets are opaque bodies, like our earth, is thought probable for the following reasons. 1. Since in Venus, Mercury, and Mars, only that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the disk illuminated by the sun is found to shine; and again, Venus and Mercury, when between the earth and the sun, appear like dark spots or macules on the sun's disk; it is evident, that Mars, Venus, and Mercury, are opaque bodies, illuminated with the borrowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the sun. And the same appears of Jupiter, from its being void of light in that part to which the shadow of the satellites reaches, as well as in that part turned from the sun; and that his satellites are opaque, and reflect the sun's light, is abundantly shown. Again, since Saturn, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> and satellites, only yield a faint light, fainter considerably than that of the fixed stars, though these be vastly more remote, and than that of the rest of the planets; it is past doubt that he too with his attendants are opaque bodies. 2. Since the sun's light is not transmitted through Mercury and Venus, when placed against him, it is plain they are dense opaque bodies; which is likewise evident of Jupiter, from his hiding the satellites in his shadow; and therefore, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, the same may be concluded of Saturn. 3. From the variable spots of Venus, Mars, and Jupiter, it is evident these planets have a changeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; which changeable atmosphere may, by a like argument, be inferred of the satellites of Jupiter; and therefore, by similitude, the same may be concluded of the other planets. 4. In like manner, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> observed in Venus, the same may be supposed in the other planets. 5. Since, then, Saturn, Jupiter, and the satellites of both, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, are opaque bodies shining with the sun's borrowed light, are furnished with mountains, and encompassed with a changeable atmosphere; they have, it is concluded, waters, seas, &c. as well as dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and are bodies like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and therefore like the earth. And hence it seems also highly probable, that the other planets have their animal inhabitants as well as our earth.

PLANETARIUM

Pages 214-214

an astronomical machine, so called from its representing the motions, orbits, &c. of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, agreeable to the Copernican system. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>.

PLANETARY

Pages 214-214

something that relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. Hence we say, planetary worlds, planetary inhabitants, &c. See PLANET.

PLANETARY SYSTEM

Pages 214-214

is the system <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, primary and secondary, moving in their respective orbits, round their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>. PLANETARY DAYS.—Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> was shared among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> planets, each planet having its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This we learn from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius and Plutarch, Symposi. I. 4. q. 7. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> adds, that it was the Egyptians who first discovered what god, that is, what planet, presides over each day; for that among this people the planets were directors. And hence it is, that in most European languages the days of the week are still Planetary denominated from the planets; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, Monday, &c. See WEEK.

PLANETARY YEARS

Pages 214-214

the periods of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in which the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> make their revolutions round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.—As from the proper revolution of the sun, the solar year takes its original; so from the proper revolutions of the rest of the planets about the earth, so many sorts of years do arise, viz. the Saturnian year, which is defined by 29 Egyptian years, 174 hours, 58 minutes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> in a round <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to 30 solar years. The Jovial year, containing 317 days, 14 hours, 59 minutes.—The Martial year, containing 321 days, 23 hours, 31 minutes. For Venus and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, as their years, when judged of with regard to the earth, are almost equal to the solar year; they are more usually estimated from the sun, the true centre of their motions: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the former is equal to 224 days, 16 hours, 40 minutes; the latter to 87 days, 23 hours, 14 minutes.

that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> which considers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and plain figures, without considering their height <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> depth. See GEOMETRY.

PLANISPHERE

Pages 214-233

signifies a projection of the sphere, and its various circles on a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, maps, whereon are exhibited the meridians and other circles of the sphere, are planispheres. See MAP. PLANT is defined to be an organic body, destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and spontaneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, adhering to another body in such a manner as to draw from it its nourishment, and having a power of propagating itself by seeds. The vegetation and economy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> is one of those subjects in which our knowledge is extremely circumscribed. A total inattention to the structure and economy of plants is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> reason of the small progress that has been made in the principles of vegetation, and of the instability and fluctuation of our theories concerning it; for which reason we shall give a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the structure of plants, beginning with the seed, and tracing its progress and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a> to a state of maturity. 1. Of Seeds.] The seeds of plants are of various figures and sizes. Most of them are divided into two lobes; though some, as those of the cereals-kind, have five; and others, as the grains of corn, are not divided, but entire. But as the essential properties of all seeds are the same, when considered with regard to the principles of vegetation, our particular descriptions shall be limited to one seed, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> garden-bean. Neither is the choice of this seed altogether arbitrary; for, after it begins to vegetate, its parts are more conspicuous than many others, and consequently better calculated for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. This seed is covered with two coats <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> membranes. The outer coat is extremely thin, and full of pores; but may be easily separated from the inner one (which is much thicker), after the bean has been boiled, or lain a few days in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. At the thick end of the bean there is a small hole visible to the naked eye, immediately over the radicle or future root, that it may have a free passage into the soil (fig. 1. A). When these coats are taken off, the body of the seed appears, which is divid- ed into two smooth portions or lobes. The smoothness of the lobes is owing to a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FILM">film</a> or cuticle with which they are covered. At the basis of the bean is placed the radicle or future root (fig. 3. A). The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of the radicle, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as it enters into the body of the feed, divides into two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> branches, one of which is inserted into each lobe, and sends off smaller ones in all directions through the whole substance of the lobes (fig. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a>). These ramifications become so extremely minute towards the edges of the lobes, that they require the finest glasses to render them visible. To these ramifications Grew and Malpighi have given the name of seminal root; because, by means of it, the radicle and plume, before they are expanded, derive their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> nourishment. The plume, bud, or germ (fig. 3.), is inclosed in two small corresponding cavities in each lobe. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and consistence is much the same with those of the radicle, of which it is only a continuation, but having a quite contrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; for the radicle descends into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and divides into a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of smaller branches or filaments; but the plume ascends into the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and unfolds itself into all the beautiful variety of stem, branches, leaves, flower, fruit, &c. The plume in corn shoots from the smaller end of the grain, and amongst maltsters goes by the name of acrospire. The next thing to be taken notice of is the substance or parenchymatous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the lobes. This is not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> concreted juice, but is curiously organized, and consists of a vast number of small bladders resembling those in the pith of trees (fig. 5.). Besides the coats, cuticle, and parenchymatous parts, there is a substance perfectly distinct from these, distributed in different proportions through the radicle, plume, and lobes. This inner substance appears very plainly in a transverse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the radicle or plume. Towards the extremity of the radicle it is one entire trunk; but higher up it divides into three branches; the middle one runs directly up to the plume, and the other two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into the lobes on each side, and spread out into a great variety of small branches through the whole body of the lobes (fig. 4.). This substance is very properly termed the seminal root: for when the seed is sown, the moisture is first absorbed by the outer coats, which are everywhere furnished with sap and air-vesicles; from these it is conveyed to the cuticle; from the cuticle it proceeds to the pulpy part of the lobes; when it has got thus far, it is taken up by the mouths of the small branches of the seminal root, and passes from one branch into another, till it is all collected into the main trunk, which communicates both with the plume and radicle, the two principal involved organs of the future plant. After this the sap or vegetable food runs in two opposite directions: part of it ascends into the plume, and promotes the growth and expansion of that organ; and part of it descends into the radicle, for nourishing and evolving the root and its various filaments. Thus the plume and radicle continue their progress in opposite directions till the plant arrives at maturity. It is here worth remarking, that every plant is really possessed of two roots, both of which are contained in the feed. The plume and radicle, when the seed is first deposited in the earth, derive their nourishment from the seminal root; but, afterwards, when the radicle begins to shoot out its filaments, and to absorb some moisture, not, however, in a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> to supply the exigencies of the plume, the two lobes, or main body of the feed, rise along with the plume, affuming the appearance of two leaves, resembling the lobes of the feed in size and shape, but having no resemblance to those of the plume, for which reason they have got the name of dissimilar leaves. These dissimilar leaves defend the young plume from the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, by absorbing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, air, &c., assist the tender radicle in nourishing the plume, with which they have still a connection by means of the seminal root above described. But when the radicle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> root has descended deep enough into the earth, and has acquired a sufficient number of filaments or branches for absorbing as much aliment as is proper for the growth of the plume; then the seminal or dissimilar leaves, their utility being entirely superfluous, begin to decay and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off. Fig. 1. A, the foramen or hole in the bean through which the radicle shoots into the soil. Fig. 2. A transverse section of the bean; the dots being the branches of the seminal root. Fig. 3. A, the radicle. B, the plume or bud. Fig. 4. A view of the seminal root branched out upon the lobes. Fig. 5. A longitudinal section of one of the lobes of the bean a little magnified, to show the small bladders of which the pulpy or parenchymatous part is composed. Figs. 6. 7. A, a transverse section of the radicle. B, a transverse section of the plume, showing the organs or vesicles of the seminal root. Fig. 8. The appearance of the radicle, plume, and seminal root, when a little further advanced in growth. Having thus briefly described the feed, and traced its evolution into three principal organic parts, viz. the plume, radicle, and seminal leaves, we shall next take an anatomical view of the root, trunk, leaves, &c. 2. Of the root.] In examining the root of plants, the first thing that presents itself is the skin, which is of various colours in different plants. Every root, after it has arrived at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> skin. The first is coeval with the other parts, and exists in the feed; but afterwards there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> sent off from the bark, and forms a second skin; e.g. in the root of the dandelion, towards the end of May, the original or outer skin appears shrivelled, and is easily separated from the new one, which is fresher, and adheres more firmly to the bark. Perennial plants are supplied in this manner with a new skin every year; the outer one always falls off in the autumn and winter, and a new one is formed from the bark in the succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. The skin has numerous cells or vesicles, and is a continuation of the parenchymatous part of the radicle. However, it does not consist solely of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENCHYMA">parenchyma</a>; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> shows that there are many tubular ligneous vessels interposed through it. When the skin is removed, the true cortical substance or bark appears, which is also a continuation of the parenchymatous part of the radicle, but greatly augmented. The bark is of very different sizes. In most trees it is exceeding thin in proportion to the wood and pith. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>, it is almost one-half of the semidiameter of the root; and, in dandelion, it is nearly twice as thick as the woody part. The bark is composed of two substances; the parenchyma or pulp, which is the principal part, and a few woody fibres. The parenchyma is exceedingly porous, and has a great resemblance to a sponge; for it shrivels considerably when dried, and dilates to its former dimensions when infused in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These pores or vessels are not pervious, so as to communicate with each other; but consist of distinct little cells or bladders, scarcely visible without the assistance of the microscope. In all roots, these cells are constantly filled with a thin watery liquor. They are generally of a spherical figure; though in some roots, as the bugloss and dandelion, they are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>. In many roots, as the horseradish, peony, asparagus, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>, &c., the parenchyma is of one uniform structure. But in others it is more diversified, and puts on the shape of rays, running from the centre towards the circumference of the bark. These rays sometimes run quite through the bark, as in lovage; and sometimes advance towards the middle of it, as in melilot and most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGUMINOUS">leguminous</a> and umbelliferous plants. These rays generally stand at an equal distance from each other in the same plant; but the distance varies greatly in different plants. Neither are they of equal sizes: in carrot they are exceedingly small, and scarcely discernible; in melilot and chervil, they are thicker. They are likewise more numerous in some plants than in others. Sometimes they are of the same thickness from one edge of the bark to the other; and some grow wider as they approach to the skin. The vessels with which these rays are amply furnished, are supposed to be air-vessels, because they are always found to be dry, and not so transparent as the vessels which evidently contain the sap. In all roots there are ligneous vessels dispersed in different proportions through the parenchyma of the bark. These ligneous vessels run longitudinally through the bark in the form of small threads, which are tubular, as is evident from the rising of the pith in them when a root is cut transversely. These ligneous sap-vessels do not run in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> through the bark, but at small distances incline towards one another, in such a manner that they appear to the naked eye to be inoculated; but the microscope discovers them to be only contiguous, and braced together by the parenchyma. These braces or coagulations are very various both in size and number in different roots; but in all plants they are most numerous towards the inner edge of the bark. Neither are these vessels single tubes; but, like the nerves in animals, are bundles of 20 or 30 small contiguous cylindrical tubes, which uniformly run from the extremity of the root, without sending off any branches or suffering any change in their size or shape. In some roots, as parsnip, especially in the ring next the inner extremity of the bark, these vessels contain a kind of lymph, which is freer than the sap contained in the bladders of the parenchyma. From this circumstance they have got the name of lymph-ducks. These lymph-ducks sometimes yield a mucilaginous lymph, as in the comfrey; and sometimes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> milky glutinous lymph, as in the angelica, fennel, burdock, scorzonera, dandelion, &c. The lymph-ducks are supposed to be the vessels from which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> and balsams are secreted. The lymph of fennel, when exposed to the air, becomes a clear transparent balsam; and that of the scorzonera, dandelion, &c., condenses into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>. The situation of the vessels is various. In some plants they stand in a ring or circle at the inner edge of the bark, as in asparagus; in others, they appear in lines or rays, as in borage; in the parsnip, and several other plants, they are most conspicuous towards the outer edge of the bark; and in the dandelion, they are disposed in the form of concentric circles. The wood of roots is that part which appears after the bark is taken off, and is firmer and less porous than the bark or pith. It consists of two distinct substances, viz. the pulpy or parenchymatous, and the ligneous. The wood is connected to the bark by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portions of the bark inserted into it. These insertions are mostly in the form of rays, tending to the centre of the pith, which are easily discernible by the eye in a transverse section of most roots. These insertions, like the bark, consist of many vessels, mostly of a round or oval figure. The ligneous vessels are generally disposed in collateral rows running longitudinally through the root. Some of these contain air, and others sap. The air-vessels are so called, because they contain no liquor. These air-vessels are distinguished by being whiter than the others. The pith is the central part of the root. Some roots have no pith, as the stramonium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOTIANA">nicotiana</a>, &c.; others have little or none at the extremities of the roots, but have a considerable quantity of it near the top. The pith, like every other part of a plant, is derived from the seed; but in some it is more immediately derived from the bark: for the insertions of the bark running in between the rays of the wood, meet in the centre, and constitute the pith. It is owing to this circumstance, that, among roots which have no pith in their lower parts, they are amply provided with it towards the top, as in columbine, lovage, &c. The bladders of the pith are of very different sizes, and generally of a circular figure. Their position is more uniform than in the bark. Their sides are not mere films, but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of small fibres or threads; which gives the pith, when viewed with a microscope, the appearance of a piece of fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. We shall conclude the description of roots with observing, that their whole substance is nothing but a congeries of tubes and fibres, adapted by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of nourishment, and of course the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> and augmentation of their parts. Fig. 9. A transverse section of the root of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMWOOD">wormwood</a> as it appears to the naked eye. Fig. 10. A section of fig. 9, magnified. AA, the skin, with its vessels. BBBB, the bark. The round holes CCC, &c., are the lymph-ducks of the bark: All the other holes are little cells and sap-vessels. DDD, parenchymatous insertions from the bark, with the cells, &c. EEEE, the rays of the wood, in which the holes are the air-vessels. N.B. This root has no pith. 3. Of the Trunk, Stalk, or Stem.] In describing the trunks of plants, it is necessary to premise, that whatever is said with regard to them applies equally to the branches. The trunk, like the root, consists of three parts, viz. the bark, wood, and pith. These parts, though substantially the same in the trunk as in the root, are in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> very different in their texture and appearance. The skin of the bark is composed of very minute bladders, interspersed with longitudinal woody fibres, as in the nettle, thistle, and most herbs. The outside of the skin is visibly porous in some plants, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>. The principal body of the bark is composed of pulp or parenchyma, and innumerable vessels much larger than those of the skin. The texture of the pulpy part, though the same substance with the parenchyma in roots, yet seldom appears in the form of rays running towards the pith; and when these rays do appear, they do not extend above half-way to the circumference. The vessels of the bark are very differently situated, and defined for various purposes in different plants. For example, in the bark of the pine, the innermost are lymph-ducts, and exceedingly small; the outermost are gum or resiniferous vessels, destined for the secretion of turpentine; and are so large as to be distinctly visible to the naked eye. The wood lies between the bark and pith, and consists of two parts, viz. a parenchymatous and a ligneous. In all trees, the parenchymatous part of the wood, though much diversified as to size and consistence, is uniformly disposed in diametrical rays, or insertions running between similar rays of the ligneous part. The true wood is nothing but a congeries of old dried lymph-ducts. Between the bark and the wood a new ring of these ducts is formed every year, which gradually loses its softness as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> season approaches, and towards the middle of winter is condensed into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> ring of wood. These annual rings, which are distinctly visible in most trees when cut through, serve as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> marks to distinguish their age (fig. ii, i2.). The rings of one year are sometimes larger, sometimes less, than those of another, probably owing to the favourable or unfavourable effects of the season. The pith, though of a different texture, is exactly of the same substance with the parenchyma of the bark, and the insertions of the wood. The quantity of pith is various in different plants. Instead of being increased every year like the wood, it is annually diminished, its vessels drying up, and affuming the appearance and structure of wood; insomuch that in old trees there is scarce such a thing as pith to be discerned. A ring of sap-vessels is usually placed at the outer edge of the pith, next the wood. In the pine, fig, and walnut, they are very large. The parenchyma of the pith is composed of small cells or bladders, of the same kind with those of the bark, only of a larger size. The general figure of these bladders is circular; though in some plants, as the thistle and borage, they are angular. Though the pith is originally one connected chain of bladders, yet as the plant grows old they shrivel, and open in different directions. In the walnut, after a certain age, it appears in the form of a regular transverse hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. In some plants it is altogether wanting; in others, as the fennel, nettle, &c., there is only a transverse partition of it at every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>. Many other varieties might be mentioned; but these must be left to the observation of the reader. Fig. ii. A transverse section of a branch of ash, as it appears to the eye. Fig. i2. The same section magnified. AA, the bark. BBB, an arched ring of sap-vessels next the skin. CCC, the parenchyma of the bark with its cells, and another arched ring of sap-vessels. DD, a circular line of lymph-ducts immediately below the above arched ring. EE, the wood. F, the first year's growth. G, the second. H, the third year's growth. III, the true wood. KK, the great air-vessels. LL, the lesser ones. MMM, the parenchymatous insertions of the bark represented by the white rays. NO, the pith, with its bladders or cells. 4. Of the Leaves.] The leaves of plants consist of the same substance with that of the trunk. They are full of nerves or woody portions, running in all directions, and branching out into innumerable small threads, interwoven with the parenchyma like fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a> or gauze. The skin of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, like that of an animal, is full of pores, which both serve for perspiration and for the absorption of dew, air, &c. These pores or orifices differ both in shape and magnitude in different plants, which is the cause of that variety of texture or grain peculiar to every plant. The pulpy or parenchymatous part consists of very minute fibres, wound up into small cells or bladders. These cells are of various sizes in the same leaf. All leaves, of whatever figure, have a marginal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a>, by which all the rest are bounded. The particular shape of this fibre determines the figure of the leaf. The vessels of leaves have the appearance of inoculating; but, when examined by the microscope, they are found only to be interwoven or laid along each other. What are called air-vessels, or those which carry no sap, are visible even to the naked eye in some leaves. When a leaf is slowly broken, they appear like small woolly fibres, connected to both ends of the broken piece. Plate Fig. i3. The appearance of the air-vessels to the eye, CCCXXI. Plate Fig. i4. A small piece cut off that leaf. Plate Fig. i5. The same piece magnified, in which the vessels have the appearance of acrew. Plate Fig. i6. The appearance of these vessels as they exist in the leaf before they are stretched out. 5. Of the Flower.] It is needless here to mention any thing of the texture, or of the vessels, &c., of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, as they are pretty similar to those of the leaf. It would be foreign to our present purpose to take any notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and distinctions of flowers. These belong to the science of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, to which the reader is referred. There is one curious fact, however, which must not be omitted, viz. That every flower is perfectly formed in its parts many months before it appears outwardly; that is, the flowers which appear this year are not properly speaking the flowers of this year, but of the last. For example, mezzereon generally flowers in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; but these flowers were completely formed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August preceding. Of this fact any one may satisfy himself by separating the coats of a tulip root about the beginning of September; and he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find that the two innermost form a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, in the centre of which stands the young flower, which is not to make its appearance till the following April or May. Fig. i8. exhibits a view of the tulip-root when dissected in September, with the young flower towards the bottom. 6. Of the Fruit.] In describing the structure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, A few examples shall be taken from such as are most generally known. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, besides the skin, which is a production of the skin of the bark, consists of a double parenchyma or pulp, sap, and air-vesicles, calcareous and acetylic. The outer parenchyma is the same substance <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from the bark, only its bladders are larger and more succulent. It is everywhere interspersed with small globules or grains, and the bladders reflect these grains as a kind of centres, every grain being the centre of a number of bladders. The sap and air-vesicles in this pulp are extremely small. Next the core is the inner pulp or parenchyma, which consists of bladders of the same kind with the outer, only larger and more oblong, corresponding to those of the pulp, from which it seems to be derived. This inner pulp is much sooner than the other, and has none of the small grains interspersed through it; and hence it has got the name of acetylic. Between the acetylic and outer pulp, the globules or grains begin to grow larger, and gradually unite into a hard stony body, especially towards the corculum or stool of the fruit; and from this circumstance it has been called the calcareous. These grains are not derived from any of the organic parts of the tree; but seem rather to be a kind of concretions precipitated from the sap, similar to the precipitation from wine, urine, and other liquors. The core is a roundish cavity in the centre of the pear, lined with a hard woody membrane, in which the seed is inclosed. At the bottom of the core there is a small duct or canal, which runs up to the top of the pear; this canal allows the air to get into the core, for the purpose of drying and ripening the seeds. Fig. 18, a transverse section of a pear, as it appears to the naked eye. A, the skin, and a ring of sap-vesicles. B, the outer parenchyma, or pulp, with its vesicles, and ligneous fibres interspersed. C, the inner parenchyma, or acetylic, with its vesicles, which are larger than the outer one. D, the core and seeds. Fig. 19, a piece cut off, fig. 19. Fig. 20, is fig. 19, magnified. A A A, the small grains or globules, with the vesicles radiated from them. Fig. 21, a longitudinal section of the pear, showing a different view of the same parts with those of fig. 18. A the channel, or duct, which runs from the top of the pear to the bottom of the core. In a lemon, the parenchyma appears in three different forms. The parenchyma of the rind is of a coarse texture, being composed of thick fibres, woven into large bladders. Those nearest the surface contain the essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of the fruit, which bursts into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> when the skin is squeezed over a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>. From this outmost parenchyma <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten infusions or lamellae are produced, which run between as many portions of the pulp, and unite into one body in the centre of the fruit, which corresponds to the pith in trunks or roots. At the bottom and top of the lemon, this pith evidently joins with the rind, without the intervention of any lamellae. This circumstance shows, that the pith and bark are actually connected in the trunk and roots of plants, though it is difficult to demonstrate the connection, on account of the closeness of their texture, and the minuteness of their fibres. Many vesicles are dispersed through the whole of this parenchyma; but the largest ones stand on the inner edge of the rind, and the outer edge of the pith, just at the two extremities of each lamella. The second kind of parenchyma is placed between the rind and the pith; is divided into distinct bodies by the lamellae; and each of these bodies forms a large bag. These bags contain a third parenchyma, which is a cluter of smaller bags, distinct and unconnected with each other, having a small stalk by which they are fixed to the large bag. Within each of these small bags are many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of bladders, composed of extremely minute fibres. These bladders contain the acid juice of the lemon. Fig. 22, a longitudinal section of a lemon. A A A, the rind with the vesicles which contain the essential oil. B B, the substance corresponding to the pith, formed by the union of the lamellae or infusions. C C, its continuation and connection with the rind, independent of the infusions. Fig. 23, a transverse section of the lemon. B B B, &c., the nine pulpy bags, or second parenchyma, placed between the rind and the pith; and the cluter of small bags, which contain the acid juice, inclosed in the large ones. C C, the large vesicles that surround the pith. D D, two of the large bags laid open, showing the seeds, and their connection with the lamellae or membranes which form the large bags. Of the Perpiration of Plants, and the quantity of moisture daily imbibed by them.—These curious particulars have been determined with great accuracy by Dr Hales. The method he took to accomplish his purpose was as follows.—In the month of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the warmest season of the year, he took a large sunflower three feet and an half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which had been purposely planted in a flower-pot when young. He covered the pot with thin milled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, leaving only a small hole to preserve a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> air, and another by which he might occasionally supply the plant with water. Into the former he inserted a glass tube nine inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and another shorter tube into the hole by which he poured in the water; and the latter was kept <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> stoppered with a cork, except when there was occasion to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it. The holes in the bottom of the pot were also stoppered up with corks, and all the crevices filled with cement.—Things being thus prepared, the pot and plant were weighed for several days; after which the plant was cut off close to the leaden plate, and the flump well covered with cement. By weighing, he found that there perpired through the unglazed porous pot two ounces every 12 hours; which being allowed for in the daily weighing of the plant and pot, the greatest perspiration, in a warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, was found to be one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> 14 ounces; the middle rate of perspiration, one pound four ounces; the perspiration of a dry warm night, without any sensible dew, was about three ounces; but when there was any sensible though small dew, the perspiration was nothing; and when there was a large dew, or some little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> in the night, the plant and pot was increased in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> two or three ounces. In order to know what quantity was perspired from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inch of surface, our author cut off all the leaves of the plant, and laid them in five several parcels, according to their several sizes; and then measured the surface of a leaf of each parcel, by laying over it a large lattice. lattice made with threads, in which each of the little squares was \( \frac{1}{4} \) of an inch; by numbering of which, he had the surface of the leaves in square inches; which, multiplied by the number of leaves in the corresponding parcels, gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of all the leaves. By this method he found the surface of the whole plant above ground to be 5616 square inches, or 39 square feet. He dug up another sunflower of nearly the same size, which had eight main roots, reaching 15 inches deep and sidewise, from the stem. It had besides a very thick bush of lateral roots from the eight main roots, extending every way in a hemisphere about nine inches from the stem and main roots. In order to estimate the length of all the roots, he took one of the main roots with its laterals, and measured and weighed them; and then weighed the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> with their laterals; by which means he found the sum of all their lengths to be 1448 feet. Supposing then the periphery of these roots at a medium to be 0.131 of an inch, then their surface will be 2276 square inches, or 15.8 square feet; that is, equal to 0.4 of the surface of the plant above ground. From calculations drawn from these observations, it appears, that a square inch of the upper surface of this plant perspires \( \frac{1}{10} \) part of an inch in a day and a night; and that a square inch of the surface underground imbibes \( \frac{1}{10} \) of an inch in the same time. The quantity perspired by different plants, however, is by no means equal. A vine-leaf perspires only \( \frac{1}{10} \) of an inch in 12 hours; a cabbage perspires \( \frac{1}{10} \) of an inch in the same time; an apple-tree \( \frac{1}{10} \) in 12 hours; and a lemon \( \frac{1}{10} \) in 12 hours. Of the circulation of the Sap in PLANTS.—Concerning this there have been great disputes; some maintaining, that the vegetable sap has a circulation analogous to the blood of animals; while others affirm, that it only ascends in the day-time, and descends again in the night. In favour of the doctrine of circulation it has been urged, that upon making a transverse incision into the trunk of a tree, the juice which runs out proceeds in greater quantity from the upper than the lower part; and the swelling in the upper lip is also much greater than in the lower. It appears, however, that when two similar incisions are made, one near the top and the other near the root, the latter expends much more sap than the former. Hence it is concluded, that the juice ascends by one set of vessels and descends by another. But, in order to show this clearly, it would be necessary first to prove that there is in plants, as in animals, some kind of centre from which the circulation begins, and to which it returns; but no such centre has been discovered by any naturalist; neither is there the least provision apparently made by nature whereby the sap might be prevented from descending in the very same vessels through which it ascends. In the lacteal vessels of animals, which we may suppose to be analogous to the roots of vegetables, there are valves which effectually prevent the chyle when once absorbed from returning into the intestines; but no such thing is observed in the vessels of vegetables; whence it must be very probable, that when the propelling force ceases, the juice descends by the very same vessels through which it ascended.—This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, however, has been cleared up almost as well as the nature of the subject will admit of by the experiments of Dr Hales. These experiments are so numerous, that for a particular account of them we must refer to the work itself; however, his reasoning against the circulation of the sap will be sufficiently intelligible without them. "We see (says he), in many of the foregoing experiments, what quantities of moisture trees daily imbibe and perspire: now the celerity of the sap must be very great, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that quantity of moisture must, most of it, ascend to the top of the tree, then descend, and ascend again, before it is carried off by perspiration.
