Most of these tracts are either planted or rendered very good corn-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> and sheepwalks. "About 30 years since, the sides of many of our little sand-hills were fown with the seeds of French furze, and when a wet season followed, they succeeded very well, and grew so fast, that once in three or four years they are cut for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and sell at a good price at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THETFORD">Thetford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDON">Brandon</a>, Harling, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWAFFHAM">Swaffham</a>, and places adjacent. This excited some public-spirited gentlemen, among whom was the late Mr <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUXTON">Buxton</a> of Shadwell-Lodge, near Thetford, to attempt the planting of Scotch and spruce firs, and other hardy forest-trees. At first they found some difficulty from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> looseness of the sand. But as there is in all this part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> marle, at about three feet depth below the land, they very judiciously thought that incorporating it with the sand in the holes where their young trees were planted, would insure success; nor were they disappointed. The method succeeded beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>; the plantations thrived exceedingly, and the roots soon reached below the sand, after which they were out of danger. This excited them to further attempts. "On the spots where they intended to raise new plantations from seeds and acorns, they laid on a thick coat of marle and clay, which after being rough spread, and lying a winter in that state, was made fine, and ploughed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> before planting. By these means the soil became fixed, and in a little time covered with grass and herbage; so that there are now vast plantations of firs, oak, and forest-trees, in the most healthy and vigorous state, where within my <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> ten acres of land would not maintain a single sheep three months. "But the benefit of plantations, whether of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, copses, or trees, is not confined to the immediate advantage, or even the future value of the wood. By annually feeding a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of leaves, which the winds disperse, and the rains wash into the soil, it is considerably improved; and whenever such copses have been stubbed up, the ground (however unfruitful before planting) has thereby been so enriched as to bear excellent crops for many years, without the additional help of manure. How much land-owners are interested in planting waste or barren spots I need not mention; and nothing but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of indolence or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> unpardonable in this enlightened age could induce them to neglect it. "Nature has furnished us with plants, trees, and shrubs, adapted to almost every soil and situation; and as the laws of vegetation are now much better understood than formerly, it is a reproach to those whose practice does not keep pace with their knowledge in making the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of her bounty. Let no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> repine and say the land is barren; for those spots which appear to be so, owe that appearance to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> negligence. Industry and art might soon render an eighth part of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> nearly as valuable as the rest, which now remains in a state unprofitable to the owners, and disgraceful to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>." Rosse's PLANTING, a method of planting in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> position of the plant or shoot is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>; the branches being set into the earth, and the root raised into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Dr Agricola mentions this monstrous method of planting, which he found to succeed very well in most all sorts of fruit-trees, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-trees, &c. Bradley affirms, that he has seen a lime-tree in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> growing with its first roots in the air, which had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out branches in great plenty, at the same time that its first branches produced roots and fed the tree. Mr Fairchild of Hoxton has practised the same with us, and gives the following directions for performing it: Make choice of a young tree of one foot, of alder, elm, willow, or any other tree that easily takes root by laying; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the shoot gently down into the earth, and so let it remain until it has taken root. Then dig about the first root, and raise it gently out of the ground, till the stem be nearly upright, and stake it up. Then prune the roots, now erected in the air, from the bruises and wounds they received in being dug up; and anoint the pruned parts with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of two ounces of turpentine, four ounces of tallow, and four ounces of beeswax, melted together, and applied pretty warm. Afterwards Planudes, towards prune off all the buds or shoots that are upon the item, and dress the wounds with the same composition, to prevent any collateral shootings, that might spoil the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the item.

PLANUDES

Pages 243-243

MAXIMUS, a Greek monk of Constantinople, towards the end of the 14th century, who published a collection of epigrams intitled Anthologia; a Greek translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Ælop, which is rather a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> than a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and some other works. We know nothing more of him, than that he suffered some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. PLASHING of HEDGES, is an operation thought by some persons to promote the growth and continuance of old hedges; but whether the fact be so <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit of some dispute. See HEDGES. It is performed in this manner: The old stubs must be cut off, &c. within two or three inches of the ground; and the best and longest of the middle-sized shoots must be left to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Some of the strongest of these must also be left to answer the purpose of stakes. These are to be cut off to the height at which the hedge is intended to be left; and they are to stand at ten feet distance one from another: when there are not proper shoots for these at the due distances, their places must be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> stakes of dead wood. The hedge is to be first thinned, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> away all but those shoots which are intended to be used either as stakes, or the other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the plashing: the ditch is to be cleaned out with the spade; and it must be now dug as at first, with sloping sides each way; and when there is any cavity on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> on which the hedge grows, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> has been washed away from the roots of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, it is to be made good by facing it, as they express it, with the mould dug from the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ditch: all the rest of the earth dug out of the ditch is to be laid upon the top of the bank: and the owner should look carefully into it that this be done; for the workmen, to spare themselves trouble, are apt to throw as much as they can upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the bank; which being by this means overloaded, is soon washed off into the ditch again, and a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of the work undone; whereas what is laid on the top of the bank always remains there, and makes a good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of an indifferent hedge. In the plashing the quick, two extremes are to be avoided; these are, the laying it too low, and the laying it too thick. The latter makes the sap run all into the shoots, and leaves the plashes without sufficient nourishment; which, with the thickness of the hedge, finally kills them. The other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of laying them too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, is equally to be avoided; for this carries up all the nourishment into the plashes, and so makes the shoots small and weak at the bottom, and consequently the hedge thin. This is a common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England. The best hedges made anywhere in England are those in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>; for they are plashed in a middle way between the two extremes, and the cattle are by that prevented both from cropping the young shoots, and from going through; and a new and vigorous hedge soon forms itself. When the shoot is bent down that is intended to be plashed, it must be cut half way through with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>: the cut must be given sloping, somewhat downwards, and then it is to be wound about the stakes, and after this its superfluous branches are to be cut off as they stand out at the sides of the hedge. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> for the first year or two, the field where a new hedge is made can be ploughed, it will thrive the better for it; but if the stubs are very old, it is best to cut them quite down, and to fence them with good dead hedges on both sides, till the shoots are grown up from them strong enough to plash; and wherever void spaces are seen, new sets are to be planted to fill them up. A new hedge raised from sets in the common way, generally requires plashing in about eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years after.

PLASSEY

Pages 243-243

is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Muxadab in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, famous for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the English under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clive, and the native Hindoos under the nabob Surajah Dowlah. The British <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> consisted of about 3200 men, of whom the Europeans did not exceed 900; while that of the nabob consisted of 50,000 foot, and 18,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disproportion, however, Lord Clive effectually routed the nabob and his forces, with the loss of three Europeans and 26 Seapoys killed, and five Europeans and 40 Seapoys wounded. The nabob's loss was estimated at about 200 men, besides oxen and elephants. See CLIVE.

PLASTER

Pages 243-245
or Plaster, in building, a composition of lime, sometimes with sand, &c. to parget, or cover the nudities of a building. See PARGETING and STUCCO. PLASTER of Paris, a preparation of several species of gypsum dug near Mount Martre, a village in the neighbourhood of Paris; whence the name. See ALABASTER, GYPSUM, and SULPHATE OF LIME, under CHEMISTRY. The best sort is hard, white, shining, and marbled; known by the name of plaster-stone or parget of Mount Martre. It will neither give fire with steel, nor ferment with aquafortis; but very freely and readily calcines in the fire into a fine plaster, the use of which in building and casting statues is well known. The method of representing a face truly in plaster of Paris is this: The person, whose figure is designed, is laid on his back, with any convenient thing to keep off the hair. Into each nostril is conveyed a conical piece of stiff paper, open at both ends, to allow of respiration. These tubes being anointed with oil, are supported by the hand of an afflatus; then the face is lightly oiled over, and the eyes being kept shut, alabaster fresh calcined, and tempered to a thinness consistence with water, is by spoonfuls nimbly thrown all over the face, till it lies near the thickness of an inch. This matter grows sensibly hot, and in about a quarter of an hour hardens into a kind of stony concretion; which being gently taken off, represents, on its concave surface, the minutest part of the original face. In this a head of good clay may be moulded, and therein the eyes are to be opened, and other necessary amendments made. This second face being anointed with oil, a second mould of calcined alabaster is made, consisting of two parts joined lengthwise. lengthwise along the ridge of the nose; and herein may be cast, with the same matter, a face extremely like the original. If finely powdered alabaster, or plaster of Paris, be put into a basin over a fire, it will, when hot, assume the appearance of a fluid, by rolling in waves, yielding to the touch, foaming, &c., all which properties it again loses on the departure of the heat; and being thrown upon paper, will not at all wet it, but immediately discover itself to be as motionless as before it was set over the fire; whereby it appears, that a heap of such little bodies, as are neither spherical nor otherwise regularly shaped, nor small enough to be below the discernment of the eye, may, without fusion, be made fluid, barely by a sufficiently strong and various agitation of the particles which compose it; and moreover lose its fluidity immediately upon the cessation thereof. Two or three spoonfuls of burnt alabaster, mixed up thin with water, in a short time coagulate, at the bottom of a vessel full of water, into a hard lump, notwithstanding the water that surrounded it. Artificers observe, that the coagulating property of burnt alabaster will be very much impaired or lost, if the powder be kept too long, especially if in the open air, before it is made use of; and when it hath been once tempered with water, and suffered to grow hard, they cannot, by any burning or powdering of it again, make it serviceable for their purpose as before. This matter, when wrought into veils, &c., is still of so loose and spongy a texture, that the air has easy passage through it. Mr. Boyle gives an account, among his experiments with the air-pump, of his preparing a tube of this plaster, closed at one end and open at the other; and on applying the open end to the cement, as is usually done with the receivers, it was found utterly impossible to exhaust all the air out of it; for fresh air from without pressed in as fast as the other, or internal air, was exhausted, though the sides of the tube were of considerable thickness. A tube of iron was then put on the engine; so that being filled with water, the tube of plaster of Paris was covered with it; and on using the pump, it was immediately seen, that the water palled through into it as easily as the air had done, when that was the ambient fluid. After this, trying it with Venice turpentine instead of water, the thing succeeded very well; and the tube might be perfectly exhausted, and would remain in that state several hours. After this, on pouring some hot oil upon the turpentine, the case was much altered; for the turpentine melting with this, that became a thinner fluid, and in this state capable of palling like water into the pores of the plaster. On taking away the tube after this, it was remarkable that the turpentine, which had pervaded and filled its pores, rendered it transparent, in the manner that water gives transparency to that singular stone called oculus mundi. In this manner, the weight of air, under proper management, will be capable of making several forts of glues penetrate plaster of Paris; and not only this, but baked earth, wood, and all other bodies, porous enough to admit water on this occasion. Plaster of Paris is used as a manure in Pennsylvania, as we find mentioned in a letter from a gentleman in that country inserted in the fifth volume of the Bath Society Papers, and which we shall insert here for the satisfaction and information of our agricultural readers. "The best kind is imported from hills in the vicinity of Paris; it is brought down the Seine, and exported from Havre de Grace. I am informed there are large beds of it in the bay of Fundy, some of which I have seen nearly as good as that from France; nevertheless several cargoes brought from thence to Philadelphia have been used without effect. It is probable this was taken from the top of the ground, and by the influence of the sun and atmosphere deprived of the qualities necessary for the purposes of vegetation. The lumps composed of flat shining specks are preferred to those which are formed of round particles like sand; the simple method of finding out the quality is to pulverize some, and put it dry into an iron pot over the fire, when that which is good will loom boil, and great quantities of the fixed air escape by ebullition. It is pulverized by first putting it in a flambing-mill. The finer its pulverization the better, as it will thereby be more generally diffused. "It is best to sow it in a wet day. The most approved quantity for grass is six bushels per acre. No art is required in sowing it more than making the distribution as equal as possible on theeward of grass. It operates altogether as a top manure, and therefore should not be put on in the spring until the principal frosts are over and vegetation hath begun. The general time for sowing with us is in April, May, June, July, August, and even as late as September. Its effects will generally appear in ten or fifteen days; after which the growth of the grass will be so great as to produce a large burden at the end of six weeks after sowing. "It must be sown on dry land, not subject to be overflowed. I have sown it on sand, loam, and clay, and it is difficult to say on which it has been answered, although the effect is sooner visible on sand. It has been used as a manure in this state for upwards of twelve years. Its duration may, from the best information I can collect, be estimated from seven to twelve years; for, like other manure, its continuance very much depends on the nature of the soil on which it is placed. "One of my neighbours sowed some of his grasses on a field five years ago, another four years ago; a great part of my own farm was sown in May 1788. We regularly mow two crops, and pasture in autumn; no appearance of failure, the present crop being full as good as any preceding. I have this season mowed fifty acres of red clover, timothy grass, white clover, &c., which was plastered last May, July, and September; many who saw the grass eliminated the produce at two tons per acre, but I calculate the two crops at three tons. Several strips were left in the different fields without plaster; these were in a measure unproductive, being scarcely worth mowing. In April 1788, I covered a piece of grass land upwards of two inches thick with barn manure; in the same worn-out field I sowed plaster, to contrast it with the dung. I mowed the dugged and plastered land twice last year and once this; in every crop the plaster has produced the most. You will remember, in all experiments with clover, to mix about one-third timothy grass seed; it is of great advantage in serving as a support for the clover; it very much facilitates the curing of clover, and when cured is a superior fodder. The plaster operates equally as well on the other grasses as on clover. Its effect is said to be good on wheat, if sown in the spring; but I cannot say this from experience. On Indian corn I know its operation..." to be great; we use it at the rate of a table spoonful for a hill, put in immediately after dressing. "From some accurate experiments last year made and reported to our Agricultural Society, it appears that nine bushels of additional corn per acre were produced by this method of using plaster." PLASTERING. See Pargetting.

PLASTIC

Pages 245-249

C denotes a thing endowed with a formative power, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of forming or fashioning a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> after the likeness of a living being. PLASTIC-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, a certain power by which, as an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, many philosophers, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have supposed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> motions in the corporeal world, and the various processes of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> and corruption, to be perpetually carried on. Among the philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, such a power was almost universally admitted. It seems, indeed, to have been rejected only by the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a> and Epicurus, who talk as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had thought gravity essential to matter, and the fortuitous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of atoms, which they held to have been from eternity, the source not only of all the regular motions in the universe, but also of the organization of all corporeal systems, and even of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and intellective, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> and in men. It is needless to say, that those men, whatever they might profess, were in reality <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">atheists</a>; and Democritus, it is universally known, avowed his atheism. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the philosophers who held the existence of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLASTIC_NATURE">plastic nature</a>, considered it not as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in the strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, but merely as an instrument in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the Deity; though even among them there were some who held no superior power, and were of course as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> atheists as Democritus himself. Such was Strato of Lampacus. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was originally of the peripatetic school, over which he presided many years, with no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reputation for learning and eloquence. He was the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> assertor of what has been termed Hylozoic atheism; a system which admits of no power superior to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or plastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, essential, ingenerable, and incorruptible, inherent in matter, but without sense and consciousness. That such was his doctrine we learn from Cicero, who makes Velleius the Epicurean say, "Nec audendus Strato qui Physicus appellatur, qui omnem vim divinam in Naturae fitam effe censet, quae causas gigantici, augendi, minuendi habeat, sed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARET">caret</a> omni sensu." That Strato in admitting this plastic principle, differed widely from Democritus, is apparent from the following account of him by the same author: Strato Lampacenus negat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> deorum le uti <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> fabricandum mundum, quaeunque sint docet omnia esse effecta naturae, nec ut illae, qui asperis, et levibus, et hamatis uncinateque corporibus concretae haec esse dicat, interjecta inani; somnia cenent haec esse Democriti, non docentis sed optantis. That the rough and smooth, and hooked and crooked, atoms of Democritus, were indeed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> and delusions, is a position which no man <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> controvert; but surely Strato was himself as great a dreamer when he made sensation and intelligence result from a certain plastic or spermatic life in matter, which is itself devoid of sense and consciousness. It is, indeed, inconceivable, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the emphatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Cudworth, "how any one in his senses should admit such a monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a> as this, that every atom of dust has in itself as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> as the greatest politician and most profound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, and yet is neither conscious nor intelligent!" It is to be observed of Strato likewise, that though he attributed a certain kind of life to matter, he by no means allowed of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> life as ruling over the whole material universe. He supposed the several parts of matter to have so many several plastic lives of their own, and seems to have attributed something to chance in the production and preservation of the mundane system. In denying the existence of a God, perpetually directing his plastic principle, and in supposing as many of these principles as there are atoms of matter, Strato deviated far from the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. The great founder of the peripatetic school, as well as his apostate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, taught that mundane things are not effected by fortuitous mechanism, but by such a nature as acts regularly and artificially for ends; yet he never considers this nature as the highest principle, or supreme Numen, but as subordinate to a perfect mind or intellect; and he expressly affirms, that "mind, together with nature, formed or fashioned this universe." He evidently considers mind as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and intelligent agent, and nature as the subservient and executive instrument. Indeed, we are strongly inclined to adopt the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the learned Moehlheim, who thinks that by nature Aristotle meant nothing more than that θεον, ουρανον, or animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to which he attributes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>, and of which he expressly says that all things are full. Be De Generatione Animalium lib. iii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. ii., this as it may, he always joins God and nature together, and affirms that they do nothing in vain. The same doctrine was taught before him by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, who affirms that "nature, together with reason, and according to it, orders all things." It must not, however, be concealed, that Plato seems to have attributed intelligence to the principle by which he supposed the world to be animated; for Chalcidius, commenting on the Timaeus, thus expresses himself: "Hec est illa ratione... <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. 53. velles anima mundi, quae gemina juxta meliorem naturam veneratione tutelam praebet infernibus, divinis dispositionibus obsequens, providentiam nativis impertiens, eorum similitudine propter cognitionem beatam."—Apologeticus, tells us, "Ilam coelestem animam, fontem animarum omnium, optimam virtutem effe genetricem, subferviri etiam Fabricatoris Deo, et pretio effe ad omnium inventione ejus." Plato pronunciavit. The doctrine of Plato has been adopted by many moderns of great eminence both for genius and for learning. The celebrated Berkeley bishop of Cloyne, after giving the view of Plato's anima mundi, which the reader will find in our article MOTION, No. 12, thus recommends the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>: "If that philosopher himself was not read only, but studied also with care, and made his own interpreter, I believe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> that now lies against him would soon wear off, or be even converted into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem, for those excellent notions, and fine hints, that sparkle and shine throughout his writings; which seem to contain not only the most valuable learning of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Greece, but also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of the most remote traditions and early science of the east." Cudworth, and the learned author of Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, are likewise strenuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for the Aristotelian doctrine of a plastic nature diffused through the material world; (see Metaphysics, No. 200, 201, 202.) and a notion very similar has lately occurred. occurred to a writer who does not appear to have borrowed it either from the Lyceum or the Academy. This writer is Mr Young, of whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fulgence, and its agency in moving bodies, some account has been given elsewhere, (see Motion). As a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> unconscious agent, immaterial, and, as he expresses himself, immental, it bears a striking resemblance to the phyletic nature or vegetable life of Cudworth; but the author holds it to be not only the principle of motion, but also the basis or fulcrum of matter itself; in the production of which, by certain motions, it may be said to be more strictly plastic than the hylarchical principle, or vis gentrix, of any other philosopher with whose writings we have any acquaintance. Though this opinion be singular, yet as its author is evidently a man who thinks for himself, unawed by the authority of celebrated names, and as one great part of the utility of such works as ours consists in their serving as indexes to science and literature, we shall lay before our readers a short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the reasonings by which Mr Young endeavours to support his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, and we shall take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of remarking upon those reasonings as we proceed. The author, after a short introduction, enters upon his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> intitled, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> of Matter in general. In that chapter there is little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>. He treats, as others have done, of primary and secondary qualities, and adheres too closely to the language of Locke, when he says, that "the nature of bodies signifies the aggregate of all those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> with which they furnish us, and by which they are made known." To say the best of it, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> is inaccurately expressed. An aggregate of ideas may be occasioned by the impulse of bodies on the organs of sense, but the effect of impulse cannot be that which impels. We should not have made this remark, which may perhaps be deemed captious, were we not persuaded that the vague and inaccurate use of terms is the source of those mistakes into which, we cannot help thinking, that the very ingenious author has sometimes fallen. Having justly observed, that we know nothing directly of bodies but their qualities, he proceeds to investigate the nature of solidity. "Solidity (he says) is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of body which principally requires our notice. It is that which fills <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, and which resists other solids, occupying the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which it occupies; thus making extension and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> real, and different from mere space and vacuity. If the fe- --- (A) We can only conceive of solidity as being a resistance of the parts of any body, to a power which endeavours to separate them, or to bring them nearer together. Now that which resists any power, and prevents its effect, is also a power. By resistance, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> here an active resistance, such as an animal can employ against an animal. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> pulls against a load, he draws it along; but if he draws against another horse, he is put to a stand, and his endeavor is defeated. When any endeavor to change the situation of the parts of any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> is in like manner prevented from taking effect, and the parts retain their situation, the situation has plainly been preserved by an active resistance or power, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to that which was fruitlessly exerted on them." Such is our author's reasoning to prove that matter is essentially active, and that from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> results our notion of its solidity: but does he not here confound solidity with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, and impenetrability with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>? He certainly does; for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is as solid, in the proper sense of the word, as adamant, and the particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> as the particles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The parts of water are, indeed, separated with ease, and those of adamant with difficulty; but it is not because the latter have more solidity than the former, but because the power of cohesion, whatever it may be, operates upon them with greater force. Solidity is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of a whole; hardness and softness result from the cohesion of parts. We do not at all perceive the propriety of the simile of the horse pulling a load, and afterwards pulling against another horse. Is it because both horses are active that one of them cannot prevail against the other, and because the load is inactive that either of them may drag along a mass of iron of half a ton <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>? which we do not perceive the force, attempted to prove that it is by an inward power, and not by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a>, that one body prevents another from occupying the same place with itself; he naturally enough infers matter to be essentially active. "But the activity of matter is to be considered in a certain limited sense, and its inertness is to be regarded in another limited sense; so that these are compatible within their respective limits. The activity of body may be considered as belonging to the parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>; its inertia as the inertia formed of those parts. The actions of the parts are everywhere opposed to each other, and equal; and hence results the inactivity of the whole." Solidity alone of the primary qualities being positive, and peculiar to bodies, and our author having resolved this into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> or power, it follows, by his analysis, that the essence of body is reduced to power likewise. But, as he properly observes, power is an idea of reflection, not acquired by the senses, but suggested by thought. Hence our knowledge of real existence in body must be such as is suggested to us by our thoughts exercised about our sensations. "We are capable of acting and producing changes in appearances; and this faculty, which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to exist in ourselves, we call power. We are conscious of the exertion of our own power; and therefore, when we see action or change happen without any exertion of ours, we refer this to other powers without us, and necessarily conclude the power to exist where the change begins or the action is exerted. This power, then, referred to bodies, must exist in them, or it can exist nowhere." In two chapters, which might easily have been compressed into one not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the shortest of them, our author analyzes atoms or the primary particles of matter, and strenuously opposes their impenetrability. He allows that there are atoms of matter not divisible by any known force; but as these, however small, must be conceived as having extension, each of them must be composed of parts held together by the same power which binds together many atoms in the same body. This power, indeed, he acknowledges to operate much more forcibly when it cements the parts of a primary atom than when it makes many atoms cohere in one mass; but still it operates in the same manner: and as the ideal analysis may be carried on ad infinitum, the only positive idea which is suggested by atoms, or the parts of atoms, is the idea of a resisting power. That this power of resistance, which constitutes what is vulgarly called the solidity of bodies, may not be absolutely impenetrable, he attempts to prove, by showing that resistance does in fact take place in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where impenetrability, and even solidity, are not supposed by any man. "Let us endeavour (says he) to bring together two like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of a magnet, and we shall experience a resistance to their approximation. Why, then, may not a piece of iron, which between our fingers resists their coming together, result by an efficacy perfectly similar, though more strongly exerted? If <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a> were to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon our bodies as upon iron, we should feel it; or were magnets endowed with sensation, they would feel that which resists their nearer approach. The resisting extension between the two magnets is permeable to all the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and reflecting none is therefore unseen; but it is easy to conceive that the same power which resists the approach of the iron might resist and reflect some rays of light. We should then have a visible object interposed between the two magnets, as we have before supposed it might be a tangible one. It is likewise easy to conceive that which is tangible and visible so applied to our organs of tasting, of smelling, and of hearing, as to excite ideas of flavours, odours, and sounds. Thus we see that an action, in which no supposition of solidity or impenetrability is involved, may be conceived to assume all the qualities of matter, by only supposing a familiar effect extended in its operation." This reasoning is exceedingly ingenious, though perhaps not original; but what is of more importance, it does not approach so near to demonstration as the author seems to imagine. If magnets operate by means of a fluid issuing from them (see Magnetism), those who hold the solidity or impenetrability of matter will maintain, that each atom of the magnetic fluid is solid and impenetrable. That we do not see nor feel these atoms, will be considered as no argument that they do not exist; for we do not see, nor in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> room feel, the atoms of the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; which yet Mr Young will acknowledge to have a real existence, and to be capable of operating upon our senses of hearing and smelling. Let us, however, suppose, that by this reasoning he has established the non-existence of every thing in the primary atoms of matter but active powers of resistance, and let us see how he conceives the actions of these powers to constitute what gives us the notion of inert and solid body; for that we have such a notion cannot be denied. To act he allows to be an attribute, and justly observes, that we cannot conceive an attribute to exist without a substance. "But (says he) we have traced all phenomena to action as to a generic idea, comprehending under it all forms of matter and motion as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of that genus. By this analysis, that complex idea we usually denominated matter, and considered as the substance or substratum to which motion appertained as an attribute, is found to change its character, and to be itself an attribute of a substance essentially active, of which one modification of motion produces matter and another generates motion." The action of this substance Mr Young determines to be motion, (see Motion, No. 16.) and he proceeds to inquire by what kind of motion it produces matter, or inert and resisting atoms. "Whatever portion of the active substance is given to form an atom, the following things are necessary to be united in such portion of active substance: 1stly, It must in some respect continually move; for otherwise it would lose its nature, and cease to be active. 2ndly, It must also in some other respect be at rest, for otherwise it could not form an inactive atom. 3rdly, It must preserve unity within itself." The author's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> If so, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> or triple the mass, and a very strange phenomenon will be the result; for we shall have an active whole compounded of two or three inactive parts, even though those parts should not be in contact! proof of the first of these positions we have given elsewhere. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> he holds to be self-evident; and the third he thinks established by the following reasoning: "Solidity is the result of those actions among the parts of any whole, whereby the unity of the whole is preserved within itself. Several uncohering things may be united by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> bond: this does not constitute these one solid; it may be one bundle: but if several things cohere, and have a unity preserved within themselves, they become one solid. An atom is the least and most simple solid." Having thus proved the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of these three requisites to the formation of an atom, he observes, that "the two first can only be united in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> of the portion of active substance about a centre or axis at rest. By such a motion, all the parts successively occupy different places in the orbit of rotation, and therefore move; the centre round which they revolve being at rest, the whole portion is also at rest; and thus the portion is at once moving and quiescent, as is required. The same kind of motion will also fulfill the terms of the third requisite; for a substance having a revolving motion around its own centre, preserves its unity by reason of all the parts preserving the same relation to the centre: and further, a motion of the active substance about a centre or axis will be an activity in the same orbit, which will act upon and resist whatever shall interfere to oppose its activity, or destroy the unity of the sphere, by diverting the course of the revolving motions. The activity or motion of a portion of active substance about a centre will, therefore, give solidity to such portion; for it will give it unity and resistance, and in a manner tie together all the parts, forming them into one mass about their common centre: for they move or are active not towards the centre, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they would be lost in non-extension; nor from the centre, where they would dilate in boundless space; but about the centre, preserving the same limits of extension: and being in this way active, they in this way resist any other activity opposed to them, that is, they resist any action which tends to penetrate or divide this sphere of revolving activity. Therefore, since any portion of active substance does, by revolving about a centre, become an united, resisting, and quiescent whole, the smallest portions of the active substance which have such motions will become atoms, or make the smallest portions of matter." Having thus shown to his own satisfaction how atoms of matter are formed, he next explains what at first he confesses may have appeared a paradox, "how the active substance, retaining its own nature and essential properties, continuing immaterial, unfold, and active, puts on at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the form of matter, and becomes material, solid, and inert. A sphere of revolving active substance, as it revolves continually about a centre, and as parts of the substance, are considered as successively passing through every point in the orbit; considered thus in its parts, and in its motions, it is active substance, immaterial, and unfold; but the whole sphere, considered unitically, collectively, and as quiescent, is in this point of view a solid atom, material, and inert." Such is the active substance of Mr Young, and such his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the formation of matter. That he has not with fertility copied from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, every reader of his book, who is not an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> stranger to Greek and Roman literature, will readily acknowledge; and yet if his theory be well founded, he has discovered a middle substance between mind and matter, more properly plastic than Aristotle or Plato, Cudworth or Berkeley, ever conceived. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> compels us to add, that to us his theory appears to labour under infuperable objections. That there may be in the universe a substance essentially active, and at the same time not intelligent, is a proposition which we are by no means inclined to controvert. Various phenomena, both in vegetable and animal life, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to suspect that there is such a substance; but it does not follow that we are inclined to adopt our author's doctrine respecting the formation of matter. He conceives his proof, indeed, to be "in its nature not at all imperfect, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of demonstration;" and if any one refuse it, he thinks it will be necessary for him to show, either that the explanation offered is not sufficient, or that some other explanation will serve equally well." To show that the explanation offered is not sufficient, will not, we apprehend, be a very arduous task; but we have no inclination to attempt ourselves another explanation, because we believe that of the formation of matter no other account can be given than that which resolves it into the fiat of the Creator. That it cannot be formed by the motion of an immaterial substance in the manner which our author has very clearly described, seems to be a truth so evident as not to admit of proof; for if motion be, as he defines it, a change of place, every thing that is moved must have the quality of extension. But all the parts of this active substance which are given to form an atom, move round a centre, and are expressly said to occupy successively different places in the orbit of rotation. Every one of these parts, therefore, is an extended being: and since, according to our author, solidity is nothing but an active power of repulsion, and the parts of this active substance, in their rotation round their centre, act upon and repel whatever interferes to oppose their activity, it follows that each of these parts is likewise a solid being. But, in the opinion of Mr Young himself, and of all mankind, whatever is extended and solid is material. This theory, therefore, exhibits a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in which atoms are formed of a substance, which, though it is said to be active, immaterial, and unfold, appears, when narrowly inspected, to be nothing else than a collection of those very atoms of which the author pretends to explain the formation. Mr Young, who examines and very freely censures some of the doctrines of Newton and others, is too much a man of science to be offended at us for stating objections to a theory which is quite new, to a transformation which he himself acknowledges may to many "appear not only problematical and difficult to conceive, but wholly impossible, and implying contradictions absolutely and forever irreconcilable." Whether this be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> character of it our readers must determine; but if we did not believe the author to be a man of ingenuity, we should not have introduced him or his work to their acquaintance. Plastic Art, the art of representing all sorts of figures by the means of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is derived from the Greek word πλαστική, which signifies the "art of forming, modelling, or casting, in a mould." A mould in general is a body that is made hollow for that purpose. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> makes use of it to form figures in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, bronze, lead, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, or any other metal or fusible substance. The mould is made of clay, stucco, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and is hollowed into the form of the figure that is to be produced; they then apply the jet, which is a sort of funnel, through which the metal is poured that is to form the figures, and that is called running the metal into the mould. It is in this manner, but with much practice and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, that the artist forms, 1. Equestrian and pedetrian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of every kind; 2. Groups; 3. Pedestals; 4. Bas-reliefs; 5. Medallions; 6. Cannons, mortars, and other pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>; 7. Ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, as capitals, bases, &c.; 8. Various sorts of furniture, as lutes, branches, &c., in every kind of metal; and in the same manner figures are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in stucco, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, or any other fusible matter. See PLASTER OF <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">PARIS</a>. Wax being a substance that is very easily put in fusion, plasters make much use of it. There are impressions which are highly pleasing in coloured wax, of medallions, bas-relief alto relievo, and of detached figures; which, however, are somewhat brittle. But this matter has been carried too far: they have not only formed moulds to represent the likeness and the bust of a living person, by applying the plaster to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> itself, and afterwards casting melted wax into the mould; but they have also painted that waxen bust with the natural colours of the face, and have then applied glass eyes and natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; to which they have joined a stuffed body and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of wax; and have, lastly, dressed their figure in a real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; and by these means have produced an object the most shocking and detestable that it is possible to conceive. It is not a statue, a bust, a natural resemblance that they form; but a dead body, a lifeless countenance, a mere carcass. The stiff air, the inflexible muscles, the haggard eyes of glass, all contribute to produce an object that is hideous and disagreeable to every man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Figures like these offend by affording too exact an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of nature. In no one of the polite arts ought imitation ever to approach so near the truth as to be taken for nature herself. Illusion must have its bounds; without which it becomes ridiculous. There is another <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> far more ingenious and pleasing, which is that wherein M. Lippart, antiquary and artist at Dresden, has so much excelled. He has found the means of resembling, by indefatigable labour, great expense, and infinite taste, that immense <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, engraved and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CAMEO">cameo</a>, which are to be seen in the most celebrated cabinets. He has made choice of those that are the most beautiful; and, with a plaster of his own invention, he takes from these stones an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> that is surprisingly accurate, and which afterwards become as marble: these impressions he calls pastes. He then gives them a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and incloses each with a gold rim; and, by ranging them in a judicious order, forms them an admirable system. They are fixed on pasteboards, which form so many drawers, and are then inclosed in cases, which represent folio volumes, and have titles wrote on their backs; so that these fictitious books may conveniently occupy a place in a library. Nothing can be more ingenious than this invention; and, by means of it, persons of moderate fortune are enabled to make a complete collection of all antiquity has left that is excellent of this kind; and the copies are very little inferior to the originals. There is also another method of taking the impressions of cameos, medals, and coins, which is as follows: They wash or properly clean the piece whose impression is to be taken, and surround it with a border of wax. They then dissolve sealing-wax in water, and make a decoction of it, mixing with it some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, to give it an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour. They pour this paste, when hot, on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or medal, to the thickness of about the tenth part of an inch; they then leave it exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, in a place free from dust. After a few days this paste becomes hard, and offers to the eye the most admirable and faithful representation of the medal that it is possible to conceive: they are then carefully placed in drawers; and thousands of these impressions, which comprehend many ages, may be included in a small compass. The proficient in plasters have likewise invented the art of casting in a mould papier-mâché or dissolved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and forming it into figures in imitation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, of ornaments and decorations for ceilings, furniture, &c., and which they afterwards paint or gild. There are, however, some inconveniences attending this art; as, for example, the imperfections in the moulds, which render the contours of the figures inelegant, and give them a heavy air: these ornaments, moreover, are not so durable as those of bronze or wood, seeing that in a few years they are preyed on by the worm. The figures that are given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, Delft <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c., belong also to plasters; for they are formed by moulds, as well as by the art of the sculptor and turner; and by all these arts united are made vases of every kind, figures, groups, and other designs, either for use or ornament. From this general article the reader is referred to FOUNDRY, CAST, GLAZING, PORCELAIN, PAPIER-MÂCHÉ, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">POTTERY</a>, DELFT WARE.

PLATA

Pages 249-250

the name of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, running through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Paraguay; whence the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is sometimes called Plata; though this name is usually bestowed only upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Paraguay. In the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it comprehends all that country bounded on the east and south-east by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; on the south, by Terra Magellonica; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUCUMAN">Tucuman</a>; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the provinces of Paraguay Proper and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARANA">Parana</a>. The great river La Plata, from which the country has its name, was first discovered, in 1515, by Juan Diaz de Solis; but denominated La Plata by Sebastian Caboto, from the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> he procured from the adjacent inhabitants, imagining it was the produce of the country, though in fact they brought it from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. The country lies between 32° and 37° of south latitude. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is pleasant and healthy. Their winter is in May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, when the nights are indeed very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but the days moderately warm; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a> is neither violent nor lasting, and the snows are very inconsiderable. The country consists mostly of plains of vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and exceeding rich <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, producing all sorts of European and American <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, wheat, maize, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, &c., and abounding with such excellent pastures, that the herds brought hither from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> are multiplied to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they are all in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> claiming any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in them, but every man takes what he hath occasion for. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, especially, is so prodigious, that many thousands of them are killed merely for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the ships go for Spain, and their carcases left to be devoured by wild beasts and birds of prey, which are also very numerous. Sometimes, when they cannot vend their hides, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> kill them for their tongues; and those who care not to be at the trouble to fetch them from the plains, may buy them for a trifle. There is a curious account in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Anson's voyage of the manner of hunting them on horseback; and of catching and killing them, by throwing a noose on their horns at full gallop, the horses being trained to the sport. Horses are also numerous, and in common like the other cattle; so that a man may have as many as he pleases for the catching; and of those that are already broke, one may buy some of the best, and of the true Spanish breed, for a piece-of-eight per head. Wild fowl also is in great plenty here; partridges in particular are more numerous, and as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and tame as our hens, so that one may kill them with a stick. Their wheat makes the finest and whitest of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and, in a word, they seem to want for nothing here, especially the natives, but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>. The former the Spaniards have brought to them from other parts; and the latter they supply themselves with, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> vast numbers of almond, peach, and other trees, which require no other trouble than putting the kernels into the ground, and by the next year, we are told, they begin to bear fruit. The return for European commodities is so great here, that it almost exceeds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>; an ordinary two-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> fetching a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> of the value of 10 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12 shillings 20 or 30 crowns, and so of the rest. The river Plata rises in Peru, and receives a great many others in its course; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which is the Paraguay. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of it is said to be very clear and sweet, and to petrify wood; and contains such plenty and variety of fish, that the people catch great quantities of them without any other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> than their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It runs mostly to the south and south-east; and is navigable the greater part of its course by the largest vessels, and full of delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. All along its banks are seen the most beautiful birds of all kinds; but it sometimes overflows the adjacent country to a great extent, and is infested by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> of a prodigious size. From its junction with the Paraguay to its mouth it is above 200 leagues. We may form some judgement of its largeness by the width of its mouth, which is said to be about 70 leagues. Before it falls into the Paraguay it is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>. See PANAMA. PLATÆÆ, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a very strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, in its situation exposed to the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> (Theophratus); burnt to the ground by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Justinus); mentioned much in the course of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>: Famous for the defeat of Mardonius, the Persian general; and for the most signal victory of the Lacedemonians and other Greeks under Pausanias the Lacedemonian, and Arissides an Athenian general (Nepos, Diodorus, Plutarch); in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of which the Greeks erected a temple to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Eleutherus, and instituted games which they called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEUTHERIA">Eleutheria</a>; and there they show the tombs of those who fell in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> (Strabo). It stood at the foot of Mount Cithaeron, between that and Thebes to the north, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, and on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> and Megaris. Now in ruins.

PLATAEA

the Spoonbill, a genus of birds belonging to the order of gallinae. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLATANUS

Pages 250-250

the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">Plane</a>-tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the magnolia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLATE

Pages 250-251

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> which denotes a piece of wrought silver, such as the shallow vessel on which meat is eaten. It is likewise used by sportsmen to express the reward given to the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> at our races. The winning a plate is not the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of a few days to the owner of the horse; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> is to be made for it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is any great dependence on the success. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> is the least <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that can be allowed to draw the horse's body clear, and to refine his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection that is attainable by art. It is first necessary to take an exact view of his body, whether he be low <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; and it is also necessary to consider whether he be dull and heavy, or brisk and lively when abroad. If he appear dull and heavy, and there is reason to suppose it is owing to too hard riding, or, as the jockeys express it, to some gout that has been dissolved in hunting, and has not been removed by scouring, then the proper remedy is half an ounce of diapente given in a pint of good sack; this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> at once remove the canic, and revive the creature's spirits. After this, for the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> of the month, he is to be fed with oats, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and split beans; giving him sometimes the one and sometimes the other as he likes best; and always leaving some in the locker, that he may feed at leisure when he is left alone. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOM">groom</a> returns at the feeding-time, whatever is left of this must be removed, and fresh given; by this means the creature will soon become high-spirited, wanton, and full of play. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> he must be rode out an airing, and every other day it will be proper to give him a little more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>; but not so much as to make him sweat too much. The beans and oats in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> are to be put into a bag, and beaten till the hulls are all off, and then winnowed clean; and the bread, instead of being chipped in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way, is to have the crust clean cut off. If the horse be in good flesh and spirits when taken up for its month's preparation, the diapente must be omitted; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> business will be to give him good food, and to much exercise as will keep him in wind, without overwearing him or tiring his spirits. When he takes larger exercises afterwards, towards the end of the month, it will be proper to have some horses in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to run against him. This will put him upon his mettle, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them will give him spirits. This, however, is to be cautiously observed, that he has not a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> given him for ten days or a fortnight before the plate is to be run for; and that the last heat that is given him the day before the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, must be in his clothes: this will make him run with greatly more vigour, when stripped for the race, and feeling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> wind on every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> week, the horse should have the same food, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATING">PLATING</a> is the art of covering baser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> with a thin plate of silver either for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> or for ornament. It is said to have been invented by a spur-maker, not for show but for real utility. Till then the more elegant spurs in common use were made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> silver, and from the flexibility of that metal they were liable to be bent into inconvenient forms by the slightest accident. To remedy this defect, a workman at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> contrived to make the branches of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of spurs hollow, and to fill that hollow with a slender rod of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Finding this a great improvement, and being desirous to add cheapness to utility, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to make the hollow larger, and of course the iron thicker and thicker, till at last he discovered the means of coating an iron spur with silver in such a manner as to make it equally elegant with those which were made wholly of that metal. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> was quickly applied to other purposes; and to numberless utensils which were formerly made of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or iron are now given the strength of these metals, and the elegance of silver, for a small additional expense.

PLATEBAND

Pages 250-250

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a border <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, along a wall, or the side of a parterre, frequently edged with box, &c. PLATEBAND of a door or window, is used for the lintel, where that is made <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, or not much marked.

PLATO

Pages 252-255

an illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of antiquity, was by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> an Athenian, though the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth was the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Egina. His lineage through his father is traced back to Codrus the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, and through his mother to Solon the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his birth is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> placed in the beginning of the 88th Olympiad; but Dr Enfield thinks it may be more accurately fixed in the third year of the 87th Olympiad, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 432 years before the Christian era. He gave early indications of an extensive and original genius, and had an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> suitable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, being instructed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of letters by the grammarian Dionysius, and trained in athletic exercises by Aristo of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>. He applied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diligence to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and made such proficiency in the latter, as to produce an epic poem, which, upon comparing it with the poems of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, he committed to the flames. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 20 he composed a dramatic piece; but after he had given it to the performers, happening to attend upon a discourse of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, he was so captivated by his eloquence, that he reclaimed his tragedy without suffering it to be acted, renounced the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, burnt all his poems, and applied himself wholly to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. It is thought that Plato's first matters in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> were Cratylus and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERMOGENES">Hermogenes</a>, who taught the systems of Heraclitus and Parmenides; but when he was 20 years old, he attached himself wholly to Socrates, with whom he remained eight years in the relation of a scholar. During this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, he frequently displeased his companions, and sometimes even his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> upon the Socratic system opinions which were taken from some other stock. It was the practice of the scholars of Socrates to commit to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the substance of their master's discourses. Plato wrote them in the form of dialogues; but with so great additions of his own, that Socrates, hearing him recite his Lyfs, cried out, "O <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>! how many things does this young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> feign of me!" Plato, however, retained the warmest <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his master. When that great and good man was summoned before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, his illustrious scholar undertook to plead his cause, and begun a speech in his defense; but the partiality and violence of the judges would not permit him to proceed. After the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a>, he presented his master with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> sufficient to redeem his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; which, however, Socrates refused to accept. During his imprisonment, Plato attended him, and was present at a conversation which he held with his friends concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; the substance of which he afterwards committed to writing in the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> intitled Phaedo, not, however, without interweaving his own opinions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The philosophers who were at Athens were so alarmed at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Socrates, that most of them fled from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> to avoid the injustice and cruelty of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>.
