Plato, whose grief upon this occasion is said by Plutarch to have been excessive, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>; where he was kindly entertained by Euclid, who had been one of Socrates's first scholars, till the storm was over. Afterwards he determined to travel in pursuit of knowledge; and from Megara he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he conferred with Eurytus, Philolaus, and Archytas. These were the most celebrated of the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, whose doctrine was then become famous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and from these the Pythagoreans have affirmed that he had all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy. He dived into the most profound and mysterious secrets of the Pythagorean doctrines; and perceiving other knowledge to be connected with them, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENE">Cyrene</a>, where he learned <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> of Theodorus the mathematician. From thence he passed into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, to acquaint himself with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of their priests, to study more nicely the proportions of geometry, and to instruct himself in astronomical observations; and having taken a full survey of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he settled for some time in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Sais, learning of the wise men there, what they held concerning the universe, whether it had a beginning, whether it moved wholly or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, &c.; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a> affirms, that he learned from these the immortality, and also the transmigration, of souls. Some of the fathers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that he had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the books of Moses, and that he studied under a learned Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>; but there is nothing that can be called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> for these assertions. St Austin once believed that Plato had some conference with Jeremiah; but afterwards discovered, that that prophet must have been dead at least 60 years before Plato's voyage to Egypt. Plato's curiosity was not yet satisfied. He travelled into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> to consult the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> about the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of that country; and he designed to have penetrated even to the Indies, and to have learned of the Brachmans their manners and customs; but the wars in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> prevented him. "He then returned into Italy, to the Pythagorean school at Tarentum, where he endeavoured to improve his own system, by incorporating with it the doctrine of Pythagoras, as it was then taught by Archytas, Timaeus, and others. And afterwards, when he visited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, he retained such an attachment to the Italic school, that, through the bounty of Dionysius, he purchased at a vast price several books which contained the doctrine of Pythagoras, from Philolaus, one of his followers. "Returning home richly stored with knowledge of various kinds, Plato settled in Athens, and executed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, which he had doubtless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> had in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>, of forming a new school for the instruction of youth in the principles of philosophy. The place which he made choice of for this purpose was a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, called the Academy, from Hecadmus, who left it to the citizens for the purpose of gymnastic exercises. Adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and sepulchres, planted with lofty <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>-trees, and intersected by a gentle stream, it afforded a delightful retreat for philosophy and the muses. Of this retreat Horace speaks: Atque Atque inter sylvas Academi quaere vereum. "Midst Academic groves to search for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>." Within this inclosure he possessed, as a part of his humble patrimony, purchased at the price of three thousand drachmas, a small garden, in which he opened a school for the reception of those who might be inclined to attend his instructions. How much Plato valued mathematical studies, and how necessary a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> he thought them for higher speculations, appears from the inscription which he placed over the door of his school: "Oubis ayos ergon houta." "Let no one who is unacquainted with geometry enter here." This new school soon became famous, and its master was ranked among the most eminent philosophers. His travels into distant countries, where learning and wisdom flourished, gave him celebrity among his brethren of the Socratic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. None of these had ventured to institute a school in Athens except Aristippus; and he had confined his instructions almost entirely to ethical subjects, and had brought himself into some discredit by the freedom of his manners. Plato alone remained to inherit the patrimony of public esteem which Socrates had left his disciples; and he possessed talents and learning adequate to his design of extending the study of philosophy beyond the limits within which it had been inclosed by his master. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, not only that young men crowded to his school from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, but that people of the first distinction in every department frequented the academy. Even females, disguised in men's clothes, often attended his lectures. Among the illustrious names which appear in the catalogue of his followers are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DION">Dion</a> the Syracusan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and the orators Hyperides, Lyscursus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>, and Ilocrates. Greatness was never yet exempted from envy. The disingenuous reputation of Plato brought upon him the hatred of his former companions in the school of Socrates, and they loaded him with detraction and obloquy. It can only be ascribed to mutual jealousy, that Xenophon and he, though they relate the discourses of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> master, studiously avoid mentioning one another. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> the Cynic ridiculed Plato's doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> speculations. In the midst of these private censures, however, the public fame of Plato daily increased; and several states, among which were the Arcadians and the Thessians, sent ambassadors with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> requests that he would come over, not only to instruct the young men in philosophy, but also to prescribe them laws of government. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRENAICS">Cyrenaics</a>, Syracusans, Cretans, and Eleans, sent also to him: he did not go to any of them, but gave laws and rules of governing to all. He lived frugally, yet soberly and chastely. He was a man of great virtues, and exceedingly affable; of which we need no greater <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, than his civil manner of conversing with the philosophers of his own times, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and envy were at their height. His behaviour to Diogenes is always mentioned in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The Cynic was vastly offended, it seems, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> and fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of Plato, and used to catch all opportunities of snarling at him. He dined one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and, trampling upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> with his dirty feet, uttered this brutish sarcasm, "I trample upon the pride of Plato;" to which Plato wisely replied, "With greater pride." The fame of Plato drew disciples to him from all parts; among whom were Speusippus an Athenian, his sister's son, whom he appointed his successor in the academy, and the great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. The admiration of this illustrious man was not confined to the breasts of a few philosophers. He was in high esteem with several princes, particularly Archelaus king of Macedon, and Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> of Sicily. At three different periods he visited the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of this latter prince, and made several bold but unsuccessful attempts to subdue his haughty and tyrannical spirit. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> relation of the particulars of these visits to Sicily may serve to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> upon the character of our philosopher; and we shall give it in the words of Dr Enfield, from whose elegant history of philosophy we have extracted by much the most valuable parts of this article. The professed object of Plato's first visit to Sicily, which happened in the 40th year of his age, during the reign of the elder Dionysius the son of Hermocrates, was, to take a survey of the island, and particularly to observe the wonders of Mount Aetna. Whilst he was resident at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, he was employed in the instruction of Dion, the king's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who possessed excellent abilities, though hitherto restrained by the terrors of a tyrannical government, and relaxed by the luxuries of a licentious court. Disgusted by the debauched manners of the Syracusans, he endeavoured to rescue his pupil from the general depravity. Nor did Dion disappoint his preceptor's expectations. No sooner had he received a taste of that philosophy which leads to virtue, than he was fired with an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of wisdom. Entertaining an hope that philosophy might produce the same effect upon Dionysius, he took great pains to procure an interview between Plato and the tyrant. In the course of the conference, whilst Plato was discoursing on the security and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of virtue, and the miseries attending injustice and oppression, Dionysius, perceiving that the philosopher's discourse was levelled against the vices and cruelties of his reign, dismissed him with high displeasure from his presence, and conceived a design against his life. It was not without great difficulty that Plato, by the assistance of Dion, made his escape. A vessel which had brought over Pollis, a delegate from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, was fortunately at that time returning to Greece. Dion engaged Pollis to take the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the philosopher, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> him safely in his native country; but Dionysius discovered the design, and obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> from Pollis, that he would either put him to death or sell him as a slave upon the passage. Pollis accordingly sold him in the island of Aegina; the inhabitants of which were then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Athenians. Plato could not long remain unnoticed: Anicerris, a Cyrenaic philosopher, who happened to be at that time in the island, discovered the stranger, and thought himself happy in an opportunity of showing his respect for so illustrious a philosopher: he purchased his freedom for 30 minae, or 84l. 10s. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> money, and sent him home to Athens. Repayment being afterwards offered to Anicerris by Plato's relations, he refused the money, saying, with that generous spirit which true philosophy always inspires, that he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> no reason why the relations of Plato should engross to themselves the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of serving him. After a short <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a>, Dionysius repented of his ill- placed resentment, and wrote to Plato, earnestly requesting him to repair his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by returning to Syracuse; to which Plato gave this high-minded answer, that philosophy would not allow him leisure to think of Dionysius. He was, however, prevailed upon by his friend Dion to accept of the tyrant's invitation to return to Syracuse, and take upon him the education of Dionysius the younger, who was heir apparent to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. He was received by Dionysius the reigning sovereign with every possible appearance of respect; but after feeling his friend banished, and being himself kept as a prisoner at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, he was by the tyrant sent back into his own country, with a promise that both he and Dion should be recalled at the end of the war in which the Sicilians were then engaged. This promise was not fulfilled. The tyrant wished for the return of Plato; but could not resolve to recall Dion. At last, however, having probably promised that the philosopher should meet his friend at the court of Syracuse, he prevailed upon Plato to visit that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> a third time. When he arrived, the king met him in a magnificent chariot, and conducted him to his palace. The Sicilians too rejoiced in his return; for they hoped that the wisdom of Plato would at length triumph over the tyrannical spirit of the prince. Dionysius seemed wholly divested of his former resentments, listened with apparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to the philosopher's doctrine, and, among other expressions of regard, presented him with eighty talents of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. In the midst of a numerous train of philosophers, Plato now possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> influence and authority in the court of Syracuse. Whilst Aristippus was enjoying himself in splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; whilst Diogenes was freely indulging his acrimonious humour; and whilst Alcines was gratifying his thirst after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>;—Plato supported the credit of philosophy with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, which his friends regarded as an indication of superior wisdom, but which his enemies imputed to pride. After all, it was not in the power of Plato to prevail upon Dionysius to adopt his system of policy, or to recall Dion from his exile. Mutual distrust, after a short interval, arose between the tyrant and the philosopher; each suspected the other of evil designs, and each endeavoured to conceal his suspicion under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> of respect. Dionysius attempted to impede upon Plato by condescending attentions, and Plato to deceive Dionysius by an appearance of confidence. At length, the philosopher became so much dissatisfied with his situation, that he earnestly requested permission to return to Greece, which was at last granted him, and he was sent home loaded with rich presents. On his way to Athens, pausing through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a> during the celebration of the Olympic games, he was present at this general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the Greeks, and engaged universal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. From this narrative it appears, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Plato visited the courts of princes, it was chiefly from the hope of seeing his ideal <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a republic realized; and that his talents and attainments rather qualified him to shine in the academy than in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> or the senate. Plato, now restored to his country and his school, devoted himself to science, and spent the last years of a long life in the instruction of youth. Having enjoyed the advantage of an athletic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, and lived all his days temperately, he arrived at the 81st, or according to some writers the 90th, year of his age, and died, through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> decay of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, in the first year of the hundred and eighth Olympiad. He passed his whole life in a state of celibacy, and therefore left no natural heirs, but transferred his effects by will to his friend Adiamantus. The grove and garden, which had been the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of his philosophical labours, at last afforded him a sepulchre. Statues and altars were erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>; the day of his birth long <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be celebrated as a festival by his followers; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> is to this day preserved in gems; but the most lasting monuments of his genius are his writings, which have been transmitted, without material injury, to the present times. The character of this philosopher has always been high. Besides the advantages of a noble birth, he had a large and comprehensive understanding, a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and good taste, great evenness and sweetness of temper, all cultivated and refined by education and travel; so that it is no wonder if he was honoured by his countrymen, esteemed by strangers, and adored by his scholars. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> thought more highly of Plato than of all their philosophers; they always called him the Divine Plato; and they seemed relieved that his deficient should be more than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>. "There are (says Apuleius) who assert Plato to have sprung from a more sublime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>; and that his mother Pericleone, who was a very beautiful woman, was impregnated by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a>." Plutarch, Suidas, and others, affirm this to have been the common report at Athens. When he was an infant, his father Aristo went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMETTUS">Hymettus</a>, with his wife and child, to sacrifice to the mutes; and while they were buried in the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, a swarm of bees came and distilled their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> upon his lips. This, says Tully, was considered as a prefigure of his future eloquence. Apuleius relates, that Socrates, the night before Plato was recommended to him, dreamed that a young swan flew from Cupid's altar in the academy, and settled in his lap; thence soared to heaven, and delighted the gods with its music; and when Aristo the next day presented Plato to him, "Friends (says Socrates), this is the twin of Cupid's academy." The Greeks loved fables: they show however in the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, what exceeding respect was paid to the memory of Plato. Tully perfectly adored him; tells us, how he was justly called by Panetius the divine, the most wise, the most sacred, the Homer of philosophers; entitled him to Atticus, Deus ille noster; thinks, that if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> had spoken Greek, he would have spoken in Plato's language, and made him so implicitly his guide in wisdom and philosophy, as to declare, that he had rather err with Plato than be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> with any one else. But, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> aside, Plato was certainly a very wonderful man, of a large and comprehensive mind, an imagination infinitely fertile, and of a most flowing and copious eloquence. Nevertheless, the strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of fancy prevailing in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> over judgement, he was too apt to soar beyond the limits of earthly things, to range in the imaginary regions of general and abstracted ideas; and on which account, though there is always a greatness and fullness in his manner, he did not philosophize so much according to truth and nature as Aristotle, though Cicero did not scruple to give him the preference. The writings of Plato are all in the way of dialogue; where he seems to deliver nothing from himself, but every thing thing as the sentiments and opinions of others, of Socrates chiefly, of Timaeus, &c. He does not mention himself anywhere, except once in his Phaedo, and another time in his Apology for Socrates. His style, as Aristotle observed, is betwixt prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; on which account, some have not scrupled to rank him with the poets. There is a better reason for doing than the elevation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of his style; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is often-times the offspring of imagination, instead of doctrines or truths deduced from nature. The first edition of Plato's works in Greek was put out by Aldus at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1513; but a Latin version of him by Marcellus Ficinus had been printed there in 1491. They were reprinted together at Lyons in 1588, and at Frankfort in 1602. The famous printer Henry Stephens, in 1578, gave a most beautiful and correct edition of Plato's works at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, with a new Latin version by Serranus, in three volumes folio; and this deservedly passes for the best edition of Plato; yet Serranus's edition is very exceptional, and in many respects, if not in all, inferior to that of Ficinus.

PLATONIC

Pages 255-255

something that relates to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, his school-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, opinions, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like. Thus, platonic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> denotes a pure spiritual affection, for which Plato was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advocate, subsisting between the different sexes, abstracted from all carnal appetites, and regarding no other object but the mind and its beauties; or it is even a sincere disinterested friendship subsisting between persons of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, abstracted from any selfish views, and regarding no other object than the person, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any such love or friendship has aught of a foundation in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. PLATONIC Year, or the Great Year, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> determined by the revolution of the equinoxes, or the space wherein the stars and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> return to their former places in respect of the equinoxes. The platonic year, according to Tycho Brahe, is 25816, according to Ricciolus 25910, and according to Caffini 24800 years. This period once accomplished, it was an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> that the world was to begin anew, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of things to turn over again.

PLATONISM

Pages 255-260

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, which was divided into three branches, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, physics, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. Under theology were comprehended <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a> and ethics, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a>. Plato wrote likewise on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALECTICS">dialectics</a>, but with such inferiority to his pupil <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, that his works in that department of science are seldom mentioned. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers always began their theological systems with some discussion on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the gods, and the formation of the world; and it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> doctrine with them, that from nothing nothing can proceed. We are not to suppose that this general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a> implied nothing more than that for every effect there must be a cause; for this is a proposition which no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> controvert who understands the terms in which it is expressed; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> believed that a proper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> is impossible even to omnipotence, and that to the production of anything a material is not less necessary than an efficient cause, (see Metaphysics, N° 264—394.) That with respect to this important question, Plato agreed with his predecessors and contemporaries, appears evident to us from the whole tenor of his Timaeus. We agree with Dr Enfield* in thinking, that Platonism, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>, which comprehends his whole doctrine on the subject of the formation of the universe, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is so manifestly spoken of as eternally co-existing with God, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his doctrine could not have been mistaken by so many learned and able writers, had they not been seduced by the desire of establishing a coincidence of doctrine between the writings of Plato and Moses. It is certain that neither Cicero† nor Apuleius‡ nor <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCINOUS">Alcinous</a>§ nor even the later commentator Lib. i. c. 6. Chalcidius, undertook their matter in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than as admitting two primary and incorruptible principles, God and matter; to which we shall afterwards see reason to add a third, namely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> quoted by those who maintain the contrary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> are by no means sufficient for their purpose. Plato, it is true, in his Timaeus, calls God the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of the universe, and in his Sophist speaks of him as "forming animate and inanimate beings, which did not before exist;" but these expressions do not necessarily imply that this offspring of Deity was produced from nothing, or that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> matter existed from which these new beings were formed. Through the whole dialogue of the Timaeus, Plato supposes two eternal and independent causes of all things; one, that by which all things are made, which is God; the other, that from which all things are made, which is matter. He distinguishes between God, matter, and the universe, and supposes the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> of the world to have formed it out of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of pre-existent matter. Matter, according to Plato, is an eternal and infinite principle. His doctrine on this head is thus explained by Cicero ||. "Matter, from which all things are produced and formed, is a substance without form or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, but capable of receiving all forms, and undergoing every kind of change; in which, however, it never suffers annihilation, but merely a solution of its parts, which are in their nature infinitely divisible, and move in portions of space which are also infinitely divisible. When that principle which we call quality is moved, and acts upon matter, it undergoes an entire change, and those forms are produced, from which arises the diversified and coherent system of the universe." This doctrine Plato unfolds at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in his Timaeus, and particularly insists upon the notion, that matter has originally no form, but is capable of receiving any. He calls it the mother and receptacle of forms, by the union of which with matter the universe becomes perceptible to the senses; and maintains, that the visible world owes its forms to the energy of the divine intellectual nature. Our author is supported in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> this inference by the testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a> Laertius, who surely understood the language and dogmas of Plato better than the most accomplished modern scholar can pretend to do; yet a learned writer* has lately expressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> surprise that any one should consider matter as having been, in Plato's opinion, uncreated; and he boldly affirms, that Laertius, instead of affirming that spirit and matter were the principles of all things, ought to have said that God alone, in Plato's estimation, was their original.—To prove this, he gives from the Timaeus a quotation, in which the founder of the academy declares that God framed heaven and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the inferior deities; and that as he fashioned, so he pervades all nature. He observes, that Cicero denominates the god of Platonism. Plato the maker, and the god of Aristotle only the governor, of the world. And, to satisfy those who may demand a particular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of Plato's having taught a real creation, he affirms that his writings abound with declarations on the subject, of which the meaning cannot be misapprehended. "With this purpose (says he) Plato denominates at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the principles or substance of all things, ἀναγεννημένων, the productions of the efficient Deity, and at others enters more particularly into the question. Thus, he observes, that many persons are ignorant of the nature and power of mind or intellect, 'as having existed at the beginning, antecedent to all bodies.' Of this mind, he observes, that it is without exception προστάτης πάντων, of all things the most ancient; and he subjoins, in order to remove all doubt of his purpose, that it is also Αγών αὐτῶν, the cause or principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>." With all possible respect for Dr Ogilvie, of whose piety and erudition we are thoroughly convinced, we must take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to say, that to us the declarations of Plato on this subject appear much less precise and explicit than they appear to him; and that the inference which he would draw from the words of Cicero seems not to flow necessarily from the sense of those words. That Plato believed God to have framed the heaven and the earth, and to have fashioned all nature, is a position which, as far as we know, has never been controverted; but between framing or fashioning the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> or νῦν ἀρχήν, and calling the universe into existence from non-entity, there is an infinite and an obvious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. The distinction made by Cicero between the God of Plato and the God of Aristotle is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> distinction, but it will not bear the superstructure which the learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> builds upon it. Aristotle maintained the eternity of the world in its present form. Plato certainly taught that the first matter was in time reduced from a chaotic state into form by the power of the Demiurgus; but we have seen nothing in his writings which explicitly declares his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that the first matter was itself created. The learned Cudworth, who wished, like Dr Ogilvie, to find a coincidence of doctrine between the theology of Plato and that of the Gospel, strained all his faculties to prove that his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> taught a proper creation; but he laboured in vain. He gives a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of quotations in support of his position; of which we shall here insert only two upon which Dr Ogilvie seems to lay the greatest stress. Plato, says the author of the Intellectual System, calls the one God (α) ὁ ὑπὸ συμβολῆς καὶ ἰδίου, καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ ἀναγεννημένων καὶ τοῦ ἀέρος, καὶ ὅσων ἂν ἀπαντῇ ἐγγεγραμμένων—He that makes earth, and heaven, and the gods, and doth all things both in heaven, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, and under the earth. And, again, "he by whole efficiency the things of the world (ἰδίᾳν εὑρεῖ, προστάτης αὐτῶν ἐν αὐτῷ) were afterwards made when they were not before." Both Cudworth and Ogilvie think this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> an explicit <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of Plato's belief in the creative power of God; but that they are mistaken has been evinced by Motheim with a force of argument which will admit of no reply. In that part of the Sophist from which the quotation is taken, Plato considers the διάνοια τούτου, of which he is treating, as belonging both to God and to man; and he defines it in general to be "a certain power which is the cause that things may afterwards be which were not before." Cudworth wishes to confine this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> to the divine power; and adds from himself to the text which he quotes the following words, which are not in Plato, or FROM AN ANTECEDENT NON-EXISTENCE BROUGHT FORTH INTO BEING! That the incomparable author intended to deceive his reader, we are far from imagining: his zeal for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> had deceived himself. Plato's definition comprehends the διάνοια τούτου, as well of man as of God; and therefore cannot infer a creative power anywhere, unless the father of the academy was so very absurd as to suppose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> artists the creators of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> which they have invented and made! Motheim thinks that Cudworth was misled by too implicit a confidence in Ficinus; and it is not impossible that Dr Ogilvie may have been swayed by the authority, great indeed, of the author of the Intellectual System. That intellect existed antecedent to all bodies is indeed a Platonic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOGMA">dogma</a>, from which Dr Ogilvie, after Cudworth, wishes to infer that the doctrine of the creation was taught in the academy; but Dr Ogilvie knows, and no man knew better than Cudworth, that Plato, with every other Greek philosopher, distinguished between body and matter; and that though he held the priority of intellect to the former, it by no means follows that he believed it to have existed antecedent to the latter. That he believed mind, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> (for he distinguishes between the two), to be the cause or principle of motion, cannot be denied; but we are not therefore authorized to conclude, that he likewise believed it to be the cause of the existence of matter. That he believed mind to be the most ancient of all things, taking the word things in the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> sense, cannot be true, since by Dr Ogilvie's own acknowledgement he held the existence and eternity of ideas, not to add that he believed τὸ ἀέρος ἢ ἀνάγεννα—the first hypostasis in his trinity, to be superior to mind and prior to it, though not in time, yet in the order of nature. When therefore he calls mind the most ancient of all things, he must be supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> only, that it is more ancient than all bodies and inferior souls. It is no reflection on the character of Plato that he could not, by the efforts of his own reason, acquire any notion of a proper creation; since we, who have the advantage of his writings, and of (A) Motheim affirms that this quotation is nowhere to be found in the writings of Plato. He therefore at first suspected that the learned author, in looking hastily over Plato's tenth book De Legibus, had transferred to God what is there said of the anima mundi, leading by its own motions every thing in the heaven, the earth, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and that he had added something of his own. He dropped that opinion, however, when he found Plato, in the tenth book of his Republic, declaring it to be as easy for God to produce the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, stars, and earth, &c. from himself, as it is for us to produce the image of ourselves, and whatever else we please, only by interposing a looking-glass. In all this power, however, there is nothing similar to that of creation. Platonism writings infinitely more valuable, to instruct us, find it extremely difficult, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not impossible, to conceive how any thing can begin to be. We believe the fact on the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; but should certainly have never agitated such a question, had it not been stated to us by writers inspired with celestial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. In the Platonic cosmogony we cannot therefore doubt but that the eternity of the ἀναγέννησις was taken for granted. Whether it was an eternal and necessary emanation from an eternal mind, is not perhaps quite so evident, though our own opinion is, that it was believed to be self-existent. But be this as it may, which is not worth disputing, one thing is certain, that Plato did not believe it to have a single form or quality which it did not receive either from the Demiurge or the Physis—the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third person of this trinity. Except Aristotle, all the Greek philosophers, who were not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATERIALISTS">materialists</a>, held nearly the same opinions respecting the origin of the world; so that in examining their systems we shall be greatly misled if we understand the terms incorporeal and immaterial as at all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. It was also a doctrine of Plato, that there is in matter a necessary but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> and refractory force; and that hence arises a propensity in matter to disorder and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, which is the cause of all the imperfection which appears in the works of God, and the origin of evil. On this subject Plato writes with wonderful obscurity: but, as far as we are able to trace his conceptions, he appears to have thought, that matter, from its nature, resists the will of the Supreme Artificer, so that he cannot perfectly execute his designs; and that this is the cause of the mixture of good and evil which is found in the material world. Plato, however, was no materialist. He taught, that there is an intelligent cause, which is the origin of all spiritual being, and the former of the material world. The nature of this great being he pronounced it difficult to discover, and when discovered, impossible to divulge. The existence of God he inferred from the marks of intelligence, which appear in the form and arrangement of bodies in the visible world: and from the unity of the material system he concluded, that the mind by which it was formed must be one. God, according to Plato, is the supreme intelligence, incorporeal, without beginning, end, or change, and capable of being perceived only by the mind. He certainly distinguished the Deity not only from body, and whatever has corporeal qualities, but from matter itself, from which all things are made. He also ascribed to him all those qualities which modern philosophers ascribe to immaterial substance: and conceived him to be in his nature simple, unencumbered in space, the author of all regulated motion, and, in fine, possessed of intelligence in the highest perfection. His notions of God are indeed exceedingly refined, and such as it is difficult to suppose that he could ever have acquired but from some obscure remains of primeval <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, gleaned perhaps from the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> or from the philosophers of the East. In the Divine Nature he certainly believed that there are two, and probably that there are three, hypostases, whom he called Platonic, τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ ὁ Ἀρετής. The first he considered as self-existent, and elevated far above all mind and all knowledge; calling him, by way of eminence, the being, or the one. The only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> which he acknowledged in this person was goodness; and therefore he frequently styles him ὁ ἀρετής—the good, or essential goodness. The second he considered as mind, the wisdom or reason of the first, and the maker of the world; and therefore he styles him νοῦς λόγος and ἀναγέννησις. The third he always speaks of as the soul of the world; and hence calls him ὁ Ἀρετής, or ὁ Ἀρετής τοῦ κόσμου. He taught that the second is a necessary emanation from the first, and the third from the second, or perhaps from the first and second. Some have indeed pretended, that the Trinity, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Platonic, was a fiction of the later Platonists, unknown to the founder of the school: but any person who shall take the trouble to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the writings of Plato, will find abundant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that he really affected a triad of divine hypostases, all concerned in the formation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the world. Thus in his tenth book of Laws, where he undertakes to prove the existence of a Deity in opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHEISTS">atheists</a>, he ascends no higher in the demonstration than to the ὁ Ἀρετής or mundane soul, which he held to be the immediate and proper cause of all the motion that is in the world. But in other parts of his writings he frequently affects, as superior to the self-moving principle, an immoveable νοῦς or intellect, which was properly the demiurge or framer of the world; and above this hypostasis one most simple and absolutely perfect being, who is considered in his Theology as ἀπόλυτος the original deity, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> from the others, who are only ἀπόλυτοι. These doctrines are to be gathered from his works at large, particularly from the Timaeus, Philotheus, Sophista and Euthyphro; but there is a passage in his second epistle to Dionysius, apparently written in answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, in which that monarch had required him to give a more explicit account than he had formerly done of the nature of God, in which the doctrine of a Trinity seems to be directly asserted. "After having said that he meant to wrap up his meaning in such obscurity, as that an adept only should fully comprehend it, he adds expressions to the following import: 'The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of Nature is surrounded on all sides by his works: whatever is exists by his permission: he is the fountain and source of excellence: around the second person are placed things of the second order; and around the third those of the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> (B)." Of this obscure passage a very satisfactory explanation is given in Dr Ogilvie's Theology of Plato, to which the narrow limits prescribed to such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as this compel us to refer the reader. We shall only say, that the account which we have given of the Platonic trinity is ably supported by the doctor. In treating of the eternal emanation of the second and third hypostases from the first, the philosophers of the academy compare them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> proceeding from the sun. Plato himself, as quoted by Dr Cudworth, illustrates his doctrine by the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a>. (B). "Περὶ τῶν πεντακοσίων βασιλεῶν, παντὶ ἐξ Ἐγγύτων εἰκόνων ἐπιτύχει. Ἐγγύτων εἰκόνα παντὶ τῶν καλῶν. Διατριβῆς δὲ πάντων ἐν ἀναγέννησι, καὶ τρίτῳ περὶ τῷ τρίτῳ. Oper. p. 1269." For "τριάδα" or the first hypostasis, is in the intellectual world the same (he says) to intellect and intelligibles that the sun is in the corporeal world to vision and visibles; for as the sun is not vision itself but the cause of vision, and as that light by which we see is not the sun but only a thing like the sun; so neither is the Supreme or Highest Good properly knowledge, but the cause of knowledge; nor is intellect, considered as such, the best and most perfect being, but only a being having the form of perfection." Again, "as the sun causes other things not only to become visible but also to be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>; so the Supreme Good gives to things not only their capability of being known, but also their very essences by which they subsist; for this fountain of the Deity, this highest good, is not itself properly essence, but above essence, transcending it in respect both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and of power." The resemblance which this trinity of Plato bears to that revealed in the gospel must be observed by every attentive reader; but the two doctrines are likewise in some respects exceedingly dissimilar. The third hypostasis in the Platonic system appears in no point of view co-ordinate with the first or second. Indeed the first is elevated far above the second, and the third funk still farther beneath it, being considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> soul immersed in matter, and forming with the corporeal world, to which it is united, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> animal. Nay, it does not appear perfectly clear, that Plato considered his ἐνεργὸς τοῦ κόσμου as a pure spirit, or as having subsisted from eternity as a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">Hypothesis</a>. "This governing spirit, of whom the earth, properly so called, is the body, consisted, according to our author's philosophy, of the same and the other; that is, of the first matter, and of pure intelligence, framed to actuate the machinery of nature. The Supreme Being placed him in the middle of the earth; which, in the vivid idea of Plato, seemed itself to live, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an influence that was felt in every part of it. From this seat his power is represented as being extended on all sides to the utmost limit of the heavens; conferring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and preserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> in the various and complicated parts of the universe. Upon this being God is said to have looked with peculiar complacency after having formed him as an image of himself, and to have given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and perfect proportion to the mansion which he was destined to occupy. According to the doctrine of Timaeus, the Supreme Being struck out from this original mind innumerable spirits of inferior order, endowed with principles of reason; and he committed to divinities of secondary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the task of investing these in material forms, and of dispersing them as inhabitants of the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies. He taught also, that at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the human soul is reunited to the ἐνεργὸς τοῦ κόσμου, as to the source from which it originally came." Such is the third person of the Platonic triad, as we find his name and attributes very accurately stated by Dr Ogilvie; and the Christian philosopher, who has no particular system to support, will not require another proof that the triad of Plato differs exceedingly from the Trinity of the Scriptures. Indeed the third hypostasis in this triad has so much the appearance of all that the ancients could mean by that which we call a creature, that the learned Cudworth, who wished, it is difficult to conceive for what reason, to find the sublime mystery of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> explicitly taught in the writings of a pagan philosopher, was forced to suppose that Plato held a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> ἐνεργὸς, or soul, one ἐνεργὸς incorporated with the material world, and the other ἐνεργὸς or supramundane, which is not the soul but the governor of the universe. We call this a mere hypothesis; for though the author displays vast erudition, and adduces many quotations in which this double ἐνεργὸς is plainly mentioned, yet all those quotations are taken from Platonists who lived after the propagation of the gospel, and who, calling themselves eclectics, freely stole from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> such dogmas as they could incorporate with their own system, and then attributed those dogmas to their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. In the writings of Plato himself, there is not so much as an allusion to this supramundane ἐνεργὸς; and it is for this reason (the ἐνεργὸς, of which he treats being so very inferior to the ἐνεργὸς ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ) that we have expressed with hesitation his ὑπόθεσις. Yet that he did admit so many, seems more than probable both from the passage illustrated by Dr Ogilvie, and from the attempt of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOTINUS">Plotinus</a>, one of his followers, to demonstrate that the number can be neither greater nor less. That his doctrine on this subject should be inaccurate and erroneous, can excite no wonder; whilst it must be confessed to have such a resemblance to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and to be incapable of being proved by reasoning from effects to causes, that we could not doubt of his having inherited it by tradition, even though we had not complete evidence that something very similar to it was taught <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before him, not only by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> and Parmenides, but by the philosophers of the east. We have said that the Demiurgus was the maker of the world from the first matter which had existed from eternity; but in Plato's cosmogony there is another principle, more mysterious, if possible, than any thing which we have yet mentioned. This is his intellectual system of ideas, which it is not easy to collect from his writings, whether he considered as independent existences, or only as archetypal forms, which had subsisted from eternity in the λόγος or divine intellect. On this subject he writes with such exceeding obscurity, that men of the first eminence, both among the ancients and the moderns, have differed about his real meaning. Some have supposed, that by ideas he meant real beings subsisting from eternity, independent of all minds, and separate from all matter; and that of these ideas he conceived some to be living and others to be without life. In this manner his doctrine is interpreted by Tertullian among the ancients, and by the celebrated Brucker among the moderns; and not by them only, but by many others equally learned, candid, and acute. Cudworth, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with his annotator Mosheim, contend, that by his ideal world Plato meant nothing more than that there existed from eternity in the λόγος or mind of God a notion or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of every thing which was in time to be made. This is certainly much more probable in itself, than that a man of enlarged understanding should have supposed, that there are somewhere in extramundane space real living incorporeal beings eating and drinking, which are the ideas of all the animals which ever have been or ever will be eating and drinking in this world. Yet Mosheim candidly acknowledges, that if the controversy were to be decided by the votes of the learned, he is doubtful whether it would be given for or against him; and Cudworth, though he pleads Platonism pleads the cause of his master with much ingenuity, owns, that on this subject his language cannot be vindicated. This indeed is most true; for Plato contends, that his ideas are not only the objects of science, but also the proper or physical causes of all things here below; that the idea of similitude is the cause of the resemblance between two globes; and the idea of dissimilitude the cause that a globe does not resemble a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>: he likewise calls them ovus, efences or fulfiances, and many of his followers have pronounced them to be animals. These wonderful expressions incline us to adopt with some hesitation the opinion stated by Dr Enfield. This historian of philosophy having observed, that some of the admirers of Plato contend, that by ideas existing in the reason of God, nothing more is meant than conceptions formed in the Divine mind, controverts this opinion with much effect. "By ideas, Plato (says he) appears to have meant something much more mysterious; namely, patterns or archetypes subsisting by themselves, as real beings, ovus ola in the Divine reason, as in their original and eternal region, and issuing thence to give form to sensible things, and to become objects of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> and science to rational beings. It is the doctrine of the Timaeus, that ἀληθεία τοῦ Θεοῦ, the reason of God, comprehends exemplars of all things, and that this reason is one of the primary causes of things. Plutarch says, that Plato supposes three principles, God, Matter, and Idea. <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-JUSTIN_MARTYR">Justin <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>, Pseudo-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, and others, affirm the same thing. "That this is the true Platonic doctrine of ideas will appear probable, if we attend to the manner in which Plato framed his system of opinions concerning the origin of things. Having been from his youth (says Aristotle) conversant with Cratylus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Heraclitus, and instructed in the doctrine of that school, that all sensible things are variable, and cannot be proper objects of science, he reasonably concluded, that if there be any such thing as science, there must exist, besides sensible objects, certain permanent natures, perceptible only by the intellect." Such natures, divine in their origin, and eternal and immutable in their existence, he admitted into his system, and called them ideas. Visible things were regarded by Plato as fleeting shades, and ideas as the only permanent substances. These he conceived to be the proper objects of science to a mind raised by divine contemplation above the perpetually varying scenes of the material world." It was a fundamental doctrine in the system of Plato, that the Deity formed the material world after a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, consisting of those ideas which had eternally subsisted in his own reason; and yet, with some appearance of contradiction, he calls this model "self-existent, indivisible, and eternally generated." Nay, he talks of it as being intelligent as well as eternal, and wholly different from the transcripts, which are subjected to our inspection. There is so much mystery, confusion, and apparent absurdity, in the whole of this system, as it has come <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us, that we must suppose the friends of Plato to have been entrusted with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> to his esoteric doctrines, which has long been lost, otherwise it would be difficult to conceive how that philosopher could have had so many admirers. With almost every ancient theist of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> the founder of the academy believed in an order of beings called daemons, which were superior to the souls of men, and Plato struck off by the Demiurge from the foul of the world. Of these the reader will find some account elsewhere: (See Daemon and Polytheism). We mention them at present because they make an important appearance in Plato's system of physics, which was built upon them and upon the doctrine which has been stated concerning God, matter, and ideas. He taught, that the visible world was formed by the Supreme Architect, uniting eternal and immutable ideas to the first matter; that the universe is one animated being *, including within its limits all animated natures; that, in the formation of the visible and tangible world, fire and earth were first formed, and were afterwards united by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; that from perfect parts one perfect whole was produced, of a spherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, as most beautiful in itself, and best fitted to contain all other figures †; that the elementary parts of the world are of regular geometrical forms, the particles of earth being cubical, those of fire pyramidal, those of air in the form of an octahedron, and those of water in that of an icosahedron; that these are adjusted in number, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, and power, in perfect conformity to the geometrical laws of proportion; that the soul which pervades this sphere is the cause of its revolution round its centre; and, lastly, that the world will remain for ever, but that by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of its animating principle, it accomplishes certain periods, within which every thing returns to its ancient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and state. This periodical revolution of nature is called the Platonic or great year. See the preceding article. The metaphysical doctrines of Plato, which treat of the human soul, and the principles of his system of ethics, have been detailed in other articles (See Metaphysics, Part III. chap. iv.; and Moral Philosophy, No. 6.); but it is worthy of observation in this place, that, preparatory to the study of all philosophy, he required from his disciples a knowledge of the elements of mathematics. In his Republic, he makes Glaucus, one of the speakers, recommend them for their usefulness in human life. "<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> for accounts and distributions; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> for encampments and mensurations; music for solemn festivals in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods; and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and the like. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, on his part, denies not the truth of all this, but still intimates that they were capable of answering an end more sublime. "You are pleasant (says he) in your seeming to fear the multitude, lest you should be thought to enjoin certain sciences that are useless. 'Tis indeed no contemptible matter, though a difficult one, to believe, that through these particular sciences the soul has an organ purified and enlightened, which is destroyed and blinded by studies of other kinds; an organ better worth saving than a thousand eyes, in as much as truth becomes visible through this alone." Concerning policy, Plato has written at large in his Republic and in his Dialogue on Laws. He was so much enamoured with his own conceptions on this subject, that it was chiefly the hope of having an opportunity to realise his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of a republic which induced him to visit the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Dionysius. But they who are conversant with mankind, and capable of calmly investigating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of human actions, will easily perceive that his projects were chimerical, and could only have originated in a mind replete with philosophical enthusiasm. Of this nothing can be a clearer proof than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of admitting: Platonism ting in his republic a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of women, in order to give reason an entire control over desire. The main object of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> institutions appears to have been, the subjugation of the passions and appetites, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> contemplation of ideas. A system of policy, raised upon such fanciful grounds, cannot merit a more distinct consideration. Such is genuine Platonism as it was taught in the old academy by the founder of the school and his immediate followers; but when Arcesilaus was placed at the head of the academics, great innovations were introduced both into their doctrines and into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of teaching (see Arcesilaus). This man was therefore considered as the founder of what was afterwards called the middle academy. Being a professed sceptic, he carried his maxim of uncertainty to such a height, as to alarm the general body of philosophers, offend the governors of the state, and bring just odium upon the very name of the academy. At length Carneades, one of the disciples of this school, relinquishing some of the more obnoxious tenets of Arcesilaus, founded what has been called the new academy with very little improvement on the principles of the middle. See Carneades. Under one or other of these forms Platonism found its way into the Roman republic. Cicero was a Platonist, and one of the greatest ornaments of the school. A school of Platonists was likewise founded in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in the second century of the Christian era; but their doctrines differed in many particulars from those taught in the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>. They professed to seek truth wherever they could find it, and to collect their dogmas from every school. They endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> some of the principles of Plato into a conformity with the doctrines of the gospel; and they incorporated with the whole many of the maxims of Aristotle and Zeno, and not a few of the fictions of the east. Their system was therefore extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a>, and seldom so rational as that of the philosopher after whose name they were called, and of whose doctrines we have given so copious a detail. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIUS">Ammonius</a>, Eclectics, and Plotinus.

PLAUTUS

Pages 260-263

Marcus Accius, a comic writer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome, born in Umbria, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His proper name was Marcus Accius, and he is supposed to have acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Plautus from having play feet. His parentage appears to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>; so that some have thought he was the son of a slave. Aulus Gellius says that Plautus was distinguished for his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and Cato for his eloquence in the forum, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and observes elsewhere from Varro, that he was so well paid for his plays as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> his stock in trading, in which he lost all he gained by the mules. He is said to have been reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> at a mill for his subsistence; but Varro adds, that his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> was his best support, as he composed three of his plays during this drudgery. He died in the first year of the elder Cato's censorship, about the year of Rome 369, and 184 before Christ. We have 20 of his plays extant, though not all of them entire. Five of them, comedies, have been elegantly translated into English by Mr B. Thornton, and published in 2 vols 8vo, 1767. PLAYS. See the following article. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">PLAYHOUSE</a>. See Theatre, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">Amphitheatre</a>, &c. The most ancient English playhouses were the Curtain in Shoreditch and the Theatre. In the time of Playhouse, Shakespeare, who commenced a dramatic writer in 1592, there were no less than 10 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> open. Four of these were private houses, viz. that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a>, the Cockpit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Phoenix in Drury-Lane, a theatre in Whitefriars, and one in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The other six were called public theatres, viz. the Globe, the Swan, the Rose, and the Hope, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">Bank</a>-side; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Bull, at the upper end of St John's street, and the Fortune in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> street. The two last were chiefly frequented by citizens. Mr Malone gives us a pretty copious account of these playhouses, in a supplement to his last edition of Shakespeare, which we shall here insert. "Most, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all (says he) of Shakespeare's plays were performed either at the Globe or at the Theatre in Blackfriars. It appears that they both belonged to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of comedians, viz. his majesty's servants, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> they assumed, after a licence had been granted to them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James in 1603, having before that time been called the servants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chamberlain. "The theatre in Blackfriars was a private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; but the peculiar and distinguishing marks of a private playhouse it is not easy to ascertain. It was very small, and plays were there usually represented by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. The Globe, situated on the southern side of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, was a hexagonal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, partly open to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, partly covered with reeds. It was a public theatre, and of considerable size, and there they always acted by daylight. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the Globe, and the other public theatres, a pole was erected, to which a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> was affixed. These flags were probably displayed only during the hours of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a>; and it should seem from a passage in one of the old comedies that they were taken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, in which season no plays were presented. The Globe, though hexagonal at the outside, was probably a rotunda within, and perhaps had its name from its circular form. It might, however, have been denominated only from its sign, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> supporting the Globe. This theatre was burnt down in 1613, but it was rebuilt in the following year, and decorated with more ornament than had been originally bestowed upon it. The exhibitions at the Globe seem to have been calculated chiefly for the lower class of people; those at Blackfriars for a more select and judicious audience. "A writer informs us, that one of these theatres was a winter and the other a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> house. As the Globe was partly exposed to the weather, and they acted there usually by daylight, it was probably the summer theatre. The exhibitions here seem to have been more frequent than at Blackfriars, at least till the year 1604 or 1605, when the Bank-side appears to have become less fashionable and less frequented than it formerly had been. Many of our ancient dramatic pieces were performed in the yards of carriers' inns; in which, in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s reign, the comedians, who then first united themselves in companies, erected an occasional stage. The form of these temporary playhouses seems to be preserved in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> theatre. The galleries are in both ranged over each other on three sides of the building. The small rooms under the lowest of these galleries answer to our present boxes; and it is observable that these, even in theatres which were were built in a subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> expressly for dramatic exhibitions, still retained their old name, and are frequently called rooms by our ancient writers. The yard bears a sufficient resemblance to the pit, as at present in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. We may suppose the stage to have been raised in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, on the fourth side, with its back to the gateway of the inn, at which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for admission was taken. Hence, in the middle of the Globe, and I suppose of the other public theatres, in the time of Shakespeare, there was an open yard or area, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people stood to see the exhibition; from which circumstance they are called by our author groundlings, and by Ben Jonson "the understanding gentlemen of the ground." "In the ancient playhouses there appears to have been a private box, of which it is not easy to ascertain the situation. It seems to have been placed at the side of the stage towards the rear, and to have been at a lower price: in this some people sat, either from economy or singularity. The galleries, or scaffolds as they are sometimes called, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the house which in private theatres was named the pit, seem to have been at the same price; and probably in houses of reputation, such as the Globe, and that in Blackfriars, the price of admission into those parts of the theatre was 6d. while in some meaner playhouses it was only 1d. in others only 2d. The price of admission into the best rooms or boxes was, I believe, in our author's time, 1s.; though afterwards it appears to have risen to 2s. and half-a-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. "From several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in our old plays, we learn, that spectators were admitted on the stage, and that the critics and wits of the time usually sat there. Some were placed on the ground; others sat on stools, of which the price was either 6d. or 1s. according; I suppose, to the commodiousness of the situation; and they were attended by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, who furnished them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, which was smoked here as well as in other parts of the house: yet it should seem that persons were suffered to sit on the stage only in the private playhouses, such as Blackfriars, &c., where the audience was more select, and of a higher class; and that in the Globe and other public theatres no such licence was permitted. "The stage was firewood with rushes, which, as we learn from Hentzner and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> de Ephemeris, was, in the time of Shakespeare, the usual covering of floors in England. The curtain which hangs in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the present stage, drawn up by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and pulleys, though not a modern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, for it was used by Inigo Jones in the masques at court, was yet an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> to which the simple mechanism of our ancient theatres had not arrived, for in them the curtains opened in the middle, and were drawn backwards and forwards on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod. In some playhouses they were woollen, in others made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>.—Towards the rear of the stage there appears to have been a balcony, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of which was probably eight or ten feet from the ground. I suppose it to have been supported by pillars. From hence, in many of our old plays, part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> was spoken; and in the front of this balcony curtains likewise were hung. "A doubt has been entertained whether in our ancient theatres there were fide and other scenes. The question is involved in so much obscurity, that it is very difficult to form any decided <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> upon it. It is certain, that in the year 1693 Inigo Jones exhibited an entertainment at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in which moveable scenes were used; but he appears to have introduced several pieces of machinery in the masques at court, with which undoubtedly the public theatres were unacquainted.
