A passage which has been produced from one of the old comedies, proves, it must be owned, that even these were furnished with some pieces of machinery, which were used when it was requisite to exhibit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of some god or saint; but from all the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> accounts, I am inclined to believe that the mechanism of our ancient stage seldom went beyond a painted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> or a trap-door, and that few, if any of them, had any moveable scenes. When King Henry VIII. is to be discovered by the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, the scenerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in the first folio, 1623, which was printed apparently from playhouse copies, is, 'the king draws the curtain, (i.e. draws it open), and sits <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> pensively;' for, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> curtains that hung in the front of the stage, they used others as substitutes for scenes. If a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>-chamber is to be exhibited, no change of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is mentioned; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is simply ordered to thrust forth a bed. When the tale requires the Roman capitol to be exhibited, we find two officers enter, 'to lay cushions, as it were, in the capitol,' &c. On the whole, it appears, that our ancient theatres, in general, were only furnished with curtains, and a single scene composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, which were sometimes, perhaps, ornamented with pictures; and some passages in our old dramas incline one to think, that when tragedies were performed the stage was hung with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. "In the early part, at least, of our author's acquaintance with the theatre, the want of scenery seems to have been supplied by the simple expedient of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the names of the different places where the scene was laid in the progress of the play, which were dispensed in such a manner as to be visible to the audience. The invention of trap-doors, however, appears not to be modern; for in an old morality, intitled All for Money, we find a marginal direction which implies that they were very early in use. The covering, or internal roof of the stage, was anciently termed the heavens. It was probably painted of a sky-blue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, or perhaps pieces of drapery tinged with blue were suspended across the stage to represent the heavens. "It is probable that the stage was formerly lighted by two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> branches, of a form similar to those now hung in churches. They gave <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in a subsequent period to small circular wooden frames, furnished with candles, eight of which were hung on the stage, four at either side, and these within a few years were wholly removed by Mr Garrick, who, on his return from France, first introduced the present commodious method of illuminating the stage by lights not visible to the audience. Many of the companies of players were formerly so thin, that one person played two or three parts; and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> on which the fate of an empire was supposed to depend was decided by half a dozen combatants. It appears to have been a common practice in their mock engagements to discharge small pieces of ordnance on the stage. Before the exhibition began, three flourishes or pieces of music were played, or, in the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, there were three soundings. Music was likewise played between the acts. The instruments chiefly used were trumpets, cornets, and hautboys." The hautboys. The band, which did not consist of more than five or six performers, sat in an upper balcony, over what is now called the stage-box. "The person who spoke the prologue was ushered in by trumpets, and usually wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> black velvet cloak, which, I suppose, was considered as best suited to a supplicatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, whatever might have been its origin, some traces remained till very lately, a black coat having been, if I mistake not, within these few years, the constant stage-habiment of our modern prologue-speakers. The dress of the ancient prologue-speaker is still retained in the play that is exhibited in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a> before the king and court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. The performers of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> generally wore periwigs, which in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Shakespeare were not in common use. It appears, from a passage in Puttenham's *Art of English Poetry*, 1589, that wigs were worn on some occasions used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> of those days; and it may be inferred, from a scene in one of our author's comedies, that they were sometimes worn in his time by those who performed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> characters; but this I imagine was very rare. Some of the female part of the audience likewise appeared in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a>. The stage-dresses, it is reasonable to suppose, were much more costly at some theatres than at others; yet the wardrobe of even the king's servants at the Globe and Blackfriars, was, we find, but scantily furnished; and our author's dramas derived very little aid from the splendor of exhibition. "It is well known, that in the time of Shakespeare, and for many years afterwards, female characters were represented by boys or young men. Sir William d'Avenant, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the foreign theatres, first introduced females in the scene, and Mrs Betterton is said to have been the first woman that appeared on the English stage. Andrew Pennyquick played the part of Matilda in a tragedy of Davenport's, in 1655; and Mr Kynaston acted several female parts after the Restoration. Downes, a contemporary of his, affirms us, 'that being then very young he made a complete stage <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, performing his parts so well, particularly Arthiope and Aglaura, that it has since been disputable among the judicious whether any woman that succeeded him touched the audience so sensibly as he.' "Both the prompter, or book-holder, as he was sometimes called, and the property-man, appear to have been regular appendages of our ancient theatres. No writer that I have met with intimates, that in the time of Shakespeare it was customary to exhibit more than a single dramatic piece on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> tragedy, or *All's One*, indeed, appears to have been one of four pieces that were represented on the same day; and Fletcher has also a piece called *Four Plays in One*; but probably these were either exhibited on some particular occasion, or were ineffectual efforts to introduce a new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of amusement; for we do not find any other instances of the same kind. Had any shorter pieces been exhibited after the principal performance, some of them probably would have been printed: but there are none extant of an earlier <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> than the time of the Restoration. The practice, therefore, of exhibiting two dramas successively in the same evening, we may be assured was not established before that period. But though the audiences in the time of our author were not gratified by the representation of more than one drama in the same day, the entertainment was diversified, and the populace diverted, by vaulting, tumbling, flight of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and morris-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, a mixture not much more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> than that with which we are daily presented, a tragedy and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a>. "The amusements of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, before the commencement of the play, were of various kinds, such as reading, playing at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, drinking ale, or smoking tobacco. It was a common practice to carry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-books to the theatre, and either from curiosity or enmity to the author, or some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>, to write down passages of the play that was represented: and there is reason to believe that the imperfect and mutilated copies of some of Shakespeare's dramas, which are yet extant, were taken down in short-hand during the exhibition. At the end of the piece, the actors, in noblemen's houses and in taverns, where plays were frequently performed, prayed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and prosperity of their patrons; and in the public theatres for the king and queen. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> sometimes made part of the epilogue. Hence, probably, as Mr Steevens has observed, the addition of *Vivat rex et <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a>* to the modern play-bills. "Plays, in the time of our author, began at one o'clock in the afternoon; and the exhibition was usually finished in two hours. Even in 1667 they commenced at three. When Goffon wrote his *School of Abuse*, in 1579, it seems the dramatic entertainments were usually exhibited on Sundays. Afterwards they were performed on that and other days indiscriminately. It appears from a contemporary writer, that exhibiting plays on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> had not been abolished in the third year of King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. "The modes of conveyance to the theatre, anciently as at present, seem to have been various; some going in coaches, others on horseback, and many by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—To the Globe playhouse the company probably were conveyed by water; to that in Blackfriars the gentry went either in coaches or on horseback, and the common people on foot. In an epigram to Sir John Davis, the practice of riding to the theatre is ridiculed as a piece of affectation or vanity, and therefore we may presume it was not very general. "The long and whimsical titles that are prefixed to the quarto copies of our author's plays, I suppose to have been transcribed from the play-bills of the time. A contemporary writer has preserved something like a play-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of those days, which seems to corroborate this observation; for if it were deprived of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>, it would bear no very distant resemblance to the title pages that stand before some of our author's dramas: "Prithee, what's the play? (The first I visited this twelvemonth day) They say "A new invented play of Purle, That jeoparded his neck to steal a girl Of twelve; and lying fast impounded for't, Has hither sent his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> his part; Against all those in open malice bent, That would not freely to the thief consent: Feigns all to's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and in the epilogue Goes out applauded for a famous rogue." —Now hang me if I did not look at first For some such stuff, by the fond people's thirst." "It is uncertain at what time the usage of giving authors a benefit on the third day of the exhibition of their pieces commenced. Mr Oldys, in one of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, intimates that dramatic poets had anciently their benefit on the first day that a new play was represented; a regulation..." Playhouse which would have been very favourable to some of the ephemeral productions of modern times. But for this there is not, I believe, any sufficient authority. From D'Avenant, indeed, we learn, that in the latter part of the reign of Queen Elizabeth the poet had his benefit on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> day. As it was a general practice in the time of Shakespeare to sell the copy of the play to the theatre, I imagine in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> an author derived no other advantage from his piece than what arose from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of it. Sometimes, however, he found it more beneficial to retain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPYRIGHT">copyright</a> in his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and when he did so, I suppose he had a benefit. It is certain that the giving authors the profit of the third exhibition of their play, which seems to have been the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> during almost the whole of the last century, was an established custom in the year 1612, for Dekker, in the prologue to one of his comedies printed in that year, speaks of the poet's third day. The unfortunate Olway had no more than one benefit on the production of a new play; and this too, it seems, he was sometimes forced to mortgage before the piece was acted. Southerne was the first dramatic writer who obtained the emoluments arising from two representations; and to Farquhar, in the year 1703, the benefit of a third was granted. When an author sold his piece to the sharers or proprietors of a theatre, it remained for several years unpublished; but when that was not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, he printed it for sale, to which many seem to have been induced, from an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> that an imperfect copy might be issued from the press without their consent. The customary price of the copy of a play in the time of Shakespeare appears to have been twenty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, or five pounds thirteen shillings and four pence. The play when printed was sold for sixpence; and the usual present from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> in return for a dedication was forty shillings. On the first day of exhibiting a new play, the prices of admission appear to have been raised; and this seems to have been occasionally practised on the benefit-nights of authors to the end of the last century. The custom of affording a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> censure on plays at their first exhibition is as ancient as the time of our author; for no less than three plays of his rival Ben Jonson appear to have been damned; and Fletcher's Faithful Shepherdess, and The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a> Pestle, written by him and Beaumont, underwent the same fate. "It is not easy to ascertain what were the emoluments of a successful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in the time of Shakespeare. They had not then annual benefits as at present. The performers at each theatre seem to have shared the profits arising either from each day's exhibition or from the whole season among them." From Ben Jonson's Poetaster we learn, that one of either the performers or proprietors had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> shares and a half; but of what integral sum is not mentioned. From the prices of admission into our ancient theatres, which have been already mentioned, I imagine the utmost that the sharers of the Globe playhouse could have received on any one day was about £5. So lately as the year 1685, Shadwell received by his third day on the representation of the Squire of Alsatia, £130.; which Downes the prompter says was the greatest receipt that had ever been taken at Drury-Lane playhouse at single prices. It appears from the MSS. of Lord Stanhope, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the chambers to King James I., that the customary sum paid to John Heminge and his company for the performance of a play at court was twenty nobles, or five pounds thirteen shillings and four pence. And Edward Alleyn mentions in his Diary, that he once had so slender an audience in his theatre called the Fortune, that the whole receipts of the house amounted to no more than three pounds and some odd shillings. "Thus scanty and meagre were the apparatus and accommodations of our ancient theatres, on which those dramas were first exhibited, that have since engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of so many learned men, and delighted to many thousand spectators. Yet even then, we are told by a writer of that age, 'that dramatic poetry was so lively expressed and represented on the public stages and theatres of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, as Rome in the age of her pomp and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it better performed; in respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> and art, not of the coit and sumptuousness.'"

PLAYERS

Pages 287-287

in fortification, denote a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> used in raising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> letting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a draw-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. They consist of two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> levers, twice as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the bridge they lift, joined together by other timbers framed in the form of a St Andrew's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> to counterpoise them. They are supported by two upright jambs, on which they swing; and the bridge is raised or let down by means of chains joining the ends of the players and bridge.

PLEA

Pages 263-267

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is what either party alleges for himself in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in a cause there depending; and in a more restrained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is the defendant's answer to the plaintiff's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>. Pleadings are usually divided into those of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas. Pleas of the crown are all suits in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s name, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a> in behalf of the king, for offences committed against his crown and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and against his peace; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, felony, &c. See ARRRAIGNMENT. Common pleas are such suits as are carried on between common persons in civil causes. These pleas are of two sorts; dilatory pleas, and pleas to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Dilatory pleas are such as tend merely to delay or put off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, by questioning the propriety of the remedy, rather than by denying the injury; pleas to the action are such as dispute the very cause of suit. 1. Dilatory pleas are, 1. To the jurisdiction of the court: alleging, that it ought not to hold plea of this injury, it arising in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> or beyond <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>: or because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in question is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> demesne, and ought only to be demanded in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s court, &c. 2. To the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a> of the plaintiff, by reason whereof he is incapable to commence or continue the suit; as, that he is an alien enemy, outlawed, excommunicated, attainted of treason or felony, under a praemunire, not in rerum natura (being only a fictitious person), an infant, a feme-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>, or a monk professed. 3. In abatement: which abatement is either of the writ, or the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a>, for some defect in one of them; as by misnaming the defendant, which is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISNOMER">misnomer</a>; giving him a wrong addition, as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ESQUIRE">esquire</a> instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>; or other want of form in any material respect. Or, it may be that the plaintiff is dead; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of either party is at once an abatement of the suit. These pleas to the jurisdiction, to the disability, or in abatement, were formerly very often used as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> dilatory pleas, without any foundation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and calculated only for delay; but now by flat. 4 & 5 Ann. c. 16, no dilatory plea is to be admitted without affidavit made of the truth thereof, or some probable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> thrown to the court to induce them to believe it true. And with respect to the pleas themselves, it is a rule, that no exception shall be admitted against a declaration or writ, unless the defendant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in the same plea give the plaintiff a better; that is, show him how it might be amended, that there may not be two objections upon the same account. All pleas to the jurisdiction conclude to the cognizance of the court; praying "judgement whether the court will have farther cognizance of the suit." Pleas to the disability conclude to the person; by praying "judgement, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the said A the plaintiff ought to be answered." And pleas in abatement (when the suit is by original) conclude to the writ, or declaration; by praying "judgement of the writ, or declaration, and that the same may be quashed," estteur, made void, or abated: but if the action be by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, the plea must pray "judgement of the bill," and not of the declaration; the bill being here the original, and the declaration only a copy of the bill. When these dilatory pleas are allowed, the cause is either dismissed from that jurisdiction, or the plaintiff is stayed till his disability be removed; or he is obliged to sue out a new writ, by leave obtained from the court, or to amend and new-frame his declaration. But when, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they are overruled as frivolous, the defendant has judgement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESPONDENT">respondent</a> ouster, or to answer over in some better manner. It is then incumbent on him to plead. 2. A plea to the action; that is, to answer to the merits of the complaint. This is done by confessing or denying it. A confession of the whole complaint is not very usual; for then the defendant would probably end the matter sooner, or not plead at all, but suffer judgement to go by default. Yet sometimes, after tender and refusal of a debt, if the creditor harasses his debtor with an action, it then becomes necessary for the defendant to acknowledge the debt, and plead the tender; adding, that he has always been ready, tout temps prif, and is still ready, uncore prif, to discharge it: for a tender by the debtor and refusal by the creditor will in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> discharge the costs, but not the debt itself; though in some particular cases the creditor will totally lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. But frequently the defendant confesses one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the complaint (by a cognovit actionem in respect thereof), and traverses or denies the rest; in order to avoid the expense of carrying that part to a formal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, which he has no ground to litigate. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this sort of confession is the payment of money into court: which is for the most part necessary upon pleading a tender, and is itself a kind of tender to the plaintiff; by paying into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the proper officer of the court as much as the defendant acknowledges to be due, together with the costs hitherto incurred, in order to prevent the expense of any farther proceedings. This may be done upon what is called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; which is an occasional application to the court by the parties or their counsel, in order to obtain some rule or order of court, which becomes necessary in the progress of a cause: and it is usually grounded upon an affidavit (the perfect tense of the verb affido), being a voluntary oath before some judge or officer of the court, to convince the truth of certain facts, upon which the motion is grounded: though no such affidavit is necessary for payment of money into court. If, after the money is paid in, the plaintiff proceeds in his suit, it is at his own peril: for if he does not prove more due than is so paid into court, he shall be nonsuited and pay the defendant's costs; but he shall still have the money so paid in, for that the defendant has acknowledged to be his due. To this head may also be referred the practice of what is called a fet off; whereby the defendant acknowledges the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the plaintiff's demand on the one hand; but on the other, sets up a demand of his own, to counterbalance that of the plaintiff, either in the whole or in part; as, if the plaintiff sues for ten pounds due on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of hand, the defendant may set off <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pounds due to himself for merchandise sold to the plaintiff; and, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he plead such fet-off, must pay the remaining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> into court. Pleas that totally deny the cause of complaint are either the general issue, or a special plea in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. 1. The general issue, or general plea, is what traverses, thwarts, and denies at once, the whole declaration, without offering any special matter whereby to evade it. As in trespas either vi et armis, or on the case, "non culpabilis, not guilty?" in debt upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, "nihil debet, he owes nothing;" in debt on bond, non est factum, it is not his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>;" on an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPSIT">assumpsit</a>, "non assumpsit, he made no such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>." Or in real actions, "nul tort, no wrong done; nul dillefin, no dillefin;" and in a writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> or issue is, that "the tenant has more right to hold than the demandant has to demand." These pleas are called the general issue, because, by importing an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and general denial of what is alleged in the declaration, they amount at once to an issue; by which we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> a fact affirmed on one side and denied on the other. 2. Special pleas in bar of the plaintiff's demands are very various, according to the circumstances of the defendant's case. As, in real actions, a general release or a fine; both of which may destroy and bar the plaintiff's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. Or, in personal actions, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, arbitration, conditions performed, nonage of the defendant, or some other fact which precludes the plaintiff from his action. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> is likewise a special plea in bar; as in actions of assault and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>, non assault dementhe, that it was the plaintiff's own original assault; in trespasses, that the defendant did the thing complained of in right of some office which warranted him so to do; or, in an action of slander, that the plaintiff is really as bad a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> as the defendant said he was. Also a man may plead the statutes of limitation in bar; or the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> limited by certain acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, beyond which no plaintiff can lay his cause of action. This, by the statute of 32 Hen. VIII. c. 2, in a writ of right is 60 years: in alizes, writs of entry, or other possessory actions real, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a> of one's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> in lands; and either of their seisin, or one's own, in rents, suits, and services, 50 years: and in actions real for lands grounded upon one's own seisin or possession, such possession must have been within 30 years. By statute 1 Mar. st. 2, c. 5, this limitation does not extend to any suit for avowons. But by the statute 21 Jac. I. c. 2, a time of limitation was extended to the case of the king; viz. 60 years precedent to 19th Feb. 1623; but, this becoming ineffectual by efflux of time, the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> of limitation was fixed by statute 9 Geo. III. c. 16, to commence and be reckoned backwards, from the time of bringing any suit or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> to recover the thing in question; so that a possession for 60 years is now a bar even against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, in derogation of the ancient maxim, Nullum tempus occurrit regi. By another statute, 21 Jac. I. c. 16, 20 years is the time of limitation in any writ of formondem: and, by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, 20 years is also the limitation in every action of ejectment; for no ejectment can be brought, unless where where the lessor of the plaintiff is entitled to enter on the lands, and by the statute 21 Jac. I. c. 16. no entry can be made by any man, unless within 20 years after his right shall accrue. Also all actions of trespass (quare clausum fregit, or otherwise), detinue, trover, replevin, account, and case (except upon accounts between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>), debt on simple contract, or for arrears of rent, are limited by the statute last mentioned to five years after the cause of action commenced; and actions of assault, menace, battery, mayhem, and imprisonment, must be brought within four years, and actions for words two years, after the injury committed. And by the statute 31 Eliz. c. 5. all suits, indictments, and informations, upon any penal statutes, where any forfeiture is to the crown, shall be sued within two years, and where the forfeiture is to a subject, within one year, after the offence committed, unless where any other time is specially limited by the statute. Lastly, by statute 10 W. III. c. 14. no writ of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, feire facias, or other suit, shall be brought to reverse any judgment, fine, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, for error, unless it be prosecuted within 20 years. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of these statutes of limitation is to preserve the peace of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and to prevent those innumerable perjuries which might ensue if a man were allowed to bring an action for any injury committed at any distance of time. Upon both these accounts the law therefore holds, that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> reipublicae ut fit finis illium: and upon the same principle the Athenian laws in general prohibited all actions where the injury was committed five years before the complaint was made. If therefore, in any suit, the injury, or cause of action, happened earlier than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> expressly limited by law, the defendant may plead the statutes of limitations in bar: as upon an affumpst, or promise to pay money to the plaintiff, the defendant may plead, Non affumpst infra <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> annos, He made no such promise within five years; which is an effectual bar to the complaint. An etoppel is likewise a special plea in bar; which happens where a man hath done some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, or executed some deed, which etops or precludes him from averring any thing to the contrary. As if a tenant for years (who hath no freehold) levies a fine to another person. Though this is void as to strangers, yet it shall <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> as an etoppel to the cognizance; for, if he afterwards brings an action to recover these lands, and his fine is pleaded against him, he shall thereby be etopped from saying, that he had no freehold at the time, and therefore was incapable of levying it. The conditions and qualities of a plea (which, as well as the doctrine of ettoppels, will also hold equally, mutatis mutandis, with regard to other parts of pleading), are, 1. That it be single and containing only one matter; for duplicity begets confusion. But by statute 4 and 5 Ann. c. 16. a man, with leave of the court, may plead two or more distinct matters or single pleas; as in an action of assault and battery, these three, Not guilty, sin assault demesne, and the statute of limitations. 2. That it be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and positive, and not argumentative. 3. That it have convenient certainty of time, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and persons. 4. That it answer the plaintiff's allegations in every material point. 5. That it be so pleaded as to be capable of trial. Special pleas are usually in the affirmative, sometimes in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, but they always advance some new fact not mentioned in the declaration; and then they must be averred to be true in the common form:—“And this he is ready to verify.”—This is not necessary in pleas of the general issue, those always containing a total denial of the facts before advanced by the other party, and therefore putting him upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of them. See PLEADINGS. PLEA to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>, the defensive matter alleged by a Blackfriar criminal on his indictment; (see ARRAIGNMENT.) This Comment is either, 1. A plea to the jurisdiction; 2. A demurrer; 3. A plea in abatement; 4. A special plea in bar; or, 5. The general issue. I. A plea to the jurisdiction, is where an indictment is taken before a court that hath no cognizance of the offence; as if a man be indicted for a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s town, or for treason at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions: in these or similar cases, he may except to the jurisdiction of the court, without answering at all to the crime alleged. II. A demurrer to the indictment, is incident to criminal cases, as well as civil, when the fact as alleged is allowed to be true, but the prisoner joins issue upon some point of law in the indictment, by which he infers, that the fact, as stated, is no felony, treason, or whatever the crime is alleged to be. Thus, for instance, if a man be indicted for feloniously stealing a greyhound; which is an animal in which no valuable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> can be had, and therefore it is not felony, but only a civil trespass to steal it; in this case the party indicted may demur to the indictment; denying it to be felony, though he confesses the act of taking it. Some have held, that if, on demurrer, the point of law be adjudged against the prisoner, he shall have judgement and execution, as if convicted by verdict. But this is denied by others, who hold, that in such case he shall be directed and received to plead the general issue, Not guilty, after a demurrer determined against him. Which appears the more reasonable, because it is clear, that if the prisoner freely discovers the fact in court, and refers it to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the court whether it be felony or not; and upon the fact thus shown, it appears to be felony, the court will not record the confession, but admit him afterwards to plead not guilty. And this seems to be a case of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, being for the most part a mistake in point of law, and in the conduct of his pleading; and, though a man by mispleading may in some cases lose his property, yet the law will not suffer him by such niceties to lose his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. However, upon this doubt, demurrers to indictments are seldom used; since the same advantages may be taken upon a plea of not guilty; or afterwards, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> of judgement, when the verdict has established the fact. III. A plea in abatement is principally for a misnomer, a wrong name, or a false addition to the prisoner. As, if James Allen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, is indicted by the name of John Allen, esquire, he may plead that he has the name of James, and not of John; and that he is a gentleman, and not an esquire. And, if either fact is found by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, then the indictment shall be abated, as writs or declarations may be in civil actions. But, in the end, there is little advantage accruing to the prisoner by means of these dilatory pleas; because, if the exception be allowed, a new bill of indictment may be framed, according to what the prisoner in his plea avers to be his true name and addition. For it is a rule, upon all pleas in abatement, that he who takes advantage of a flaw, must at the same time show how it may be amended. Let us therefore next consider a more substantial kind of plea, viz. IV. Special pleas in bar; which go to the merits of the indictment, and give a reason why the prisoner ought not to answer it at all, nor put himself upon his trial for the crime alleged. These are of four kinds: a former acquittal, a former conviction, a former attainder, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. There are many other pleas which may be pleaded in bar of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>; but these are applicable to both appeals and indictments. 1. First, the plea of auterfoits acquit, or a former acquittal, is grounded on this universal maxim of the common law of England, that no man is to be brought into jeopardy of his life, more than once, for the same offence. And hence it is allowed as a consequence, that when a man is once fairly found not guilty upon any indictment, or other prosecution, before any court having competent jurisdiction of the offence, he may plead such acquittal in bar of any subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> for the same crime. 2. Secondly, the plea of auterfoits convict, or a former conviction for the same identical crime, though no judgement was ever given, or perhaps will be (being suspended by the benefit of clergy or other causes), is a good plea in bar to an indictment. And this depends upon the same principle as the former, that no man ought to be twice brought in danger of his life for one and the same crime. 3. Thirdly, the plea of auterfoits attaint, or a former attainder, is a good plea in bar, whether it be for the same or any other felony. For wherever a man is attainted of felony, by judgement of death either upon a verdict or confession, by outlawry, or heresiofore by abjuration, and whether upon an appeal or an indictment; he may plead such attainder in bar to any subsequent indictment or appeal, for the same or for any other felony. And this because, generally, such proceeding on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> prosecution cannot be to any purpose; for the prisoner is dead in law by the first attainder, his blood is already corrupted, and he hath forfeited all that he had: so that it is absurd and superfluous to endeavour to attain him a second time. Though to this general rule, as to all others, there are some exceptions; wherein, cestant ratione, estat et ipsa lex. 4. Lastly, a pardon may be pleaded in bar; as at once destroying the end and purpose of the indictment, by remitting that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, which the prosecution is calculated to inflict. There is one advantage that attends pleading a pardon in bar, or in the arrest of judgement before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> is past; which gives it by much the preference to pleading it after sentence or attainder. This is, that by stopping the judgement it stops the attainder, and prevents the corruption of the blood: which, when once corrupted by attainder, cannot afterwards be restored otherwise than by act of parliament. V. The general issue, or plea of not guilty, upon which plea alone the prisoner can receive his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> judgement of death. In case of an indictment of felony or treason, there can be no special justification put in by way of plea. As, on an indictment for murder, a man cannot plead that it was in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against a robber on the highway, or a burglar; but he must plead the general issue, Not guilty, and give this special matter in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. For (besides that these pleas do in effect amount to the general issue; since, if true, the prisoner is most clearly not guilty) as the facts in treason are laid to be done proditoriae et contra ligamentis sine debitione; and, in felony, that the killing was done felonice; these charges, of a traitorous or felonious intent, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> and very gist of the indictment, and must be answered directly, by the general negative, Not guilty; and the jury upon the evidence will take notice of any defensive matter, and give their verdict accordingly as effectually as if it were or could be specially pleaded. So that this is, upon all accounts, the most advantageous plea for the prisoner. When the prisoner hath thus pleaded not guilty, non culpabilis, or nient culpable: which was formerly used to be abbreviated upon the minutes, thus, Non (or nient) cul, the clerk of the affize, or clerk of arraigns, on behalf of the crown, replies, that the prisoner is guilty, and that he is ready to prove him so. This is done by two monosyllables in the same spirit of abbreviation, (cul pri); which signifies first that the prisoner is guilty, (cul culpable, or culpabilis); and then that the king is ready to prove him so, (pri, pretio firm, or paratus, sacrificare). By this replication the king and the prisoner are therefore at issue: for when the parties come to a fact which is affirmed on one side and denied on the other, then they are said to be at issue in point of fact; which is evidently the case here, in the plea of non cul, by the prisoner; and the replication of cul, by the clerk. How the courts came to express a matter of this importance in so odd and obscure a manner, can hardly be pronounced with certainty. It may perhaps, however, be accounted for by supposing, that these were at first short notes, to help the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the clerk, and remind him what he was to reply; or else it was the short method of taking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in court, upon the minutes, the replication and averment; cul pri; which afterwards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of succeeding clerks adopted for the very words to be by them spoken (A). But however it may have arisen, the joining of issue seems to be clearly the meaning of this obscure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>; which has puzzled our most ingenious etymologists, and is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> understood as if the clerk of the arraigns, immediately on plea pleaded, had fixed an opprobrious name on the prisoner, by asking him, "culprit, how wilt thou be tried?" for immediately upon issue joined it is inquired of the prisoner, by what trial he will make his innocence appear. This form has at present reference to appeals and approvements only, wherein the appellee has his choice, either to try the accusation by --- (A) Of this ignorance we may see daily instances, in the abuse of two legal terms of ancient French: one the prologue to all proclamations, "Oyez, or Hear ye," which is generally pronounced, most unmeaningly, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OYES">Oyes</a>;" the other, a more pardonable mistake, viz. when a jury are all sworn, the officer bids the oyer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> them, for which the word in law-French is, "Countez;" but we now hear it pronounced in very good English, "Count thele." PLEA But upon indictments, since the abolition of ORDEAL, there can be no other trial but by jury, per pais, or by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and therefore, if the prisoner refuses to put himself upon the inquest in the usual form, that is, to answer that he will be tried by God and the country, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONER">commoner</a>; and, if a peer, by God and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>; the indictment, if in treason, is taken pro confesso; and the prisoner, in cases of felony, is judged to stand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, and, if he perseveres in his obstinacy, shall now be convicted of the felony. When the prisoner has thus put himself upon his trial, the clerk answers in the humane <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the law, which always hopes that the party's innocence rather than his guilt may appear, "God send thee a good deliverance." And then they proceed, as soon as conveniently may be, to the trial. See the article TRIAL.

PLEADINGS

Pages 267-270

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, are the mutual alterations between the plaintiff and defendant, (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">SUIT</a>, WRIT, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">PROCESS</a>). They form the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stage of a fact; and at present are set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and delivered into the proper office in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>; though formerly they were usually put in by their counsel ore tenus, or viae voce, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and then minuted down by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> clerks or prothonotaries; whence, in our old law-French, the pleadings are frequently denominated the parol. The first of these is the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a>, anciently called the tale; in which the plaintiff sets forth his cause of complaint at length: being indeed only an amplification or exposition of the original writ upon which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> is founded, with the additional circumstances of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, when and where, the injury was committed. In local actions, where possession of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is to be recovered, or damages for an actual trespass, or for waste, &c., affecting land, the plaintiff must lay his declaration, or declare his injury to have happened in the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> and place that it really did happen; but in transitory actions, for injuries that might have happened anywhere, as debt, detinue, flander, and the like, the plaintiff may declare in what county he pleads, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> must be in that county in which the declaration is laid. Though, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the defendant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make affidavit that the cause of action, if any, arose not in that but another county, the court will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> a change of the venue or vicinie (that is, the vicinia or neighbourhood in which the injury is declared to be done), and will oblige the plaintiff to declare in the proper county. For the statute 6 Ric. II. c. 2. having ordered all writs to be laid in their proper counties, this, as the judges conceived, impowred them to change the venue, if required, and not to insist rigidly on abating the writ: which practice began in the reign of James I. And this power is discretionally exercised, so as not to cause but prevent a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Therefore the court will not change the venue to any of the four northern counties previous to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> circuit; because there the assizes are holden only once a-year, at the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> circuit. And it will sometimes remove the venue from the proper jurisdiction (especially of the narrow and limited kind), upon a suggestion, duly supported, that a fair and impartial trial cannot be had therein. It is generally usual, in actions upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to set forth several <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, by different counts in the same declaration; so that if the plaintiff fails in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of one, he may succeed in another. As in an action on the case upon an assumptio for goods sold and delivered, the plaintiff usually counts or declares, first, upon a fettered and agreed price between him and the defendant; as, that they bargained for £20.; and left he should fail in the proof of this, he counts likewise upon a quantum valebat; that the defendant bought other goods, and agreed to pay him so much as they were reasonably worth: and then avers that they were worth other £20. and so on in three or four different shapes; and at last concludes with declaring, that the defendant had refused to fulfil any of these agreements, whereby he is endangered to lose a value. And if he proves the case laid in any one of his counts, though he fails in the rest, he shall recover proportionable damages. This declaration always concludes with these words, "and thereupon he brings suit," &c. (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> producit seetam, &c.) By which words, suit or seeta (a sequela), were anciently understood the witnesses or followers of the plaintiff. For in former times, the law would not put the defendant to the trouble of answering the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> till the plaintiff had made out at least a probable case. But the actual production of the suit, seeta, or follower, is now antiquated, and hath been totally disused, at least ever since the reign of Edward III., though the form of it still continues. At the end of the declaration are added also the plaintiff's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pledges of prosecution, John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a> and Richard Roe; which, as we elsewhere observe, (see WRIT), are now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> names of form; though formerly they were of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to answer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> for the arrearsment of the plaintiff, in case he were nonjusticed, barred of his action, or had a verdict and judgment against him. For if the plaintiff neglects to deliver a declaration for two terms after the defendant appears, or is guilty of other delays or defaults against the rules of law in any subsequent stage of the action, he is adjudged not to follow or pursue his remedy as he ought to do; and thereupon a nonjustit, or non prosequitur, is entered, and he is said to be non-press'd. And for thus deferring his complaint, after making a false claim or complaint (pro falso clamore fio), he shall not only pay costs to the defendant, but is liable to be amerced to the king. A retraxit differs from a nonjustit, in that the one is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> and the other positive: the nonjustit is a default and neglect of the plaintiff, and therefore he is allowed to begin his suit again upon payment of costs; but a retraxit is an open and voluntary renunciation of his suit in court; and by this he for ever loses his action. A discontinueance is somewhat similar to a nonjustit; for when a plaintiff leaves a claim in the proceedings of his cause, as by not-continuing the process regularly from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to day, and time to time, as he ought to do, the suit is discontinued, and the defendant is no longer bound to attend; but the plaintiff must begin again, by suing out a new original, usually paying costs to his antagonist. When the plaintiff hath stated his case in the declaration, it is incumbent on the defendant, within a reasonable time, to make his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and put in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a>; or else the plaintiff will at once recover judgment by default, or nihil dicit, of the defendant. Defence, in its true legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, signifies not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a>, protection, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, which is now its popular signification; but merely an opposing or denial (from the French verb defendre) of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> or validity of the complaint. pleadings complaint. It is the *contestation* of the civilians: a general assertion that the plaintiff hath no ground of action; which assertion is afterwards extended and maintained in his plea. Before defence made, if at all, cognizance of the suit must be claimed or demanded; when any person or body-corporate hath the franchise, not only of holding pleas within a particular limited jurisdiction, but also of the cognizance of pleas; and that either without any words exclusive of other courts, which intitle the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the franchise, whenever any suit that belongs to his jurisdiction is commenced in the courts at Westminster, to demand the cognizance thereof; or with such exclusive words, which also intitle the defendant to plead to the jurisdiction of the court. Upon this claim of cognizance, if allowed, all proceedings shall cease in the superior court, and the plaintiff is left at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to pursue his remedy in the special jurisdiction. As, when a scholar or other privileged person of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> is impleaded in the courts at Westminster, for any cause of action whatsoever, unless upon a question of freehold. In these cases, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of those learned bodies, confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, or vice-chancellor, may put in a claim of cognizance; which, if made in due time and form, and with due proof of the facts alleged, is regularly allowed by the courts. It must be demanded before full defence is made or appearance prayed; for these are a submission to the jurisdiction of the superior court, and the delay is a *laches* in the lord of the franchise: and it will not be allowed if it occasions a failure of justice, or if an action be brought against the person himself who claims the franchise, unless he hath also a power in such case of making another judge. After defence made, the defendant must put in his plea. But before he defends, if the suit is commenced by *capias* or *libet*, without any special original, he is intitled to demand one *imparlance*, or *licentia loquendi*; and may, before he pleads, have more granted by consent of the court, to see if he can end the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> amicably without farther suit, by talking with the plaintiff: a practice which is supposed to have arisen from a principle of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, in obedience to that precept of the gospel, "agree with thine adversary quickly, whilst thou art in the way with him." And it may be observed, that this gospel-precept has a plain reference to the Roman law of the twelve tables, which expressly directed the plaintiff and defendant to make up the matter while they were in the way, or going to the praetor:—*in via, rem uti pacient orato*. There are also many other previous steps which may be taken by a defendant before he puts in his plea. He may, in real actions, demand a view of the thing in question, in order to ascertain its identity and other circumstances. He may crave *quer* of the writ, or of the bond, or other specialty upon which the action is brought; that is, to hear it read to him; the generality of defendants in the times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> simplicity being supposed incapable to read it themselves: whereupon the whole is entered *verbatim* upon the record; and the defendant may take advantage of any condition, or other part of it, not stated in the plaintiff's declaration. In real actions also the tenant may pray in aid, or call for the assistance of another, to help him to plead, because of the feebleness or imbecility of his own estate. Thus a tenant for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> may pray in aid of him that hath the inheritance in remainder or rever- fission; and an incumbent may pray in aid of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> and ordinary; that is, that they shall be joined in the action, and help to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. *Voucher* also is the calling in of some person to answer the action, that hath warranted the title to the tenant or defendant. This we still make use of in the form of common recoveries, which are grounded on a writ of entry; a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of action that relies chiefly on the weakness of the tenant's title, who therefore vouches another person to warrant it. If the voucher appear, he is made defendant instead of the voucher; but if he afterwards makes default, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> shall be had against the original defendant; and he shall recover an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> in value against the deficient vouchee. In assizes, indeed, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> question is, whether the demandant or his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were or were not in possession till the outset happened, and the title of the tenant is little (if at all) difficult, there no voucher is allowed; but the tenant may bring a writ of *warrantia chartae* against the warrantor, to compel him to affit him with a good plea or defence, or else to render damages and the value of the land, if recovered against the tenant. In many real actions also, brought by or against an infant under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 21 years, and also in actions of debt brought against him, as heir to any deceased ancestor, either party may suggest the nonage of the infant, and pray that the proceedings may be deferred till his full age, or, in our legal phrase, that the infant may have his age, and that the *parol* may *demur*, that is, that the pleadings may be laid; and then they shall not proceed till his full age, unless it be apparent that he cannot be prejudiced thereby. But by the statutes of Westminster, 3 Edw. I. c. 46. and of Glocester, 6 Edw. I. c. 2. in writs of entry *for differi* in some particular cases, and in actions ancestrally brought by an infant, the parol shall not demur; otherwise he might be deprived of his whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and even want a maintenance, till he came of age. So likewise in a writ of dower the heir shall not have his age; for it is necessary that the widow's claim be immediately determined, else she may want a present subsistence. Nor shall an infant patron have it in a *quare impedit*, since the law holds it necessary and expedient that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> be immediately filled. When these proceedings are over, the defendant must then put in his excuse or plea. See *PLEA*. It is a rule in pleading, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be allowed to plead specially such a plea as amounts only to the general issue, or a total denial of the charge; but in such case he shall be driven to plead the general issue in terms, whereby the whole question is referred to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>. But if the defendant, in an assize or action of trespass, be desirous to refer the validity of his title to the court rather than the jury, he may state his title specially; and at the same time give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the plaintiff, or suppose him to have an appearance or colour of title, bad indeed in point of law, but of which the jury are not competent judges. As if his own true title is, that he claims by seisinment with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> from A, by force of which he entered on the lands in question, he cannot plead this by itself, as it amounts to no more than the general issue, *null tort, null differi*, in assize, or not guilty in an action of trespass. But he may allege this specially, provided he goes farther, and says, that the plaintiff claiming by colour of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> of seisinment, without PLE Pleadings out livery, entered; upon whom he entered; and may then refer himself to the judgement of the court which of these two titles is the best in point of law. When the plea of the defendant is thus put in, if it does not amount to an issue or total <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> of the declaration, but only evades it, the plaintiff may plead again, and reply to the defendant's plea: Either traversing it, that is, totally denying it; as if, on an action of debt upon bond, the defendant pleads falsum ad diem, that he paid the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> when due; here the plaintiff in his replication may totally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> this plea, by denying that the defendant paid it: Or he may allege new matter in contradiction to the defendant's plea; as when the defendant pleads no award made, the plaintiff may reply, and set forth an actual award, and assign a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>: Or the replication may confess and avoid the plea, by some new matter or distinction, consistent with the plaintiff's former declaration; as in an action for trespassing upon land whereof the plaintiff is seized, if the defendant shows a title to the land by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, and that therefore he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to enter, and gives colour to the plaintiff, the plaintiff may either traverse and totally deny the fact of the descent; or he may confess and avoid it, by replying, that true it is that such descent happened, but that since the descent the defendant himself demised the lands to the plaintiff for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of life. To the replication the defendant may rejoin, or put in an answer called a rejoinder. The plaintiff may answer the rejoinder by a fur-rejoinder; upon which the defendant may rebut, and the plaintiff answer him by a fur-rebutter. Which pleas, replications, rejoinders, fur-rejoinders, rebutters, and fur-rebutters, answer to the exceptio, replicatio, duplicatio, triplicatio, and quadruplicatio, of the Roman laws. The whole of this process is denominated the pleading; in the several stages of which it must be carefully observed, not to depart or vary from the title or defence which the party has once insisted on. For this (which is called a departure in pleading) might occasion endless altercation. Therefore the replication must support the declaration, and the rejoinder must support the plea, without departing out of it. As in the case of pleading no award made in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a bond of arbitration, to which the plaintiff replies, setting forth an actual award; now the defendant cannot rejoin that he hath performed this award, for such rejoinder would be an entire departure from his original plea, which alleged that no such award was made: therefore he has now no other choice, but to traverse the fact of the replication, or else to deny upon the law of it. Again, all duplicity in pleading must be avoided. Every plea must be simple, entire, connected, and confined to one single point: it must never be entangled with a variety of distinct independent answers to the same matter; which must require as many different replies, and introduce a multitude of issues upon one and the same dispute. For this would often embarrass the jury, and sometimes the court itself, and at all events would greatly enhance the expense of the parties. Yet it frequently is expedient to plead in such a manner as to avoid any implied admission of a fact, which cannot with propriety or safety be positively affirmed or denied. And this may be done by what is called a protestation; whereby the party interposes an oblique allegation or denial of some fact, protesting (by the gerund, protestan- do) that such a matter does or does not exist; and at the same time avoiding a direct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> or denial. Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> hath defined a protestation (in the pithy dialect of that age) to be, "an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of a conclusion." For the use of it is, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the party from being concluded with respect to some fact or circumstance which cannot be directly affirmed or denied without falling into duplicity of pleading; and which yet, if he did not thus enter his protest, he might be deemed to have tacitly waived or admitted. Thus, while <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> in villainage subsisted, if a villain had brought an action against his lord, and the lord was inclined to try the merits of the demand, and at the same time to prevent any conclusion against himself that he had waived his figuory; he could not in this case both plead affirmatively that the plaintiff was his villain, and also take issue upon the demand; for then his plea would have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, as the former alone would have been a good <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> to the action: but he might have alleged the villainage of the plaintiff by way of protestation, and then have denied the demand. By this means the future vafalage of the plaintiff was saved to the defendant, in case the issue was found in his (the defendant's?) favour; for the protestation prevented that conclusion which would otherwise have resulted from the rest of his defence, that he had enfranchised the plaintiff, since no villain could maintain a civil action against his lord. So also if a defendant, by way of inducement to the point of his defence, alleges (among other matters) a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEISIN">seisin</a> or tenure which the plaintiff is unwilling to admit, and yet desires to take issue on the principal point of the defence, he must deny the seisin or tenure by way of protestation, and then traverse the defensive matter. So, lastly, if an award be set forth by the plaintiff, and he can assign a breach in one part of it (viz. the non-payment of a sum of money), and yet is afraid to admit the performance of the rest of the award, or to aver in general a non-performance of any part of it, lest something should appear to have been performed; he may save to himself any advantage he might hereafter make of the general non-performance, by alleging that by protestation, he can plead only the non-payment of the money. In any stage of the pleadings, when either side advances or affirms any new matter, he usually (as was said) avers it to be true; "and this he is ready to verify." On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, when either side traverses or denies the facts pleaded by his antagonist, he usually tenders an issue, as it is called; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of which is different according to the party by whom it is tendered: for if the traverse or denial comes from the defendant, the issue is tendered in this manner, "And of this he puts himself upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>," thereby submitting himself to the judgement of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>: but if the traverse lies upon the plaintiff, he tenders the issue or prays the judgement of the peers against the defendant in another form; thus, "and this he prays may be inquired of by the country." But if either side (as, for instance, the defendant) pleads a special negative plea, not traversing or denying anything that was before alleged, but disclosing some new negative matter; as where the suit is on a bond conditioned to perform an award, and the defendant pleads, negatively, that no award was made; he tenders no issue upon this plea, because it does not yet appear whether... PLE Pleadings, whether the fact will be disputed, the plaintiff not having yet asserted the existence of any award; but when the plaintiff replies, and seeks forth an actual specific award, if then the defendant traverses the replication, and denies the making of any such award, he then, and not before, tenders an issue to the plaintiff. For when in the course of pleading they come to a point which is affirmed on one side and denied on the other, they are then said to be at issue; all their debates being at last contracted into a single point, which must now be determined either in favour of the plaintiff or of the defendant. See Issue.

PLEASING

Pages 270-276

art of. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">Politeness</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">PLEASURE</a> is a word so universally understood as to need no explanation. Lexicographers, however, who must attempt to explain every word, call it "the gratification of the mind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> senses." It is directly opposite to PAIN, and constitutes the whole of positive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, as that does of misery. The Author of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> has furnished us with many pleasures, as well as made us liable to many pains; and we are susceptible of both in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as soon as we have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and are endowed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>. A French writer, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>* which once raised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> expectations, contends, that a child in the womb of its mother feels neither pleasure nor pain. "These sensations (says he) are not innate; they have their origin from without; and it is at the moment of our birth that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> receives its first impressions; impressions slight and superficial at the beginning, but which by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and repeated acts leave deeper traces in the sensorium, and become more extensive and more lasting. It is when the child emits forth its first cries that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> or the faculty of sensation is produced, which in a short time gathers strength and stability by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects. Pleasure and pain not being innate, and being only acquired in the same manner as the qualities which we derive from instruction, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, it follows that we learn to suffer and enjoy as we learn any other science." This is strange reasoning and strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. That sensations are not innate is universally acknowledged; but it does not therefore follow that the soul receives its first impressions and first sensations at the moment of birth. The child has life, the power of locomotion, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of touch, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before it is born; and every mother <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> tell this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, that an infant unborn exhibits symptoms both of pain and of pleasure. That many of our organs of sense are improved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is incontrovertible; but it is so far from being true that our sensible pleasures become more exquisite by being often repeated, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> contrary is experienced of far the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of them; and though external objects, by making repeated impressions on the senses, certainly leave deeper traces on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> than an object once perceived can do, it by no means follows that these impressions become the more delightful the more familiar that they are to us. That we learn to suffer and enjoy as we learn any other science, is a most extravagant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>; for it is self-evident that we cannot live without being capable in some degree both of suffering and enjoyment, though a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may certainly live to old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> in profound <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of all the sciences. The same writer assures us, indeed, that sensation is not necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life. "Philosophers (says he) make mention of a man who had lost every kind of feeling in every member of his body: he was pinched or pricked to no purpose. Meanwhile this man made use of all his members; he walked without pain, he drank, ate, and slept, without perceiving that he did so.
