Sensible neither to pleasure nor pain, he was a true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> machine." To the tale of these anonymous philosophers our author gives implicit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, whilst he favours us at the same instant with the following argumentation, which completely proves its falsehood. "It is true that sensation is a relative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, susceptible of increase and diminution; that it is not necessary to existence; and that one might live without it: but in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> he would live as an automaton, without feeling pleasure or pain; and he would possess neither idea, nor reflection, nor desire, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, nor will, nor sentiment; his existence would be merely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>, he would live without knowing it, and die without <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>." But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this man of the philosophers, whom our author calls an automaton, and a true natural machine, had neither idea, nor desire, nor passion, nor will, nor sentiment (and without sensation he certainly could have none of them), what induced him to walk, eat, or drink, or to cease from any of these operations after they were accidentally begun? The instances of the automata which played on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> and at chefs are not to the purpose for which they are adduced; for there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> between them and this natural machine, unless the philosophers wound up their man to eat, drink, walk, or sit, as Vacanson and Kempeler wound up their automata to play or cease from playing on the German flute and at chefs. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROIDES">ANDROIDES</a>. Our author having for a while sported with these harmless paradoxes, proceeds to put the credulity of his reader to the test with others of a very contrary tendency. He institutes an inquiry concerning the superiority, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and degree, of the pleasures enjoyed by the different orders of men in society; and labours, not indeed by argument, but by loose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a>, to propagate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that happiness is very unequally distributed. The pleasures of the rich, he says, must be more numerous and exquisite than those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; the nobleman must have more enjoyments than the plebeian of equal wealth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, according to him, must be the happiest of all men. He owns, indeed, that although "birth, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, honours, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, add to happiness, a man is not to be considered as miserable because he is born in the lower conditions of life. A man may be happy as a mechanic, a merchant, or a labourer, provided he enters into the spirit of his profession, and has not imbibed by a misplaced education those sentiments which make his condition insupportable. Happiness is of easy acquisition in the middling stations of life; and though perhaps we are unable to know or to rate exactly the pleasure which arises from contentment and mediocrity, yet happiness being a kind of aggregate of delights, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and of advantages more or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, every person must have a share of it; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is not exactly made, but all other things equal, there will be more in the elevated than in the inferior conditions of society; the enjoyment will be more felt, the means of enjoying more multiplied, and the pleasures more varied. Birth, rank, fortune, talents, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, genius, Pleasure, genius, and virtue, are then the great sources of happiness; those advantages are so considerable, that we see men contented with any one of them, but their union forms supreme felicity. "There is so vast a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>," says Voltaire, "between a man who has made his fortune and one who has to make it, that they are scarcely to be considered as creatures of the same kind. The same thing may be said of birth, the greatest of all advantages in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> society; of rank, of honours, and of great abilities. How great a difference is made between a person of high birth and a tradesman; between a Newton or Descartes and a simple mathematician? Ten thousand <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> are killed on the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and it is scarcely mentioned; but if the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and especially if he be a man of courage and abilities, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> are filled with the news of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> is universal. "Frederick the Great, king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, felt in a more lively manner than perhaps any other man the value of great talents. I would willingly renounce," said he to Voltaire, "everything which is an object of desire and ambition to man; but I am certain if I were not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> I should be nothing. Your merit alone would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> you the esteem and envy, and admiration of the world; but to secure respect for me, titles, and armies, and revenues, are absolutely necessary." For what purpose this account of human happiness was published, it becomes not us to say. Its obvious tendency is to make the lower orders of society discontented with their state, and envious of their superiors; and it is not unreasonable to suppose, that it contributed in some degree to excite the ignorant part of the author's countrymen to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of those atrocities of which they have since been guilty. That such was his intention, the following extract will not permit us to believe; for though in it the author attempts to support the same false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of human happiness, he mentions virtuous kings with the respect becoming a loyal subject of the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, whose character he seems to have intentionally drawn, and whose death by the authority of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> he has in effect foretold. "Happiness, in a state of society, takes the most variable forms: it is a Proteus susceptible of every kind of metamorphosis; it is different in different men, in different ages, and in different conditions, &c. The pleasures of youth are very different from those of old age: what affords enjoyment to a mechanic would be supreme misery to a nobleman; and the amusements of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> would appear insipid in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Is there then nothing fixed with regard to happiness? Is it of all things the most variable and the most arbitrary? Or, in judging of it, is it impossible to find a standard by which we can determine the limits of the greatest good to which man can arrive in the present state? It is evident that men form the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the beautiful and sublime in nature, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and wrong in morality, provided they have arrived at that degree of improvement and civilization of which human nature is susceptible; and that different opinions on these subjects depend on different degrees of culture, of education, and of improvement. The same thing may be advanced with regard to happiness: all men, if equal with respect to their organs, would form the very same ideas on this subject if they reached the degree of improvement of which we are presently speaking; and in fact, do we not see in the great circles at Rome, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, that those who are called people of fashion, who have received the same education, have nearly the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the same desires, and the same spirit for enjoyment? there is doubtless a certain degree of happiness to be enjoyed in every condition of life; but as there are some conditions preferable to others, so are there degrees of happiness greater and less; and if we were to form an idea of the greatest possible in the present state, it perhaps would be that of a sovereign, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a great empire, enjoying good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and a moderate spirit; endowed with piety and virtue; whose whole life was employed in acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and mercy, and who governed by fixed and unmovable laws. Such a king is the image of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and he must be the idol of a wise people. His whole life should present a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the most august felicity. Although such sovereigns are rare, yet we are not without examples of them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> affords us Titus and Marcus Aurelius, and the present age can boast of piety and munificence in the character of some of its kings. This state of the greatest happiness to which man can reach not being ideal, it will serve as a standard of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> by which happiness and misery can be estimated in all civilized countries. He is as happy as a king, is a proverbial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, because we believe with justice that royalty is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> limit of the greatest enjoyments; and in fact, happiness being the work of man, that condition which comprehends all the degrees of power and of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, which is the source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and of dignity, and which supposes in the person invested with all means of enjoyment either for himself or others, leaves nothing on this earth to which any reasonable man would give the preference. "We can find also in this high rank the extreme of the greatest evils to which the condition of nature is exposed. A king condemned to death and perishing on a scaffold, by the authority of a faction, while at the same time he had endeavoured by every means in his power to promote the general happiness of his subjects, is the most terrible and striking example of human misery; for if it be true that a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is the greatest of all blessings, then the loss of it, and at the same time the loss of life by an ignominious and unjust <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, are of all calamities the most dreadful. "It is also in the courts of kings that we find the most amiable and perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; and it is there where true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, true politeness, the best tone of manners, the most amiable graces, and the most eminent virtues, are completely established. It is in courts that men seem to have acquired their greatest improvement: Whoever has seen a court, says La Bruyere, has seen the world in the most beautiful, the most enchanting, and attractive colours. The prejudices of mankind in behalf of the great are so extensive, that if they inclined to be good they would be almost the objects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>." In this passage there are doubtless many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> observations; but there is at least an equal number of others both false and dangerous. That a crown is the greatest of earthly blessings, and that it is in the courts of kings that we meet with the most amiable and perfect characters, are positions which a true philosopher will not admit but with great limitations. The falsehood of the author's pleasure. But all pains do not proceed from an excess of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Many of them arise from reducing the body or the mind to a state below indifference. Thus, if a person have just sufficient warmth in his body to keep him barely at ease or in a state of indifference, by withdrawing this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> a state of uneasiness or pain is produced; and if in a calm state of mind one be made acquainted with a melancholy event, his quiet is interrupted, and he sinks below indifference into a painful state of mind. If now, without communicating any new source of positive pleasure, we remove in the former case the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and in the latter the grief, the persons from whom they are removed will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> real pleasure. Thus, then, whether pain arises from excess or deficiency of action, the gradual or the sudden removal of it must be in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> attended with pleasure.* It is equally true that the gradual or sudden removal of pleasure is attended with pain. We are now prepared to examine our French author's account of the pleasures and pains of savages. "Every age (says he) has its different pleasures; but if we were to imagine that those of childhood are equal to those of confirmed age, we should be much mistaken in our estimation of happiness. The pleasures of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, either natural or moral, are not unfolded to the infant; the most perfect music is a vain noise; the most exquisite perfumes and dishes highly seasoned offend his young organs instead of affording delight; his touch is imperfect; forty days elapse before the child gives any sign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> or of weeping; his cries and groans before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> are not accompanied with tears; his countenance expresses no passion; the parts of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> bear no relation to the sentiments of the soul, and are moreover without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>. Children are but little affected with cold; whether it be that they feel less, or that the interior heat is greater than in adults. In them all the impressions of pleasure and pain are transitory; their memory has scarcely begun to unfold its powers; they enjoy nothing but the present moment; they weep, laugh, and give tones of satisfaction without consciousness, or at least without reflection; their joy is confined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> of their little whims, and constraint is the greatest of their misfortunes; few things amuse, and nothing satisfies them. In this happy condition of early infancy nature is at the whole expense of happiness; and the only point is not to contradict her. What desires have children? Give them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in all their movements, and they have a plenitude of existence, an abundance of that kind of happiness which is confined in some sort to all the objects which surround them: but if all beings were happy on the same conditions, society would be at no expense in procuring the happiness of the different individuals who compose it. Sensation is the foundation of reflection; it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of the soul; it is by this that man is elevated to sublime speculations, and secures his dominion over nature and himself. This quality is not <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a>, but susceptible, like all other relative qualities, of increase and decay, of different degrees of strength and intensity: it is different in different men; and in the same man it increases from infancy to youth, from youth to confirmed manhood: at this period it stops, and gradually declines as we proceed to old age and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> childhoods. Considered physically, it varies according to age, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, and food; considered in a moral point of view, it... Pleasure of view, it takes its different appearances from individual education, and from the habits of society; for man in a state of nature and society, with regard to sensation and the unfolding of his powers, may be considered as two distinct beings: and if one were to make a calculation of pleasure in the course of human life, a man of fortune and capacity enjoys more than ten thousand savages. "Pleasure and pain being relative qualities, they may be almost annihilated in the moment of vehement passion. In the heat of battle, for example, ardent and animated spirits have not felt the pain of their wounds; and minds strongly penetrated with sentiments of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, enthusiasm, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, have supported the most cruel torments with courage and fortitude. The sensibility of some persons is so exquisitely alive, that one can scarcely approach them without throwing them into convulsions. Many diseases show the effect of sensibility pushed to an extreme; such as hysterical affections, certain kinds of madness, and some of those which proceed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, and from the bite or sting of certain animals, as the viper and the tarantula. Excessive joy or grief, fear and terror, have been known to destroy all sensation, and occasion death." Having made these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> observations on pleasure and pain in infancy, and as they are increased or diminished by education, and the different conditions of body and mind, our author proceeds to consider the capability of savages to feel pleasure and pain. "By savages he understands all the tribes of men who live by hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, and on those things which the earth yields without cultivation. Those tribes who possess herds of cattle, and who derive their subsistence from such possessions, are not to be considered as savages, as they have some idea of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Some savages are naturally compassionate and humane, others are cruel and sanguinary. Although the physical constitution of man be everywhere the same, yet the varieties of climate, the abundance or scarcity of natural productions, have a powerful influence to determine the inclinations. Even the fierceness of the tiger is softened under a mild sky; now nature forms the manners of savages just as society and civil institutions form the manners of civilized life. In the one case climate and food produce almost the whole effect; in the other they have scarcely any influence. The habits of society every moment contend with nature, and they are almost always victorious. The savage devotes himself to the dominion of his passions; the civilized man is employed in restraining, in directing, and in modifying them: so much influence have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, laws, society, and the fear of censure and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, over his soul. "It is not to be doubted that savages are susceptible of both pleasure and pain; but are the impressions made on their organs as sensible, or do they feel pain in the same degree with the inhabitants of a civilized country? "Their enjoyments are so limited, that if we confine ourselves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> will be sufficient to describe them: our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> must therefore be confined to pain, because the manner in which they support misfortune, and even torture, presents us with a view of character unequalled in the history of civilized nations. It is not uncommon in civilized countries to see men <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> death, meeting it with cheerfulness, and even not uttering complaints under the torture; but they do not infuse the executioners of public vengeance, and defy pain in order to augment their torments; and those who are condemned by the laws suffer the punishment with different degrees of fortitude. On those mournful occasions, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ranks of mankind in general die with less firmness: those, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, who have received education, and who, by a train of unfortunate events, are brought to the scaffold, whether it be the fear of being reproached with cowardice, or the consideration that the stroke is inevitable, such men discover the expiring sighs of self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> even in their last moments; and those especially of high rank, from their manners and sentiments, are expected to meet death with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>: but an American savage in the moment of punishment appears to be more than human; he is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of the first order, who braves his tormentors, who provokes them to employ all their art, and who considers as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> glory to bear the greatest degree of pain without shrinking (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">AMERICA</a>, No. 14, 27, 28, 29.). The recital of their tortures would appear exaggerated, if it were not attested by the best authority, and if the savage nations among whom those customs are established were not sufficiently known; but the excess of the cruelty is not so astonishing as the courage of the victim. The European exposed to sufferings of the same dreadful nature would rend heaven and earth with his piercing cries and horrible groans; the reward of martyrdom, the prospect of eternal life, could alone give him fortitude to endure such torments; but the savage is not animated with this exalted hope. What supports him then in scenes of so exquisite suffering? The feeling of shame, the fear of bringing reproach on his tribe, and giving a stain to his fellows never to be wiped away, are the only sentiments which influence the mind of a savage, and which always present to his imagination, animate him, support him, and lend him spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. At the same time, however powerful those motives may be, they would not be alone sufficient, if (a) There are instances of persons who have died at the noise of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> without being touched. A man frightened with the fall of a gallery in which he happened to be, was immediately seized with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>. M. le Cat mentions a young person on whom the influence of another made such an impression, that his countenance became at first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and then changed into black, in such a manner that in less than eight days he appeared to wear a mask of black velvet: he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this state for four months, without any other symptom of bad health or any pain. A sailor was so terrified in a storm, that his face sweated blood, which like ordinary sweat returned as it was wiped off. Stahl, whose testimony cannot be called in question, cites a similar case of a girl who had been frightened with soldiers. The excess of fear, according to many physicians, produces madness and epilepsy. Pleasure, the savage felt pain in the same degree with the European. Sensibility, as we have already observed, is increased by education; it is influenced by society, manners, laws, and government; climate and food work it into a hundred different shapes; and all the physical and moral causes contribute to increase and diminish it. The habitual existence of a savage would be a state of suffering to an inhabitant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. You must cut the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of the one and tear it away with your nails, before you can make him feel in an equal degree to a scratch or prick of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> in the other. The savage, doubting, suffers under torture, but he suffers much less than an European in the same circumstances: the reason is obvious; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> which the savages breathe is loaded with fog and moist vapours; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> not being confined by high banks, are by the winds as well as in floods spread over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> fields, and deposit on them a putrid and pernicious slime; the trees squeezed one upon another, in that rude and uncultivated country serve rather as a covering to the earth than an ornament. Instead of those fresh and delicious shades, those openings in the woods, and walks crossing each other in all directions, which delight the traveller in the fine forests of France and Germany; those in America serve only to intercept the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and to prevent the benign influence of his beams. The savage participates of this cold humidity; his blood has little heat, his humours are grofs, and his constitution phlegmatic. To the powerful influence of climate, it is necessary to join the habits of his life. Obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> vast deserts for subsistence, his body is accustomed to fatigue; food not nourishing, and at the same time in no great plenty, blunts his feelings; and all the hardships of the savage state give a rigidity to his members which makes him almost incapable of suffering. The savage in this state of nature may be compared to our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-women and street-porters, who, though they possess neither great vigour nor strength, are capable of performing daily, and without complaint, that kind of labour which to a man in a different condition of life would be a painful and grievous burden. Feeling, in less perfection with the savage, by the effects of climate and food, and the habits of his life, is still farther restrained by moral considerations. The European is less a man of nature than of society: moral restraints are powerful with him; while over the American they have scarcely any influence. This latter then is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> condition of imperfection with regard to us; his senses are blunted, and his moral powers are not disclosed. Now, pleasure and pain depending on the perfection of the senses and the unfolding of the intellectual faculties, it cannot be doubted, that in enjoyments of any kind savages experience less pleasure, and in their sufferings less pain, than Europeans in the same circumstances. And in fact, the savages of America possess a very feeble constitution. They are agile without being strong; and this agility depends more on their habits than on the perfection of their members: they owe it to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of hunting; and they are moreover so weak, that they were unable to bear the toil which their first oppressors imposed on them. Hence a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of men in all respects imperfect could not endure torment under which the most robust European would sink, if the pain which they feel were really as great as it appears to be. Feeling is then, and must necessarily be, less in the savage condition; for pleasure, this faculty disclosing itself by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of all the physical and moral qualities, must be less as they are less exercised. Everything shows the imperfection of this precious quality, this source of all our affections, in the American savages. "All the improvements in Europe have had a tendency to unfold sensibility: the air is purified that we may breathe more freely; the morals are drained, the rivers are regulated in their courses, the food is nourishing, and the houses commodious. With the savages, on the contrary, every thing tends to curb it; they take pleasure even in hardening the organs of the body, in accustoming themselves to bear by degrees the most acute pain without complaining. Boys and girls among the savages amuse themselves with tying their naked arms together, and laying a kindled coal between them, to try which of them can longest suffer the heat; and the warriors who aspire to the honour of being chief, undergo a course of suffering which exceeds the idea of torture inflicted on the greatest criminals in Europe." These observations on the pleasures and pains of savages appear to be well-founded, and, as the attentive reader will perceive, are perfectly agreeable to the theory of Dr Sayers. If indeed that theory be just, as we believe it to be, it will follow, that the few pleasures of sense which the American enjoys, he ought to enjoy more completely than any European, because to him they recur but seldom. This may very possibly be the case; and certainly would be so, were not his fibres, by climate and the habits of his life, rendered more rigid than those of the civilized part of the inhabitants of Europe. But if we agree with our author * in what he says of the pains and pleasures of savages, we cannot admit, without many exceptions, his theory of the enjoyments of children. It is so far from being true, that few things amuse, and that nothing satisfies them, that the direct contrary must have been observed by every man attentive to the operations of the infant mind, which is amused with everything new, and often completely satisfied with the merest trifle. The pleasures of philosophy are not indeed unfolded to the infant; but it by no means follows that he does not enjoy his rattle and his drum as much as the philosopher enjoys his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> and air-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>; and if there be any truth in the science of physiognomy, the happiness of the former is much more pure and exquisite than that of the latter. That the most perfect music is vain noise to an infant, is far from being self-evident, unless the author confines the state of infancy to a very few months; and we are not disposed to believe, without better <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> than we have yet received, that the relish of exquisite perfumes and highly-scented dishes adds much to the sum of human felicity. But however much we disapprove of many of these reflections, the following we cordially adopt as our own. "If we compare (says our author) the pleasures of sense with those which are purely intellectual, we shall find that the latter are infinitely superior to the former, as they may be enjoyed at all times and in every situation of life. What are the pleasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, says Cicero, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, and of women, compared with the delights of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>? This taste increases with age, and no happiness... Pleasure, happiness is equal to it. Without knowledge and study, say Cato, life is almost the image of death (9). The pleasures of the soul are such, that it is frequent enough to see men preserve their gaiety during their whole life, notwithstanding a weak, defeated, and debilitated body. Scaron, who lived in the last century, was an example of this. Balzac, speaking of him, says, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, and Philocetes, in profane, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> in sacred history, said many great things while they were afflicted with violent pain; but Scaron alone said pleasant things. I have seen, continues he, in many places of ancient history, constancy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and eloquence, accompanying affliction; but he is the only instance wherein I have seen pleasantry. There are men whose understandings are constantly on the stretch, and by this very means they are improved; but if the body were as constantly employed in the pursuit of sensual gratification, the constitution would soon be destroyed. The more we employ the mind we are capable of the greater exertion; but the more we employ the body we require the greater repose. There are besides but some parts of the body capable of enjoying pleasure; every part of it can experience pain. A toothache occasions more suffering than the most considerable of our pleasures can procure of enjoyment. Great pain may continue for any length of time; excessive pleasures are almost momentary. Pleasure carried to an extreme becomes painful; but pain, either by augmenting or diminishing it, never becomes agreeable. For the moment, the pleasures of the senses are perhaps more satisfactory; but in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> those of the heart and mind are infinitely preferable. All the sentiments of tenderness, of friendship, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, and of generosity, are sources of enjoyment for man in a state of civilization. The damned are exceedingly unhappy, said St Catherine de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, if they are incapable of loving or being beloved. Pleasure, continued for a great length of time, produces languor and fatigue, and excites <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>; the continuation of pain is productive of none of these effects. Many suffer pain for eight days and even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> without interruption; an equal duration of excessive pleasure would occasion death. Time is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> relative idea with regard to pleasure and pain; it appears long when we suffer, and short when we enjoy. If there existed no regular and uniform movement in nature, we would not be able from our sensations alone to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> time with any degree of exactness, for pain lengthens and pleasure abridges it. From the languor of unoccupied time has arisen the proverb expressive of our desire to kill it. It is a melancholy reflection, and at the same time true, that there is no enjoyment which can effectually secure us from pain for the remainder of our lives; while there are examples of evils which hold men in constant sorrow and pain during their whole existence. Such then is the imperfection of the one and the power of the other. Pleasure and pain are the sources of morality; an action is just or unjust, good or otherwise, only as its natural tendency is to produce suffering or enjoyment to mankind. No crime could be committed against a being altogether indefensible, nor could any good be bestowed on it. Unless he were endowed with the desire of pleasure and the apprehension of pain, man, like an automaton, would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> from necessity, without choice and without determination. All our passions are the development of sensibility. If we were not possessed of feeling, we should be destitute of passions; and as sensibility is augmented by civilization, the passions are multiplied; more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and vigorous in an extensive and civilized empire than in a small state; more in the latter than among barbarous nations; and more in these last than among savages (see Passion). There are more passions in France and England than in all the nations of Europe; because every thing which serves to excite and foster them is always in those countries in the greatest state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>. The mind is active; the ideas great, extensive, and multiplied. And is it not the soul, the mind, and heart, which are the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of all the passions? But wherever the passions are multiplied, the sources of pleasure and pain are multiplied with them. This being the case, it is impossible to prescribe a fixed and general rule of happiness suited to every individual. There are objects of pleasure with regard to which all men of a certain education are agreed; but there are perhaps many more, owing to the variety of temperaments and education, about which they differ. Every man forms ideas of enjoyment relative to his character; and what pleases one may be utterly detested by another. In proportion as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is civilized and extensive, those differences are remarkable. Savages, who are not acquainted with all the variety of European pleasures, amuse themselves with very few objects. Owing to the want of civilization, they have scarcely any choice in the objects of taste. They have few passions; we have many. But even in the nations of Europe pleasure is infinitely varied in its modification and forms. Those differences arise from manners, from governments, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> customs, and chiefly from education. Meanwhile, however different and variable the ideas of pleasure may be among nations and individuals, it still remains a fact, that a certain number of persons in all civilized states, whether distinguished by birth, rank, or fortune, or talents, as they have nearly the same education so they form nearly the same ideas of happiness; but to possess it a man must give his chief application to the state of his mind; and notwithstanding all his efforts it is of uncertain duration. Happiness is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of life: we enjoy it frequently at great intervals; and it is therefore necessary to know how to use (B) "Savages, barbarians, and peasants, enjoy little happiness except that of sensation, The happiness of a civilized and well-informed man consists of sensations, of ideas, and of a great number of affinities, altogether unknown to them. He not only enjoys the present, but the past and the future. He recalls the agreeable idea of pleasures which he has tasted. It is great happiness, says an ancient, to have the recollection of good actions, of an upright intention, and of promises which we have kept." PLE Pleasure. All the productions of art perish; the largest fortunes are dissipated; rank, honour, and dignity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away like a fleeting shadow; the memory is impaired; all the faculties of the soul are extinguished; the body sinks under the infirmities of old age; and scarcely has one reached the boundaries of happiness marked out by his imagination, when he must give <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to another, and renounce all his pleasures, all his hopes, all his illusions; the fugitive images of which had given happiness to the mind. There are pleasures, however, on which the mind may securely rest, which elevate man above himself, dignify his nature, fix his attention on spiritual things, and render him worthy of the care of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. These are to be found in true religion; which procures for those who practise its duties ineffable happiness in a better country, and is in this world the support of the weak, and the sweet consolation of the unfortunate.

PLEBEIAN

Pages 276-276

any person of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people. It is chiefly used in speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who were divided into senators, patricians, and plebeians. The distinction was made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> the founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; who confined all dignities, civil, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and sacerdotal, to the rank of patricians. But to prevent the seditions which such a distinction might produce through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of the higher order and the envy of the lower, he endeavoured to engage them to one another by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> ties and obligations. Every plebeian was allowed to choose, out of the body of the patricians, a protector, who should be obliged to assist him with his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and substance, and to defend him from oppression. These protectors were called patrons; the protected, clients. It was the duty of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> to draw up the contracts of the clients, to extricate them out of their difficulties and perplexities, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> against the artifices of the crafty. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the patron was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, his clients were obliged to contribute to the portions of his daughters, the payment of his debts, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of him and his children if they happened to be taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The client and patron could neither accuse nor bear witness against each other; and if either of them was convicted of having violated this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the crime was equal to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and any one might with impunity slay the offender as a victim devoted to Pluto and the infernal gods. For more than 600 years we find no dissensions <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> jealousies between the patrons and their clients; not even in the times of the republic, when the people frequently mutinied against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and powerful.

PLECTRANTHUS

Pages 276-276

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42nd order, Verticillatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLEDGE

Pages 276-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, a surety <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gage, either real or personal, which the plaintiff or defendant is to find for his prosecuting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>. The word is sometimes also used for FRANK Pledge, which see. To PLEDGE, in drinking, denotes to warrant, or be surety to one, that he shall receive no harm while he is taking his draught. The phrase is referred by antiquaries to the practice of the Danes heretofore in England, who frequently used to stab or cut the throats of the natives while they were drinking. PLEDGE OF GOODS FOR <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">MONEY</a>. See PAWN.

PLEDGERY

Pages 276-276
or PLEGGERY, in Law, suretship, or an undertaking or answering for another.

PLEGED

Pages 276-276

BOLSTER, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> COMPRESS, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a kind of flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> laid over a wound, to imbibe the superfluous humours, and to keep it clean.

PLEIADES

Pages 276-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an assemblage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> stars, in the neck of the constellation Taurus. They are thus called from the Greek πλεια, navigare, "to sail;" as being terrible to mariners, by reason of the rains and storms that frequently rise with them. The Latins called them vergilie, from ver, "<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>;" because of their rising about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the vernal equinox. The largest is of the third magnitude, and is called <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LUCIDA">lucida</a> pleiadaum.

PLENARY

Pages 276-276

something complete <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> full. Thus we say the pope grants plenary indulgences; i.e., full and entire remissions of the penalties due to all sins. See INDULGENCES.

PLENIPOTENTIARY

Pages 276-276

a person vested with full power to do anything. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">AMBASSADOR</a>.

PLENITUDE

Pages 276-276

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a thing that is full, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that fills another. In medicine, it chiefly denotes a redundancy of blood and humours.

PLENUM

Pages 276-276

in Physics, denotes, according to the Cartesians, that state of things wherein every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of space is supposed to be full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, in opposition to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">VACUUM</a>, which is a space supposed devoid of all matter.

PLENUS FLOS

Pages 276-277

a full flower; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> expressive of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of luxuriance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a>. Such flowers, although the most delightful to the eye, are both vegetable monsters, and, according to the sexualists, vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>; the unnatural increase of the petals constituting the first; the consequent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the stamina <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, the latter. The following are well-known examples of flowers with more petals than one; ranunculus, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">anemone</a>, marigold, columbine, fennel-flower, poppy, peony, pink, gillyflower, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPION">campion</a>, viscous campion, lily, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> imperial, tulip, narcissus, rocket, mallow, Syrian mallow, apple, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, peach, cherry, almond, myrtle, rose, and strawberry. Flowers with one petal are not so subject to fullness. The following, however, are instances: polyanthus, hyacinth, primrose, crocus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>-saffron, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">thorn</a>-apple; though Kramer has asserted that a full flower with one petal is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> in terms. In flowers with one petal, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of luxuriance, or impletion, is by a multiplication of the divisions of the limb or upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; in flowers with more petals than one, by a multiplication of the petals or nectarium. To take a few examples. Columbine is rendered full in three different ways: 1. By the multiplication of its petals, and total exclusion of the nectaria; 2. By the multiplication of the nectaria, and exclusion of the petals; or, 3. By such an increase of the nectaria only as does not exclude the petals, between each of which are interjected three nectaria, placed one within another. Again, fennel-flower is rendered full by an increase of the nectaria only; narcissus, either by a multiplication of its cup and petals, or of its cup only; larkspur <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> by an increase of the petals and exclusion of the spur, which is its nectarium. In *Japonaria concava anglica*, the impletion is attended with the finger-like effect of incorporating the petals, and reducing their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> from five to one; and in gilder-rofe, the luxuriance is effected by an increase both in magnitude and number of the circumference or margin of the head of flowers, in the plain, wheel-shaped, barren florets; and an exclusion of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-shaped hermaphrodite florets of the centre or disk. Hitherto we have treated of plenitude in simple flowers only: the instance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now adduced seems to connect the different modes of impletion in them and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> flowers. Before proceeding farther, however, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be improper to premise, that as a simple luxuriant flower is frequently, by beginners, mistaken for a compound flower in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, such flowers may always be distinguished with certainty by this rule: That in simple flowers, however luxuriant, there is but one pistillum or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> organ; whereas in compound flowers, each floret, or partial flower, is furnished with its own proper pistillum. Thus in hawk-weed, a compound flower, each flat or tongue-shaped floret in the aggregate has its five stamens and naked seed, which last is in effect its pistillum; whereas, in a luxuriant lychis, which is a simple flower, there is found only one pistillum or female organ <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the whole. In a compound radiated flower, which generally consists of plain florets in the margin or radius, and tubular or hollow florets in the centre or disk, plenitude is effected either by an increase of the florets in the margin, and a total exclusion of those in the disk; which mode of luxuriance is termed *impletion by the radius*, and resembles what happens in the gilder-rofe: or by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELONGATION">elongation</a> of the hollow florets in the centre, and a less profound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of their brims; which is termed *impletion by the disk*. In the first mode of luxuriance, the florets in the centre, which are always hermaphrodite or male, are entirely excluded; and in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> succeed florets similar in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> to those of the radius. Now as the florets in the margin of a radiated compound flower are found to be always either female, that is, furnished with the pistillum only; or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEUTER">neuter</a>, that is, furnished with neither stamens nor pistillum; it is evident, that a radiated compound flower, filled by the radius, will either be entirely female, as in feverfew, daisy, and African marigold; or entirely neuter, as in sunflower, marigold, and centaury: hence it will always be easy to distinguish such a luxuriant flower from a compound flower with plain florets in a natural state; as these flowers are all hermaphrodite, that is, furnished with both stamens and pistillum. Thus the full flowers of African marigold have each floret furnished with the pistillum or female organ only: the natural flowers of dandelion, which, like the former, is composed of plain florets, are furnished with both stamens and pistillum. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> mode of luxuriance, termed *impletion by the disk*, the florets in the margin sometimes remain unchanged: but most commonly adopt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of those in the centre, without, however, suffering any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in point of sex; so that confusion is less to be apprehended from this mode of luxuriance than from the former; besides, the length to which the florets in the centre run out is of itself a sufficient distinction, and adapted to excite at once an idea of luxuriance. Daisy, feverfew, and African marigold, exhibit instances of this as well as of the former mode of impletion. In luxuriant compound flowers with plain florets, the *semiflora* of Tournefort, the stigma or summit of the style in each floret is lengthened, and the seed-buds are enlarged and diverge; by which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> such flowers may always be distinguished from flowers of the same kind in a natural state. Scorzonera, nipple-wort, and goat's-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, furnish frequent instances of the plenitude alluded to. Lastly, the impletion of compound flowers with tubular or hollow florets, the *flocculus* of Tournefort, seems to observe the same rules as that of radiated flowers just delivered. In everlastings-flower, the *xeranthemum* of Linnæus, the impletion is finger-like, being effected by the enlargement and expansion of the inward chaffy scales of the calyx. These scales, which become coloured, are greatly augmented in length, so as to overtop the florets, which are scarce larger than those of the same flower in a natural state. The florets too in the margin, which in the natural flower are female, become, by luxuriance, barren; that is, are deprived of the pistillum; the style, which was very short, spreads, and is of the length of the chaffy scales; and its summits, formerly two in number, are metamorphosed into one. Full flowers are more easily referred to their respective genera in methods founded upon the calyx, as the flower-cup generally remains unaffected by this highest degree of luxuriance.

PLEONASM

Pages 277-277

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in *<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>*, whereby we <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> words seemingly superfluous, in order to express a thought with the greater energy; such as, "I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it with my own eyes," &c. See *Oratory*, No. 67.

PLESCOW

Pages 277-277

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> in Russia, between the duchies of Novogorod, Lithuania, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, and Ingria.

PLESSIS-LES-TOURS

Pages 277-277

formerly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of France, within half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>. It was built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. and in it he died in the year 1483. It is situated in a plain surrounded by woods, at a small distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is yet handsome, though built of brick, and converted to purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>.

PLETHORA

Pages 277-277

in *Medicine*, from πληθος, "plenitude." A plethora is when the vessels are too much loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. The plethora may be sanguine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> febrile. In the first there is too much effervescence in the blood, in the latter too little. In the sanguine plethora, there is danger of a fever, inflammation, apoplexy, rupture of the blood-vessels, obstructed secretions, &c.; in

PLEURA

Pages 277-278

in Anatomy, a thin membrane covering the inside of the thorax. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLEURONECTES

Pages 278-278

a genus of fishes belonging to the order of thoracici. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLEURS

Pages 278-278

a town in France, which was buried under a mountain in the year 1618. Of this fatal circumstance, Bishop Burnet, in his Travels, p. 96, gives the following account. "Having mentioned (says the Bishop) some falls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in these parts (viz. near the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>), I cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by the extraordinary fate of the town of Pleurs, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from Chavennes to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>.—The town was half the size of Chavennes, but much more nobly built; for, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the Francken, that cost some millions, there were many other palaces built by rich factors both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> and the other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, who, liking the situation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, as well as the freedom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, gave themselves all the indulgences that a vast wealth could furnish. By one of the palaces that was a little distant from the town, and was not overwhelmed with it, one may judge of the rest. It was an out-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of the family of the Francken, and yet it may compare with many palaces in Italy. The voluptuousness of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> became very crying; and Madame de Salis told me that she heard her mother often relate some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of a Protestant minister's sermons that preached in a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> there, who warned them often of the terrible judgements of God which were hanging over their heads, and which he believed would suddenly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out upon them. "On the 25th of August 1618, an inhabitant came and told me to be gone, for he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the mountains cleaving; but he was laughed at for his pains. He had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> whom he prevailed to leave all and go with him; but when she was safe out of town, she called to mind that she had not locked the door of a room in which she had some things of value, and so she went back to do that, and was buried with the rest; for at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> the hill fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and buried the town and all the inhabitants, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 2200, so that not one person escaped. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the mountains did so fill the channel of the river, that the first news of Chavennes had of it was by the failing of their river; for three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four hours there came not a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, but the river wrought for itself a new course, and returned to them. "I could hear no particular character of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who escaped (continues the Bishop); so I must leave the secret reason of so singular a preservation to the great discovery, at the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, of those steps of Divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> that are now to unaccountable. Some of the family of the Francken got some miners to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> underground, to find out the wealth that was buried in their house; for, besides their plate and furniture, there was a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of cash and many jewels in the house. The miners pretended they could find nothing; but they went to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Tyrol and built fine houses, and a great wealth appeared, of which no other visible account could be given but this, that they had found some of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>."

PLEXUS

Pages 278-278

among anatomists, a bundle of small vessels interwoven in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; thus a congeries of vessels within the brain is called plexus choroides, reticularis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> retiformis. See Anatomy. A plexus of nerves is the union of two or more nerves, forming a sort of ganglion or knot. PLICÁ POLONICA, or plaited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> peculiar to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; whence the name. See Medicine, No. 355. Mr Cox, who gives a short account of it, attempts likewise to give the physical causes of it. Many causes of this kind, he tells us, have been supposed to concur in rendering the plica more frequent in those regions than in other parts. It would be an endless work to enumerate the various conjectures with which each person has supported his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>.—The most probable are those assigned by Dr Vicat: The first cause is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the Polish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which is rendered insalubrious by numerous woods and marshes, and occasionally derives an uncommon keenness even in the midst of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> from the position of the Carpathian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; for the southern and south-easterly winds, which usually convey warmth in other regions, are in these chilled in their passage over their snowy summits. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is, unwholesome <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; for although Poland is not deficient in good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people usually drink that which is nearest at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, taken indiscriminately from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and even stagnant pools. The third cause is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> inattention of the natives to cleanliness; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> shows, that those who are not negligent in their persons and habitations, are less liable to be afflicted with the plica than others who are deficient in that particular. Thus persons of higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are less subject to this disorder than those of inferior stations; the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> than those of small villages; the free peasants than those in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> state of vassalage; the natives of Poland Proper than those of Lithuania. Whatever we may determine as to the possibility that all or any of these causes, by themselves, or in conjunction with others, originally produced the disorder; we may venture to assert, that they all, and particularly the last, assist its propagation, inflame its symptoms, and protract its cure. In a word, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLICA_POLONICA">plica polonica</a> appears to be a contagious distemper; which, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, still prevails among a people ignorant in medicine, and inattentive to check its progress, but is rarely known in those countries where proper precautions are taken to prevent its spreading.

PLIMPTON

Pages 278-279

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, in England, seated on a branch of the river Plym, which had once a castle, now in ruins. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. ment; is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles E. of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, and 218 W. by S. of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 40° 0' N. Lat. 50° 22'.

PLINIA

Pages 279-279

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra class of Linnæus. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLINTH

Pages 279-280
ORLE, or Orlo, in Architecture,** is a flat square member, in the form of a brick. It is used as the foundation of columns, being that flat square table under the moulding of the base and pedestal at the bottom of the whole order. It seems to have been originally intended to keep the bottom of the original wooden pillars from rotting. Vitruvius also calls the Tuscan abacus *plinth*. **PLINTH of a Statue, &c.** is a base, either flat, round, or square, that serves to support it. **PLINTH of a Wall,** denotes two or three rows of bricks advancing out from a wall; or, in general, any flat high moulding, that serves in a front-wall to mark the floors, to sustain the eaves of a wall, or the larmier of a chimney. **PLINY the Elder,** or *Cæcilius Plinius Secundus*, one of the most learned men of ancient Rome, was descended from an illustrious family, and born at Verona. He bore arms in a distinguished post; was one of the college of augurs; became intendant of Spain; and was employed in several important affairs by Vespasian and Titus, who honoured him with their esteem. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius, which happened in the year 79, proved fatal to him. His nephew, Pliny the Younger, relates the circumstances of that dreadful eruption, and the death of his uncle, in a letter to Tacitus. Pliny the Elder wrote a href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History in 37 books, which is still extant, and has had many editions; the most esteemed of which is that of Father Hardouin, printed at Paris in 1723, in two volumes folio. **PLINY the Younger,** nephew of the former, was born in the ninth year of Nero, and the 62d of Christ, at Novocomum, a town upon the lake Larius, near which he had several beautiful villas. Cæcilius was the name of his father, and Plinius Secundus that of his mother's brother, who adopted him. He brought into the world with him fine parts and an elegant taste, which he did not fail to cultivate early; for, as he tells us himself, he wrote a Greek tragedy at 14 years of age. He lost his father when he was young; and had the famous Virginius for his tutor or guardian, whom he has set in a glorious light. He frequented the schools of the rhetoricians, and heard Quintilian; for whom he ever after entertained so high an esteem, that he bestowed a considerable portion upon his daughter at her marriage. He was in his 18th year when his uncle died; and it was then that he began to plead in the forum, which was the usual road to dignities. About a year after, he assumed the military character, and went into Syria with the commission of tribune: but this did not suit his taste any more than it had done Tully's; and therefore we find him returning after a campaign or two. He tells us, that in his passage homewards he was detained by contrary winds at the island Icaria, and how he employed himself in making verses: he enlarges in the same place upon his poetical exercises; yet poetry was not the shining part of his character any more than it had been of Tully's. Upon his return from Syria, he married a wife, and settled at Rome: it was in the reign of Domitian. During this most perilous time, he continued to plead in the forum, where he was not more distinguished by his uncommon abilities and eloquence, than by his great resolution and courage, which enabled him to speak boldly, when scarcely one else durst speak at all. On these accounts he was often singled out by the senate to defend the plundered provinces against their oppressive governors, and to manage other causes of a like important and dangerous nature. One of these was for the province of Batavia, in their prosecution of Baebius Maffa; in which he acquired so general an applause, that the emperor Nerva, then a private man, and in banishment at Tarentum, wrote to him a letter, in which he congratulated not only Pliny, but the age which had produced an example so much in the spirit of the ancients. Pliny relates this affair in a letter to Cornelius Tacitus; and he was so pleased with it himself, that he could not help entreating this friend to record it in his history. He entreats him, however, with infinitely more modesty than Tully had intreated Lucceius upon the same occasion; and though he might imitate Cicero in the request, as he professes to have constantly let that great man before him for a model, yet he took care not to transgress the bounds of decency in his manner of making it. He obtained the offices of quaestor and tribune, and luckily went unhurt through the reign of Domitian: there is, however, reason to suppose, if that emperor had not died just as he did, that Pliny would have shared the fate of many other great men; for he tells us himself, that his name was afterwards found in Domitian's tables, among the number of those who were destined to destruction. He lost his wife in the beginning of Nerva's reign, and soon after married his beloved Calpurnia, of whom we read so much in his Epistles. He had not, however, any children by any of his wives: and hence we find him thanking Trajan for the *jus trium liberorum*, which he afterwards obtained of that emperor for his friend Suetonius Tranquillus. He hints also, in his letter of thanks to Trajan, than he had been twice married in the reign of Domitian. He was promoted to the consulship by Trajan in the year 100, when he was 38 years of age; and in this office pronounced that famous panegyric, which has ever since been admired, as well for the copiousness of the topics as the elegance of address. Then he was elected augur, and afterwards made proconsul of Bithynia; whence he wrote to Trajan that curious letter concerning the primitive Christians; which, with Trajan's receipt, is happily extant among his Epistles. Pliny's letter, as Mr McIlmoth observes in a note upon the passage, is esteemed as almost the only genuine monument of ecclesiastical antiquity relating to the times immediately succeeding the apostles, it being written at most not above 40 years after the death of St Paul. It was preserved by the Christians themselves, as a clear and unsuspicious evidence of the purity of their doctrines, and is frequently appealed to by the early writers of the church against the calumnies of their adversaries. It is not known what became of Pliny after his return from Bithynia; whether he lived at Rome, or what time he spent at his country houses. Antiquity is also silent as to the time of his death: but it is conjectured that he died either a little before or soon after that excellent prince, his admired Trajan; that is, about the year of Christ 116. Pliny was one of the greatest wits, and one of the worthiest worthiest men among the ancients. He had five parts, which he cultivated to the utmost; and he accomplished himself with all the various kinds of knowledge which could serve to make him either useful or agreeable. He wrote and published a great number of things; but nothing has escaped the wreck of time except the books of Letters, and the panegyric upon Trajan. This has ever been considered as a masterpiece; and if he has, as some think, almost exhausted all the ideas of perfection in a prince, and gone perhaps a little beyond the truth, yet it is allowed that no panegyric was ever possessed of a finer subject, and on which he might better indulge in all the flow of eloquence, without incurring the suspicion of flattery and lies. His letters seem to have been intended for the public; and in them he may be considered as writing his own memoirs. Every epistle is a kind of historical sketch, wherein we have a view of him in some striking attitude either of active or contemplative life. In them are preserved anecdotes of many eminent persons, whose works have come down to us, as Suetonius, Silius Italicus, Martial, Tacitus, and Quintilian; and of curious things, which throw great light upon the history of those times. They are written with great politeness and spirit; and if they abound too much in turn and metaphor, we must impute it to that degeneracy of taste which was then accompanying the degenerate manners of Rome. Pliny, however, seems to have preserved himself in this latter respect from the general contagion: whatever the manners of the Romans were, his were pure and incorrupt. His writings breathe a spirit of transcendent goodness and humanity: his only imperfection is, he was too desirous that the public and posterity should know how humane and good he was. We have two elegant English translations of his Epistles; the one by Mr Mead, and the other by Lord Orrery. PLOCAMÁ, a genus of plants belonging to the pentandra class. See Botany Index. PLOCE. See Oratory, p. 433.

PLOCKSKO
