a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Regal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, on the east by the palatinate of Mazovia, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>, and on the west by the palatinate of Inowladilaw. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town is of the same name. PLOEN is a town of Germany in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and capital of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. It stands on the banks of a lake of the same name, and gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, till by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the last duke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue it escheated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> in 1761. The ducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, rising in the midst of the town, on an elevated spot of ground, and overlooking the lake, is a very picturesque object. The town stands 22 miles north-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUBECK">Lubeck</a>, and 10 south-east of Kiell. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 30. N. Lat. 54. 11.

PLOMO

Pages 280-280

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, is a name given by the Spaniards, who have the care of the silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, to the silver ore, when found adhering to the surface of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and when it incrusts their cracks and cavities like small and loose grains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-powder. Though these grains be few in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> have no silver in it, yet they are always very happy when they find it, as it is a certain token that there is a rich vein somewhere in the neighbourhood. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> forwards they still meet with these grains, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the plomo in greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, it is a certain sign that they are getting nearer and nearer the good vein.

PLOT

Pages 280-280

Dr Robert, a learned antiquarian and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Sutton-barn, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Borden in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the year 1641, and studied in Magdalen-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, and afterwards in University-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1682 he was elected secretary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and published the Philosophical Transactions from No. 143 to No. 166 inclusive. The next year Elias Ashmole, Esq., appointed him first keeper of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, and about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the vice-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> nominated him first professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> in the university of Oxford. In 1687 he was made secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Marshal, and the following year received the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Historiographer to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James II. In 1690 he resigned his professorship of chemistry, and likewise his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of keeper of the museum, to which he presented a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> collection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities; which were those he had described in his histories of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>: the former published at Oxford in 1677, folio, and reprinted with additions and corrections in 1705; and the latter was printed in the same size in 1686. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1694-5, Henry Howard, Earl Marshal, nominated him Maberay-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> extraordinary; two days after which he was constituted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; and, on the 30th of April 1696, he died of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Borden. As Dr Plot delighted in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the above works were designed as essays towards a Natural History of England; and he had actually formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of travelling through England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> for that purpose. He accordingly drew up a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of his scheme in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the learned Bishop Fell; which is inserted at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of Leland's Itinerary, of the edition of 1744. Amongst several MSS. which he left behind him were large materials for the "Natural History of Kent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>." Besides the above works, he published De origine fontium tenimmen philosophicum, 8vo, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> papers in the Philosophical Transactions. Plot, in dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, is sometimes used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of a tragedy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>; but more properly for the knot or intrigue, which makes the embarrassment of any piece. See Poetry. Plot, in Surveying, the plan or draught of any field, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, surveyed with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, and laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and dimensions.

PLOTINUS

Pages 280-282

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> in the third century. He was born at Lycompis, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in 204; and began very early to show a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> singularity both in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and manners: for, at eight years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when he went to school, he used to run to his nurse, and uncover her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to suck; and would have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> that practice longer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had not been discouraged by her. At 28 years of age he had a strong desire to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, on which occasion he was recommended to the most famous professors of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. He was not satisfied with their lectures; but, Plotinus, upon hearing those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIUS">Ammonius</a>, he confessed that this was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> he wanted. He studied for 11 years under that excellent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and then went to hear the Persian and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> philosophers: for in 243, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Gordianus intended to wage <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Persians, he followed the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, but probably repented of it; for it was with difficulty he could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by flight, after the emperor had been slain. He was then 39; and the year following he went to Rome, and read philosophical lectures in that city; but avoided following the example of Erennius and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, his fellow-pupils, who, having promised with him not to reveal some hidden and excellent doctrines they had received from Ammonius, had nevertheless forfeited their word. Plotinus continued ten years in Rome, without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> anything; but, in his 50th year, Porphyry became his scholar; who, being of an exquisitely fine genius, was not satisfied with superficial answers, but required to have all difficulties thoroughly explained; and therefore Plotinus, to treat things with greater accuracy, was obliged to write more books. He had before written 21 books, and during the six years of Porphyry's stay with him he wrote 24, and 9 after Porphyry's leaving Rome, in all 54. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> veneration for him; and he passed for a man of such judgement and virtue, that many persons of both sexes, when they found themselves dying, intrusted him, as a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> angel, with the care of their estates and children. He was the arbiter of numberless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-suits; and constantly behaved with such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and rectitude of mind, that he did not create himself one enemy during the 26 years he resided in Rome. He, however, did not meet with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> from all of his own profession; for Olympias a philosopher of Alexandria, being envious of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, used his utmost endeavours, though in vain, to ruin him. The emperor Gallienus, and the empress Salonina, had a very high regard for him; and, had it not been for the opposition of some jealous courtiers, they would have had the city of Campania rebuilt, and given to him with the territory belonging to it, to establish a colony of philosophers, and to have it governed by the ideal laws of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s commonwealth. He laboured under various disorders during the last year of his life, which obliged him to leave Rome, when he was carried to Campania to the heirs of one of his friends, who furnished him with everything necessary; and he died there in the year 270, at the age of 66, and in the noblest manner that an heathen philosopher could do, these being his words as he breathed his last: "I am labouring with all my might to return the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of me to the Divine Whole which fills the universe." We have already remarked that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of Plotinus were singular and extraordinary; and we shall now show that they were so. He was ashamed of being lodged in a body, for which reason he did not care to tell the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family. The contempt he had for all earthly things, was the reason why he would not permit his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> to be drawn: and when his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> Amelius was urgent with him upon this head, "Is it not enough (said he) to drag after us, whithersoever we go, that image in which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has shut us up? Do you think that we should likewise transmit to future ages an image of that image, as a sight worthy of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>?" From the same principle, he refused to attend to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; for he never made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of preservatives or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and did not even eat the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of tame animals. He ate but little, and abstained very often from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; which joined to his intense meditation, kept him very much from sleeping. In short, he thought the body altogether below his notice; and had so little respect for it, that he considered it as a prison, from which it would be his supreme <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to be freed. When Amelius, after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, inquired about the state of his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, he was told, "that it was gone to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the blessed, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, joy, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of the union with God prevail." And the reason given for it, as related by Porphyry, is, "that Plotinus had been peaceable, gracious, and vigilant; that he had perpetually elevated his thoughts foul to God; that he had loved God with his whole heart; that he had disengaged himself, to the utmost of his abilities, from this wretched life; that, elevating himself with all the powers of his soul, and by the several gradations taught by Plato, towards that Supreme Being which fills the universe, he had been enlightened by him; had enjoyed the vision of him without the help or interposition of ideas; had, in short, been often united to him." This is the account of Porphyry, who tells us also, that he himself had once been favoured with the vision. To this account, however, we need scarcely add, that little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> is due: it agrees pretty much with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> enthusiasm and the reveries of Eckhaimists. Plotinus had also his familiar spirit, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>; but, according to Porphyry, it was not one of those called demons, but of the order of those who are called gods; so that he was under the protection of a genius superior to that of other men. The superiority of his genius puffed him up not a little: for when Amelius desired him to share in the sacrifices, which he used to offer up on solemn festivals, "It is their business (replied Plotinus) to come to me, not mine to go to them;" "which lofty answer (says Porphyry) no one could guess the reason of, or dared to ask." Porphyry put the 54 books of Plotinus in order, and divided them into five enneads. The greater part of them turn on the most high-flown ideas in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>; and this philosopher seems, in certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, not to differ much from Spinoza. He wrote two books to prove, that "all being is one and the same;" which is the very doctrine of Spinoza. He inquires, in another book, "Whether there are many souls, or only one?" His manner of composing partook of the singularity of his nature: he never read over his compositions after he had written them; he wrote a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and was not exact in his orthography: he stood in need, therefore, of a faithful friend to revise and correct his writings; and he chose Porphyry for this purpose before Amelius, who had, however, been his disciple 24 years, and was very much esteemed by him. Some have accused Plotinus of plagiarism, with regard to Numenius; a slander which Amelius refuted. Longinus was once much prejudiced against our great philosopher, and wrote against his Treatise of Ideas, and against Porphyry's answer in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of that treatise. He afterwards conceived a high esteem for him; fought industriously for all his books; and, in order to have them very correct, desired Porphyry to lend him his copy; but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wrote to him in the following manner: "I always observed to you, when we were together," PLU Plotius Pluche. gether, when we were at a distance from one another, as well as when you lived at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>, that I did not comprehend many of the subjects treated of by Plotinus; but that I was extremely fond of his manner of writing, the variety of his knowledge, and the order and disposition of his questions, which are altogether philosophical." "This fingle passage (says Bayle) flows the exalted genius, the exquisite discernment, and judicious penetration of Longinus. It cannot be denied, that most subjects which this philosopher examines are incomprehensible; nevertheless, we discover in his works a very elevated, fruitful, and capacious genius, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> way of reasoning. Had Longinus been an injudicious critic, had he not possessed an exalted and beautiful genius, he would not have been so sensible of Plotinus's obscurity: for no person complains less of the obscurity of a book, than those whose thoughts are confused and undertaking is shallow." Marius Ficinus, at the request of Cosmo de Medicis, made a Latin version of the works of Plotinus, with a summary and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of each book; which was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, first by himself, in 1559, and afterwards with the Greek in 1580, folio. His life was written by Porphyry, the most illustrious of his disciples.

or Darter, a genus of birds belonging to the order Anseres. See Ornithology Index.

PLOUGH

Pages 282-282

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, a machine for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> up the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of cattle, contrived to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, labour, and expense, which, without this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, must have been employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> the ground, and fitting it for receiving all sorts of seed. See Agriculture.

PLOUGHING

Pages 282-282

in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> up the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>. See Agriculture, pafsim.

PLOUGHMAN

Pages 282-282

the person who guides the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> in the operation of tilling.

PLOVER

Pages 282-282

the English name of several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Charadrius. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLOWDEN

Pages 282-282

Edmund, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, was born in 1517, and was first a student of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he spent three years in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and medicine. He then removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where, having <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his former studies about four years more, in 1552 he was admitted to the practice of physic and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>: but probably finding the practice of the art of healing less agreeable than the study, he entered himself of the Middle Temple, and began to read law. Wood says, that in 1557 he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> reader to that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>-reader three years after, being then sergeant and oracle of the law. He died in the year 1584, aged 67; and was buried in the Temple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He wrote, 1. Commentaries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Reports of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">Cases</a>, &c. in the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward VI. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, and Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1571, 78, 99, 1613, &c. Written in the old Norman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. 2. Queries, or a Moot-book of cases, &c. translated, methodized, and enlarged, by H. B. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn. London, 1662, 8vo.

PLUCHE

Pages 282-283

Antony, a celebrated French writer, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a> in 1688, and having distinguished himself by his engaging manners and proficiency in the belles-lettres, was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> in the university of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Two years after he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and was admitted into holy orders. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a> (Clermont) informed of his talents, conferred upon him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of his episcopal city. By his industry and superior knowledge, a proper order and subordination soon took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in it; but some peculiar opinions respecting the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> disturbed his tranquillity, and obliged him to quit his office. The intendant of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, at the request of the celebrated Rollin, entrusted him with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his son. Abbé Pluche having filled that place with success and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to himself, left Rouen and went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of some literary friends and his own excellent writings, he acquired a very distinguished reputation for learning. He published, 1. Le Spectacle de la <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> (Nature Displayed), in 9 vols in 12mo. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which is equally instructive and entertaining, is written with perspicuity and elegance; but the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> which is adopted has rendered it rather prolix. The speakers, who are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a>, and Countess, are not distinguished by any striking feature; but they have all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> character, which is tolerably pleasing, not excepting even that of the little chevalier de Breuil, who is, however, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> scholar. This is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which Abbé Desfontaines has formed of this work. Though the author has given the conversations a pretty ingenious turn, and even some vivacity, yet now and then they assume the tone of the college. 2. Histoire du Ciel, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Heavens, in 2 vols in 12mo. In this performance we find two parts almost independent of one another. The first contains some learned inquiries into the origin of the poetic heavens. It is nearly a complete <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, founded upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which are new and ingenious. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the history of the opinions given by philosophers respecting the formation of the world. The author shows the insufficiency, the inconstancy, and uncertainty, of the most esteemed systems; and concludes with pointing out the excellence and sublime simplicity of the Mosaic account. Besides a noble and well-turned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, we find in it an erudition which does not fatigue the mind. As to the foundation of the system explained in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, though it appears extremely plausible, we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not take upon us to say how far it is true: Voltaire called it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">Fable</a> du Ciel, or a Fable of the Heavens. 3. De Linguarum artificio; a work which he translated with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, La Mécanique des Langues, in 12mo. In this treatise he proposes a short and easy method of learning languages, which is by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of translations instead of themes or exercises; his reflections on that subject are judicious and well expressed. 4. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">Harmony</a> of the Psalms and the Gospel, or a Translation of the Psalms and Hymns of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, with Notes relative to the Vulgate, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> Text, printed at Paris in 1764, in 12mo. In 1749, Abbé Pluche retired to Varenne St Maure, where he gave himself up entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. Having become deaf that he could not hear without the help of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> afforded him little entertainment. It was in this retreat that he died of an apoplexy on the 20th of November 1761, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 73 years. He possessed those qualities which form the scholar, the honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and the Christian: temperate in his meals, true to his word, an affectionate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, a sensible friend, and a humane <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; he gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> of virtue in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> as well as his writings. His submission to all the dogmas of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> was very great. Some Deists having been surprized that, in matters of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he should think and speak like the vulgar, his answer was, "I <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> in doing so: It is infinitely more rational to believe the word of God, than to follow the glimmering lights of a reason which is limited and subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>."

PLUG

Pages 283-283

certain pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, formed like the frustum of a cone, and used to stop the nausie-holes and the breaches made in the body of a ship by cannon-balls; the former of which are called haule-plugs, and the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>-plugs, which are formed of various sizes in proportion to the holes made by the different sizes of shot, which may penetrate the ship's sides <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bottom in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; accordingly they are always ready for this purpose.

PLUKENET

Pages 283-283

Leonard, a physician who flourished in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. was one of the most excellent and laborious botanists of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was author of the Physiography Plukenetiana, the Almagesticum Britannicum, and other works of the like kind, on which he spent the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and fortune. His Phytopraphy is mentioned with the highest encomiums in the Philosophical Transactions for February 1696-7. His <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> Botanica, with cuts, were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 6 vols folio, in 1720. PLUM-TREE. See PRUNUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PLUMAGE

Pages 283-283

the feathers which serve birds for a covering. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">ORNITHOLOGY</a>.

PLUMB-LINE

Pages 283-283

among artificers, denotes a perpendicular to the horizon; so called, as being <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> erected by means of a plummet.

PLUMBAGO

Pages 283-283
LEAD-WORT; a genus of plants belonging to the pentandrae clas. See BOTANY Index.

PLUMBERY

Pages 283-284

the art of casting and working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and using it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. As this metal melts soon and with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, it is easy to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it into figures of any kind, by running it into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> of brafs, clay, platter, &c. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> article in plumbery is sheets and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of lead; and as these make the basis of the plumber's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, we shall here give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of making them. In casting sheet-lead, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mould is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, which consists of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces of wood well jointed, and bound with bars of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> at the ends; on the sides of which runs a frame consisting of a ledge or border of wood, three inches thick and four inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> from the mould, called the sharps: The ordinary width of the mould, within these sharps, is from four to five feet; and its length is 16, 17, or 18 feet. This should be something longer than the sheets are intended to be, in order that the end where the metal runs off from the mould may be cut off, because it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> thin or uneven, or ragged at the end. It must stand very even or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> in breadth, and something falling from the end in which the metal is poured in, viz. about an inch or an inch and a half in the length of 16 or 17 feet or more, according to the thickness of the sheets wanted; for the thinner the sheet, the more declivity the mould should have. At the upper end of the mould stands the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, which is a concave triangular prism, composed of two planks nailed together at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and two triangular pieces fitted in between them at the ends. The length of this pan is the whole breadth of the mould in which the sheets are cast; it stands with its bottom, which is a sharp edge, on a form at the end of the mould, leaning with one side against it; and on the opposite side is a handle to lift it up by, to pour out the melted lead; and on that side of the pan next the mould are two iron hooks to take hold of the mould, and prevent the pan from slipping while the melted lead is pouring out of it into the mould. This pan is lined on the inside with moistened sand, to prevent it from being fired by the hot metal. The mould is also spread over; about two inches thick, with sand fitted and moistened, which is rendered perfectly level by moving over it a piece of wood called a strike, and smoothing it over with a smoothing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, which is a plate of polished <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, about one-fourth of an inch thick and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, turned up on all the four edges, and with a handle fitted on to the upper or concave side. The sand being thus smoothed, it is fit for casting sheets of lead; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they would cast a cistern, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> out the signs of the four sides; and having taken the dimensions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> or fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, make <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDINGS">mouldings</a> by prefixing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slips of wood, which contain the same mouldings, into the level sand; and form the figures of birds, beasts, &c. by prefixing in the same manner leaden figures upon it, and then taking them off; and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> smoothing the surface where any of the sand is raised up by making these impressions upon it. The rest of the operation is the same in casting either cisterns or plain sheets of lead. But before we proceed to mention the manner in which that is performed, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary to give a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the strike. The strike, then, is a piece of board about five inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and something longer than the breadth of the mould on the inside; and at each end is cut a notch about two inches deep, so that when it is used it rides upon the sharps with those notches. Before they begin to cast, the strike is made ready by tacking on two pieces of an old hat on the notches, or by flipping a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> over each end, in order to raise the under side about one-eighth of an inch or something more above the sand, according as they would have the sheet to be in thickness; then they tally the under edge of the strike, and lay it across the mould. The lead being melted, it is put into the pan with ladles, in which, when there is a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> for the present purpose, the scum of the metal is swept off with a piece of board to the edge of the pan, letting it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> on the sand, which is by this means prevented from falling into the mould at the pouring out of the metal. When the lead is cool enough, which must be regulated according to the thickness of the sheets wanted, and is known by its beginning to stand with a shell or wall on the sand round the pan, two men take the pan by the handle, or else one of them lifts it by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> and chain fixed to a beam in the ceiling, and pour it into the mould, while another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> stands ready with the strike, and, as soon as they have done pouring in the metal, puts on the mould, sweeps the lead forward, and draws the overplus into a trough prepared to receive it. The sheets being thus cast, nothing remains but to roll them up or cut them into any measure wanted: but if it be a cistern, it is bent into four sides, so that the two ends may join the back, where they are soldered together; after which the bottom is soldered up. The method of casting pipes without soldering.—To make Plumbery make these pipes they have a kind of little mill, with arms or levers to turn it withal. The moulds are of braids, and consist of two pieces, which open and shut by means of hooks and hinges, their inward calibre or diameter being according to the size of the pipe, usually two feet and a half. In the middle is placed a core or round piece of braids or iron, somewhat longer than the mould, and of the thickness of the inward diameter of the pipe. This core is passed through two <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> runnels, one at each end of the mould, which they serve to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>; and to these is joined a little copper tube about two inches long, and of the thickness the leaden pipe is intended to be of. By means of these tubes, the core is retained in the middle of the cavity of the mould. The core being in the mould, with the runnels at its two ends, and the lead melted in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, they take it up in a ladle, and pour it into the mould by a little aperture at one end, made in the form of a funnel. When the mould is full, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> a hook into the end of the core, and, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the mill, draw it out; and then opening the mould, take out the pipe. If they desire to have the pipe lengthened, they put one end of it in the lower end of the mould, and pass the end of the core into it; then shut the mould again, and apply its runnel and tube as before, the pipe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> cast serving for a runnel, &c., at the other end. Things being thus replaced, they pour in fresh metal, and repeat the operation till they have got a pipe of the length required. For making pipes of sheet-lead, the plumbers have wooden cylinders, of the length and thickness required; and on these they form their pipes by wrapping the sheet around them, and soldering up the edges all along them. The lead which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> the Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-boxes is reduced to a thinness which we are informed European plumbers cannot imitate. The following account of the process by which the plates are formed was communicated to a writer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> by an intelligent officer of an East Indiaman. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a> sits by a pot containing the melted metal; and has two large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the under one fixed, the upper moveable, directly before him. He raises the upper <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> by pressing his foot upon the side of it, and with an iron ladle pours in the opening a proper quantity of the fluid metal. He then immediately lets <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> the upper stone, and by that means forms the lead into a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> plate, which is afterwards cut into a proper shape. The surfaces of the stones, where they touch each other, are exactly ground together.

PLUMBING

Pages 284-284

among miners, is the method of using a mine-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIAL">dial</a>, in order to know the exact <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> where to sink <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-shaft, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to bring an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADIT">adit</a> to the work, or to know which way the load inclines when any flexure happens in it. It is performed in this manner: A skilful person with an afflatus, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> line, and a mine-dial, after his guess of the place above ground, descends into the adit or work, and there fastens one end of the line to some fixed thing in it; then the incited <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> is let to rest, and the exact point where it rests is marked with a pen: he then goes on farther in, the line still fastened, and at the next flexure of the adit he makes a mark on the line by a knot or otherwise; and then letting down the dial again, he there likewise notes down that point at which the needle stands in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> position. In this manner he proceeds, from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to turning, marking down the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and marking the line, till he comes to the intended place: this done, he ascends and begins to work on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> what he did in the adit, bringing the first knot in the line to such a place where the mark of the place of the needle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> again answer its pointing, and continues this till he come to the desired place above ground, which is certain to be perpendicular over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mine into which the air-shaft is to be sunk.

PLUMBUM

Pages 284-284
Lead.** See **LEAD**, Chemistry Index. **PLUMBUM Corneum**, or muriate of lead, a combination of lead with muriatic acid. See **LEAD**, Chemistry Index.

PLUME

Pages 284-284
or **Plumula**, in Botany, the bud or germ. See **GEMMA**.

PLUMIER

Pages 284-284
Charles**, a learned Minim, born at Marseilles, and one of the most able botanists of the 17th century. He was instructed by the famous Maiguen, who taught him mathematics, turnery, the art of making spectacles, burning-glasses, microscopes, and other works. He at length went to Rome to perfect himself in his studies, and there applied himself entirely to botany under a skilful Italian. At his return to Provence, he settled in the convent at Bornes, a maritime place near Hieres, where he had the conveniency of making discoveries in the fields with respect to simples. He was some time after sent by the French king to America, to bring from thence such plants as might be of service in medicine. He made three different voyages to the Antilles, and visited the island of St Domingo. The king honoured him with a pension; and he at last settled at Paris. However, at the desire of M. Fagon, he prepared to go a fourth time to America, to examine the tree which produces the Jesuits bark; but died at the port of Santa Maria, near Cadiz, in 1756. He wrote several excellent works; the principal of which are: 1. A volume of the Plants in the American Islands. 2. A Treatise on the American Fern. 3. The Art of Turnery; a curious work embellished with plates.

PLUMMET

Pages 284-284

**PLUMB-Rule**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **Plumb-line**, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used by carpenters, masons, &c., in order to judge whether walls, &c., be upright planes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>, or the like. It is thus called from a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, fastened to the end of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which usually constitutes this instrument. Sometimes the string descends along a wooden ruler, &c., raised perpendicularly on another; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it becomes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>.

PLUMOSE

Pages 284-284

something formed in the manner of a feather, with a stem and fibres issuing from it on each side; such are the antennae of certain moths, butterflies, &c.

PLURAL

Pages 284-284

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an epithet applied to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> and verbs which is used when we speak of more than one thing. See **GRAMMAR**.

PLURALITY

Pages 284-285

a discrete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, consisting of two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the same kind; thus we say, a plurality of gods, &c. See the article **<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>**, No. 157, for the arguments both for and against a plurality of worlds. Plurality of Benefices, or Livings, is where the same clerk is possessed of two or more spiritual preferments with cure of souls. See Benefice. The finality of some benefices first gave rise to pluralities; for an ecclesiastic, unable to subsist on a single one, was allowed to hold two; and at length the number increased without bounds. A remedy was attempted for this abuse at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Lateran under Alexander III. and Innocent III. in the year 1215, when the holding more than one benefice was forbidden by a canon under the penalty of deprivation; but the same canon granting the pope a power to dispense with it in favour of persons of distinguished merit, the prohibition became almost useless. They were also restrained by statute 21 Hen. VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 13, which enacted, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any person having one benefice with cure of souls, of the yearly value of £1, or above (in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s books), accepts any other with cure of souls, the first shall be adjudged in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to be void, &c., though the same statute provides for dispensation in certain <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. In England, in order to procure a dispensation, the prelate must obtain of the bishop, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> the livings are, two certificates of the values in the king's books, and the reputed values and distance; one for the archbishop, and the other for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>. And if the livings <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in two dioceses, then two certificates of the same kind are to be obtained from each bishop. He must also show the archbishop his presentation to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> living; and bring with him two testimonials from the neighbouring clergy concerning his behaviour and conversation, one for the archbishop and the other for the lord-chancellor; and he must also show the archbishop his letters of orders, and a certificate of his having taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts at the least, in one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of this realm, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the registrar. And if he be not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> or bachelor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, nor doctor nor bachelor of law, he is to procure a qualification of a chaplain, which is to be duly registered in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> office, in order to be tendered to the archbishop, according to the statute. And if he hath taken any of the aforesaid degrees, which the statute allows as qualifications, he is to procure a certificate thereof as already mentioned, and to show the same to the archbishop; after which his dispensation is made out at the faculty office, where he gives security according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the canon. He must then repair to the lord-chancellor for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>; and he must apply to the bishop of the diocese where the living lies for his admission and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. By the several stamp acts, for every skin, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, &c., on which any dispensation to hold two <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> dignities or benefices, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and a benefice, shall be engrossed or written, there shall be paid a treble 4s. stamp duty. We have also a regulation in regard to pluralities; but it is often dispensed with: for, by the faculty of dispensation, a plurality is required, in that benefice from which he shall happen to be most absent, to preach 13 sermons every year, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> hospitality for two months yearly. In Germany the pope grants dispensation for possessing a plurality of benefices, on pretence that the ecclesiastical princes there need <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> revenues to bear up against the Protestant princes.

PLUSH

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, &c., a kind of stuff, having a fort of velvet knap <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> on one side, composed regularly of a woof of a single woollen thread and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> warp; the one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, of two threads twisted; the other goats or camel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>; though there are some plashes entirely of worsted, and others composed wholly of hair.

PLUTARCH

Pages 285-286

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and historian of antiquity, who lived from the reign of Claudius to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a>, was born at Chaeronia, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Eoetia in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. Plutarch's family was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> in Chaeronia; his grandfather Lamprias was eminent for his learning and a philosopher; and is often mentioned by Plutarch in his writings, as is also his father. Plutarch was initiated early in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, to which he was naturally inclined; and was placed under the care of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIUS">Ammonius</a>, an Egyptian, who, having taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> with great reputation at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, from thence travelled into Greece, and settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Under this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> he made great advances in knowledge; and like a thorough philosopher, more apt to regard things than words, he purified this knowledge to the neglect of languages. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was not only the language of Rome, but of Greece also: and much more used there than the French is now in England. Yet he was so far from regarding it then, that, as we learn from himself, he became not conversant in it till the declension of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: and, though he is supposed to have resided in Rome near 40 years at different times, yet he never seems to have acquired a competent skill in it. But this was not the worst: he did not cultivate his mother-tongue with any great exactness; and hence that harshness, inequality and obscurity in his style, which has so frequently and justly been complained of. After he was principled and grounded by Ammonius, having an inextinguishable thirst for knowledge, he resolved to travel. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> was at that time, as formerly it had been, famous for learning; and probably the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of their doctrine might tempt him, as it had tempted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> and others, to go and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with the priesthood of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This appears to have been particularly his bent, by his travels Of Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>: in which he shows himself versed in the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and philosophy of the wise men. From Egypt he returned into Greece; and visiting in his way all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the philosophers, gathered from them many of those observations with which he has abundantly enriched posterity. He does not seem to have been attached to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, but culled from each of them whatever he thought excellent and worthy to be regarded. He could not bear the paradoxes of the Stoics, but yet was more averse from the impiety of the Epicureans: in many things he followed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; but his favourites were <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> he revered to highly, that he annually celebrated their birth-days with much solemnity. Besides this, he applied himself with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> diligence to collect not only all books that were excellent in their kind, but also all the sayings and observations of wise men which he had heard in conversation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had received from others by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; and likewise to consult... Plutarch fulf the records and public instruments preserved in cities which he had visited in his travels. He took a particular journey to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, to search the archives of that famous commonwealth, to understand thoroughly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of their legislators, their kings, and their ephori; and digested all their memorable deeds and sayings with much care. He took the same methods with regard to many other commonwealths; and thus was enabled to leave us in his works such a rich cabinet of observation upon men and manners, as, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Montaigne and Bayle, have rendered him the most valuable author of antiquity. The circumstances of Plutarch's life are not known, and therefore cannot be related, with any exactness. According to the learned Fabricius, he was born under Claudius, 50 years after the Christian era. He was married to a most amiable woman of his own native town, whose name, according to the probable conjecture of Rualdus, was Timoxena, and to whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and virtue he has borne the most affectionate testimony in his moral works. He had several children, and among them two sons; one called Plutarch after himself, the other Lamprias in memory of his grandfather. Lamprias was he, of all his children, who seems to have inherited his father's philosophy; and to him we owe the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> or catalogue of Plutarch's writings, and perhaps also his aphorisms. He had a nephew, Sextus Chaeronius, who taught the learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Marcus Aurelius the Greek tongue, and was much honoured by him. Some think, that the critic Longinus was of his family; and Apuleius, in the first book of his Metamorphoses, affirms himself to be defended from him. On what occasion, and at what time of his life, he went to Rome, how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> he lived there, and when he finally returned to his own country, are all uncertain. It is probable, that the fame of him went thither before him, not only because he had published several of his works, but because immediately upon his arrival, as there is reason to believe, he had a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to hear him: for he tells us himself, that he was taken up in giving lectures of philosophy to the great men of Rome, that he had not time to make himself master of the Latin tongue, which is one of the first things that would naturally have engaged his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It appears that he was several times at Rome; and perhaps one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> for his living there was the intimacy he had contracted in some of these journeys with Soffius Senecio, a great and worthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who had been four times <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, and to whom Plutarch has dedicated many of his lives. But the great inducement which carried him first to Rome, was undoubtedly that which had carried him into so many other parts of the world; namely, to make observations upon men and manners, and to collect materials for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the lives of the Roman worthies, in the same manner as he had already written those of the Grecian: and accordingly he not only conversed with all the living, but searched the records of the Capitol, and of all the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. Not but, as we learn from Suidas, he was instructed also with the management of public affairs in the empire, during his residence in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. "Plutarch (says he) lived in the time of Trajan, who befriended him the consular ornaments, and also caused an edict to be passed, that the magistrates or officers of Illyria should do nothing in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> without his knowledge and approbation." When and how he was made known to Trajan is likewise uncertain: but it is generally supposed that Trajan, a private man when Plutarch first came to Rome, was, among other nobility, one of his auditors. It is also supposed, that this wise emperor made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of him in his councils; at least, much of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his reign has been imputed to Plutarch. Fabricius asserts that he was Trajan's preceptor, and that he was raised to the consular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> by him, and made procurator of Greece in his old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> by the emperor Adrian. We are equally at a loss concerning the time of his abode in the imperial city; which, however, at different times, is not imagined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> much short of 40 years. The desire of visiting his native country, so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to all men, and especially when growing old, prevailed with him at length to leave <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>: and at his return he was unanimously chosen archon or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of Chaeronia, and not long after admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the Delphic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>'s priests. We have no particular account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, either as to the manner of it or the year; only it is evident that he lived, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his studies, to a good old age. The most probable conjecture is that of Fabricius, who says he died in the fifth year of Adrian, at the age of 70. His works have been divided, and they admit of a pretty equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, into Lives and Morals: the former of which, in his own estimation, were to be preferred as more noble than the latter. His style, as we have already observed, has been excepted to with some reason: he has also been criticised for some mistakes in Roman antiquities, and for a little partiality to the Greeks. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he has been justly praised for the copiousness of his fine sense and learning, for his integrity, and for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of goodness which appears in all he wrote. His bufnells was not to please the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, but to instruct and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> the mind; and in this none ever went beyond him. Of his moral writings it is to be regretted that we have no elegant English translation. Even his Lives were chiefly known to the English reader by a motley and miserable version, till a new one executed with fidelity and spirit was presented to the public by the Langhorns in 1770. On the whole, it is to be wished that this most amiable moralist and biographer had added a life of himself to those which he has given to the world of others, as the particulars which other writers have preferred of his personal history are very doubtful and imperfect.

PLUTO

Pages 286-287

in Pagan worship, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the infernal regions, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Ops, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. This deity finding himself childless and unmarried, mounted his chariot to visit the world; and arriving in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, fell in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with Proserpine, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> gathering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> with her companions in the valley of Enna, near Mount Etna: when, forcing her into his chariot, he drove her to the river Chamarus, through which he opened himself a passage back to the realms of night. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">CERES</a> and PROSERPINE. Pluto is usually represented in an ebony chariot drawn by four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> horses; sometimes holding a sceptre, to denote his power; at others, a wand, with which he drives away the ghosts; and at others, some keys, to signify that he had the keys of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> observes, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of rendering the wearer invisible, and that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> borrowed it in order to be concealed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a> when he fought against the Trojans. Pluto was greatly revered both by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who erected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and altars to him. To this god sacrifices were offered in the night, and it was not lawful to offer them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

PLUTUS

Pages 287-287

in Pagan worship, the god of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, is frequently confounded with Pluto. He was represented as appearing lame when he approached, and with wings at his departure; to show the difficulty of amassing wealth, and the uncertainty of its enjoyment. He was also frequently represented <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, to show that he often bestowed his favours on the most unworthy, and left in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> those who had the greatest merit.

PLUVIUS

Pages 287-287

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. He was invoked by that name among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> whenever the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was parched up by continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and was in want of refreshing rains. He had an altar in the temple on the capitol.

PLYING

Pages 287-287

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of making, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> endeavouring to make, a progress against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Hence a ship that advances well in her course in this manner of sailing, is said to be a good player. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">Beating</a>, Pitching, and Tacking.

PLYMOUTH

Pages 287-288

in New England, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> PLY Plymouth, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSACHUSETTS">Massachusetts</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It is remarkable for having been the first settlement in New England, and for having had the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of worship. It is seated at the fourth end of Plymouth bay. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 70° 10' N. Lat. 41° 58'.

PLYNTERIA

Pages 288-288

a Grecian festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Aglauros, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>, who received from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Cecrops the name of Aglauros. The word is derived from πλάνων, laurae, because during the solemnity they undressed the statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> and washed it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which it was observed was looked up-

PNEUMATICS

Pages 372-395

Pneumatic engines may offer of making them highly useful. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> may thus be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> by a machine that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> cost little, and hardly go out of repair. The last pneumatic engine which we shall speak of at present is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fanners, used for winnowing grain, and for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> out of a room; and we have but few observations to make on them. The wings of the fanners are inclosed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> drum, whose circular sides have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> opening BDE (fig. 102.) round the centre, to admit the air. By <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the wings rapidly round, the air is hurried round along with them, and thus acquires a centrifugal tendency, by which it presses strongly on the outer rim of the drum: this is gradually detached from the circle as at KI, and terminated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> IHGF, which goes off in a tangential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; the air therefore is driven along this passage. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the wings were disposed in planes passing through the axis C, the compression of the air by the anterior surface would give it some tendency to escape in every direction, and would obstruct in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the arrival of more air through the side-holes. They are therefore reclined a little backward, as represented in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. It may be shown that their best form would be that of a hyperbolic spiral \(a b c\); but the straight form approaches sufficiently near to the most perfect shape. Much labour is lost, however, in carrying the air round those parts of the drum where it cannot escape. The fanners would either draw or discharge almost twice as much air if an opening were made all round one side. This could be gradually contracted (where required for winnowing) by a surrounding cone, and thus directed against the falling grain: this has been verified by actual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. When used for drawing air out of a room for ventilation, it would be much better to remove the outer side of the drum entirely, and let the air fly freely off on all sides; but the flat sides are necessary, in order to prevent the air from arriving at the fanners any other way but through the central holes, to which trunks should be fitted leading to the apartment which is to be ventilated. --- PNEUMATOSIS. See MEDICINE, No. 336. PNEUMONIA. See MEDICINE, No. 183.

PNEUMONICS

Pages 395-395

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines proper in diseases of the lungs, in which respiration is affected.

PO

Pages 395-395

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and celebrated river of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which has its source at Mount Vif in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and on the confines of Dauphiny. It runs through Piedmont, Montferrat, the Milanese, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>; from thence it runs to the borders of the Parmesan, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Modenese; and having entered the Ferrarese, it begins to divide at Ficheruolo, and proceeds to discharge itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> by four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mouths. As it passes along, it receives several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and often overflows its banks, doing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of mischief: the reason of which is, that most of those rivers descend from the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and are increased by the melting of the snow.

POCOCKE

Pages 395-396

Dr. Edward, a learned oriental scholar, was the eldest son of the Rev. Edward Pococke; and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1604, where he was also educated. In 1628 he was admitted probationer-fellow of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, and about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> had prepared an edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Epistle of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, the Second and Third of St John, and that of St Jude, in Syriac and Greek, with a Latin Translation and Notes. In 1629 he was ordained <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and appointed chaplain to the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> five <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> six years; in which time he distinguished himself by his fortitude and zeal while the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> raged there. At length returning to England, he was in 1636 appointed reader of the Arabic lectures founded by Archbishop Laud. Three years after he went to Constantinople, where he prosecuted his studies of the eastern tongues, and procured many valuable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. After near four years stay in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, he embarked in 1640; and taking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in his way, visited Gabriel Sionita the famous Maronite, and Hugo Grotius. In 1643 he was presented to the rectory of Childrey in Berks; and about three years after married the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Thomas Burdett, Esq. About the middle of 1647 he obtained the restitution of the salary of his Arabic lecture, which had been detained from him about three years.
