In 1648 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., who was then prisoner in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight, nominated Mr Pococke to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and the canonry of Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> annexed to it; but in 1650 he was ejected from his canonry for refusing to take the engagement, and soon after a vote passed for depriving him of his Hebrew and Arabic lectures; but several governors of houses, &c. presenting a petition in his favour, he was suffered to enjoy both these places. He had some years before published his Specimen Historiae Arabum; and now appeared his Porta Moysis; and soon after the English Polyglot edition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>, to which he had largely contributed, and also Eutychius's Annals, with a Latin version. At the Restoration, he was restored to the canonry of Christ-church, and also received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He then published his Arabic version of Grotius's Treatise of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">Truth</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>; and an Arabic poem entitled Laimato P Ajam, with a Latin translation and notes. Soon after he published Gregory Abul Pharaeus's Historia Dynastiarum. In 1674 he published an Arabic version of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> parts of the Liturgy of the Church of England; and a few years after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on the Prophecies of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MICAH">Micah</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, Hosea, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOEL">Joel</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> died in 1691, after having been for many years confessedly the first person in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> for eastern learning; and was no less worthy of admiration for his uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>. POE modesty and humility, and all the virtues that can adorn a Christian. His theological works were republished at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1749, in two volumes in folio.

PODALIRIUS

Pages 396-396

son of Æsculapius and Epione, was one of the pupils of the Centaur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIRON">Chiron</a>, under whom he made himself such a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of medicine, that during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> the Greeks invited him to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to stop a pestilence which had baffled the skill of all their physicians. Some suppose, however, that he went to the Trojan war, not in the capacity of a physician in the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, but as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, attended by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Machaon, in 30 ships, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> from Oechalia, Ithome, and Trica. At his return Podalirius was shipwrecked on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, where he cured the falling sickness <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. He fixed his habitation there; and built two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, one of which he called Syrna, after his wife. The Carians, on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, built him a temple, and paid him divine honours.

PODOLIA

Pages 396-396

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, bounded on the east by Volhynia and the river Ucrain; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-east, by Budiac <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>; on the south-east, by the river Niester, which separates it from Bessarabia and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLDAVIA">Moldavia</a> in European <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> on the south-west; and by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Ruthia on the north-west. It is usually divided into the Upper and Lower. In the Upper, which is the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Kamieck, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Podolia, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a>. In the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eastern part of Podolia the chief town is Bracklaw, the capital of a palatinate.

PODOPHYLLUM

Pages 396-396

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 27th order, Rheedeae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

PODURA

Pages 396-396
or SERINGTAIL, a genus of insects of the order of aptera. See Entomology Index. POE-BIRD is an inhabitant of some of the South sea islands, where it is held in great esteem and veneration by the natives. It goes by the name of kogo in New s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand; but it is better known by that of poe bird. It is somewhat less than our blackbird, and is remarkable for the sweetness of its note, as well as the beauty of its plumage. Its flesh is also delicate food. POECILE was a famous portico at Athens, which received its name from the variety (ποικίλος) of paintings which it contained. Zeno kept his school there; and there also the stoics received their lessons, whence their name, ἡ στοά, a porch. The Precile was adorned, among many others, with a picture of the siege and taking of Troy, the battle of Theseus against the Amazons, and the fight between the Macedonians and Athenians at Oenoe in Argolis. The only reward which Miltiades obtained after the battle of Marathon was to have his picture drawn more conspicuous than that of the rest of the officers that fought with him, in the representation which was made of the engagement, and which was hung up in the Precile in commemoration of that celebrated victory.

POESTUM

Pages 396-396
or POSIDONIA, an ancient city of Grecia Magna, now part of the kingdom of Naples. It was founded by one of those colonies from Greece which in the early ages established themselves in Italy; and it flourished before the foundation of Rome itself. It was destroyed by the Goths on the decline of the Roman empire, who in their barbarous zeal for the Christian religion overturned every place of Pagan worship which was exposed to their ravages. Since that time it has been in ruins; and these ruins were unknown till they were discovered in the following manner: "In the year 1735 (says the author of the Antiquities, History, and Views of Positum), an apprentice to a painter at Naples, who was on a visit to his friends at Capaccio, by accident took a walk to the mountains which surround the territory of Positum. The only habitation he perceived was the cottage of a farmer, who cultivated the best part of the ground, and reserved the rest for pasture. The ruins of the ancient city made a part of this view, and particularly struck the eyes of the young painter; who, approaching nearer, saw with astonishment walls, towers, gates and temples. Upon his return to Capaccio, he consulted the neighbouring people about the origin of these monuments of antiquity. He could only learn, that this part of the country had been uncultivated and abandoned during their memory; that about ten years before, the farmer, whose habitation he had noticed, established himself there; and that having dug in many places and searched among the ruins that lay round him, he had found treasures sufficient to enable him to purchase the whole. At the painter's return to Naples, he informed his master of these particulars, whose curiosity was so greatly excited by the description, that he took a journey to the place, and made drawings of the principal views. These were shown to the king of Naples, who ordered the ruins to be cleared, and Positum arose from the obscurity in which it had remained for upwards of 700 years, as little known to the neighbouring inhabitants as to travellers." Our author gives the following description of it in its present state. It is, says he, of an oblong figure, about two miles and a half in circumference. It has four gates, which are opposite to each other. On the key stone of the arch of the north gate, on the outside, is the figure of Neptune in bas-relief, and within a hippocampus. The walls which still remain are composed of very large cubical stones, and are extremely thick, in some parts 18 feet. That the walls have remained unto this time is owing to the very exact manner in which the stones are fitted to one another (a circumstance observed universally in the masonry of the ancients), and perhaps in some measure to a stalactite concretion which has grown over them. On the walls here and there are placed towers of different heights; those near the gates being much higher and larger than the others, and evidently of modern workmanship. He observes, that, from its situation among marshes, bituminous and sulphurous springs, Positum must have been unwholesome; a circumstance mentioned by Strabo, Morbofam eam facit fluvius in paludes diffusus. In such a situation the water must have been bad. Hence the inhabitants were obliged to convey that necessity of life from purer springs by means of aqueducts, of which many vestiges still remain. The principal monuments of antiquity are a theatre, an amphitheatre, and three temples. The theatre and amphitheatre are much ruined. The first temple is hexastylos,

POETRY

Pages 396-442

A MIDST those thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> which envelope the first ages of the world, reason and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> throw some lights on the origin and primitive employment of this divine art. Reason suggests, that before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of letters, all the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> had no other method of transmitting to their descendants the principles of their worship, their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies, their laws, and the renowned actions of their sages and heroes, than by poetry; which included all these objects in a kind of hymns that fathers sung to their children, in order to engrave them with indelible strokes in their hearts. History not only informs us, that Moses and Miriam, the first authors that are known to mankind, sung, on the borders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, a song of divine praise, to celebrate the deliverance which the Almighty had vouchsafed to the people of Israel, by opening a passage to them through the waters; but it has also transmitted to us the song itself, which is at once the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monument and a masterpiece of poetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The Greeks, a people the most ingenious, the most animated, and in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the most accomplished, that the world ever produced—strove to rival from the Hebrews the precious gift of poetry, which was vouchsafed them by the Supreme Author of all <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that they might ascribe it to their false deities. According to their ingenious fictions, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> became the god of poetry, and dwelt on the hills of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHOCIS">Phocis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, whose feet were washed by the waters of Hippocrene, of which each mortal that ever drank was seized with a sacred delirium. The immortal swans floated on its waves. Apollo was accompanied by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>—those <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>—the daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">Memory</a>: and he was constantly attended by the Graces. Pegasus, his winged courier, transported him with a rapid flight into all the regions of the universe. Happy emblems! by which we at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> embellish our poetry, as no one has ever yet been able to invent more brilliant images. The literary annals of all nations afford vestiges of poetry from the remotest ages. They are found among the most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> of the ancient barbarians, and the most desolate of all the Americans. Nature asserts her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Tacitus mentions the verses and the hymns of the Germans, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when that rough people yet inhabited the woods, and while their manners were still savage. The first inhabitants of Russia and the other northern countries, those of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBION">Albion</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a>, Aquitania, and other nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, had their poetry, as well as the ancient people of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and of the known borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. But the simple productions of nature have constantly something unformed, rough, and savage. The Divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> appears to have placed the ingenious and polished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind on the earth, in order to refine that which comes from her bosom rude and imperfect: and thus art has polished poetry, which issued quite naked and savage from the brains of the first of mankind. But what is Poetry? It would be to abridge the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> limits of the poetic empire, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> the sphere of poetry. This divine art, should we say, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of all the dictionaries and other treatises on verification, that poetry is the art of making verses, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> periods that are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a> or metre. This is rather a grammatical explanation of the word, than a real definition of the thing, and it would be to degrade poetry thus to define it. The father of criticism has denominated poetry τέχνη μυθοπλασίας, an imitative art: but this, though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> in itself, is too general for a definition, as it does not discriminate poetry from other arts which depend equally on imitation. The justest definition seems to be that given by Baron Bielfeld *, That poetry is the *Elem. of art of expressing our thoughts by fiction. In fact, it is an art. Under this manner (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we reflect with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>) that all the metaphors and allegories, all the various kinds of fiction, form the first materials of a poetic edifice: it is thus that all images, all comparisons, allusions, and figures, especially those which personify moral subjects, as virtues and vices, concur to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> of such a structure. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, therefore, that is filled with invention, that incessantly presents images which render the reader attentive and affected, where the author gives interlacing sentiments to every thing that he makes speak, and where he makes speak by sensible figures all those objects which would affect the mind but weakly when clothed in a simple prosaic style, such a work is a poem. While that, though it be in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which is of a didactic, dogmatic, or moral nature, and where the objects are presented in a manner quite simple, without fiction, without images or ornaments, cannot be called poetry, but merely a work in verse; for the art of reducing thoughts, maxims, and periods, into rhyme or metre, is very different from the art of poetry. An ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, a lively and interesting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, the sublime narrative of the actions of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, such as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a> of M. Fenelon, though written in prose, but in measured prose, is therefore a work of poetry: because the foundation and the superstructure are the productions of genius, as the whole proceeds from fiction; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> itself appears to have employed an innocent and agreeable deception to instruct with efficacy. This is so true, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> also, in order to please and affect, has recourse to fiction; and this part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> is called the *poetic composition of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>*. It is therefore by the aid of fiction that poetry, so to speak, paints its expressions, that it gives a body and a mind to its thoughts, that it animates and exalts that which would otherwise have remained arid and insensible. It is the peculiar privilege of poetry to exalt inanimate things into animals, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> into persons. The former licence is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, that it is now considered as nothing more than a characteristic dialect appropriated by the poets to distinguish themselves from the writers of prose; and it is at the same time so essential, that we question much if this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of composition could subsist without it: for it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perhaps, upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, be found, that in every poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> some of the qualities of Animal Nature are ascribed to things not having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Every work, therefore, where the thoughts are expressed by fictions or images, is poetical; and every work where they are expressed naturally, simply, and without ornament, although it be in verse, is prose. Verse, however, is not to be regarded as foreign or superfluous to poetry. To reduce those images, those fictions, into verse, is one of the greatest difficulties in poetry, and one of the greatest merits in a poem: and for these reasons, the cadence, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of sounds, particularly that of rhyme, delight the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and the mind infensibly repeats them while the eye reads them. There results therefore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to the mind, and a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to these ornaments; but this pleasure would be frivolous, and even childish, if it were not attended by a real utility. Verses were invented in the first ages of the world, merely to aid and to strengthen the memory: for cadence, harmony, effectual and especially rhyme, afford the greatest affluence to poetry, one of the memory that art can invent; and the images, or of its excellent fictions, that strike our senses, affix in graving them with such deep traces in our minds, as even time itself frequently cannot efface. How many excellent apophthegms, sentences, maxims, and precepts, would have been buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> of oblivion, if poetry had not preserved them by its harmony? To give more efficacy to this lively <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, the first poets sung their verses, and the words and phrases must necessarily have been reduced, at least to cadence, or they could not have been susceptible of musical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> excellencies, therefore, though not a necessary constituent of poetry, consists in its being expressed in verse. See Part III. **Part I. General Principles of the Art.** **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. Of the Essence and End of Poetry.** The essence of Polite Arts in general, and consequently of poetry in particular, consists in expression; and we think that, to be poetical, the expression must necessarily arise from fiction, or invention. (See the article Art, particularly from No. 12. to the end.) This invention, which is the fruit of happy genius alone, arises: 1. From the subject itself of which we undertake to treat; 2. From the manner in which we treat that subject, or the species of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of which we make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; 3. From the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> that we propose to follow in conformity to this manner; and, 4. From the method of executing this plan in its full detail. Our first guides, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, afford us no lights that can elucidate all these objects in general. The precepts which <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> lays <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, relate to epic and dramatic poetry only; and which, by the way, confirms our idea, that antiquity itself made the essence of poetry to consist in fiction, and not in that species of verse which is delusive of it, or in that which is not capable of it. But since this art has risen to a great degree of perfection; and as poetry, like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, communicates its fire to every thing it touches, and animates and embellishes whatever it treats; there seems to be no subject in the universe to which poetry cannot be applied, and which it cannot render equally brilliant and pleasing. From this universality of poetry, from its peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of expression by fiction, which is applicable to all subjects, have arisen its different species, of which a particular description will be given in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part. Horace, in a well-known verse, has been supposed to declare the end of poetry to be twofold, to please, or to instruct: *Aut prodere volunt, aut declarare poetae.* But Dr Beattie maintains, that the ultimate end of this art is to instruct; instruction being only one of the poetry means (and not always a necessary one) by which that end is to be accomplished. The passage rightly understood, he observes, will not appear to contain any part of thing inconsistent with this doctrine. The author is chap. i. there stating a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the Greek and Roman writers, with a view to the poetry of the stage; and, after commending the former for their correctness, and for the liberal spirit wherewith they conducted their literary labours, and blaming his countrymen for their inaccuracies. End of Poetry. Hor. Ar. Poet. 333—347. Hor. Carm. Mb. iv. ode 9. Hor. Sat. fib. i. sat. 4. ver. 42. Sect. II. Of the Standard of Poetical Invention. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s beautiful description of the heavens and earth, as they appear in a calm evening by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> and stars, concludes with this circumstance, "And the heart of the shepherd is glad." Madame Dacier, from the turn she gives to the passage in her version, seems to think, and Pope, in order perhaps to make out his couplet, inferrates, that the gladness of the shepherd is owing to his sense of the utility of those luminaries. And this may in part be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; but this is not in Homer; nor is it a necessary consideration. It is true, that, in contemplating the material universe, they who discern the causes and effects of things must be more rapturously entertained than those who perceive nothing but shape and size, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Yet, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> outside of Nature's work, there is a splendour and a magnificence to which even untutored minds cannot attend without great delight. Not that all peasants or all philosophers are equally susceptible of these charming impressions. It is strange to observe the callousness of some men, before whom all the glories of heaven and earth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in daily succession, without touching their hearts, elevating their fancy, or leaving any durable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. Even of those who pretend to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>, how many are there to whom the lustre of the rising or setting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; the sparkling concave of the midnight sky; the mountain-forest tossing and roaring to the storm, or warbling with all the melodies of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>-evening; the sweet interchange of hill and dale, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> and sunlight, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which an extensive landscape offers to the view; the scenery of the ocean, so lovely, so majestic, and so tremendous; and the many pleasing varieties of the animal and vegetable kingdoms, could never afford so much real satisfaction, as the teams and noise of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>-room, the insipid fiddling and squeaking of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>, or the vexations and wranglings of a card-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>! But some minds there are of a different make; who, even in the early part of life, receive from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of Nature a species of delight which they would hardly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for any other, and who, as avarice and ambition are not the infirmities of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, would, with equal sincerity and rapture, exclaim, I care not, Fortune, what you me deny; You cannot rob me of free Nature's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; You cannot shut the windows of the sky, Through which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> shows her bright'ning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; You cannot <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> my constant feet to trace The woods and lawns by living stream at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>. Caffe of Indolence. Such minds have always in them the seeds of true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and frequently of imitative genius. At least, though their enthusiastic or visionary turn of mind (as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the world would call it) should not always incline them to practice poetry or painting, we need not scruple to affirm, that without some portion of this enthusiasm no person ever became a true poet or painter. For he who would imitate the works of nature, must first accurately observe them; and accurate observation is to be expected from those only who take great pleasure in it. To a mind thus disposed no part of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> is indifferent. In the crowded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and howling wilderness; in the cultivated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> and solitary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a>; in the murmur of the rivulet and in the uproar of the ocean; in the radiance of summer and gloom of winter; in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of heaven and in the whisper of the breeze; he still finds something to rouse or to soothe his imagination, to draw forth his affections, or to employ his understanding. And from every mental energy that is not attended with pain, and even from some of those that are, as moderate terror and pity, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> mind derives satisfaction; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> being equally necessary to the body and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and to both equally productive of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and pleasure. This happy sensibility to the beauties of nature should be cherished in young persons. It engages them to contemplate the Creator in his wonderful works; it purifies and harmonizes the soul, and prepares it for moral and intellectual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; it supplies an endless source of amusement; it contributes even to bodily health; and, as a first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> subsists between material and moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, it leads the heart by an easy transition from the one to the other; and thus recommends virtue for its transcendent loveliness, and makes vice appear the object object of contempt and abomination. An intimate acquaintance with the best descriptive poets, Spenser, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, and Thomson, but above all with the divine Georigic, joined to some practice in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, will promote this amiable sensibility in early years: for then the face of nature has <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> superadded to its other charms, the passions are not pre-engaged, the heart is free from care, and the imagination warm and romantic. But not to insist longer on those ardent emotions that are peculiar to the enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of nature, may it not be affirmed of all men, without exception, or at least of all the enlightened part of mankind, that they are gratified by the contemplation of things <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, as opposed to unnatural? Monstrous sights please but for a moment, if they please at all; for they derive their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> from the beholder's amazement, which is quickly over. We read indeed of a man of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>*, who chooseth to adorn his villa with pictures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of most unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>: but it is a singular instance; and one would not be much more surprized to hear of a person living without food, or growing fat by the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>. To say of any thing, that it is contrary to nature, denotes censure and disapprobation on the part of the speaker; as the epithet natural intimates an agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and seems for the most part to imply, that a thing is as it ought to be, suitable to our own taste, and congenial with our own <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Think with what sentiments we should peruse a poem, in which nature was totally misrepresented, and principles of thought and of operation supposed to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, repugnant to every thing we had seen or heard of:—in which, for example, avarice and coldness were ascribed to youth, and prodigality and passionate attachment to the old; in which men were made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> at random, sometimes according to character, and sometimes contrary to it; in which cruelty and envy were productive of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and beneficence and kind affection of hatred; in which beauty was invariably the object of dislike, and ugliness of desire; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> was rendered happy by atheism and the promiscuous perpetration of crimes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and fortitude were held in universal contempt. Or think, how we should relish a painting, where no regard was had to the proportions, colours, or any of the physical laws, of Nature:—where the ears and eyes of animals were placed in their shoulders; where the sky was green and the grass crimson; where trees grew with their branches in the earth and their roots in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; where men were seen fighting after their heads were cut off, ships sailing on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, lions entangled in cobwebs, sheep preying on dead carcases, fishes sporting in the woods, and elephants walking on the sea. Could such figures and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> give pleasure, or merit the appellation of sublime or beautiful? Should we hesitate to pronounce their author mad? And are the absurdities of madmen proper subjects either of amusement or of imitation to reasonable beings? Let it be remarked, too, that though we distinguish our internal powers by different names, because otherwise we could not speak of them so as to be understood, they are all but so many energies of the same individual mind; and therefore it is not to be supposed, that what contradicts any one leading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> should yield permanent delight to the rest. That cannot be agreeable to reason, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> disapproves; nor can that gratify imagination, which is repugnant to reason.—Besides, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> and acquiescence of mind are pleasant, as distrust and disbelief are painful; and therefore, that only can give <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and general satisfaction, which has something of plausibility in it; something which we conceive it possible for a rational being to believe. But no rational being can acquiesce in what is obviously contrary to nature, or implies palpable absurdity. Poetry, therefore, and indeed every art whose end is to please, must be natural; and if so, must exhibit real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact, or something like it; that is, in other words, must be either according to truth or according to verisimilitude. And though every part of the material universe abounds in objects of pleasurable contemplation, yet nothing in nature so powerfully touches our hearts, or gives so great variety of exercise to our moral and intellectual faculties, as man. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> affairs and human feelings are universally interesting. There are many who have no great relish for the poetry that delineates only irrational or inanimate beings; but to that which exhibits the fortunes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and the conduct of men, there is hardly any person who does not listen with sympathy and delight. And hence to imitate human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, is considered by Aristotle as essential to this art; and must be allowed to be essential to the most pleasing and most instructive part of it, Epic and Dramatic composition. Mere descriptions, however beautiful, and moral reflections, however just, become tiresome, where our passions are not occasionally awakened by some event that concerns our fellow-men. Do not all readers of taste receive peculiar pleasure from those little tales or episodes with which Thomson's descriptive poem on the Seasons is here and there enlivened? and are they not sensible, that the thunder-form would not have been half so interesting without the tale of the two lovers (Simm. v. 1171); nor the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, without that of Palemon and Lavinia (Aut. v. 177.) nor the driving snows, without that exquisite picture of a man perishing among them (Winter, v. 276.) It is much to be regretted, that Young did not employ the same artifice to animate his Night-Thoughts. Sentiments and descriptions may be regarded as the pilasters, carvings, gildings, and other decorations of the poetical fabric: but human actions are the columns and the rafters that give it stability and elevation. Or, changing the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHOR">metaphor</a>, we may consider these as the soul which informs the lovely frame; while those are little more than the ornaments of the body. Whether the pleasure we take in things natural, and our dislike to what is the reverse, be the effect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> or of constitution, is not a material inquiry. There is nothing absurd in supposing, that between the foul, in its first formation, and the rest of nature, a mutual harmony and sympathy may have been established, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> may indeed confirm, but no perverse habits could entirely subdue. As no sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> could make man believe the contrary of a self-evident <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a>, great influence should imagine, that our love of nature and regularity of sentiment might still remain with us in some degree, though we had never been born and bred in the Sicilian villa above-mentioned, of course and never heard any thing applauded but what deserved upon cenure, nor cenured but what merited applause. Yet poetry, habit must be allowed to have a powerful influence over the the sentiments and feelings of mankind; for objects to which we have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> accustomed, we are apt to contract a fondness: we conceive them readily, and contemplate them with pleasure; nor do we quit our old tracks of speculation or practice without reluctance and pain. Hence in part arises our attachment to our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, our old acquaintance, our native <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, our homes, and to the very hills, streams, and rocks in our neighborhood. It would therefore be strange, if man, accustomed as he is from his earliest days to the regularity of nature, did not contract a liking to her productions and principles of operation. Yet we neither expect nor desire, that every human invention, where the end is only to please, should be an exact transcript of real existence. It is enough, that the mind acquiesce in it as probable or plausible, or such as we think might happen without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> opposition to the laws of nature:—Or, to speak more accurately, it is enough that it be consistent, either, first, with general experience; or, secondly, with popular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; or, thirdly, that it be consistent with itself, and connected with probable circumstances. First: If a human invention be consistent with general experience, we acquiesce in it as sufficiently probable. Particular experiences, however, there may be, so uncommon, and so little expected, that we should not admit their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, if we did not know them to be true. No man of sense believes, that he has any likelihood of being enriched by the discovery of hidden <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; or thinks it probable, on purchasing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a>-ticket, that he shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>; and yet great wealth has actually been acquired by such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>. But we should look upon these as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> expedients in a play or romance for bringing about a happy catastrophe. We expect that fiction should be more consonant to the general tenor of human affairs; in a word, that not possibility, but probability, should be the standard of poetical invention. Secondly: Fiction is admitted as conformable to this standard, when it accords with received opinions. These may be erroneous, but are not often apparently repugnant to nature. On this account, and because they are familiar to us from our infancy, the mind readily acquiesces in them, or at least yields them that degree of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> which is necessary to render them pleasing: hence the fairies, ghosts, and witches of Shakespeare, are admitted as probable beings; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> obtain a place in religious pictures though we know that they do not now appear in the scenery of real life. A poet who should at this day make the whole action of his tragedy depend upon enchantment, and produce the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> events by the assistance of supernatural agents, would indeed be censured as transgressing the bounds of probability, be banished from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> to the nursery, and condemned to write <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">fairy</a> tales instead of tragedies. But Shakespeare was in no danger of such censures: In his days the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a> was established both by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and by the fashion; and it was not only unpolite, but criminal, to doubt it. Now indeed it is admitted only by the vulgar; but it does not therefore follow that an old poem, invented built upon it should not be acceptable to the learned themselves. When a popular opinion has long been exploded, and has become repugnant to philosophical belief, the fictions built upon it are still admitted as natural, both because we all remember to have listened to them in childhood with some degree of credit, and because we know that they were accounted natural by the people to whom they were first addressed; whose sentiments and views of things we are willing to adopt, when, by the power of pleasing description, we are introduced into their scenes, and made acquainted with their manners. Hence we admit the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> of the ancient poets, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> and Tartarus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a> and Charybdis, Cyclops and Circe, and the rest of those "beautiful wonders" (as Horace calls them) which were believed in the heroic ages; as well as the demons and enchantments of Fafo, which may be supposed to have obtained no small degree of credit among the Italians of the 16th century, and are suitable enough to the notions that prevailed universally in Europe not long before (a). In fact, when poetry is in other respects true, when it gives an accurate display of those parts of nature about which we know that men in all ages must have entertained the same opinion, namely, those appearances in the visible creation, and those feelings and working of the human mind, which are obvious to all mankind:—when poetry is thus far according to nature, we are very willing to be indulgent to what is fictitious in it, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> a temporary allowance to any system of fable which the author pleases to adopt; provided that he lay the scene in a distant country, or fix the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> to a remote period. This is no unreasonable piece of complaisance; we owe it both to the poet and to ourselves; for without it we should neither form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> estimate of his genius, nor receive from his works that pleasure which they were intended to impart. Let him, however, take care, that his system of fable be such as his countrymen and contemporaries (to whom his work is immediately addressed) might be supposed capable of yielding their assent to; for otherwise we should not believe him to be in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a>; and let him convey it as much as he can with probable circumstances, and make it appear in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of events consistent with itself. For (thirdly) if this be the case, we shall admit his story as probable, or at least as natural, and consequently be interested in it, even though it be not warranted by general experience, and derive but slender authority from popular opinion. Caliban, in the Tempest, would have shocked the mind as an improbability, if we had not been made acquainted with his origin, and seen his character displayed in a series of consistent behaviour. But when we are told that he sprung from a witch and a demon, a connection not contrary to the laws of nature, as they were understood in Shakespeare's time, and find his manners conformable to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, we are easily reconciled to the fiction. In the same sense, the Lilliputians of (a) In the 14th century, the common people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> believed that the poet Dante went down to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>; that the Inferno was a true account of what he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> there; and that his fellow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, and stunted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> (which seemed by its growth and colour to have been too near the fire), were the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his passing so much of his time in that hot and smoky region. See Vicende della Letteratura del Sig. G. Denina, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4. of Swift may pass for probable beings; not so much because we know that a belief in pignies was once current in the world (for the true ancient pigny was at least thrice as tall as those whom Gulliver visited), but because we find that every circumstance relating to them accords with itself, and with their supposed character. It is not the size of the people only that is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a>; their country, seas, ships, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, are all in exact proportion; their theological and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles, their passions, manners, customs, and all the parts of their conduct, betray a levity and littleness perfectly suitable; and so simple is the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>, and apparently so artless and sincere, that we should not much wonder if it had imposed (as we have been told it has) upon some persons of no contemptible understanding. The same degree of credit may perhaps for the same reasons be due to his giants. But when he grounds his narrative upon a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to nature; when he presents us with rational <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, and irrational men; when he tells us of horses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses for habitation, milking cows for food, riding in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, and holding conversations on the laws and politics of Europe; not all his genius (and he there exerts it to the utmost) is able to reconcile us to so monstrous a fiction: we may smile at some of his absurd exaggerations; we may be pleased with the energy of style, and accuracy of description, in particular places; and a malevolent heart may triumph in the satire; but we can never relish it as a fable, because it is at once unnatural and self-contradictory. Swift's judgement seems to have forsaken him on this occasion: he wallows in nastiness and brutality: and the general run of his satire is downright defamation. Lucian's True History, is a heap of extravagancies put together without order or unity, or any other apparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> than to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and manner of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> authors. His ravings, which have no better right to the name of fable, than a hill of rubbish has to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, are destitute of every colour of plausibility. Animal trees, ships sailing in the sky, armies of monstrous things travelling between the sun and moon on a pavement of cobwebs, rival nations of men inhabiting woods and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in a whale's belly,—are like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> of a bedlamite than the inventions of a rational being. If we were to prosecute this subject any farther, it would be proper to remark, that in some kinds of poetical invention a stricter probability is required than in others:—that, for instance, Comedy, whether dramatic or narrative (B), must seldom deviate from the ordinary course of human affairs, because it exhibits the manners of real and even of familiar life.—that the tragic poet, because he imitates characters more exalted, and generally refers to events little known, or long since past, may be allowed a wider range; but must never attempt the marvellous fictions of the epic muse, because he addresses his work, not only to the passions and imagination of mankind, but also to their eyes and ears, which are not easily imposed on, and refuse to be gratified with any representation that does not come very near the truth:—that the epic poem may claim still ampler privileges, because its fictions are not subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a> of any outward sense, and because it conveys information in regard both to the highest human characters, and the most important and wonderful events, and also to the affairs of unseen worlds and superior beings. Nor would it be improper to observe, that the several species of comic, of tragic, of epic composition, are not confined to the same degree of probability: for that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> may be allowed to be less probable than the regular comedy; the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASQUE">masque</a> than the regular tragedy; and the mixed epic, such as the Fairy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>, and Orlando Furioso, than the pure epopee of Homer, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, and Milton. But this part of the subject seems not to require further illustration. Enough has been said to show, that nothing unnatural can please; and that therefore poetry, whose end is to please, must be according to nature. And if so, it must be either according to real nature, or according to nature somewhat different from the reality. Sect. III. Of the System of Nature exhibited by Poetry. To exhibit real nature is the business of the historian; who, if he were strictly to confine himself to his own sphere, would never record even the minutest circumstance of any speech, event, or description, which was not warranted by sufficient authority. It has been the language of critics in every age, that the historian ought to relate nothing as true which is false or dubious, and their works to conceal nothing material which he knows to be true, by fiction. But it is to be doubted whether any writer of profane and make history has ever been so scrupulous. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> himself, who began his history when that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> began which he records, and who set down every event soon after it happened, according to the most authentic information, seems, however, to have indulged his fancy not a little in his harangues and descriptions, particularly that of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>: and the same thing has been practised, with greater latitude, by Livy and Tacitus, and more or less by all the best historians both ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Nor are they to be blamed for it. By these improved or invented speeches, and by the heightenings thus given to their descriptions, their work becomes more interesting, and more useful; nobody is deceived, and historical truth is not materially affected. A medium is, however, to be observed in this, as in other things. When the historian lengthens a description into a detail of fictitious events, as Voltaire has done in his account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Fontenoy, he loses his credit with us, by raising a suspicion that he is more intent upon a pretty story than upon the truth. And we are disgusted with his insincerity, when, in defiance even of verisimilitude, he puts long elaborate orations in the mouth of those, of whom we know, either from the circumstances that they could not, or from more authentic records that they did not, make any such orations; as Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a> has done in the case of Volumnia haranguing her son Coriolanus, and Flavius Josephus in that of Judah addressing his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> as viceroy of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. From what these historians relate, one would conjecture (B) Fielding's Tom Jones, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMELIA">Amelia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Andrews, are examples of what may be called the Epic or Narrative Comedy, or more properly perhaps the Comic Epopee. Of Nature conjecture that the Roman matron had studied at Athens under some long-winded rhetorician, and that the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> must have been one of the most flowery orators of antiquity. But the fictitious part of history, or of story-telling, ought never to take up much room; and must be highly blameable when it leads into any mistake either of facts or of characters. Now, why do historians take the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to embellish their works in this manner? One reason, no doubt, is, that they may display their talents in oratory and narration; but the chief reason, as hinted already, is, to render their composition more agreeable. It would seem, then, that something more pleasing than real nature, or something which shall add to the pleasing qualities of real nature, may be devised by human fancy. And this may certainly be done. And this it is the poet's business to do. And when this is in any degree done by the historian, his narrative becomes in that degree poetical. The possibility of thus improving upon nature must be obvious to every one. When we look at a landscape, we can fancy a thousand additional embellishments. Mountains lovelier and more picturesque; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> more copious, more limpid, and more beautifully winding; smoother and wider lawns; valleys more richly diversified; caverns and rocks more gloomy and more stupendous; ruins more majestic; buildings more magnificent; oceans more varied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, more splendid with shipping, or more agitated by storms, than any we have ever seen—it is easy for human imagination to conceive. Many things in art and nature exceed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>; but nothing sensible transcends or equals the capacity of thought—a striking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the human soul! The finest woman in the world appears to every eye susceptible of improvement, except perhaps to that of her lover. No wonder, then, if in poetry events can be exhibited more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and of more pleasing variety, than those delineated by the historian, and scenes of inanimate nature more dreadful or more lovely, and human characters more sublime and more exquisite, both in good and evil. Yet still let nature supply the groundwork and materials, as well as the standard, of poetical fiction. The most expert painters use a layman, or other visible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, to direct their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and regulate their fancy. Homer himself founds his two poems on authentic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; and tragic as well epic poets have followed the example. The writers of romance, too, are ambitious to interweave true adventures with their fables; and when it can be conveniently done, to take the outlines of their plan from real life. Thus the tale of Robinson Crusoe is founded on an incident that actually befell one Alexander Selkirk, a seafaring man, who lived several years alone in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Juan Fernandez: Smollet is thought to have given us several of his own adventures in the history of Roderic Random; and the chief characters in Tom Jones, Joseph Andrews, and Pamela, are said to have been copied from real originals. Dramatic comedy, indeed, is for the most part purely fictitious: for if it were to exhibit real events as well as present manners, it would become too personal to be endured by a well-bred audience, and degenerate into downright abuse; which appears to have been the case with the old comedy of the Greeks*. But in general, hints taken from real existence will be found to give no little grace and stability to fiction, even in the most fanciful poems. These hints, however, may be improved by the poet's imagination, and let off with every probable ornament that can be devised, confitently with the design and genius of the work; or in other words, with the sympathies that the poet means to awaken in the mind of his reader. For mere poetical ornament, when it fails to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> the affections, is not only useless, but improper; all true poetry being addressed to the heart, and intended to give pleasure by raising or soothing the passions—the only effectual way of pleasing a rational and moral creature. And therefore we would take Horace's maxim to be universal in poetry:** "Non satis est pulchra effe poema; dulcia junto."*** "It is not enough that poems be beautiful; let them also be affecting."**** For that this is the meaning of the word dulcia in this place, is admitted by the best interpreters, and is indeed evident from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a>.***** That the sentiments and feelings of perceiving beings and when expressed in poetry, should call forth our affections, is natural enough; but can descriptions of inanimate things also be made affecting? certainly they can; as to the more they affect, the more they please us, and make them the more poetical we allow them to be. Virgil's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GEORGIC">Georgic</a> is a noble specimen (and indeed the noblest in the world) of this sort of poetry. His admiration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> nature gains upon a reader of taste, till it rise to perfect enthusiasm. The following observations will perhaps explain this matter. Every thing in nature is complex in itself, and bears innumerable relations to other things; and may therefore be viewed in an endless variety of lights, and consequently described in an endless variety of ways. Some descriptions are good, and others bad. An historical description, that enumerates all the qualities of any object, is certainly good, because it is true; but may be as uninteresting as a logical definition. In poetry, no uninteresting description is good however conformable to truth: for here we expect not a complete enumeration of qualities (the chief end of the art being to please), but only such an enumeration as may give a lively and interesting idea. It is not memory, or the knowledge of rules, that can qualify a poet for this sort of description; but a peculiar liveliness of fancy and sensibility of heart, the nature whereof we may explain by its effects, but we cannot lay down rules for the attainment of it. When our mind is occupied by any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, we naturally use words and meditate on things that are suitable to it and tend to encourage it. If a man were to write a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> when he is very angry, there would probably be something of vehemence or bitterness in the style, even though the person to whom he wrote were not the object of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>. The same thing holds true of every other strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> or emotion:—while it predominates in the mind, it gives a peculiarity to our thoughts, as well as to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, gesture, and countenance: And hence we expect, that every performance introduced in poetry should see things through the medium of his ruling passion, and that his thoughts and language should be tinged accordingly. A melancholy man walking in a grove, attends to those things that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and encourage his melancholy; the sighing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> in the trees, the murmuring of waters, the murmuring of darknes and solitude of the shades: A cheerful man in a garden... Of Nature the same place, finds many subjects of cheerful meditations, in the fingering of birds, the brisk motions of the babbling stream, and the liveliness and variety of the verdure. Persons of different characters, contemplating the same thing, a Roman triumph, for instance, feel different emotions, and turn their view to different objects. One is filled with wonder at such a display of wealth and power; another exults in the idea of conquest, and pants for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> renown; a third, stung with clamour, and harried with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTUSION">contusion</a>, wishes for silence, security, and solitude; one melts with pity to the vanquished, and makes many a sad reflection upon the insignificance of worldly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, and the uncertainty of human things; while the buffoon, and perhaps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, considers the whole as a vain piece of pageantry, which, by its solemn procedure, and by the admiration of so many people, is only rendered the more ridiculous;—and each of these persons would describe it in a way suitable to his own feelings, and tending to raise the same in others. We see in Milton's Allegro and Penorolo, how a different <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of mind produces a variety in the manner of conceiving and contemplating the same rural scenery. In the former of these excellent poems, the author personates a cheerful man, and takes notice of those things in external nature that are suitable to cheerful thoughts, and tend to encourage them: in the latter, every object described is serious and solemn, and productive of calm reflection and tender melancholy; and we should not be easily persuaded, that Milton wrote the first under the influence of sorrow, or the second under that of gladness. We often see an author's character in his works; and if every author were in earnest when he writes, we should oftener see it. Thomson was a man of piety and benevolence, and a warm admirer of the beauties of nature; and every description in his delightful poem on the Seasons tends to raise the same laudable affections in his reader. The parts of nature that attract his notice are those which an impious or hard-hearted man would neither attend to, nor be affected with, at least in the same manner. In Swift we see a turn of mind very different from that of the amiable Thomson; little relish for the sublime or beautiful, and a perpetual succession of violent emotions. All his pictures of human life seem to show, that deformity and meanness were the favourite objects of his attention, and that his soul was a constant prey to indignation (c), disgust, and other gloomy passions, arising from such a view of things. And it is the tendency of almost all his writings (though it was not always the author's design), to communicate the same passions to his reader: inasmuch, that notwithstanding his erudition and knowledge of the world, his abilities as a popular orator and man of bufonics, the energy of his style, the elegance of some of his verses, and his extraordinary talents in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and humour, there is reason to doubt, whether by studying his works any person was very much improved in piety or benevolence. And thus we see, how the compositions of an ingenious author may operate upon the heart, whatever be the subject. The affections that prevail in the author of Nature himself, direct his attention to objects congenial, and give a peculiar bias to his inventive powers, and a peculiar colour to his language. Hence his work, as well as face, if nature is permitted to exert herself freely in it, will that poetry exhibit a picture of his mind, and awaken correspondent affections in the reader. When these are favourable to virtue, which they always ought to be, the work will have that sweet pathos to which Horace alludes in the passage above mentioned; and which we so highly admire, and so warmly approve, even in those parts of the Georgic that describe inanimate nature. Horace's account of the matter in question differs not from what is here given. "It is not enough (says he) *Ar. Poet. that poems be beautiful; let them be affecting, and v.99—111 agitate the mind with whatever passions the poet wishes to impart. The human countenance, as it smiles on those who smile, accompanies also with sympathetic tears those who mourn. If you would have me weep, you must first weep yourself; then, and not before, shall I be touched with your misfortunes.—For nature first makes the emotions of our mind correspond with our circumstances, infusing real joy, sorrow, or resentment, according to the occasion; and afterwards gives the true pathetic utterance to the voice and language." This doctrine, which concerns the orator and the player no less than the poet, is strictly philosophical, and equally applicable to dramatic, to descriptive, and indeed to every species of interesting poetry. The poet's sensibility must first of all engage him warmly in his subject, and in every part of it; otherwise he will labour in vain to interest the reader. If he would paint external nature, as Virgil and Thomson have done, so as to make her amiable to others, he must first be enamoured of her himself; if he would have his heroes and heroines speak the language of love or sorrow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> or courage, ambition or anger, benevolence or pity, his heart must be susceptible of those emotions, and in some degree feel them, as long at least as he employs himself in framing words for them; being assured, that He best shall paint them who can feel them most. Pope's Eloisa, v. 366. The true poet, therefore, must not only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> nature, and know the reality of things, but must also possess fancy, to invent additional decorations; judgment, to direct him in the choice of such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> with verisimilitude; and sensibility, to enter with ardent emotions into every part of his subject, so as to transmute into every part of his work a pathos and energy sufficient to raise corresponding emotions in the reader. "The historian and the poet (says Aristotle *) differ in this, that the former exhibits things as they are, i.e., in that state of perfection which is consistent with probability, and in which, for the sake of our own gratification, we wish to find them. If the poet, after all the liberties he is allowed to take with the truth, can produce nothing more exquisite than is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to be met with in history, his reader (c) For part of this remark we have his own authority, often in his letters, and very explicitly in the Latin epitaph which he composed for himself:—"ubi sevæ indignatio ulterius cor lacere nequit." See his last will and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. Of Nature reader will be disappointed and dissatisfied. Poetical representations must therefore be framed after a pattern of the highest probable perfection that the genius of the work will admit;—external nature must in them be more picturesque than in reality; action more animated; sentiments more expressive of the feelings and character, and more suitable to the circumstances of the speaker; personages better accomplished in those qualities that raise admiration, pity, terror, and other ardent emotions; and events more compact, more clearly connected with causes and consequences, and unfolded in an order more flattering to the fancy, and more interesting to the passions. But where, it may be said, is this pattern of perfection to be found? Not in real nature; otherwise history, which delineates real nature, would also delineate this pattern of perfection. It is to be found only in the mind of the poet; and it is imagination, regulated by knowledge, that enables him to form it. In the beginning of life, and while experience is confined to a small circle, we admire every thing, and are pleased with very moderate excellence. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> thinks the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of his landlord the finest apartment in the universe, listens with rapture to the strutting ballad-finger, and wonders at the rude wooden cuts that adorn his ruder compositions. A child looks upon his native village as a town; upon the brook that runs by as a river; and upon the meadows and hills in the neighborhood as the most spacious and beautiful that can be. But when, after long absence, he returns in his declining years, to visit once before he die, the dear spot that gave him birth, and those scenes whereof he remembers rather the original charms than the exact proportions; how is he disappointed to find every thing so debased and so diminished! The hills seem to have sunk into the ground, the brook to be dried up, and the village to be forsaken of its people; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, stripped of all its fancied magnificence, is become low, gloomy, and narrow; and the fields are now only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> of what they were. Had he never left this spot, his notions might have remained the same as at first; and had he travelled but a little way from it, they would not perhaps have received any material enlargement. It seems then to be from observation of many things of the same or similar kinds, that we acquire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> of forming ideas more perfect than the real objects that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> immediately around us; and these ideas we may improve gradually more and more, according to the technical fancy, vivacity of our mind, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of our experience, till at last we come to raise them to a degree of perfection superior to anything to be found in real life. There cannot be any mystery in this doctrine; for we think and speak to the same purpose every day. Thus nothing is more common than to say, that each an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> excels all we have ever known in his profession, and yet that we can still conceive a superior performance. A morality, by bringing together into one view the separate virtues of many persons, is enabled to lay down a system of duty more perfect than any he has ever seen exemplified in human conduct. Whatever be the emotion the poet intends to raise in his reader, whether admiration or terror, joy or sorrow; and whatever be the object he would exhibit, whether Venus or Tityphone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, a palace or a pile of ruins, a dance or a battle; he generally copies an idea of his own imagination; considering each quality as it is found to exist in several individuals of a species, and hence forming an assemblage more or less perfect in its kind, according to the purpose to which he means to apply it. Hence it would appear, that the ideas of poetry are poetical rather general than singular; rather collected from the examination of a species or class of things, than copied from an individual. And this, according to Aristotle, is in fact the case, at least for the most part; whence that critic determines, that poetry is something more exquisite and more philosophical than history. The historian may describe Bucephalus, but the poet delineates a war-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; the former must have seen the animal he speaks of, or received authentic information concerning it, if he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to describe it historically; for the latter, it is enough that he has seen several animals of that sort. The former tells us, what Achilles actually did and said; the latter, what such a species of human character as that which bears the name of Achilles would probably do or say in certain given circumstances. It is indeed true, that the poet may, and often does, copy after individual objects. Homer, no doubt, took his characters from the life; or at least, in forming them, was careful to follow tradition as far as the nature of his plan would allow. But he probably took the freedom to add or heighten some qualities, and take away others; to make Achilles, for example, stronger, perhaps, and more impetuous, and more eminent for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> affection, and Hector more patriotic and more amiable than he really was. If he had not done this, or something like it, his work would have been rather a history than a poem; would have exhibited men and things as they were, and not as they might have been; and Achilles and Hector would have been the names of individual and real heroes; whereas, according to Aristotle, they are rather to be considered as two distinct modifications or species of the heroic character.
